issues.title: ‘Pay attention and stay curious’: Réka Matyas on her charming little worlds filled with spotty dogs and polka-dog cats
issues.summary: The Budapest-based illustrator fills her colourful drawings with curious characters and unexpected details, encouraging us to slow down and find joy in the everyday. Spend a few minutes in Réka Mátyás...
issues.author: Ayla Angelos
issues.content_html:
The Budapest-based illustrator fills her colourful drawings with curious characters and unexpected details, encouraging us to slow down and find joy in the everyday.

Spend a few minutes in Réka Mátyás’ portfolio, and you’ll meet two spotty dogs gazing at each other across a green meadow, a polka-dot cat posing beside an equally polka-dot tabi shoe, and a woman with ladybugs crawling through her golden hair. Polka-dot sisters, three cats stretched out across a chocolate-brown page, and a figure cradling a birthday cake with a single lit candle appear. It all feels soft, warm and slightly odd, splashed in a playful palette of bubblegum pinks, grassy greens and buttery yellows.

The Budapest-based illustrator and motion designer was born in Transylvania, Romania, and began her creative journey at university, where she studied Fine Arts and graduated with a BA in 2022. She experimented with all sorts of materials and mediums, though pencil sketches and realistic drawing were her real loves. By the end of her degree, she admits, she “felt quite lost”, with plenty of pressure to find her own style. So she took a year off and landed a role at a small creative studio as a motion designer, where she picked up the software, dabbled in graphic design, and started to see new possibilities. That led her to Budapest for a master’s in Graphic Design, which she completed in 2025. Today, she works full-time as a motion designer at Artbinary, “an amazing agency where I feel like part of the family”, while illustration fills her free time, along with the occasional graphic design project when something resonates.

For a long while, Réka felt she had to pick one path out of the three. “It stressed me out quite a bit,” she says. “But over time, I’ve learned to embrace all three, and I finally feel like I’ve found my place. I’ve also realised that switching between them keeps me creatively fresh. Each discipline gives me a different perspective and a little breathing room from the others, allowing me to return to my work with new ideas and push it in directions I might not have discovered otherwise. Now, rather than seeing these different paths as competing with each other, I see them as things that feed into and strengthen one another.”

With the world around her as her muse, Réka’s ideas usually come from everyday moments. “I’m interested in observing people, their lives and the little moments that might seem insignificant at first,” she says. Réka then jots these observations down or makes quick sketches in a notebook, where an idea might sit for months before it finds its way into an illustration. Nature, music, films and whatever book she’s reading chip in too, because “you just have to pay attention and stay curious”.

When the time comes to make something, Réka sits quietly for a few minutes and lets her mind wander, imagining a little scenario around the theme. Then comes lots of tiny, rough pencil or coloured-pen sketches. “They’re usually pretty ugly, and I almost always hate all of them at first!” she laughs, but this messy stage is where the final concept tends to appear, often somewhere completely different from where she started. Once something feels right, she plays with the composition, mood and colour, then moves to her iPad, which she says is usually the quickest part.

Among her favourites is an illustration for ZEITmagazine, commissioned by art director Viola Hasse, and her first editorial job. She had never drawn older people before, so she dived straight into sketching, starting with the couple at the centre – looking lovingly into each other’s eyes – and building a story around them with symbols and perspectives. Look closely, and you’ll spot a bird with a broken wing, which denotes the woman’s gradual loss of independence; pills; a pair of glasses; a water droplet and a character looking longingly in the distance. “I wanted the storytelling to feel subtle, rather than too literal, with little details that you could discover as you looked at the image,” she says. “I really enjoyed finding ways to translate the different layers of the story into small visual elements.”

Réka loves to build worlds in her illustrations – artworks that make people smile, ask their viewers to slow down and take in the beauty around them. And each piece comes with its own set of characters and plots, using tiny details she would have spotted in her own reality.

“I usually try to include a small, unexpected detail in my illustrations, something that might surprise people or make them look twice,” she says. “I like the idea of creating images that reveal a little more the longer you spend with them. Ultimately, I don’t think every illustration needs to carry a big message. Sometimes, making someone smile or helping them see something familiar in a slightly different way is more than enough.”

issues.title: Pattern Coffee is what happens when a Belfast branding studio becomes its own client
issues.summary: Fluent Format’s David Lewis on Pattern Coffee, the Belfast speciality coffee brand he’s built with Andile Cebekhulu as a side project, and what it taught them about clients. I’m a big fan of side proj...
issues.author: Katy Cowan
issues.content_html:
Fluent Format’s David Lewis on Pattern Coffee, the Belfast speciality coffee brand he’s built with Andile Cebekhulu as a side project, and what it taught them about clients.

I’m a big fan of side projects. Creative Boom began as one, and look at it now. It seems I’m not alone. Every studio has one. The passionate thing on the side that gets talked about on a Friday afternoon, sketched out on paper, and then quietly forgotten about when Monday’s deadlines come in.

David Lewis and Andile Cebekhulu actually made theirs come true. David is the founder and creative director of Belfast brand and digital consultancy Fluent Format; Andile is its lead developer. By day, the pair build brands and digital experiences for other people. Alongside all that, they’ve been finding the time to build Pattern Coffee, a speciality coffee brand of their own.

Much like my platform, it began with no plan to be a business at all. The two friends spent nine months sourcing and trying coffees from around the world before deciding there was an opportunity. “We’re both dads with young families, busy jobs and a real love of coffee,” says David. “We joke that coffee is what keeps us going, but it’s also something we genuinely enjoy.”

What’s with the name, though? It came about during a phone call after work, when the pair got talking about how coffee had become part of their daily ritual – a moment to step away, reset and go again. Cue Pattern, along with a brand philosophy, ‘Your daily sweet spot’.

Listening to their own advice

Graphic designers spend their working lives telling clients that brand matters. So can you imagine the pressure when it’s your own name on the packaging, and your own money behind it?

“We’ve always believed that a great brand can make a real difference to a business,” says David. “It’s not just about having a nice logo or packaging. It’s about creating something people recognise, connect with and want to be part of. Pattern gave us the chance to connect with and want to be part of. It gave us the chance to explore that from the very beginning, with complete creative freedom.”

I’m familiar with that freedom. It lets you go crazy without constraints. For David and Andile, it showed up most in the packaging. Because rather than go for the usual coffee tin, they developed a sleeve that follows the same silhouette of the bag, so the overall shape stays the same while each batch of coffee gets its own visual identity.

“We knew how the bag looked on a shop shelf was just as important as how it looked on someone’s kitchen counter,” explains David. “We wanted to create something people would enjoy having around.”

Wings, rugby and a snowball effect

Amazingly, there’s been no traditional marketing. Instead, Pattern has grown through small brand activations, like collaborations with running clubs and gyms, and even pop-ups at chicken wing shops – not, I admit, where I expected a speciality coffee brand to show up. But there you go.

The pair has also sponsored grassroots rugby, including women’s sports events, schools and universities, and supported Cancer Fund for Children on several occasions.

“We’ve found that the smallest things often have the biggest impact,” says David. “One collaboration leads to another, someone discovers the coffee and shares it with a friend, and before you know it, there’s a real snowball effect. It’s allowed us to build the brand and community we always wanted, without forcing it.”

But speciality coffee can feel intimidating when you think of all the tasting notes and brew ratios. Pattern is having none of that. “We love good coffee, but we don’t think you should have to know everything about it to enjoy it,” David continues. “We wanted Pattern to feel approachable, welcoming and something everyone could be part of.”

The key takeaways?

So what are the lessons from running a coffee brand on the side when you build brands for a living? Quite a lot. “It’s been a proper hustle getting it off the ground,” says David. “When you’re the one sourcing products, packing orders and investing your own money, you develop a completely different appreciation for the start-up founders you work with.”

At this point, neither founder takes a penny out of the business – everything goes back into the brand. Well, almost everything. They did treat themselves to a La Marzocco Linea Mini, which now travels around Belfast serving coffee at pop-up events.

These days, David and Andile call Pattern their “creative sandpit” because it’s somewhere to play and test out new things. Experiment with packaging and photography while finding out firsthand what it takes to build a coffee business.

“We’re lucky to work on brilliant projects every day, but there’s something special about creating something of your own,” says David. “Pattern started as a passion project, and that’s exactly what it still is. We’re just enjoying seeing where it takes us.”

issues.title: Why Victorious Festival stopped selling its headliners and started selling Portsmouth
issues.summary: Portsmouth’s August bank holiday festival had a bit of a problem. Too many people were buying a ticket for one act on one day, then disappearing. Wildish & Co.’s solution is an identity that puts...
issues.author: Katy Cowan
issues.content_html:
Portsmouth’s August bank holiday festival had a bit of a problem. Too many people were buying a ticket for one act on one day, then disappearing. Wildish & Co.’s solution is an identity that puts the city first.

Who doesn’t love a good festival? I’ve been to my fair share over the last thirty years, and I can always tell you which bands were playing. The Prodigy in 1995 and Bowie in 2000, both at Glastonbury. Cypress Hill at V Festival in 2022 along with Asian Dub Foundation, I think it was. Björk at Bluedot a few years ago. Fun times.

If you’re running an event like this, you’ll know a lot hangs on your line-up. If it isn’t good enough, people simply won’t book. Victorious Festival knows this only too well. For more than a decade, the three-day event on Southsea seafront has drawn crowds from across the south of England, including Kings of Leon, Jamiroquai and Kasabian. But many of those only bought a ticket for a particular day, saw their fave act and went home. As such, each day felt like a different crowd, and that transience can be hard to build a community around.

Cue London agency Wildish & Co., which has given Victorious a new brand strategy, verbal identity and visual system that helps sell the festival as more than its line-up. Yeah, the headliners are still there - Black Eyed Peas, Pet Shop Boys and The Kooks are on the 2027 bill – but they’re no longer the sole attraction. Portsmouth is.

The idea is to sell the weekend, not just one day or act. Which is why the new positioning makes sense: ‘The People’s Classic’. It’s a line inspired by the ones who keep coming back, from families and festival veterans to traders, volunteers and first-timers. A second line, ‘Portsmouth Says Welcome’, ties the brand to the city that hosts it. Perfect.

It’s smart because you can’t own a line-up but you can own a seafront, a city, and something to look forward to every August. It’s something no rival festival can compete with. If you shift the story from who’s on stage to where you actually are and who you’re with, then a day ticket starts to look like you’re missing out.

The history behind the festival is also lovely. Victorious grew out of Portsmouth’s own music scene – its founders previously ran local venue Little Johnny Russell’s – and the new strategy includes a celebration of those humble roots.

Going back to the warm welcome, who’s it for? The identity launches alongside the 2027 line-up with large-scale posters at London Waterloo, Clapham Junction and Brighton, which shows you the target market.

Looking at the logo, it swaps the O in Victorious for a starburst borrowed from the sun on Portsmouth’s own coat of arms. Will you look at that – the city is quite literally in the middle of the name. The starburst also acts as an icon and is used across social, merchandise, wristbands and wayfinding.

There’s a custom headline typeface called Victorious Bold, which has tall, narrow capitals which stand out beautifully on everything from posters to stage screens. And the palette is taken right off the seafront – Navy, Sky, Sunset and Sunrise colours are complemented by secondary hues such as Sun Burn, Sea Spray and Sea Weed. A wave device runs through the lot, framing tickets, flags and signage. This was clearly a fun brief.

Then there are the illustrations, drawn in an engraving style and celebrating people enjoying themselves: a crab in headphones, for example, plus a sandcastle built from speakers and a seagull in a bucket hat. Remember those? Bucket hats were very handy when you needed to roll something out of the wind. Ahem.

A really nice touch is that every artist’s press photo gets a custom risograph-inspired treatment, so every act looks like part of the same thing. In other words, the headliners have been made to fit into Victorious’s world, when it has previously been the other way round.

Is the client happy? “Wildish & Co. got Victorious straight away,” says Leah Hennessy-Williams, head of PR and marketing at the festival. “They understood that what makes this festival special isn’t just who’s on stage, it’s the sea air, the city and the people who come back every single year. The new brand captures all of that and more, and it’s given the whole team a fresh sense of pride in what we’ve built.”

I can almost hear the seagulls on the breeze...Whether the new identity shifts people from a day ticket to the full weekend, only time will tell. But we love the sentiment behind it. As Sam Fresco, managing director at Wildish & Co., puts it: “Victorious sells you Portsmouth, and it belongs to whoever turns up.”

issues.title: Freytag Anderson serves up branding with bounce for a Scottish padel startup
issues.summary: The Glasgow studio built the Edinburgh company’s brand from the ground up, from naming to rackets. If you haven’t heard of padel yet, don’t worry: your life will be fine without it. At the same time,...
issues.author: Tom May
issues.content_html:
The Glasgow studio built the Edinburgh company’s brand from the ground up, from naming to rackets.

If you haven’t heard of padel yet, don’t worry: your life will be fine without it. At the same time, it’s nice to know that this trendy racket sport, which is kind of a cross between tennis and squash, is making a lot of people very happy right now; mainly in North America, but increasingly in the UK too.

Inevitably, there’s already a crowded market of kit brands all competing for padel fans’ attention. And the latest to catch our attention, at least, is CCO: an Edinburgh-based startup aiming to become a premium international padel brand.

This new brand has been crafted from the start by Glasgow studio Freytag Anderson, four-time winner of Scottish Design Agency of the Year.

Start to finish

Their work has included naming, positioning, visual identity, product architecture, racket design, and packaging, while for the website and e-commerce side, they teamed up with Form, a studio based in Aberdeen and Glasgow.

Readers of Creative Boom might read CCO as “Chief Creative Officer”, but that’s not what most padel players will think in practice. In any case, the name here is an acronym for “Control Creates Opportunity”. That will make perfect sense to fans of the game, where patience and placement tend to beat brute force.

The overall positioning of the brand, meanwhile, blends technical performance with a refined, lifestyle-led feel. This is captured simply but precisely in the tagline: “Performance. Synced.”

Logo design

At the heart of the visual identity is a stepped typemark inspired by the movement of a padel ball. The two Cs and the O read almost like frames from a slow-motion replay, as if the ball is gradually coming into focus.

It’s a simple idea, but it’s been executed brilliantly, and is flexible enough to stretch across the brand’s three racket ranges, along with balls, apparel and accessories. The design particularly comes to life on the rackets themselves, where the mark is stacked, mirrored and multiplied to create bold, radiating patterns that echo the rhythm of the game.

A similar use of pattern repetition carries across to the campaign images, captured by photographer Beth Chalmers, in which players appear in staggered, multiple-exposure frames.

The colour palette – mostly blacks, whites and greys – evokes an understated, premium feel. This, along with the clean, sans-serif typography and restraint, helps the brand stand out in a sporting category not known for its subtlety.

“For the digital experience, we brought in Cameron Fraser and Kyle McKenzie at Form Digital,” says Daniel Freytag, creative director at Freytag Anderson. “They’re exceptionally good at what they do, particularly when it comes to creating thoughtful, intuitive digital experiences that also work commercially. Together we translated the brand into a Shopify-powered e-commerce platform.”

issues.title: Programa extension brings SketchUp models and product schedules into one workflow
issues.summary: Studio operations software Programa has introduced a SketchUp extension that connects 3D models with its product Schedules, freeing designers from duplicating information and giving them more creative time. According to Programa, the extension is designed to reduce duplicate data entry by connecting a 3D model in SketchUp with a project’s Schedule in Programa. Programa’s Schedules […] The post Pro
issues.author: Dezeen staff
issues.content_html:
Studio operations software Programa has introduced a SketchUp extension that connects 3D models with its product Schedules, freeing designers from duplicating information and giving them more creative time.

According to Programa, the extension is designed to reduce duplicate data entry by connecting a 3D model in SketchUp with a project’s Schedule in Programa.

Programa’s Schedules function acts as a streamlined alternative to spreadsheets, detailing each item’s code, supplier, finish, dimensions, quantity and price.

The extension runs inside SketchUp and allows designers to link components in the model to matching products in the Schedule.

As a result, designers can track an item from the first 3D sketch through to its final specification, without entering the same information separately in SketchUp and Programa.

From the model, designers can send a component to a chosen Schedule, or link it to a product that is already listed there.

Programa explained that linking to an existing product creates a connection without adding a duplicate line item, keeping the Schedule "clean" as the design is fleshed out.

Before anything is added, designers can review and edit the product’s information.

The Schedule entry combines the details available from the component with anything entered during that review.

Programa said this gives studios a chance to check the specification before it is used for pricing or procurement.

The extension also provides access to Programa’s Product Library within SketchUp.

Designers can place saved 3D models directly into their designs, and use product images as material swatches to bring selected finishes into the model.

In this way, the products (and finishes) a studio has chosen can be seen in the visuals as well as listed in the Schedule.

The process also works in reverse, starting from the Schedule. A product with a compatible 3D model attached can be placed straight into SketchUp.

If there is no model, designers can choose a stand-in from SketchUp’s 3D Warehouse, or from elsewhere in the current model, to represent the product.

Once a component and a product are connected, supported changes can be reviewed and applied in either direction.

For example, adding another copy of a connected chair in SketchUp generates a quantity change, which the designer can then apply to the Schedule.

The company added that changes are presented for review “before the corresponding update is applied”.

This means the model and the specification can move together as a design develops, while the Schedule is only updated once the designer has chosen to apply a change.

Programa stressed that responsibility remains with the studio.

Designers stay in charge of “selecting the right product, checking its details and deciding when the model or Schedule should change”, the company said.

The aim, it explained, is to carry information between the model and the specification rather than make those decisions on the designer’s behalf.

The extension is aimed at studios that model in SketchUp and manage their specifications in Programa.

The Programa extension works with SketchUp desktop on Mac and Windows.

To learn more, visit Programa’s website or its extension setup guide.

The post Programa extension brings SketchUp models and product schedules into one workflow appeared first on Dezeen.

issues.title: Estúdio 41 wraps coastal Brazilian house in white brise-soleil
issues.summary: Estúdio 41 has completed the Guaratuba House, which features exterior screens and a structural system that "explores the architectural expression of exposed precast concrete". The post Estúdio 41 wraps coastal Brazilian house in white brise-soleil appeared first on Dezeen .
issues.author: Jenna McKnight
issues.content_html:
Brazilian firm Estúdio 41 has completed Guaratuba House, which features exterior screens and a structural system that "explores the architectural expression of exposed precast concrete".

Located in the seaside community of Prainha, which sits within the city of Guaratuba in southern Brazil, the holiday home was designed for a family to serve as "a refuge between the mountains and the sea".

"One of their main requirements was, therefore, a strong visual connection between the interior spaces and the surrounding natural landscape," said Estúdio 41, an architectural firm based in Curitiba.

Drawings and photographs

    Drawings and photographs

    Rectangular in plan, the 375-square-metre house has two floors. It is wrapped in folding screens made of perforated melamine panels.

    The screens filter natural light and reduce solar gain on glass surfaces. When opened up, they reveal views of the scenic landscape.

    "At night, the transparency and geometric patterns of the house's skin give it the appearance of a lantern within the landscape," the team said.

    To protect against flooding, as the coastal site has been affected by storm surges in the past, the building was lifted up 70 centimeters (2.3 feet).

    It has a prefabricated concrete structural system that was assembled in only six hours, with the concrete structural elements left visible.

    The system consists of six columns, four beams and 20 double-tee slabs, also known as "π" (pi)-shaped slabs. The latter are pre-stressed concrete panels with a cross-section that resembles the Greek letter π.

    "The project explores the architectural expression of exposed precast concrete," said the team.

    Read:

    Sabella Arquitetura crowns Brazilian house with gridded timber roof

    "The conception of a very simple and easily executable construction system reflects a concern for the realities of the local workforce," it contniued.

    "The construction technique, the modular arrangement of the structural components, and the ribs of the double-tee floor slabs are all clearly legible."

    Rooms feature artful decor and a neutral colour palette. The ground level contains an open-plan kitchen, dining area and living room, along with service areas and a guest bedroom.

    The communal area opens toward a garden, and beyond it, a sheltered barbecue terrace and a swimming pool.

    "The social areas were conceived as one large veranda in direct contact with the beach sand, with views of both the sea and mountains," the team said.

    The upper level contains four bedrooms, including the primary suite, and a family room. A bridge passes over the garden below and connects to a concrete terrace with sweeping views of the sea.

    Other projects by Estudio 41 include a small white house in Brazil with a roof garden, and a prefabricated, teal-coloured research station in Antarctica.

    Project credits:

    Architecture: Estúdio 41
    Structural engineering: Da Rocha Engenharia, Greco Engenharia
    Foundation engineering: Da Rocha Engenharia, Greco Engenharia
    Electrical engineering, plumbing, air conditioning: PD Engenharia
    Brise-soleil: Favegroup, Lamitech
    Concrete: Da Rocha Engenharia, Greco Engenharia

issues.title: Texas reveals proposal for US Space Academy in Houston
issues.summary: The Texas Space Commission has published a proposal for the newly created United States Space Academy, which would be built in Houston. The post Texas reveals proposal for US Space Academy in Houston appeared first on Dezeen .
issues.author: Tom Ravenscroft
issues.content_html:
The Texas Space Commission has published a proposal for the newly created United States Space Academy. It would be located in Houston on a site alongside NASA's Johnson Space Center, which was formerly home to Mission Control.

Revealed earlier this week, the proposals show clusters of buildings arranged in a flower-like shape, with petals surrounded by water. The renders place the facility on a currently vacant site alongside the NASA facility.

Renderings

    Renderings

    The proposal was created as a response to a request for information from the American space agency, which is looking to find a permanent home for the academy.

    It follows an executive order issued earlier this year by president Donald Trump that established a presidential commission to determine how the proposed NASA-led institution could be formed.

    In the order, he stated that the United States Space Academy would be established with the aim of training the "next generation of astronauts, scientists, engineers, operators, entrepreneurs, civil servants, and warfighters".

    The proposed academy would contain facilities for academic and more hands-on training.

    It has received bipartisan support in Texas, with Republican senator Ted Cruz and Democrat senator-elect James Talarico issuing a joint statement in support of the bid.

    Read:

    NASA says "living and working on the moon will become reality" after 2032

    "Texas has maintained a leading role in America’s human spaceflight program for decades, from training astronauts to directing missions at Johnson Space Center," said the pair in the statement.

    "The Lone Star State has developed an extensive space industry, infrastructure, and expertise. Texas is best suited to train the next generation of American space leaders and is the natural home for the U.S. Space Academy."

    According to the Texas Space Commission, the scheme was designed to align with NASA's proposed timeline, which envisions groundbreaking commencing next year.

    NASA recently announced plans for a permanent moon base, with a multi-phased plan culminating in “semi-permanent habitation models”.

    The post Texas reveals proposal for US Space Academy in Houston appeared first on Dezeen.

issues.title: Ambidestro clads coastal home in Brazil with rough local stone
issues.summary: Contrasting volumes of smooth plaster and rough local Morelo stone define this coastal home in Brazil, designed by local architecture practice Ambidestro. The post Ambidestro clads coastal home in Brazil with rough local stone appeared first on Dezeen .
issues.author: Jon Astbury
issues.content_html:
Contrasting volumes of smooth plaster and rough local Morelo stone define this coastal home in Brazil, designed by local architecture practice Ambidestro.

Named Casa Los Cobos, the home is located in Xangri-Lá on Brazil's southern coast, and was designed to make the most of panoramic views out over the sea from the rear of the site.

Drawings and exterior photographs

    Drawings and exterior photographs

    Set back from the road, a series of routes both through and around the home "reveal the landscape gradually," including a path beneath a timber canopy and via a paved veranda screened by lush plants.

    "The main opportunity was the merging of two adjoining lots into a single site that extends to the rear, where the landscape opens onto the water," Ambidestro co-founder João Pedro Crescente told Dezeen.

    The ground floor of Casa Los Cobos has been given over almost entirely to a single large living, dining and kitchen space, wrapped by service spaces and bathrooms.

    Full-height sliding glass doors allow this space to be opened out onto a large sheltered terrace alongside a swimming pool, with a lawn that slopes down to a nearby waterway.

    "The ground floor is free of partitions: living, dining and the entertaining kitchen are integrated and turned toward the greenery, accommodating everything from a weeknight dinner to a Saturday party," Crescente told Dezeen.

    "Between the living room and the water lie, in sequence, the veranda, the garden and the pool, which wraps around the house. The eye passes through these layers before reaching the backdrop," he added.

    Both the exterior and interior have been given contrasting finishes of rough Morelo stone and white plaster and paint, with the rear terrace framed by white-painted masonry.

    Interior photographs

      Interior photographs

      This is complemented internally with bespoke carpentry in pale oak, including a floating timber bar supported by a concrete column that defines one edge of the living space.

      "The intention was to use natural, local materials in light, warm tones repeated inside and out, making the transition between spaces almost imperceptible," said Crescente.

      "Moledo stone clads the facades and changes in appearance from morning to late afternoon. Other natural stones continue onto the floors and wet areas," he added.

      A skylit staircase leads up to the more compartmentalised first floor of the home, which contains six en-suite bedrooms, two of which open onto a balcony overlooking the sea.

      To provide both shading and privacy from the road, sliding timber shutters can be pulled down over the full-height bedroom windows.

      Read:

      Studio Arthur Casas affixes dramatic cantilever to Brazilian house

      Other homes in Brazil recently featured on Dezeen include a home in São Paolo by Studio Arthur Casas featuring dramatic overhangs and cantilevers, and a low-lying dwelling by Sabella Arquitetura that is topped by a gridded timber roof.

issues.title: The Most Read Books on Goodreads This Week
issues.summary: The most read books on Goodreads this week include romantasy books, thrillers, and a Young Adult dystopian novel.
issues.author: Community
issues.content_html:
Last week, I noted that Yesteryearhad been pushed out of the top five—but that didn’t last long! It has climbed its way back into the #5 spot this time around. Sarah J. Maas is no longer in the #1 spot. Can you guess which title overtookA Court of Splintered Harmony? Here’s a hint: it was published in 2025.

Two New Books Out This Week You Should Know About

Unfortunately, the most read books on Goodreads tend not to be diverse by any definition of the word. So, here are a couple of new books out this week that deserve wider readership.

For the Love of K-Dramas by Lyla Lee

The behind-the-scenes drama is just as compelling as the on-screen in the world of K-dramas. When Clara Kim gets her big break on a new romantasy show, she’s laser-focused on succeeding. But her co-star, Shin Min-joon, might ruin her chance. Min-joon has criticized Clara on social media in the past. Since they’re thrown together for this job, they focus on understanding each other and making the chemistry look real. —Julia Rittenberg

In Your Skin by Aditya Bidikar, illustrated by Som

Never have I seen a book with a description involving “Bollywood body horror” before this one, and I am heartily intrigued. Not only that, but in this age of parasocial relationships, I’m kind of surprised we haven’t seen the IRL version of this play out. It starts with Priyanka, who has grown up watching Bollywood starring Ayesha San all her life. She’s seen all the movies, and knows every step to all the dances. When she gets the chance to meet the Bollywood star, Priyanka’s life gets a wrench thrown in it: Ayesha is retiring. Priyanka has a solution to Ayesha not wanting to live right, though; she’ll just take over her life… —Erica Ezeifedi

The Most Read Books on Goodreads This Week

#5:

Yesteryear by Caro Claire Burke

Back in the top five is Yesteryear, which came out in April. It’s one of several buzzy tradwife novels out this year. In this one, a tradwife influencer wakes up one day in the time period she’s been romanticizing, and real-life homesteading turns out to be much more difficult—and dangerous—than it looks on Instagram. Yesteryear was read by almost 21,000 users this week and has a 3.8 average rating.

#4:

Threshing Day by Rebecca Yarros

The fourth book in the Empyrean series still doesn’t have a release date, so fans likely have a long time to wait. In the meantime, they can revisit the world in this new novella, which follows 13 characters on their Threshing Days, when they endure a deadly trial in attempts to bond with a dragon. It was read by 21,000 users this week and has a 4.4 average rating.

#3:

The Witch by Freida McFadden

The reigning queen of thrillers is back, this time with an October-appropriate story. After losing her job, Julia moves in with her elderly grandmother in their family’s 17th-century estate in Massachusetts. Soon, she begins to suspect the house is haunted by a woman executed for witchcraft in 1692. It was read by 24,000 users this week and has a 4.0 average rating.

#2:

A Court of Splintered Harmony (A Court of Thorns and Roses #6) by Sarah J. Maas

Sarah J. Maas is the author of 11 of the top 50 most read books this week, and the latest A Court of Thorns and Roses book is her most popular of the moment. It’s the first in the Valkyrie Cycle, following the Night Court as they face off against the return of Koschei the Deathless. The next book in the Valkyrie Cycle comes out in January. This one was read by almost 46,000 users this week and has a 3.8 average rating.

#1:

Sunrise on the Reaping by Suzanne Collins

This prequel novel in the Hunger Games series was published in 2025, but it’s getting new interest ahead of the movie adaptation, which came out November 20th. It follows Haymitch’s Hunger Games, 24 years before the events of the first novel. It was read by almost 50,000 users this week and has a 4.5 average rating.

If you’re looking for more buzzy books, check out The Bestselling Books of the Week, According to All the Lists.

issues.title: Fear is the Mind Killer: Comics for DUNE Fans
issues.summary: With the next movie due out in theaters soon, prepare by reading your way into these comics for DUNE fans.
issues.author: Megan Mabee
issues.content_html:
While I’ve always aspired to read the Dune series, I never seem to find the time before the next Dune movie comes out. The books are long, and the new movies directed by Denis Villeneuve are so good. I have found success reading the Dune series through comics though.

Frank Herbert’s son, Brian Herbert, along with Kevin J. Anderson, have adapted the iconic series into graphic novel format. These books have given me a satisfying taste of the story paired with beautiful art of the desolate yet mesmerizing world of Dune.

The series includes three volumes, Dune: The Graphic Novel Book 1, Book 2: Muad’Dib, and Book 3: The Prophet. The gorgeous illustrations by Raúl Allén and Patricia Martín immerse you right into the landscape of the bleak and breathtaking desert planet. The character art is compelling and helps show their feelings and motivations, rather than just tell them through narrative.

The new Dune film, Dune: Part Three, releases in theaters December 18th. While the Dune graphic novels offer a great way to catch up on the series before you see the movie, I also have comics for Dune fans who want to fall into similar stories.

Each comic below touches upon various themes that make Dune special. Between their pages, you’ll travel across wasteland planets crawling with curious creatures, immerse in political intrigue amongst warring nobility, and follow space wanderers on desperate quests.

Comics for Dune Fans

Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind by Hayao Miyazaki

Hayao Miyazaki’s manga series is a must-read for Dune fans. Like Paul Atreides, Nausicaä steps into a prophesied savior role in her story, though Nausicaä strives for peace over war. Her world shares many similarities with Dune, with its barren landscapes and powerful Ohmu creatures reminiscent of Dune’s sandworms. As various kingdoms wage war on each other in an effort to control ancient, destructive technology, Nausicaä sets out to try and negotiate peace.

Count by Ibrahim Moustafa

Alexandre Dumas’s The Count of Monte Cristo is a classic tale of corruption, oppression, and revenge, and these themes strongly align with the story of Dune. Ibrahim Moustafa does an incredible job of adapting Dumas’s classic into a sci-fi graphic novel. After getting framed for treason and locked away in a hover-prison, Redxan Samud makes his great escape, puts his new fortune to use, and seeks revenge on those who ruined his life.

Monstress, Volume 1: Awakening by Marjorie M. Liu, Illustrated by Sana Takeda

This epic graphic novel by Marjorie M. Liu includes stunning illustrations by Sana Takeda. The story takes place in an alternate matriarchal 1900’s Asia. Like Paul Atreides, teen Maika possesses powerful psychic abilities. As Maika tries to survive in a dark, war-stricken world, she navigates a curious connection to a monster that will put them both in danger.

On a Sunbeam by Tillie Walden

While this sweet graphic novel by Tillie Walden offers a more quietly-paced sci-fi story than Dune, it does include the theme of searching for someone across space. Just as the Bene Gesserit seek the Kwisatz Haderach in Dune, the protagonist in this book, Mia, looks for her long-lost love. Fans of the epic cinematography of the Dune movies and the vivid descriptions of sci-fi landscapes in the Dune books will also appreciate the breathtaking art of this moving graphic novel.

Like Dune, I hope these comics offer you windows into awe-inspiring and compelling sci-fi worlds. For more good reads for Dune fans, check out these 14 Fascinating Books Like DUNE, or these Best Science Fiction Books of the Century (So Far).

issues.title: I Share a Closet With His Emotional Baggage
issues.summary: How to Live Rent-Free in Someone’s Head I took Jacob up on his offer. Yes, it was soon-ish to make such a big move—just a month and change since we got together officially—but we’d known each other for longer, and I felt like it could be something real. My lease was up. He said there […] The post I Share a Closet With His Emotional Baggage appeared first on Electric Literature .
issues.author: Kate Francia
issues.content_html:
How to Live Rent-Free in Someone’s Head

I took Jacob up on his offer. Yes, it was soon-ish to make such a big move—just a month and change since we got together officially—but we’d known each other for longer, and I felt like it could be something real. My lease was up. He said there was space. My sister was being dramatic about how I would lose my identity and become nothing more than the idea of me in his mind. But honestly, the bigger thing I was worried about was Marnie.

I was not made aware that Marnie would be there. That first day, I walked in and found her stretched out on the futon, painting her toenails green.

“Hi!” she said. “You must be Jill. Jacob’s told me so much about you.”

Obviously I knew who Marnie was. I was probably the world’s living expert on Marnie after all the time I spent listening to Jacob cry about her, back before he and I got together.

“Is that all you brought?” She pointed to my garbage bag. I twisted my hands through the pull strings. Most of my things were in storage in my sister’s basement. “It’s just temporary,” I said. “Until we can get a real place.” Then Marnie offered to help me unpack, which, no.

I had been looking forward to that part, the taking things out of the bag and putting them in places, that new-drawer feeling. But there was no drawer. Jacob had said he would clear one out for me, but every drawer I opened was full of random stuff, clothes and socks and stacks of receipts but also a conch shell, a box full of plastic straws, a sewing kit, a saxophone—and of course I started to wonder if all of this stuff was Jacob’s or if some of it was Marnie’s.

It was like a regular apartment. Except it had no windows and too many doors, most of them locked, and the unlocked ones opening into closets packed with junk that fell on you if you opened them. It’ll be just like having our own place, he’d said, and it sort of was, except most of the time he wasn’t there. It smelled like him, and I remembered all the times I had lain awake in my old apartment wishing I could be there. But at odd moments I’d be brushing my teeth or sweeping the floor and Marnie would walk by, crunching her way through a giant bag of crackers. Also I was pretty sure she was using my shampoo.

“I’m not,” said Marnie. “You’re using my shampoo.”

I pulled a chunk of my hair to my nose and sniffed it.

You might wonder why I’d bother washing my hair there. But I always thought Jacob might come in at any second. When he was there, there were things like a kitchen table and a TV and a bed, things that made it feel like home. He almost never came in during the day, though, even though to me the whole benefit of our situation was that theoretically he could check in anytime.

Hey babe what time are you—

“He’s not coming,” said Marnie. “It’s game night.” She pulled out her guitar and started singing the same song, over and over and over.

When he was there, though, it was so great. One night he came in full of all this energy and curled his arms around me, burrowed his head into my shoulder. ”I don’t know how you put up with this place. God, what a mess.” He clomped around, pulling open all the closets and opening boxes of stuff. He dumped things out on the futon: a winter coat, a fondue maker with two little silver sticks. He wanted to make space for me, to give me the kind of place I deserved.

“Check these out!” He spread baseball cards on the floor. “I haven’t looked at these in ages. I bet some of them are worth a lot.” He formed stacks, then shuffled them all together and formed different stacks.

“He’s not going to clean it up, you know,” said Marnie, hours later. She sat cross-legged in a nest of flannel green plaid camping blankets. I couldn’t see the futon or any of the furniture. Jacob was gone for the night.

“Maybe I could just start with some of the big things.” I pulled an empty box and started putting things in it. Old sporting equipment, school papers, a guitar. I wrote “high school” on a label. Marnie watched from her nest.

“You could help,” I said.

“Why would I do that?”

“Maybe because you live here too?”

“You should leave it. It’s his crap.” She sounded like my sister.

“I’m his girlfriend. A good girlfriend.” I tried to pull another box down and sent a cascade of stuff tumbling down over the box I’d just packed. Marnie snorted.

“What are you even doing here?” I said. “No one wants you.”

“Ouch. I’m devastated.” She took a long slurp of Diet Coke.

I made a lot of progress over the next few days. Or, I think they were days. I didn’t like to admit it, but if Jacob forgot to check in after work, it was hard to tell one day from another. But it was nice to have a project, a purpose. And that weekend, Jacob and I had plans to spend some quality time together, just us. I straightened a stack of books, fluffed a bunch of silk flowers I’d found scattered among some old vintage dresses.

“Sorry I’m late, babe. I don’t know why you put up with me.”

I jumped up and wrapped my arms around him. The way he smelled, the laundry soap and the buzz of his voice against my chest. It felt real. We were going to spend the evening just watching bad TV in a clean room and maybe we could talk about the future, about us. “Hey,” he said, “where are my baseball cards?”

He tore through box after box. “Why would you do this? I didn’t say you could touch my stuff!”

“I was trying to help.” I picked at a strand of my hair, the ends split and split again. “Marnie left it really messy.”

“Marnie? What are you talking about?” He dumped boxes one by one, strewing items across the floor. “Marnie doesn’t live here.”

A stack of boxes fell over and Marnie was there, doubled over, coughing. “Yes, she does,” I said. “She’s literally right there.”

“Wow.” He stopped dumping boxes for a second and just stared at me. “I thought you were more mature than this.”

I crawled into a little space next to the futon and covered my face. I could hear Jacob shuffling around the room, ripping open boxes. For the first time in a long time, I thought about leaving. Not leaving leaving, just getting some space. I could crash on my sister’s couch for a while, just until I found a real place.

Marnie was right next to me, breathing. “Why are you even here?” I said.

She took a sip from a water bottle covered in faded stickers. “Honestly, I’m not sure. I had everything packed at one point. But there’s no door. They all just lead to closets.”

I dug my knuckles into my eyes. My breath hiccuped in my throat.

“Ugh,” said Marnie. “Here.” She wrapped her green camping blanket around my shoulders. Her hair smelled like apples.

A while later Jacob crawled in next to me. Marnie scooted over. “I’m sorry,” he said into my hair. “I know I’m the worst.”

“It’s fine.”

“Shoot. You’re mad.”

“I’m not mad.”

He wrapped his arms around me. “This is what I love about you, Jill. You’re so chill.” I was mad, and then, like that, I wasn’t. I was chill, just like he said. On the floor around us, his baseball cards were all lined up, tiny faces looking at me in the dark. It wasn’t that messy, really. It was probably all in my head.

issues.title: Electric Lit’s Top 10 Nonfiction Books of 2026
issues.summary: This year, I read more nonfiction books than ever before. It wasn’t planned, though I suppose it had something to do with wanting to understand a world that seems increasingly fractured and confounding. For years, one political crisis has given way to another, each arriving with its own predictions of what terrible thing awaits us […] The post Electric Lit’s Top 10 Nonfiction Books of 2026 appeare
issues.author: Electric Literature
issues.content_html:
This year, I read more nonfiction books than ever before. It wasn’t planned, though I suppose it had something to do with wanting to understand a world that seems increasingly fractured and confounding. For years, one political crisis has given way to another, each arriving with its own predictions of what terrible thing awaits us next. Reading nonfiction offered a way of making sense of it all, beyond the endless stream of news on my screen.

Curiously, the books that helped me best think about the future were often concerned with the past. In Turn (W)here, Chet’la Sebree reckons with America’s history of racism as she considers what it would mean to raise a Black child in a country still shaped by that history. The past can make the future feel all too predictable. These days, it’s hard not to imagine what’s coming in dystopian terms, from climate catastrophe to forever wars to—new fear unlocked—AI-driven human extinction.

And yet, history has a way of defying our expectations. The recent victories of the political left in this year’s midterm elections felt like a fulcrum—the whole country tilted blue and another future became imaginable. Of course, I am wary of getting carried away by optimism; the past is full of futures that never arrived. In An Army of Lovers Cannot Fail, Hélène Giannecchini recovers forgotten forms of intimacy and solidarity through the stories of queer people whose lives and ways of living have been largely overlooked.

If the past is riddled with unrealized possibilities, perhaps the task is not simply to recover them, but to imagine new ones. I ended the year reading Camonghne Felix’s Let the Poets Govern, which draws on Black radical poetic traditions to imagine new forms of collective life. And while there’s no telling what the future might bring, this year’s crop of our top nonfiction books reminded me that the catastrophes we’re warned about, however real their threats, are not the only futures available to us. It is precisely this uncertainty that makes hope possible.

Here are our favorite nonfiction books of 2026.

–Evander James Reyes
Communications Manager

Editor’s note: The following books were hand-selected by Electric Literature staff and interns, with the help of our community of contributors, readers, and friends of the organization. Books by current staff or board members are not eligible for consideration. The 10 titles below are presented alphabetically by title; they are not ranked.

An Army of Lovers Cannot Fail by Hélène Giannecchini, translated by Anna Moschovakis

In An Army of Lovers Cannot Fail, Hélène Giannecchini follows queer relationships that taught her a history her family could not pass down: friends, lovers, mentors, and strangers whose lives survive in photographs, diaries, and remembered gestures. Moving from Casa Susanna to Donna Gottschalk’s images and a record of a French man living with HIV, the book asks how people find one another across time. Giannecchini approaches research as an intimate encounter, letting uncertainty and the desire to locate herself among these lives guide what she discovers. You can read an excerpt of the book here, which is also the first translation published in EL’s Personal Narrative! It is a fitting place to begin: a hybrid work about how one life opens onto many others.
–Shandela Contreras, Editorial Intern

Feels Like Trouble by Helen Betya Rubinstein

By expertly weaving personal narrative with much-needed critique on academia and craft, Helen Betya Rubinstein has created a delightfully probing and compulsively readable collection of essays or, as the title (quite accurately) calls them, “provocations.” Feels Like Trouble takes a scalpel to the writing life, laying bare the problems at the center of how we teach and talk about what makes writing “good.” This book is a salve for anyone who’s been unmoored from their artistic instincts by instruction that harmed more than it helped. It’s also an instructive call to action for how we might rethink the status quo. Rubinstein may have experienced teachers who tried to quash her voice along the way, but in this book, it’s on full display: sharp, rebellious, and clear-eyed. Read an excerpt of the book in EL’s personal narrative.
–Katie Henken Robinson, Deputy Editor

The Flower Bearersby Rachel Eliza Griffiths

In The Flower Bearers, Rachel Eliza Griffiths navigates a season of devastating rupture: the sudden death of her closest friend, poet Kamilah Aisha Moon, followed swiftly by the public stabbing of her husband, Salman Rushdie. Through the catastrophe, Griffiths grounds her story in the sanctuary of Black literary circles and the lifelong practice of making art, framing this memoir as a profound mediation on witness. Moving from alienated graduate workshops to hospital bedside vigils, Griffiths shows that carrying love through grief requires stubborn, daily attention. She tenders a rare, vivid record of how we rebuild ourselves in the company of what survives.
–Shandela Contreras, Editorial Intern

Let the Poets Governby Camonghne Felix

Having worked inside political strategy and speechwriting, Camonghne Felix knows intimately how institutional language sanitizes violence and manages dissent. In Let the Poets Govern, she turns away from legislative compromise to position Black radical poetics as an essential blueprint for liberation. Blending memoir, philosophy, and manifesto, Felix redacts oppressive legal codes and colonial white papers, literally carving freedom out of the grammar of subjugation. Felix demonstrates that form itself is where self-determination is practiced, offering an ethical compass for building collective life far beyond paternalistic power.
–Shandela Contreras, Editorial Intern

London Falling by Patrick Radden Keefe

This book starts as nearly all books about true crime do: On November 29th, 2019 someone dies. From there, however, the book unfurls into a sprawl of deception, corruption, and unjustifiable wealth. Keefe pulls off a masterful balancing act, layering the stories of a young man trying to make something of himself with tragic results, of parents grieving a child they didn’t know they didn’t know, and of London’s seedy underbelly. He sidesteps the darker elements of true crime by holding the deepest empathy for both victim and parents, always centering the human element of this tragedy while asking: Who, exactly, wove the web that caught their son? And who benefits from making sure it isn’t destroyed?
–Rachel Maybee, Editorial Intern

On Morrison by Namwali Serpell

This year, I found myself returning to Toni Morrison, as everyone should, again and again. Namwali Serpell’s On Morrison arrived as the perfect companion for a deeper engagement with her work. While Morrison’s political and thematic concerns often overshadow her formal innovations, Serpell’s meticulous close readings reveal how her literary techniques are inseparable from the meaning of her novels, and how their difficulty is deliberate, demanding, and deeply rewarding. It’s the kind of criticism I love, the kind that makes me want to become an ever more attentive reader.
–Evander James Reyes, Communications Manager

She Was Wild Grass by Katie Bennett

Like many aspiring writers who once dreamed of living in New York, I went through a phase of obsessively reading the Beat Generation writers. I was captivated by their lives as much as their writing, though I knew far less about the women in their circle. In She Was Wild Grass, Katie Bennett recovers the story of Joan Vollmer, a voracious reader and intellectual force in the early Beat movement, whose legacy has been largely defined by her murder at the hands of William S Burroughs. Weaving Vollmer’s life into her own struggles to become a writer, Bennett examines the unequal freedoms afforded to men and women who pursue artistic lives. What stayed with me was her refusal to let Vollmer’s murder become the whole story, even as she reckons with how much of that story can never be recovered.
–Evander James Reyes, Communications Manager

Spawning Season by Joseph Osmundson

In Spawning Season, Joseph Osmundson’s genre-bending memoir of his journey toward queer parenthood, we begin with a meditation on birth, followed by the introduction of Fry—his imagined, and deeply hoped for, progeny. Fry floats through the book, so much so that I wondered how a being who may, or may not, come to be can come across as ghostly? As though they had seen this world and left it? Osmundson’s National Book Award Finalist memoir is an extraordinary achievement, filled with questions of intimacy, legacy, whom we build families with, and why we build them. It’s quiet, but it’s heartbeat is powerful.
–Denne Michele Norris, Executive Director and Publisher

Turn (W)here by Chet’la Sebree

In her interview with Jordan Bolden Majewski for The Adroit Journal, Chet’la Sebree says, “One of the things that I enjoy most as a poet is to be abandoned inside something alongside the speaker.” This technique—placing the reader inside a moment and allowing it to unfold—is also at play in Sebree’s radiant essay collection, Turn (W)here. Sebree chronicles her search for an elusive home, merging her desire for transience with her hope for lasting stability. These questions come to a head during the COVID pandemic, and with the deaths of George Floyd and Breonna Taylor. Sebree asks what it means to move through a world laced with violence, especially as she grapples with the responsibility that accompanies bringing another life into that world. A hybrid text that blends personal and political history, Turn (W)here drops readers into its pages with abandon, but never leaves us without meaning and delight.
–Lennie Roeber-Tsiongas, Assistant Editor

We Radiant Things by Franny Choi

Franny Choi turns their mastery of poetic language toward cultural criticism in this debut essay collection about how technological progress intersects with the perception of who will play what roles in our increasingly automated future. Trawling through the collective American cultural consciousness, Choi pulls up examples of stories where cyborgs wear the faces of East Asian women before removing that mask to dissect the circuitry of oppression underneath. Drawing on their own experiences as a queer, feminist Korean American, Choi’s journey into the uncanny valley has never felt so personal. You can read an excerpt of the memoir here, where Choi pairs roombas and heterosexist (and racist) ideas about cleaning.
–Rachel Maybee, Editorial Intern

George Orwell understood that what is missing often tells you more than what is there. In Nineteen Eighty-Four, there is a slot in the wall covered by a wire grate. They call it the memory hole. When a document becomes inconvenient to the authorities – a photograph that contradicts the official line, a newspaper that remembers the wrong promise, a name that is no longer supposed to exist – you simply feed it into the slot, whereupon it is whirled away on a current of warm air to enormous hidden furnaces where it burns.

The Party doesn’t argue with the past. It removes it. Controlling the past is one of its central tools of power: “Who controls the past controls the future: who controls the present controls the past.”

issues.title: The Metaphor Zoo by Jeremy Butterfield review – how animals influence our language
issues.summary: A lexicographer reveals the surprising origins of common zoological turns of phrase, from fat cats to fur babies Anyone who has grown up in the country knows that cows come home. They do it at tea time, like clockwork, because an unmilked cow is an uncomfortable cow. So how did “till the cows come home” come to mean never? Stranger still, when the phrase first appears in a 1587 commentary on St Pa
issues.author: Kathryn Hughes
issues.content_html:
A lexicographer reveals the surprising origins of common zoological turns of phrase, from fat cats to fur babies

Anyone who has grown up in the country knows that cows come home. They do it at tea time, like clockwork, because an unmilked cow is an uncomfortable cow. So how did “till the cows come home” come to mean never? Stranger still, when the phrase first appears in a 1587 commentary on St Paul’s epistle to the Galatians, there is only one cow. By the time playwrights Beaumont and Fletcher take it up a few decades later, their characters are kissing and drinking till the cow – still single – comes home. What began as a promise of endless pleasure has become a sigh of futility.

Jeremy Butterfield’s Metaphor Zoo is full of such linguistic metamorphoses. Butterfield is a lexicographer by trade, the man the OUP entrusted with revising Fowler’s Modern English Usage. His guiding text is Lakoff and Johnson’s Metaphors We Live By (1980), which argues that metaphors don’t just colour how we speak but structure our thinking. In this sprightly but well-grounded book (metaphor alert), Butterfield asks what mental patterns lie behind the hundreds of animal phrases in English. Then in Johnsonian fashion, he sets about tracing the original, dating each through the Oxford English Dictionary and watching as it goes walkabout.

Out of the many daily puzzles available online, the New York Times’ Connections game is one of the trickiest. For those playing for the first time, the goal of Connections is to divide a block of 16 words into four common themes. Some of these – for example, grouping four types of fish – can be very straightforward, while others can be far more abstract. If you’ve found yourself stumped by the latter, we’ve put together Connections answers and hints for today (November 28) below.

  • READ MORE: Globle answer today – here’s the answer and hints for November 28

If you already know how to play Connections, you can skip this paragraph to jump straight into today’s solution. But if this is your first time attempting the New York Times’ puzzle (or you just need a refresher), we suggest thinking outside of the box for your answers.

Some groups are deliberately deceptive – using a previous day’s puzzle as an example, you may think ‘Heart’, ‘Cell’, ‘Body’ and ‘Nucleus’ are all connected through biology. But you’d be wrong, as ‘Heart’ and ‘Nucleus’ were actually two of four “Nexus” words on the day we’ve used as an example. Think beyond what a word means literally, try to see subtle patterns, and your luck with Connections will improve drastically. That being said, some days are still fiendishly difficult – and if you’re still stuck, check below for the Connections answer for today.

issues.title: Globle answer today – here’s the answer and hints for November 28

Looking for a variant of the popular Wordle game? Here’s one for you that can be rather challenging: Globle. Like Wordle, players are tasked with guessing the game’s selected country for the day.

  • READ MORE: Wordle answer for today

However, unlike Wordle, players have unlimited guesses for Globle so you won’t have to worry about losing unless you’re ready to concede defeat. Even for geography aficionados, guessing the Globle answer each day can be a real challenge. To help you out, we’ve included some hints in this page to help steer towards the right answer. If you’d rather just know the answer to keep your streak going, we have that too.

What’re you waiting for? Let’s get guessing!

How to play Globle

To play Globle, you’re first going to have to access the game’s website. To start playing, simply enter in the name of any country of your choice. You’ll then get a colour match for that country indicating how close to or far away you are from the answer.

The deeper the colour, the closer you are. After a couple of guesses you will slowly be able to narrow down the answer. A good tip is to pick larger countries that share borders with other countries. You can clear large sections of the map this way. Early on, you might also want to try varying your guesses between countries in different continents to narrow down your options.

Globle hint for today (November 28)

To help get you closer to today’s Globle answer, we’ve included some hints below. We’ll start off fairly vague, before giving bigger clues.

  • The country is in East Asia
  • The country begins with the letter ‘T‘

Here’s the final hint for today’s answer. This one should really narrow things down for you.

  • The country’s capital is Tokyo

Globle answer for today (November 28)

This is your final chance to walk away before getting today’s Globle answer spoiled for you. If you’re sure you can’t guess today’s country, keep reading for today’s answer.

Today’s Globle answer is Japan. This is the answer for November 28 with a new puzzle coming tomorrow. Stay tuned for more fun with geography!

issues.summary: You’ve been framed The post Framed answer today – here’s the solution for November 28 appeared first on NME .
issues.author: NME
issues.content_html:
The last couple of years have seen a huge rise in browser-based puzzle games, tasking players with working out a certain kind of answer using limited guesses. Framed is one of the newest, following in the footsteps of Wordle, but offering a slightly different twist. You’ll still need to work out the answer using limited information and only six tries, but it’ll be movies that you’ll be guessing.

  • READ MORE: ‘Connections’ answers and hints for today

You see, Framed focuses on individual frames, or stills, of an ever-changing roster of movies. Some show a fair amount of action at the start, while others will take careful analysis and decent trivia knowledge to crack. With each wrong guess, a new still is revealed, hopefully adding enough extra information and context for you to guess the correct movie title.

With only six guesses at your disposal, you may need a little help guessing today’s Framed answer. To give you a hint, we’ve included some clues that will tease the title of the movie picked as today’s puzzle. If you’ve already failed today’s puzzle, or would just like to know the answer, we’ve detailed that as well.

How to play Framed

To play Framed you just need to follow these steps, in your browser of choice. Note that any Framed versions you find elsewhere on app stores or other storefronts are likely to be fakes.

  • Go into your browser and visit framed.wtf
  • Take a look at the still for today
  • Make a guess, if it’s correct, you will see the rewards screen
  • If incorrect, you have five more chances, each showing a new still.

Framed hint for today

Today’s puzzle is an American period drama film.

  • Released in 1992
  • Directed by Robert Redford
  • Stars Craig Sheffer, Brad Pitt, Tom Skerritt

Framed answer for today (November 28)

The answer for Framed today is A River Runs Through It. This is the answer for November 28 with a brand new puzzle tomorrow. Check back in if you need any help!

Previous Framed answers

Sometimes, when trying to solve the Framed puzzle of the day, it can be extremely advantageous to know previous answers. Here are the answers from the last few days.

  • Jaws
  • Goodfellas
  • Jersey Girl
  • Finch
  • Sisters
  • Jay And Silent Bob Strike Back
  • Fury

That’s all you need to know about Framed, and the answer for today. For more puzzle-game goodness, check out our hints for today’s Connections.

issues.title: The Cutthroat Business of Shipwrecks
issues.summary: For centuries, lost cargo sparked fierce battles over who had the right to claim treasures washed ashore. The post The Cutthroat Business of Shipwrecks appeared first on JSTOR Daily .
issues.author: Amelia Soth
issues.content_html:
In 1627, treasures started to wash up on the beaches of France: diamonds, ebony, precious porcelain, spices, ivory, ambergris, and bezoars. Two Portuguese ships, so huge they were referred to as “floating cities,” had shipwrecked off the coast of Bordeaux, spilling luxury goods into the waves.

The disaster quickly threatened to become an international incident. The owners of the cargo (unsurprisingly) wanted their goods back—but the coast dwellers claimed that anything that washed up on shore was theirs by the ancient droit du naufrage, the “right of wreck.”

The “right of wreck” was a long-lived and widespread custom, one that shaped the very architecture of seaside towns.

It’s easy to understand why a beachcomber who found a diamond in the sand might want to hold onto it, but there was a legal basis for their claims. The “right of wreck” was a long-lived and widespread custom, one that shaped the very architecture of seaside towns: in his travels through Norfolk, Daniel Defoe wrote that the “country people had scarce a barn, or a shed, or a stable…but what was built of old planks, beams, wales and timbers, &c. the wrecks of ships, and ruins of mariners and merchants’ fortunes.”

That said, in legal terms, the right of wreck was a little more complicated than “finders keepers.” In many places, it wasn’t actually the person who stumbled on the shipwrecked goods who held the right to them; rather, they became the property of the local lord. In the earliest iterations of this idea, poor shipwreck survivors could find themselves roughly stripped of all their goods—as King Richard I of England found when his fleet was unlucky enough to wash up off the coast of Cyprus, circa 1191. His fiancée and his sister were taken as captives by the emperor of the island, who also helped himself to all the treasure they’d been traveling with. (This didn’t end well for the emperor, who lost his throne in the ensuing war.)

Neither wealthy merchants nor traveling kings were particularly enthusiastic about the idea that an accident at sea could mean forfeiting all their cargo. On the other hand, powerful landowners were eager to preserve their right to the occasional random windfall. As international trade increased, the right of wreck was slowly reshaped by centuries of legal wrangling. Courts battling over who could keep what ended up creating, for instance, highly specific legal definitions for terms like “flotsam” (goods that just happened to float to the surface after a wreck) and “jetsam” (goods intentionally tossed from a ship to make it lighter).

More to Explore

Lonely Diarist of the High Seas

April White July 21, 2025 As ship stewardess, Ella Sheldon tended to upper-crust women onboard and battled a range of workplace demons. Her journals tell her story.

The resulting patchwork of rules meant that every shipwreck was a complex negotiation between competing interests. Usually, the owners of the shipwrecked goods were entitled to their property back, in exchange for some kind of fee. Whether that was a ransom or a fair reward for helping salvage the goods is a matter of perspective.

In 1236, King Henry III of England issued an edict stating that if “man, dog, or cat” escaped the shipwreck alive, finders were obligated to hold on to the wrecked goods for three months, allowing the survivors to claim them in that time. There is a bit of an issue with that rule: it’s easy to see how it could create an incentive for shore dwellers to do away with shipwreck survivors in order to claim their goods (whether those survivors be man, dog, or cat)

Legends of these dark deeds swirled for centuries, but there’s little evidence they really happened. Still, people could be rough in their efforts to “salvage.” In Estonia, for instance, where the local lords were entitled to rewards if they helped to save ships in distress, people developed a habit of launching into enthusiastic “rescue” operations, whether or not there was any real danger.

Weekly Newsletter

" * " indicates required fields

A particularly good wreck could spark a feeding frenzy. An account of the wreck of the Golden Grape in 1641 gives a sense of the chaos:

The first arrivals on the beach contented themselves with staving in barrels and filling linen bags and pockets with raisins or, stripping off their waistcoats, used the sleeves as bags. But soon bands of men appeared from the various villages… Some gangs or men took away a score or two of barrels of raisins or the same number of jars of oil, but they were lucky if they did not have to share their booty with a stronger gang before they could gain a place of safety.

Not everything washes ashore, of course; many of the treasures lost in wrecks sank under the waves. There were fortunes to be made, but in a time before diving equipment, the trouble was how to reach it. In the early modern era, for the most part, even European sailors could hardly swim. But Africans living by the sea in Senegambia and the Gold Coast were highly skilled swimmers and divers—leading them to be targeted by enslavers, who knew their specialized skills could be turned to the recovery of underwater riches. As historian Kevin Dawson writes in “History Below the Waterline: Enslaved Salvage Divers Harvesting Seaports’ Hinter-Seas in the Early Modern Atlantic”:

The African-honed expertise that enslaved underwater divers carried throughout the Atlantic world allowed them to quickly recover several tons of gold, silver, and other items from shipwrecks, especially old Spanish treasure hulks. Possessing proficiencies held by few in the world, divers exchanged their unique ability to rapidly produce capital for semi-independent lives of privileged exploitation.

Their skills were so irreplaceable that they were able to negotiate for better treatment than most enslaved people, including a share of what they salvaged. Though, of course, a share isn’t much when you’re doing all the work.
