issues.title: Flax Seeds of Revolution
issues.summary: Revolutionary-era women spun flax as resistance against British rule and colonial gender norms. The post Flax Seeds of Revolution appeared first on JSTOR Daily .
issues.author: Jonathan Aprea
issues.content_html:
250 years ago, as the leaves changed and the weather turned colder, General George Washington and the Continental Army marched across Pennsylvania and New Jersey. In the evenings, Washington retreated to his marquee tents, which served as both the center of field command and the general’s private quarters. Through the rain and the ice, Washington camped under a canopy made of linen—trusty, waterproof, and American-made.

In the 1760s, as taxes on British imported goods rose under King George III (r. 1760–1820), American colonists turned to homespun textiles as symbols of resistance and ultimately, independence. One of these textiles was linen, spun and woven from the fibers of the flax plant. Washington’s tent was made by a Pennsylvania upholsterer rather than in private homes, but for women, spinning bees and weaving contests became a way of participating in Revolutionary activities while navigating complex gender dynamics. While cotton is king in the history of American textiles, flax played an important role in the cultural front of the American Revolution, uniting soon-to-be Americans in industriousness and self-sufficiency.

A Brief History of Flax

Flax, or Linum usitatissimum, is one of the oldest continuously cultivated plants in the world, with fibers discovered in the Alps dating back to 5000 BCE. It typically grows in sandy loam and temperate climates, creating blankets of slender stalks and blue flowers in the springtime. Flaxseeds can be ground and eaten or pressed into flaxseed oil or linseed oil. The former is edible and rich in mega-3s, and the latter is used in commodities ranging from paints to linoleum (a material named after the words “linen” and “oil”). But far and away, the most common use of flax is to create the durable, breathable textile—linen.

In ancient Egypt, linen made from flax was ubiquitous, appearing in everything from mummy wrappings to everyday attire. It quickly spread to Europe and beyond. In 789, the future emperor Charlemagne decreed that all households should cultivate their own flax and produce domestic textiles at home.

By the seventeenth century, the weaving of linen was a skilled craft in Europe. Peasants would typically grow, process, and spin their own flax yarn and then bring it to a local artisan—who was usually male—to weave into cloth. As the colonial world expanded, so did the linen trade. Both the Virginia Company and the Massachusetts Bay Company had unsuccessfully encouraged settlers at Jamestown and Massachusetts to cultivate flax in the early seventeenth century, but later efforts to grow the crop in North America succeeded. Linen plants were soon growing up and down the East Coast, along with the most productive colonies in the mid-Atlantic region.

The (Flax)seeds of Revolution

In seventeenth-century North America, women spun thread but did not weave; weaving was considered a skilled craft that only a man could hone and monetize. However, by the mid-eighteenth century, the gender norms of linen production were changing. The economy of the thirteen colonies developed rapidly, with complex networks of trade connecting the settlers to mainland England and beyond. Despite the common misconception of early American self-sufficiency, the average colonist spent more than one-quarter of their budget on imports.

The act of turning flax into usable textile products became part of the daily lives of women, who, as Ulrich explains, “measured their days, not in coffee spoons, but in knots and skeins.”

Even so, they were no strangers to taxation that caused shockwaves in the homegrown textile economy. The Wool Act of 1699 prevented colonists from exporting their wool to protect the English textile industry. Weaving became a way for daughters to contribute wealth to the household at a time when it was unseemly for them to work in the field or accept wages. As historian Laurel Thatcher Ulrich writes, the development of weaving among American women was “neither an artifact of rural poverty nor a response to frontier exigency. It was a colonial adaptation to an expanding mercantile economy.” By the 1770s, the American textile industry was developing rapidly. As such, the act of turning flax into usable textile products became part of the daily lives of women, who, as Ulrich explains, “measured their days, not in coffee spoons, but in knots and skeins.”

Linen was not the only useful flax product in early America. When clothing, tablecloths, and bedsheets wore out, the material was reused for two other essential colonial industries: bookbinding and papermaking. Flax was the material of choice for bookbinding thread due to its durability and strength. Nearly every book printed in the thirteen colonies was stitched with linen thread.

Before paper came to be made by pulping wood, it was crafted from old linen rags. An advertisement in The Massachusetts Spy from October 18, 1779, sought “all Linen & Cotton and Linen Rags, be they ever so small, as they are equally good for the purpose of making paper.” In fact, in 1776, before later transcribing it onto speciallyprepared vellum, the Declaration of Independence was drafted on flax paper. From textile to text, flax bound and dressed the story of America from the very beginning, making the concept of America itself legible for the first time.

Spinning Freedom

For British rule in North America, however, the writing was on the wall as plainly as it would soon be written on the flax. Growing economic dissatisfaction sowed discontent with mainland England. In 1765, the government of King George III passed the Stamp Act, which required written materials such as legal documents and magazines to be printed on London-milled paper embossed with a special stamp. The act enraged the colonial printing industry and papermaking, spurring the slogan “no taxation without representation.” This legislation was soon deemed unenforceable and repealed.

The Stamp Act was only one of many taxes and trade restrictions implemented by Britain that attempted to force the colonists to import goods at higher prices. In response, Patriots boycotted English goods, leading to shortages of textile products and the rags needed to make paper. Across the colonies, people opted to make their own goods, rejecting English rule in favor of American ingenuity. A wheelwright in Lexington, Massachusetts, reported significantly more business in spinning wheels in the lead-up to the revolution.

Spinning was catapulted into the public eye as a patriotic act. Eighteenth-century newspapers reported dozens of spinning bees where everyone from elderly women to young girls spun yarn and thread to do their part for the Revolution. This work could even take on a competitive edge. In 1769, two Connecticut women went head-to-head in a competition that was covered in several papers:

On the 16th Instant, the Wife of Mr. John Vaughan of Lebanon agreed upon a spinning Match with a neighbouring young woman; they began their work three Quarters of an Hour after Sunrise, and left off at Nine O’Clock in the Evening of the same Day.

After that marathon, they had spun nearly fourteen skeins of fine linen yarn.

Homespun cloth was not only a symbol of rejecting British control, but a religious symbol of piety and humility in the face of European luxuries, which were seen as mere vanity. In the late eighteenth century, spinning one’s own linens was considered a sign of good character, with reference made to the biblical verse (Proverbs 31:10–31) in which the “Wife of Noble Character” “selects wool and flax / and works with eager hands” on behalf of the household.

The respectable sheen of spinning one’s own yarn from flax enabled women to engage with both revolutionary ideology and manual labor without sullying themselves in the eyes of their peers. Newspapers like The Providence Gazette commended their work, describing these women as “Daughters of Liberty” with “good reputation.” These passionate yet respectable young women working for the cause contrasted with the Sons of Liberty, the revolutionary group known for starting riots and initiating the Boston Tea Party. As historians have argued, this negotiation between Revolutionary fervor and female respectability politics revealed a deeper tension between the desire for freedom and fears of unbridled chaos.

More to Explore

How War Revolutionized Ireland’s Linen Industry

Matthew Wills June 7, 2019 During the Napoleonic Wars, Irish women, who had traditionally only spun flax into thread, took over the traditionally male job of weaving linen as well.

As the revolution wore on, linen became a potently political sartorial choice. Remarking on the clothing worn by the ladies at a 1769 spinning bee held on Long Island, a columnist from Massachusetts called them “true Female Patriots,” who, by wearing homespun, demonstrated the intensity of their disdain for British rule. As historian Mathilde Frances Lind writes, “people wearing cloth spun and woven at home were physically enveloped in the fabric of the revolution, bodily experiencing and displaying their allegiance to the colonists’ cause.” Wearing homespun cloth became a desirable characteristic of marriageable elite women. Just as women sought men willing to die for the revolution, so too did men seek wives who were willing to clothe themselves in it.

Flax Fortunes

Long before women held prominent roles in the workforce, their weaving was a tangible, valuable economic production that showed their active role in the early American economy. Spinning flax into linen was a way for women to express their political preferences and participate in revolutionary economic tactics. In 1774, Abigail Adams, known for her sharp intellect, wrote to her husband, future President John Adams, about the increasing political tension in Massachusetts and his proximity to it. “As for me, I will seek wool and flax, and work willingly with my hands; and indeed there is occasion for all our industry and economy.”

With the nineteenth century came the invention of the cotton gin, the exploitation of chattel slavery, and developments in foreign markets that caused the bulk of America’s textile outputs to shift to cotton. As the Civil War boiled over, cotton constituted 61 percent of the value of all US exports. Linen production largely morphed into more specialized markets for industrial products and luxury goods.

Weekly Newsletter

" * " indicates required fields

Nonetheless, linen and the “Age of the Homespun” had taken on a mythological valence. Orators and politicians referenced an earlier, simpler age when political change looked like industrious, virtuous women spinning flax yarn together. The Daughters of the American Revolution—a hereditary association founded in 1890 and run by descendants of revolutionaries—adopted an insignia that captured the patriotic spirit of Revolutionary-era women from whom they’d descended. As an homage to the women who supported the boycotts by making their own cloth, they chose a spinning wheel in front of a distaff filled with flax.

The economic and symbolic impact of flax on the American origin story is still visible today, if you know where to look. George Washington’s visage underscores its importance: linen made from flax constitutes 25% of every American dollar bill.

Flax became a product and driver of the American Revolution, enabling women to demonstrate their virulent patriotism within the gender norms of their society. The Plant Humanities Initiative at Dumbarton Oaks seeks to uncover these complexities, revealing the ways that plants tangle with and influence major geopolitical events like the founding of America.

issues.title: Union Veterans and the Bitter Aftermath of the Civil War
issues.summary: As the nation embraced reconciliation, former Union soldiers questioned whether their sacrifices had been in vain. The post Union Veterans and the Bitter Aftermath of the Civil War appeared first on JSTOR Daily .
issues.author: Livia Gershon
issues.content_html:
In the decade following the Civil War, many white northerners wanted nothing more than to put the carnage behind them and reunify the country. But, historian Brian Matthew Jordan writes, one group that generally wasn’t ready to forgive and forget was Union veterans.

Jordan writes that the returning soldiers found a society that was happy to hail them as heroes but often offered them little material support. Many employers refused to hire men who they believed were too mentally or physically wounded to function.

“The momentous events of less than ten years ago are too fresh in memory to be forgotten at the command of any party that may be benefitted by ignoring them.”

And veterans’ efforts to ask for more were frequently dismissed. In the summer of 1865, just months after the war’s end, The New York Times complained that returning military men “prefer to live by begging.”

But Jordan argues that the veterans’ anger was not just about their own needs. Many felt that efforts to move past the conflict insulted their sacrifices. Those who returned with disabilities, painful wounds, and post-traumatic stress were reminded constantly of the war, and some worked to remind their neighbors, staging mock battles on town greens to show the “stay at homes” what the fighting had looked like. One wrote that “the momentous events of less than ten years ago are too fresh in memory to be forgotten at the command of any party that may be benefitted by ignoring them.”

More to Explore

Capturing the Civil War

Susanna Ashton May 23, 2024 The images, diaries, and ephemera in Grand Valley State University’s Civil War and Slavery Collection reveal the cold realities of Abraham Lincoln’s world.

A prime symbol of this neglect for many was the Confederacy’s president, Jefferson Davis. Soon after the war’s end, one veteran wrote to President Andrew Johnson, saying that he believed he had been “spared to witness the close of this wicked and unjust rebellion” and would be honored to help build a scaffold for Davis’s execution. Instead, despite being accused of treason, Davis was released two years after the war’s end and became a symbol of the Lost Cause. One Union veteran from Massachusetts complained that he had lost an arm “in vain” since “Jefferson Davis is today a hero, and more care is taken of him than the soldiers who fought to preserve the Union.”

Jordan writes that the Grand Army of the Republic (GAR), which was founded in 1866 and quickly became a national organization with 2,000 posts, focused primarily on supporting veterans, widows, and orphans, including by lobbying for benefits. But it also protested the appointment of “rebels and traitors” to government offices that could have gone to former Union soldiers.

Weekly Newsletter

" * " indicates required fields

GAR soon became a controversial group, with some northern civilians arguing that its demands and remembrances kept too much bitterness alive and made it difficult for the country to move forward.

In some cases, military service had also introduced northern soldiers to ideas about racial justice that their neighbors back home didn’t embrace. While not every white veteran became a supporter of Black Americans’ rights, Jordan suggests that it wasn’t uncommon. As the planter class attempted to reinstate a system of virtual slavery with the Black Codes and vigilante violence, some wondered if they would end up having to fight the war all over again.

issues.title: What happened to King Harold's children after the battle of Hastings?
issues.summary: William the Conqueror had conquered and launched a new era in England under the Normans, but he had to keep an eye on the heirs of his fallen foe
issues.author: Jonny Wilkes
issues.content_html:
The battle of Hastings was over: from the bloody fighting on 14 October 1066, William, Duke of Normandy, emerged as King of England while Harold Godwinson, after less than a year on the throne, was dead.

The Norman Conquest had begun, yet the family of the fallen king still posed a threat to William the Conqueror. Yes, three of Harold’s brothers also died that same year: Tostig had allied with Harald Hardrada and been killed at the battle of Stamford Bridge, while Gyrth and Leofwine perished alongside Harold at Hastings.

But in the early years of William’s reign Harold’s mother Gytha became a figurehead of rebellion in Exeter, and there were concerns that his seven children may one day seek to restore their line.

Who were Harold Godwinson’s children?

Harold Godwinson had five sons and two daughters. With his first wife, Edith Swanneck, he had three boys, Godwin, Edmund and Magnus, and two girls, Gunhild and Gytha. He had two more boys, Harold and Ulf, possibly with his second wife, Ealdgyth, although the lack of historical records means there remains confusion over who gave birth to Ulf.

  • Read more | What if Harold died at Stamford Bridge, not Hastings?

What happened to Harold’s wives?

Details are scant, but it seems that Edith Swanneck – also called Edith the Fair or the Handfasted Queen as she may have been unofficially married to Harold – survived the immediate aftermath of the battle of Hastings. According to legend, it was she who identified Harold’s body on the battlefield.

Ealdgyth, or Edith of Mercia, was married to Harold in early 1066 as part of a political alliance. After Hastings, her brothers, the earls of Mercia and Northumberland, took her to Chester for safety. It was possibly there that she gave birth to Ulf.

  • Read more | In 1066, King Harold was meant to save England. How did it all go wrong?

What happened to Harold’s sons?

The eldest sons, Godwin and Edmund, were teenagers in 1066 and fled to Ireland, where they lived under the protection of Diarmait, King of Leinster. Twice, they launched a campaign to western England in the hopes of overthrowing the Norman regime.

In 1068, leading a force of Dublin Norse mercenaries, they failed in their initial aim of seizing Bristol before losing a decisive battle in Somerset. They found no support from their father’s former allies, who had made peace with William. The following years, they returned with a fleet of ships and headed for Exeter, but again failed.

Instead, Godwin and Edmund raided parts of Devon and Cornwall, then, with no hopes of success, they fled again, this time to the court of their relative, Sweyn II of Denmark.

It is possible that their younger brother Magnus accompanied them, but only clues remain in the historical sources. He may have died during Godwin and Edmund’s doomed campaigns, or became a monk in Sussex or a count in modern-day Poland.

Accounts suggest that Harold (junior) found his way to the court of Olaf III of Norway, the son of Harald Hardrada. Despite Harold Godwinson defeating and killing Hardrada, he spared Olaf’s life at Stamford Bridge, so Olaf welcomed the young Harold into his service. It appears that he participated in expeditions to the Orkneys, Hebrides, Isle of Man and Anglesey.

Ulf, however, had been immediately captured after Hastings and was imprisoned in Normandy until William’s death in 1087. By then, any thoughts of opposition had been stamped out: in fact, he became a knight of the new Duke of Normandy.

  • Read more | How well did Harold Godwinson and William the Conqueror know each other prior to the battle of Hastings?

What happened to Harold’s daughters?

Gunhild was at a nunnery at Wilton Abbey in 1066 and remained in England. She married one of William’s inner circle, Alan the Red, possibly a strategic alliance to help Alan secure his lands, which had belonged to Gunhild’s mother. When he died shortly afterwards, she ended up with his brother, Alan the Black.

Gytha, meanwhile, escaped to Denmark and married Vladimir II Monomakh, ruler of Smolensk and Chernigov and the future Grand Prince of Kiev. They had several children together, with one of them becoming known as Harald; a small way of honouring Gytha’s father, since reclaiming the English crown was out of reach.

issues.title: Your scrambled eggs aren’t just breakfast — scientists found eating at least five a week is linked to a 27 percent lower Alzheimer’s risk
issues.summary: You may not need to eat eggs every morning for them to matter as you age. Large-scale research suggests that even occasional egg consumption — compared with skipping them altogether — tracks with a noticeably lower risk of Alzheimer's disease.
issues.author: PsyPost
issues.content_html:
If you’ve ever stood in front of an open fridge wondering what actually matters for keeping your mind sharp as you get older, it’s easy to assume the answer has to be complicated. A strict eating plan, maybe, or cutting out half the grocery store.

Rarely does anyone point at the carton of eggs sitting right on the shelf. Yet a large new analysis suggests this ordinary breakfast staple — whether you scramble it on a Sunday morning or eat it without thinking inside baked goods — tracks with a noticeably lower risk of Alzheimer’s disease later in life.

Even more surprising? You didn’t have to be a daily egg-eater to show up on the right side of the data.

Why skipping eggs stood out most

When people hear about a food linked to brain aging, the first question is usually how much of it you have to eat for it to count. In this case, the real twist wasn’t only at the top of the chart — it was at zero.

To see how everyday eating habits line up with formal diagnoses, epidemiologist Jisoo Oh, principal investigator Joan Sabaté, and their colleagues at Loma Linda University School of Public Health looked at dietary surveys from nearly 40,000 older adults in the United States and matched them to Medicare records over more than a decade and a half. Their findings appeared in The Journal of Nutrition.

People who ate at least five eggs a week had up to a 27 percent lower risk of developing Alzheimer’s compared to those who rarely or never ate them. Yet even folks who had eggs just one to three times a month saw a 17 percent lower risk.

Meanwhile, avoiding eggs altogether stood out for tracking with higher risk — a curve that caught the team’s attention. “We were also interested to observe that even relatively modest intake (such as 1-3 times per month) was associated with lower risk,” Oh said. “The nonlinear pattern, where zero intake was associated with higher risk, was also an unexpected and intriguing observation.”

That pattern held up even after the researchers accounted for the rest of a person’s diet, sleep, exercise, and other medical conditions. PsyPost’s full coverage of the study walks through every intake bracket and explains what happened when the team modeled swapping eggs for other proteins like nuts, seeds, and legumes.

What’s actually inside the shell

Why would such a plain grocery item show up alongside brain aging at all? Eggs happen to bundle several nutrients that aging brains depend on, especially inside the yolk.

They pack choline for memory and nerve-cell communication, omega-3 fats that help keep brain cells structurally sound, and yolk phospholipids needed for smooth brain signaling. On top of that, eggs carry lutein and zeaxanthin — two carotenoids that settle into brain tissue and track with less oxidative stress.

Just as telling, the researchers didn’t limit their count to boiled, fried, or scrambled eggs on a morning plate. They also tracked hidden eggs folded into baked goods and packaged foods, capturing the quiet, everyday ways eggs slip into a normal routine.

One piece of the plate, not a shield

Before anyone treats a weekend scramble like a medical guarantee, the researchers are clear about what the numbers can and can’t say. Regular egg-eaters had lower risk than people who avoided them. “However, this does not mean eggs prevent Alzheimer’s disease, but rather that they may be one component of a brain-healthy dietary pattern,” Oh said.

The study contributes to the scientific understanding of how everyday whole foods relate to healthy cognitive aging. However, because the work was observational and only recorded participants’ diets once at the start, it cannot prove that eggs caused the lower risk — and because the group studied was unusually health-conscious with low rates of smoking and alcohol use, the findings may not apply identically to more diverse populations.

For the researchers’ full interview comments, the study’s funding details, and a closer look at how Medicare claims were used to verify physician diagnoses, read PsyPost’s in-depth report on the research. As for the everyday takeaway, it’s a refreshingly grounded one: supporting an aging brain may have less to do with chasing complicated fixes, and more to do with ordinary, nutrient-rich foods already sitting in the kitchen.

issues.summary: Trusting science over church rules doesn't always erase superstition—it just shifts it away from traditional miracles. Research shows ghosts, curses, and everyday rituals resonate most with people who pair a scientific outlook with lingering ties to faith, not strict atheists.
issues.author: PsyPost
issues.content_html:
If you’ve ever felt a twinge of unease touring a house with a grim past—or caught yourself quietly dodging a jinx even though you consider yourself a rational, science-minded person—you’re in familiar territory. Most of us assume that trusting science and brushing off official church rules gradually dries up superstition.

Actually, the pattern runs the other way, and it doesn’t belong to the group you might expect. Strict atheists aren’t the ones pairing a scientific worldview with ghosts, curses, and minor rituals. Instead, that combination turns up most strongly in people straddling two worlds—relying on science over religious doctrine while still keeping one foot in faith, whether that means believing in God, claiming a religious affiliation, or attending church services.

When science replaces church rules, not wonder

We tend to picture reason and the supernatural as a simple seesaw: when science goes up, everything eerie or mystical drops out. In everyday life, though, stepping away from institutional authority rarely flips an off switch on curiosity about unseen forces.

What fades first is the official, church-approved version of the supernatural. People who lean on science to understand the world and prefer making moral choices from human experience rather than religious teachings are much less likely to believe in traditional, God-created miracles.

Yet that same independent outlook tracks with stronger belief in everyday superstitions—like performing small rituals to ward off bad outcomes, avoiding jinxes, or feeling uncomfortable buying a home where a murder happened—alongside magical ideas like ghosts, curses, predicting the future, and spirits inhabiting objects.

The sweet spot between strict faith and total disbelief

That split emerged in research published in Social Forces by Baylor University sociologist Paul Froese, alongside Isaiah King of Carson-Newman University and Ruiqian Li of American University. Drawing on the 2025 Baylor Religion Survey of 1,812 American adults, the team compared respondents’ commitment to science and independent spiritual judgment against three categories of belief: traditional miracles, magic, and everyday superstitions.

When they separated committed nonbelievers from people with lingering religious habits, the picture sharpened. Among strict nonbelievers and people who never attended church, valuing science didn’t give magical thinking or superstition a boost. The link largely vanished.

Where magic and superstition really flourished was in the middle. Sociologists refer to this dynamic as bounded affinity: keeping some tie to faith leaves the door open to unseen forces, while adopting a secular, scientific mindset loosens a church’s grip on which supernatural ideas stay off-limits.

PsyPost’s full coverage of the study breaks down how the researchers built their belief scales, how demographic factors like income and education played out—including the finding that education didn’t significantly predict any of the three supernatural categories—and how magical thinking historically overlapped with early science.

Why magic feels surprisingly compatible with logic

Why would a science-minded person warm up to magic in the first place? Part of the answer comes down to how magic works. Unlike organized religion, which centers on formal theology and a shared moral community devoted to a higher power, magic operates more like a toolkit—transactional efforts aimed at nudging unseen forces for practical, worldly results.

In a strange way, that mindset mirrors a mechanical, problem-solving outlook. Even when people want nothing to do with official dogma, the notion that hidden forces can be decoded or worked with can offer a sense of personal agency and optimism in a chaotic world.

The study contributes to the scientific understanding of how supernatural beliefs evolve as organized religion loses institutional authority. However, because the survey captured a single moment in time, it cannot prove that adopting a science-first outlook directly causes someone to embrace ghosts or superstitions, and its broad umbrella of magic bundles very different concepts—from casual jinxes to psychic phenomena—together. Readers interested in the full caveats and how online wellness gurus might fuel these blended beliefs can explore them in PsyPost’s in-depth report.

So if a fiercely practical friend rolls their eyes at church rules yet still refuses to tempt fate or keeps an open mind about ghosts, there’s nothing contradictory about it. Stepping back from organized doctrine doesn’t automatically erase the appetite for mystery—for many people, it simply moves that mystery out of the church and into everyday life.

issues.title: I Looked at a Packed October and Chose 2 Outcomes
issues.summary: In October 2024 I reviewed my month. It was already packed. Personal events. Travel. You know that feeling when the month is full before it starts? A 3-day commitment can consume 5 or 6 days once you include preparation, travel, recovery, and catching up. That’s the estimate I use on my own calendar. Ignore the […]
issues.author: Thanh Pham
issues.content_html:
In October 2024 I reviewed my month. It was already packed. Personal events. Travel.

You know that feeling when the month is full before it starts?

A 3-day commitment can consume 5 or 6 days once you include preparation, travel, recovery, and catching up. That’s the estimate I use on my own calendar. Ignore the surrounding time. The month is already overcommitted.

I allow at most 3 outcomes in a month. The number is a ceiling. I stopped at 2. Launch an online course. Book an overseas trip. The course and the trip were the targets I wrote down. A realistic plan was the result I was after.

The month has 3 boxes

Anchor events. Outcomes. Key tasks. That’s the whole monthly template.

Anchor events go in first. Anything that takes a full day or longer. Travel, conferences, and vacations. Any personal or work commitment that swallows a day goes on that list too. I want those visible before I choose goals. Then the remaining capacity is easy to see.

Outcomes go in second. Only what fits the days you have left. Up to 3. Each outcome needs a yes-or-no finish line. Research filing taxes is a task. Taxes filed is an outcome. You might still collect receipts, organize records, and get professional help. Work, family, and personal results can sit side by side.

Key tasks go in last. These are the actions that produce the outcomes. Those tasks give your weekly plan a place to start.

I put this session on the calendar about a week before the month begins. Same note every time. Plan the month you have.

Someone asked me about a detailed annual plan. I prefer 90 days. You get room for real progress. The deadline still feels close. A year-long target can lose urgency for months and turn into a scramble near the end. Keep a longer direction if you want one. Annual themes can guide the quarter. Turn 1 aspiration into an outcome for the next 90 days. Name the piece this month will carry.

Review before you repeat the week

If you keep overcommitting every week, the missing habit may be the review. Without it, the next plan reuses the same assumptions.

Before you plan next week, write 3 answers. What did I finish? What held me back? What should change? Look at what you intended. Look at what happened. Let that difference shape the workload.

You can review and plan in 1 session. You can also split them. The review still has to inform the plan.

A useful week names outcomes. At most 3. Same yes-or-no test. Then schedule the tasks that deliver them. The cap hits major priorities. Smaller tasks still belong on the list. For the day I pick up to 3 priority tasks. Other work still happens around them.

Course-correct tomorrow

Daily planning checks the weekly plan. Will today’s actions move it forward?

Do it the night before or the morning of. Pull the next steps for today. Resolve any prerequisite those steps still need.

Practice can sit on the calendar and still be impossible. I use a pickleball example for this. No court booked. No partner confirmed. The time is reserved. The session can’t happen. Find that hole. Fix it. Leave the rest of the schedule alone.

If you get distracted or overwhelmed, add an early-afternoon reminder. Where am I, and what needs to change? That check lets you adjust the rest of the day.

Reassess priorities at least once a day. Do it more often when work is moving fast. Capture the new request. Before you start it, compare it with the outcome you already chose. A genuine deadline, a service commitment, or an emergency can move first. Arrival order is a weak way to choose the next task.

I packed a day into 15-minute increments. A short meeting ran long. The rest of the day had to be reworked. That grid created more administrative work than useful structure. The stress spread forward. I still block time. Open pockets give a normal delay somewhere to land. I don’t have to rebuild the whole day. Leave visible margin between commitments when you plan the next workday.

Back to neutral

Feel like quitting the day before you even plan it?

A bigger routine can be the wrong first step when you’re buried. I compare it to money. Someone struggling to pay the next bill has little room to think about investing. Time works the same way. Process your inbox. Organize your projects. Breathing room makes it easier to look past today’s emergencies.

Neutral can include unfinished work. You need the inbox and your active projects clear enough to look ahead.

Start by planning tomorrow. Add weekly planning once that is consistent. Add the monthly template after that. All 3 horizons work together. The month identifies projects and deadlines. The week turns them into commitments you can keep. The day keeps execution on track. You decide what matters, make room for it, and adjust as life happens.

This is how I teach organizing time inside the 25X productivity system.

Tonight, plan tomorrow. Check your weekly plan. Write the next steps. Fix 1 missing prerequisite. Set an early-afternoon reminder: Where am I, and what needs to change?

issues.title: I Said Family Mattered. My Calendar Spent the Year on Work.
issues.summary: I sat down for an annual review in a year when I wanted more time with my family. I looked at where my time, energy, and attention had actually gone. Most of it had gone to work. Stated priority on one side. Actual allocation on the other. The review gave me a concrete direction for […]
issues.author: Thanh Pham
issues.content_html:
I sat down for an annual review in a year when I wanted more time with my family. I looked at where my time, energy, and attention had actually gone. Most of it had gone to work.

Stated priority on one side. Actual allocation on the other. The review gave me a concrete direction for the next year: change where those resources went.

You know that feeling when the thing you care about barely shows up in the week? I treat it as an awareness exercise. Taking a vacation belongs on the page. So does sustaining a useful habit. They sit next to the professional milestones. Leave the grading alone.

Answer 5 questions before you set a goal

Set aside a quiet session. Answer these before you set anything new.

What were my biggest accomplishments?

Write the ones that were real. That list can include a useful habit you kept alive all year.

What worked well?

Find the habits and strategies that worked. Decide which ones to continue, repeat, or expand. A better year does not necessarily require adding anything new. Protecting an effective routine can be a better annual-plan decision than replacing it with another ambitious commitment. Write a “keep doing” list before you write new resolutions.

January messaging equates progress with more goals, more tools, or more effort. Start from what already worked.

What did not go as planned?

Name the goal. Write what actually happened.

What obstacles affected my goals?

Notice which obstacles are still in play. Next year’s goals need to account for unexpected caregiving once it becomes an ongoing responsibility. Someone asked me about this in a session. Treat the care as a real planning priority. Explore routines around it. Ask for help. Share responsibilities where you can. A goal that ignores an existing commitment can create a conflict that better scheduling alone cannot solve. Intention does not make caregiving easy. Practical help is not available to everyone. List your ongoing responsibilities before you commit to new goals. Identify 1 source of support to explore.

Where did my time, energy, and attention go, and did that match what mattered most?

This question caught me. I wanted more time with my family. Work is where the year went. Put your answer beside your top priority and see if they match.

Sort last year like a closet

I compare an annual review to cleaning out a closet. Keep the wins and the lessons that still serve you. Remove habits or goals that no longer fit. Identify the strategies that need replacing. Make room for what belongs in your life now. Skip judging the old wardrobe.

Make 3 columns: Keep, Let go, and Replace. Sort the past year’s routines and commitments into them.

Reflect, refocus, recharge

I use the 3 Rs with TEA. Reflect, Refocus, and Recharge. TEA means time, energy, and attention.

Reflect on what happened. You do that with the 5 questions and the closet sort.

Refocus on 3 priorities.

Recharge turns those priorities into measurable goals and supporting habits. The recharge work here is the goals, the habits, and the milestones. I want the daily actions to match what matters.

One move for time, for energy, and for attention

Ask 1 question for each pillar. Then choose 1 action.

Time. Where should I spend more time? Where should I spend less? An action can be as simple as protecting a focus block.

Energy. Which activities fuel you? Which activities drain you? Scheduling 3 weekly workouts showed up as an example in a session I taught. Use it only if it fits your life.

Attention. Which distractions or low-value tasks can you reduce? I put my phone face down and on airplane mode during focused time. I practice this one myself.

Write the plan in 3 rows. Time, energy, attention. One action on each row.

The habit might live next to the goal

The habit that supports a goal may happen somewhere other than the goal itself.

Say you want to protect 2 hours of family time each weekend. Put the hours on the calendar if you want. Then name the recurring behavior that makes room for them. That behavior might be a boundary around checking work messages. It might be a Friday weekly review that helps you close out work. Pick 1 goal and ask what habit would make this easier to follow through on. A supporting habit improves the odds. It does not guarantee the result.

Give it a 90-day finish line

An annual direction gets more actionable when you pair it with a 90-day milestone. I favor this window because the finish line feels close enough to motivate action. You still have room for meaningful progress and a course correction. This is my preferred planning approach. I’m no researcher. I don’t have a study that proves 90 days is the optimum.

Give the milestone a deadline, a specific result, and a way to measure it. Finishing 2 books on a chosen topic within the next 90 days is a clean version.

Use AI once you understand the manual version

AI can help with a hard step in goal planning. Take a desired outcome and turn it into a supporting habit and an action plan. I built a custom GPT that asks questions and generates a plan. I teach the manual process first. Understand your priorities and your constraints. Learn how a goal connects to a habit. Then let AI draft.

Give an assistant 1 goal, your available time, and your constraints. Ask it to propose a supporting habit. Assess what it gives you. I won’t promise that draft is fast or accurate.

Compare the priority with the year

Block a quiet session. Write down your stated top priority. Next to it, write where your calendar and your energy actually went. Change where the time, energy, and attention go if those two lines don’t match.

issues.title: Stop Waiting for a Convenient Moment
issues.summary: I kept waiting for a convenient moment to spend time with people who matter to me. It never arrived…so I booked the trip. I was still working while I was there. Connection belongs in my wellness routine. Meaningful time with family needs a spot on the calendar. Sound familiar? You know the thing that would […]
issues.author: Thanh Pham
issues.content_html:
I kept waiting for a convenient moment to spend time with people who matter to me. It never arrived…so I booked the trip.

I was still working while I was there. Connection belongs in my wellness routine. Meaningful time with family needs a spot on the calendar.

Sound familiar? You know the thing that would help. You wait for a clear week anyway.

Trying to improve work-life balance without defining it is like driving through fog. You cannot see clearly enough to choose a direction. Describe the actual day you want. When does work start? When does it end? Who are you working with? What happens afterward? That picture makes boundaries easier to set. Planning a week that supports your life gets easier too.

A clear vision guides your choices. It does not remove external constraints. Sketch the day on a page. Circle 1 boundary that would move your current schedule closer to it.

Keep that boundary for a week.

If you’re retired, write the day around purpose and daily activities. What is the day for? Who is in it? What do you do with the hours?

Resilience means raising your baseline. The valleys still come. Sleep, movement, nutrition, and supportive relationships build the capacity you bring into a difficult day. Setbacks will still happen. The goal is to meet them with more resources. I used to wait until I was depleted to begin taking care of myself. Now I do that work on ordinary days.

A baseline-and-valleys graph is the picture I teach with. Higher line through the week. It is a metaphor. It does not predict recovery speed or severity.

This is the core of my resilience masterclass. Resilience is a productivity skill you can practice. A hard week can still hurt. This practice does not replace mental health care.

Within the time, energy, and attention framework, resilience primarily protects energy and attention. It helps you respond to a setback without letting it consume all your capacity to work.

Practice solving problems

When a problem feels overwhelming I use 3 moves. I break it into smaller parts. I talk to someone who has handled something similar. I write down at least 20 possible solutions.

The point of 20 has no magic in it. The longer list pushes you past the first 1 or 2 obvious answers so more options can show up. Asking is part of being resourceful. It is not evidence that you lack resilience.

I use this exercise with coaching clients. It is a way to explore responses to a challenge. Some painful situations cannot be fixed this way.

In the masterclass I used a family vacation because “plan the trip” hides dozens of decisions. I broke it into choosing a destination, booking travel and accommodation, creating an itinerary, and packing. A participant who had been putting the planning off wrote down a small task to get started. The vacation plan stayed unfinished. What changed was the size of the next action.

Replace 1 oversized to-do with its next concrete action. For the full pass, make space for the smaller subproblems, someone to consult, and 20 possible solutions.

Build a stronger baseline

I attach movement to something I already do. Eating. After a meal I take a 5 to 10 minute walk. When I can’t walk I do something physically active like cleaning the house. I used to rely only on dedicated workouts. Now I look for small openings inside the day I already have.

Try 1 tweak a week. After 1 daily meal, move for 5 to 10 minutes. Walk if you can. Clean the house if you can’t. Do it for a week. My habit. Not a prescribed exercise regimen.

If you add only 1 recovery routine, start with a bedtime wind-down. I prioritize this among my relaxation practices. Begin about 1 hour before bed. Step away from screens. Choose calming activities: journaling, reading, stretching, meditation, or talking with your partner. You give the end of the day a structure. Bedtime stops being whatever work or entertainment is still running.

Schedule a wind-down reminder. Pick a simple sequence for the coming week. This routine will not resolve a sleep disorder.

Before your next busy period, choose 1 baseline-building habit. Sleep. Movement. Nutrition. A supportive relationship. Start with that.

Make self-care a daily routine

This is the walk after a meal, the wind-down, and the person you schedule on purpose.

What if overwhelm has already turned into numbness or lethargy? Skip the dramatic productivity overhaul. Start with professional help and social support. Then pick a manageable action. Make breakfast. Or walk for 5 minutes. Don’t pressure yourself to recover on a deadline.

Small habits can support you. They are not treatment for depression. Identify 1 person you can contact and 1 manageable action for today. Do both today.

A hobby has no commercial outcome

Entrepreneurs, my challenge. Your business does not count as your hobby just because you enjoy it. A hobby gives you something to do for pleasure without a commercial outcome. That is my practical definition of a restorative hobby. I am not writing a universal rule about every paid creative pursuit.

Ask what you enjoyed as a child. Ask what you could do for hours for fun. Ask what you stopped doing when work became busy. Put 1 of those on next week’s calendar. No income goal. No performance goal.

Arrange 1 visit, 1 call, or 1 shared activity with someone important to you. I waited for a convenient moment that never arrived. Put it on the calendar today.

issues.title: My Tasks Got Faster. My Week Got Busier.
issues.summary: I’ve consciously taken on more because AI increased my capacity. Individual tasks got faster. My week got busier. Brooks finds that automation frees him to do more work. I chose the extra work on purpose. So where should the saved time go? More output. Better work. Or breathing room. Any of those can be the […]
issues.author: Thanh Pham
issues.content_html:
I’ve consciously taken on more because AI increased my capacity. Individual tasks got faster. My week got busier.

Brooks finds that automation frees him to do more work. I chose the extra work on purpose.

So where should the saved time go? More output. Better work. Or breathing room. Any of those can be the right answer…you have to choose on purpose.

You know that feeling when the work gets faster and the week still feels packed? That was me.

Building the team took months

I compare adopting AI agents to building a team. Delegation initially creates more work because someone has to provide context, establish the infrastructure, and supervise execution. The workload eases after those foundations are in place.

I spent roughly 6-8 months getting there. My agents could move work forward with less intervention. I finally had some breathing room. That timeline is mine (yours will be different).

More capacity led me to take on more. Reliable delegation took effort. Better-supported agents eventually reduced my involvement.

I chose 1 recurring responsibility. I gave that workflow clear instructions, relevant context, and a review process. I expanded after it was holding.

The brief comes first

I use a 10-80-10 split for AI-assisted work. You define the task and what done means. AI executes the bulk of the work. You review and sign off. Treat the percentages as a conceptual allocation.

A weak opening brief pushes that work into repeated clarification and correction later.

My reusable brief covers the goal, the source material, the constraints, and the definition of done.

Write the brief before your next handoff. If done is vague the review gets long. You already know how that feels.

Ask what a 2-minute review needs

Running several AI tasks at once moved my bottleneck from execution to the review queue.

I asked what would have to be true for a review that takes 1 hour to take 2 minutes. I wanted completed work that was easier to evaluate and approve.

My weekly planning and review now takes 10-15 minutes. That figure is for weekly planning and review. The 2-minute version is the question I ask when a review is still taking 1 hour.

Apply it to 1 recurring deliverable. Define the evidence or the summary you need for a confident decision.

I fixed the decks 1 bottleneck at a time

Frequent workshops meant I kept rebuilding decks and replacing outdated screenshots.

First I created an AI-assisted deck builder. Then I added computer-use capabilities so the assistant could visit an app, check whether a screenshot was outdated, and capture a replacement. What helped was reducing the recurring work of keeping the slides current.

Scope the computer access. Review sensitive screen content before you publish it.

Brooks protects the message and delegates more of the mechanics. He gathers the material, shapes the story, and provides a reference version of the slides. Then he lets AI help assemble the presentation. He reviews the result. Less of his evening goes to formatting. More of his attention stays on what the audience needs to understand.

On your next presentation, separate the story decisions from the slide-production tasks. You shape the story and provide a reference version. The assistant helps assemble. You review.

Identify the repetitive update that slows a recurring deliverable down. Automate that step before you redesign the whole workflow.

Describe the pain and ask

Brooks has caught himself assuming a tool could not handle something simply because he could not see the mechanism. He describes the pain point and asks the assistant to suggest an approach. He keeps legitimate limits on what it should handle. Some reasons not to delegate are valid. The question explores feasibility.

Pick 1 repetitive task you have dismissed as unsuitable for AI. Ask for a proposed workflow before you decide.

Missing context is a possible diagnosis when an assistant keeps asking questions. Relevant source material can let it answer questions that would otherwise come back to you. Brooks describes how read-only access to a team’s code repository can enrich the assistance even for nontechnical work such as marketing.

Start with narrowly scoped read-only access. Notice the next question your assistant asks. Identify the approved source that could answer it.

What Brooks sees at work

Brooks describes 3 workplace responses to AI. These are his informal observations.

The enthusiast voluntarily takes on more. The employee sees targets rise because management expects AI-powered output. The quiet overachiever finishes early and worries about being found out.

He has encountered online anecdotes about finishing a week’s work in 3 hours. Those are anecdotes. Unverified.

Each response has its own problem. Managing commitments. Negotiating expectations. Deciding how to use newly available capacity.

Which situation resembles your workplace?

Talk about outcomes and workload. Hours spent looking busy is a weak scoreboard once the work speeds up.

Stay with the tool you can use

Get good at the tool your workplace already permits. Build practical experience on real work. Chasing the current winner can wait until you have those reps.

Brooks makes the complementary point. Using a capable tool is often more valuable than waiting to identify the best one.

Choose 1 approved assistant. Use it on a recurring task before you consider a switch.

Block the time

Before you automate another task, decide where the recovered time should go. More output, better work, or breathing room. Protect that choice in your calendar. Block it today.

issues.title: My 2019 Annual Review
issues.summary: Another year complete. Here’s a quick recap of 2019, which also happened to be one of the craziest years of my life. As always, this Annual Review will answer three questions. What went well this year? What didn’t go so well this year? What did I learn? Before we begin, it is worth noting that […]
issues.author: James Clear
issues.content_html:
Another year complete. Here’s a quick recap of 2019, which also happened to be one of the craziest years of my life.

As always, this Annual Review will answer three questions.

  1. What went well this year?
  2. What didn’t go so well this year?
  3. What did I learn?

Before we begin, it is worth noting that every Annual Review is a personal process. This is simply an overview of what my year looked like, not advice for how you should live your life. (That said, you are always welcome to use this general format for your own Annual Review.)

1. What went well this year?

I had a lot to celebrate this year.

Book sales.Atomic Habits launched in October 2018, which meant that 2019 was the first full calendar year it had been available. I came in with big aspirations, but I think it’s fair to say that book sales have outpaced my expectations.

As of December 2019:

  • Over 1.3 million copies sold worldwide
  • 12 consecutive months on the New York Times bestseller list
  • 4.8/5 stars on Amazon with over 1,800 reviews
  • 4.8/5 stars on Audible with over 25,000 ratings
  • Over 15 national TV segments in the United States, Canada, and Australia
  • Translated into 40+ languages

This has been a wild ride to say the least.

Of course, the greatest reward has been hearing from readers. It seems like nearly every day someone tells me that Atomic Habits helped them lose weight or start a business or make some positive change in their life. People are finding real value in the ideas and it feels great to produce something useful.

3-2-1 Newsletter. My new project for 2019 was launching the 3-2-1 newsletter, which shares 3 ideas from me, 2 quotes from others, and 1 question to ponder each week. I had been struggling to write consistently during the first half of the year (discussed below) and this new format offered something I knew I could stick with despite a busy schedule. (Sometimes I have to take my own medicine and scale my habits down.)

I didn’t realize it at the time, but it turns out to have been a good idea. I feel good because I’m producing new work each week and the response from subscribers has been quite favorable. Many readers tell me it’s the only newsletter they actually read as soon as it hits their inbox.

Audience growth. I didn’t write many new articles this year, but thanks to the buzz generated by Atomic Habits and the momentum of the 3-2-1 newsletter, audience growth remained strong.

Here’s what the year looked like:

  • 5 new articles published this year (fewest ever; discussed in next section)
  • 353,970 new email subscribers in 2019
  • 586,638 total email subscribers as of December 31, 2019
  • 10,848,250 unique visitors in 2019
  • 47,308,712 total visitors since launching on November 12, 2012

Even after doing this for a few years, the scale of the internet still blows me away. I’m grateful to have the opportunity to share my work with so many people.

Twitter and Instagram. I didn’t put much energy into social media for a long time, but the web has evolved in the last five years and social media plays an important role now. This was the first year I put consistent effort into Twitter and Instagram, and it paid off. My audience doubled on both platforms this year. Feel free to join the fun and follow me on Twitter and on Instagram.

Travel. This was the craziest travel year of my life and, in all likelihood, the craziest I will ever have. I spent a total of 158 nights away from home this year, which means I spent 43% of the year not sleeping in my own bed. It’s a pace I will probably (hopefully?) never match again.

Here’s the rundown…

18 states (0 new) – Arizona, California (5x!), Colorado (2x), Florida (2x), Georgia, Hawaii, Illinois (2x), Indiana (3x), Maryland, Nebraska (2x), Nevada, New York (5x!), Ohio, Pennsylvania (3x), Tennessee (2x), Texas (2x), Utah, and Virginia.

14 countries (7 new) – Australia (2x!), Canada (2x), Croatia, Denmark, Greece, England, Iceland, Ireland, Japan, Malaysia, Singapore, Spain, Sweden, and the United Arab Emirates.

While I love traveling, I did feel a bit guilty about the number of flights I took this year and the resulting pollution. In response, I decided to buy carbon offsets not only to cover my flights, but also to be entirely carbon neutral for 2019. I bought mine through Project Wren, and it wasn’t nearly as expensive as I expected.

New restaurants. Whenever I travel to a new city, I like to ask for restaurant recommendations on Twitter. Oh man, did you all set me up this year. I had so many great meals thanks to reader suggestions.

I feel compelled to repay you all by sharing some of my favorites (in no order):

  • Los Angeles, CA — fundamental LA
  • Denver, CO — Mercantile Provisions
  • Honolulu, HI — Marukame Udon
  • New York, NY — Manhatta (my meal of the year)
  • Philadelphia, PA — Zahav (runner up)
  • Melbourne, Australia — Chin Chin
  • Sydney, Australia — NOMAD
  • Sydney, Australia — Mr. Wong
  • Toronto, Canada — PAI
  • Dubrovnik, Croatia — Pantarul
  • Dubrovnik, Croatia — Taj Mahal
  • London, England — Nopi
  • London, England — Dishoom
  • Athens, Greece — Atitamos
  • Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia — Village Park Restaurant
  • Singapore — Artichoke
  • Singapore — Maxwell Food Court
  • Madrid, Spain — El Charrua
  • Madrid, Spain — Ten Con Ten

For more ideas (including specific dishes), check out my full list of recommended restaurants.

Speaking. I delivered 31 paid keynote speeches in 2019. This is far and away the most I’ve ever given in a calendar year. Obviously, this is tied directly to the success of Atomic Habits, but I’ve improved my speaking skills as well. My biggest takeaway is that if you write about a topic for years and are forced to clarify your thinking in a well-structured book, then speaking about that topic for one hour becomes much easier to do. (Note: If you’d like me to speak at your company or event, you can submit a request here.)

2. What didn’t go so well this year?

Many wonderful things happened in 2019, but I suffered plenty of growing pains as well.

Writing. For years, my business was built on the consistency of my writing. I published a new article every Monday and Thursday from 2012 to 2015. From 2016 to 2018, I spent most of my time writing Atomic Habits. Overall, those six years were filled with writing.

Then 2019 arrived and the book began to sell far and wide. My attention shifted to promotion mode: interviews, speeches, book signings. It was all great, but there was very little time left for writing. Honestly, I probably wrote more words on Twitter last year than in new articles.

Thankfully, I began to course correct during the second half of the year by writing the 3-2-1 newsletter (as mentioned previously). We’ll see what things look like in 2020, but if I’m going to write another book at some point, I will need to carve out more time to write.

Weightlifting. Everything has a tradeoff. It turns out that it is hard to maintain consistency in the gym when you are on the road for nearly half the year. In 2019, I completed 91 workouts for an average of 7.6 per month, which is better than nothing, but a steep drop off from previous years.

Workouts per month in 2019:

  • January – 16
  • February – 6
  • March – 4
  • April – 8
  • May – 4
  • June – 2(!)
  • July – 12
  • August – 8
  • September – 9
  • October – 15
  • November – 1(!)
  • December – 6

When looking at these numbers, the thing that sticks out to me is that my worst months were the months I had lots of international travel (March, June, and November). I’ll need a better plan for exercising in foreign locations in the future.

Given how inconsistent things were, I didn’t bother with max lifts this year and just did rep work most days. As a result, my best lifts of the year were:

  • Back Squat – 330 lbs (150 kg) for 5 rep
  • Bench Press – 245 lbs (111 kg) for 5 rep
  • Deadlift – 415 lbs (188 kg) for 5 rep

This marks the second year in a row when I failed to hit an all-time PR in any major lift. Admittedly, it’s unlikely you’re going to reach a personal best every year anyway, but nonetheless I have a lot of catching up to do in the gym in 2020.

Email. I joked earlier this year that my email response time is either 3 minutes or 3 months. Problem is… it’s not really a joke. I’m terrible at answering email. Honestly, this wouldn’t bother me except for one reason: it bothers other people.

My poor email response times came back to burn me multiple times this year. Sometimes it was a missed opportunity due to a delayed reply. Other times people became annoyed or frustrated, or thought I was intentionally ignoring them.

I’m not sure the best way to handle this. I get more email than I can manage and answering emails is certainly not as important as writing the next article or book. And yet, people expect responses within a day or two. One thing is for sure, I’ll probably need a new email approach in 2020.

3. What did I learn this year?

Some of my major lessons from this year include:

Move fast. The importance of moving fast was clarified for me over the last year. The original release date for Atomic Habits was set for March 2019. I pushed to move the date forward six months to October 2018 because I didn’t want to miss out on holiday sales around Christmas. My publishing team agreed, everyone worked their tails off, and we had a fabulous launch in October.

What happened next was even more important: The book was available in January when everyone was thinking about New Year’s Resolutions. As a result, Atomic Habits jumped out to a very strong start during the fall and winter. By the time we arrived at the original launch date in March, we had already sold nearly 500,000 copies.

In this case, the difference between waiting and acting was massive. We all know exactly what would have happened if we had waited: time would have flown by, somehow planning the launch would have expanded to fill all of that time, and six months of sales would have vanished.

Growing up takes time. For the last three years my business has been stuck in that awkward pre-teen stage where one minute it acts like a full-fledged adult and the next minute you realize it’s covered in pimples and doesn’t know how to control all four limbs at the same time.

But in 2019—maybe!—it turned a corner. The to-do list is still endless, but that’s what running a business is like. It does feel like I’m starting to find my footing, however. The strategy is becoming more clear. The products are gaining a foothold. The fog is lifting ever-so-slightly. I have spent nearly a decade as a full-time entrepreneur, but I’m finally uncovering a clear roadmap of what the future of the business looks like.

A life well-lived is a life well-edited. My biggest area of growth this year was prioritization. I had to become much better at saying no— and I’m still not very good at it!

In short: Prune away the inessential. Pour yourself into what remains.

That’s it! As always, thanks for reading. Happy New Year! 1
