issues.title: The Ultimate Productivity Hack is Saying No
issues.summary: The ultimate productivity hack is saying no. Not doing something will always be faster than doing it. This statement reminds me of the old computer programming saying, “Remember that there is no code faster than no code.” The same philosophy applies in other areas of life. For example, there is no meeting that goes faster […]
issues.author: James Clear
issues.content_html:
The ultimate productivity hack is saying no.

Not doing something will always be faster than doing it. This statement reminds me of the old computer programming saying, “Remember that there is no code faster than no code.” 1

The same philosophy applies in other areas of life. For example, there is no meeting that goes faster than not having a meeting at all.

This is not to say you should never attend another meeting, but the truth is that we say yes to many things we don’t actually want to do. There are many meetings held that don’t need to be held. There is a lot of code written that could be deleted.

How often do people ask you to do something and you just reply, “Sure thing.” Three days later, you’re overwhelmed by how much is on your to-do list. We become frustrated by our obligations even though we were the ones who said yes to them in the first place. 2

It’s worth asking if things are necessary. Many of them are not, and a simple “no” will be more productive than whatever work the most efficient person can muster.

But if the benefits of saying no are so obvious, then why do we say yes so often?

Why We Say Yes

We agree to many requests not because we want to do them, but because we don’t want to be seen as rude, arrogant, or unhelpful. Often, you have to consider saying no to someone you will interact with again in the future—your co-worker, your spouse, your family and friends. 3

Saying no to these people can be particularly difficult because we like them and want to support them. (Not to mention, we often need their help too.) Collaborating with others is an important element of life. The thought of straining the relationship outweighs the commitment of our time and energy.

For this reason, it can be helpful to be gracious in your response. Do whatever favors you can, and be warm-hearted and direct when you have to say no.

But even after we have accounted for these social considerations, many of us still seem to do a poor job of managing the tradeoff between yes and no. We find ourselves over-committed to things that don’t meaningfully improve or support those around us, and certainly don’t improve our own lives.

Perhaps one issue is how we think about the meaning of yes and no.

The Difference Between Yes and No

The words “yes” and “no” get used in comparison to each other so often that it feels like they carry equal weight in conversation. In reality, they are not just opposite in meaning, but of entirely different magnitudes in commitment.

When you say no, you are only saying no to one option. When you say yes, you are saying no to every other option.

I like how the economist Tim Harford put it, “Every time we say yes to a request, we are also saying no to anything else we might accomplish with the time.”4 Once you have committed to something, you have already decided how that future block of time will be spent.

In other words, saying no saves you time in the future. Saying yes costs you time in the future. No is a form of time credit. You retain the ability to spend your future time however you want. Yes is a form of time debt. You have to pay back your commitment at some point.

No is a decision. Yes is a responsibility.

The Role of No

Saying no is sometimes seen as a luxury that only those in power can afford. And it is true: turning down opportunities is easier when you can fall back on the safety net provided by power, money, and authority. But it is also true that saying no is not merely a privilege reserved for the successful among us. It is also a strategy that can help you become successful.

Saying no is an important skill to develop at any stage of your career because it retains the most important asset in life: your time. As the investor Pedro Sorrentino put it, “If you don’t guard your time, people will steal it from you.” 5

You need to say no to whatever isn’t leading you toward your goals. You need to say no to distractions. As one reader told me, “If you broaden the definition as to how you apply no, it actually is the only productivity hack (as you ultimately say no to any distraction in order to be productive).”

Nobody embodied this idea better than Steve Jobs, who said, “People think focus means saying yes to the thing you’ve got to focus on. But that’s not what it means at all. It means saying no to the hundred other good ideas that there are. You have to pick carefully.” 6

There is an important balance to strike here. Saying no doesn’t mean you’ll never do anything interesting or innovative or spontaneous. It just means that you say yes in a focused way. Once you have knocked out the distractions, it can make sense to say yes to any opportunity that could potentially move you in the right direction. You may have to try many things to discover what works and what you enjoy. This period of exploration can be particularly important at the beginning of a project, job, or career.

Upgrading Your No

Over time, as you continue to improve and succeed, your strategy needs to change.

The opportunity cost of your time increases as you become more successful. At first, you just eliminate the obvious distractions and explore the rest. As your skills improve and you learn to separate what works from what doesn’t, you have to continually increase your threshold for saying yes.

You still need to say no to distractions, but you also need to learn to say no to opportunities that were previously good uses of time, so you can make space for great uses of time. It’s a good problem to have, but it can be a tough skill to master.

In other words, you have to upgrade your “no’s” over time.

Upgrading your no doesn’t mean you’ll never say yes. It just means you default to saying no and only say yes when it really makes sense. To quote the investor Brent Beshore, “Saying no is so powerful because it preserves the opportunity to say yes.” 7

The general trend seems to be something like this: If you can learn to say no to bad distractions, then eventually you’ll earn the right to say no to good opportunities.

How to Say No

Most of us are probably too quick to say yes and too slow to say no. It’s worth asking yourself where you fall on that spectrum.

If you have trouble saying no, you may find the following strategy proposed by Tim Harford, the British economist I mentioned earlier, to be helpful. He writes, “One trick is to ask, “If I had to do this today, would I agree to it?” It’s not a bad rule of thumb, since any future commitment, no matter how far away it might be, will eventually become an imminent problem.” 8

If an opportunity is exciting enough to drop whatever you’re doing right now, then it’s a yes. If it’s not, then perhaps you should think twice.

This is similar to the well-known “Hell Yeah or No” method from Derek Sivers. If someone asks you to do something and your first reaction is “Hell Yeah!”, then do it. If it doesn’t excite you, then say no. 9

It’s impossible to remember to ask yourself these questions each time you face a decision, but it’s still a useful exercise to revisit from time to time. Saying no can be difficult, but it is often easier than the alternative. As writer Mike Dariano has pointed out, “It’s easier to avoid commitments than get out of commitments. Saying no keeps you toward the easier end of this spectrum.” 10

What is true about health is also true about productivity: an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure.

The Power of No

More effort is wasted doing things that don’t matter than is wasted doing things inefficiently. And if that is the case, elimination is a more useful skill than optimization.

I am reminded of the famous Peter Drucker quote, “There is nothing so useless as doing efficiently that which should not be done at all.”

Footnotes

  1. Taligent’s Guide to Designing Programs. Hat tip to Kevlin Henney

  2. Even worse, people will occasionally fight to do things that waste time. “Why can’t you just come to the meeting? We have it every week.” Just because it is scheduled weekly doesn’t mean it is necessary weekly. You don’t have to agree to something just because it exists.

  3. Saying no to your superiors at work can be particularly difficult. In these situations, I like the approach recommended in Essentialism by Greg McKeown. He writes, “Remind your superiors what you would be neglecting if you said yes and force them to grapple with the trade-off. For example, if your manager comes to you and asks you to do X, you can respond with “Yes, I’m happy to make this the priority. Which of these other projects should I deprioritize to pay attention to this new project?” Hat tip to my friend, Shane Parrish, at Farnam Street who shared this insight from McKeown in the article, “Eight Ways to Say No With Grace and Style.”

  4. Tim Harford, The Power of Saying No

  5. Pedro Sorrentino, [Stoic Capital #21] On productivity, time and wealth

  6. Jobs had another great quote about saying no: “I’m actually as proud of the things we haven’t done as the things I have done. Innovation is saying no to 1,000 things.”

  7. Brent Beshore on Twitter

  8. This is similar to Shane Parrish’s rule of thumb for meetings: “If you wouldn’t do it right now, say no.” A similar philosophy could be extended to many areas of life.

  9. Derek Sivers, No “yes.” Either “HELL YEAH!” or “no.”

  10. Mike Dariano, Start with “no” for a better “yes”

issues.title: 30 One-Sentence Stories From People Who Have Built Better Habits
issues.summary: In this article, I’d like to share 30 “one-sentence stories” about building better habits. (They are not all exactly one sentence, but they are very short.) None of these stories are mine. They were sent to me by readers of Atomic Habits. My hope is that these examples will illustrate how real people are putting […]
issues.author: James Clear
issues.content_html:
In this article, I’d like to share 30 “one-sentence stories” about building better habits. (They are not all exactly one sentence, but they are very short.)

None of these stories are mine. They were sent to me by readers of Atomic Habits. My hope is that these examples will illustrate how real people are putting the book into practice. They will show you what people are actually doing to build good habits and break bad ones. And hopefully, they will spark some ideas for how you can do the same.

I have divided the stories into categories that roughly correspond to different sections or ideas in the book.

Identity-based habits

One of the central ideas in the book is the concept of building “identity-based habits”, which essentially recommends focusing on the type of person you wish to become rather than the outcome you wish to achieve.

One reader named Roland used the idea to improve his eating habits.

“I stopped eating unhealthy food via identity change,” he wrote. “I tried many times in the past, but it became easy — natural — only after I had made the conscious decision that I want to be someone who eats healthy. Instead of aiming for I want to stop eating bad food, I tried changing the mindset to I am someone that eats healthy and lives a healthy life. It changes how you approach things.”

Another reader named Robert employed this idea to help him quit smoking. He wrote, “I recently stopped smoking and the difference between I don’t smoke and I can’t smoke is a powerful trainer of my brain. The positive message of I don’t smoke is that I have not “given up” anything. I am not sacrificing a pleasure. I am investing in my future happiness and wellbeing.”

Like most strategies in the book, the concept of identity-based habits can be combined with other habit building tactics. For instance, one reader used an external reward of $10 to reinforce the desired identity. “I told myself, I am no longer a drinker. Then, after each day of non-drinking, I gave myself $10 to buy something nice rather than poison (like clothes and household items). Today, I no longer need the allowance and I’m six years sober.”

Chapter 2 of Atomic Habits covers these strategies in much greater detail.

Changing the Cues

Another way you can change a habit is by identifying and altering the cues that prompt your behavior. This is precisely what many readers have done.

One woman named Lisa cultivated a reading habit by increasing her exposure to books. “I’ve read more books by continually having 20-30 books on hold at the library,” she said. “It saves time on browsing for books. I always have new things to read with a three-week deadline.”

Heather used a similar strategy to reinforce the simple habit of drinking more water. “I use color and placement for visual reminding and motivation. I poured water in a bright aqua water bottle – my favorite color – and placed it on my nightstand so I couldn’t miss it when I woke up.”

Other readers have done the opposite. They reduced exposure to negative cues. One man named Max managed to eliminate his e-cigarette habit. “I quit e-cigarettes with a combination of determination and also quitting coffee at the same time, which was a trigger for me as I’d smoke and drink coffee together in the morning.”

Habit Stacking

Another popular tactic in the book is something I call “habit stacking.” It’s strategy I first learned from Stanford professor B.J. Fogg. He refers to it as “anchoring” because you anchor—or stack—your new habit onto a current habit.

One reader used habit stacking to create a simple rule for learning a new language.

“When I first moved to China and started to learn Mandarin, I committed to strike up a conversation with the taxi driver whenever I went into a cab (I took a lot of cab rides, 5+ daily). I did it for 2 years no matter the time of day or how tired I was. I now speak fluent Chinese.”

Similarly, a reader named David told me, “I meditate for 20 minutes after brushing my teeth in the morning. Linking new habits onto a keystone one seems to work.”

You’ll find all sorts of habit stacking examples in Chapter 5 of Atomic Habits.

Environment Design, Part I

I have written about the power of the environment and the importance of choice architecture in the past. The simple truth is our environment often shapes our behavior. Many readers are using this fact to their benefit by installing some of the environment design strategies I share in the book.

For starters, you can break a bad habit by increasing the friction in your environment.

One woman named Cyd curtailed her snacking habit with the following strategy. “My husband still loves his Pringles, as do I, but they’re now kept in a locked car that’s parked in the cold. It works!”

Multiple readers are learning to wake up earlier.

One reader named Daniel told me, “I jump out of bed every morning without any hesitation. The reason? The only way to turn off my alarm is to scan a QR Code I keep in the bathroom. This worked wonders for me.”

Chris utilized both environment design and habit stacking to stop sleeping in. He wrote, “I have a bad habit: Hitting snooze. To eliminate it, I “made it hard” and put phone in the bathroom. The phone then became a habit stack. The first thing I do when I wake up: turn off alarm, go to bathroom, brush teeth, etc.”

One of my favorite examples was sent to me by J. Money, the personal finance blogger. He wrote, “I brush my teeth right after putting my kids to bed every night (8pm), which has prevented me from eating or drinking (alcohol) at night for years… ‘Cuz who wants to re-brush them again!”

It’s a great example of creating just enough friction to keep your bad habits at bay.

Environment Design, Part II

Typically, we think of designing physical spaces, but you can use the same principles to shape your digital environment as well. For instance, a reader named Matthew wrote to me and said, “I significantly cut down on mindless Instagram time. Simply logging out of the app makes a big difference.”

Another reader named Viet went even further. “I used my own laziness to my own advantage with my bad habit of browsing Facebook. Deleting Facebook and having to go through the one extra step of going to website and logging in manually was enough barrier for me to not get back on.”

And Rahul did something similar to kill his video game habit. “For gaming addiction, I removed my graphic card,” he wrote. “For excessive net surfing on mobile, I uninstalled apps and removed the Chrome browser.”

Environment Design, Part III

On the flip side, you can foster good habits by reducing the friction in your environment.

Natalie started picking up her cluttered clothes and building better cleaning habits simply by reducing the number of steps between her and the laundry basket. “I quit leaving my socks all over the floor by putting a little basket beside the door to collect them in.”

Similar strategies can be particularly useful for building new exercise habits.

One reader named Justin sent me the following message: “I started going to a gym that was less than a mile from my house. This took away the time and inconvenience excuses. I was never consistent at exercise, but now I work out 8-10x a week. Crossfit, running, and cycling. I’ve been going strong for 2.5 years.”

Another reader wrote, “I’ve been running at 6 A.M. for the past two years. I always put my running gear (Garmin, compression sleeves, shoes, etc.) into a neat pile the night before. When I get up, I just get dressed and go out the door.”

I’ve even heard from readers who go to sleep wearing their running clothes. All they have to do is stumble out the door in the morning.

For more on environment design, see Chapters 6 and 12 of Atomic Habits.

Habit Substitution

In many cases, it can be more effective to replace your bad habit than to merely try to eliminate it.

The beautiful thing about habit substitution is that you can build a good habit and break a bad one at the same time. One reader told me, “At home I would go out to my backyard to smoke, so I put a weight bench out there and every time I wanted to smoke I’d go out and do some reps instead. After that, my craving was reduced.”

I thought the following idea was interesting. One reader replaced biting their nails with cutting their nails. “I stopped biting my fingernails mostly by making sure clippers were always close at hand – especially at work.”

Many readers have substituted a new habit in a “stair step” fashion. They gradually shift from the old habit to something healthier.

Mark, for example, shared the following strategy. “I significantly cut back on beer consumption. I used flavored sparkling water to replace the beer and I asked my wife to stop having beer in the fridge for a while. Once I replaced the habit (it was mostly stress drinking after work), I was able to add beer back into my life.”

And another reader, also named Marc, curtailed his drinking in a similar way. “I replaced drinking beer every day in a succession of replacements, going through fruit juice, then iced tea, then seltzer water. I did it over about nine months by having one less drink a week. Once I finally quit, I got past the cravings in only two weeks. I haven’t had a drink in over a year now.”

Shawn used this approach to stop smoking. “I decided to quit smoking and used a fun-sized Snickers candy bar as a substitute until the major cravings went away. I’m still smoke-free years later.”

Substitution can even be useful in a broader sense. Suraj wrote, “I was addicted to drugs and alcohol. To beat my addiction, I started working out. Now I am planning to compete in powerlifting meets.”

To a certain degree, habit substitution allows you to look for a healthier obsession. Some people are hooked on alcohol. Others are hooked on exercise. Either one can be unhealthy if taken too far, but generally speaking it’s a lot better to spend a few hours exercising each day than to spend a few hours drinking each day.

Mindset Tricks

Sometimes I like to employ clever little mental tricks to stick with a good habit.

One reader named Caelan wrote, “I quit smoking by assigning my cheat days progressively farther in the future. I never quit “for good,” I only quit until my next cheat day. This helped with cravings, because the choice wasn’t between “right now” or “never,” it was “right now” or “later.”

Ken applied a similar strategy to his habit of eating fast food. “I started small when I quit bad habits like eating McDonalds all the time and drinking soda. I told myself I’d take a week off, then said two weeks. That continued. This month, I made it four years without McDonalds and 15 months without soda.”

Another person used the Pointing-and-Calling strategy I discussed in Chapter 4. They wrote, “I quit smoking by saying a mantra out loud every time I wanted a cigarette (“your brain tricks you”) which I think changed my thinking from the subconscious part of my brain to the logical part.”

Qiana used a little math and a clever visual trick. “I stopped drinking soda,” she wrote. “I added up all the sodas I drank for the week and counted how many tablespoons of sugar were in those soda cans and bottles. I began to scoop the amount of sugar into an enormous bowl The visual did it for me. I had to break that habit.”

Habit Tracking

Finally, I’d like to close with one of my favorite strategies: habit tracking.

Here’s how a few readers are using it…

Cindy sent me an email saying, “I purchased a large wall calendar and started building the chains. This really works for me. I like to build that chain. There are 6 months of red X’s on my calendar. I am healthier, have lost 30 pounds, feel stronger, exercise more, garden, read more, work on my small business, and practice my French.”

The easiest way to start tracking your habits is to use the templates provided in the Habit Journal. It will make the whole process a breeze.

My favorite approach is to pick a very tiny version of your habit and track that. For example, I have been tracking the habit of “reading 1 page” for the last month. One reader named Günter did something similar. “I’ve done a simple workout every day for over half a year now. I managed to stick to it by changing the scope: when I don’t have time for a full set or don’t feel like it, instead of skipping altogether, I do an abbreviated session. I also mark it in my calendar.”

Hopefully, these short stories give you some ideas on how to build better habits in your own life. If you’d like to learn more about the strategies discussed above, check out Atomic Habits. And if you’re interested in a notebook that makes it easier to build better habits, try the Habit Journal.

But no matter what, keep taking action in small ways each day. It is so gratifying for me to see people making real changes in their life because of these ideas. As always, thanks for reading.

issues.title: BermudAir adds 18 routes, 10 new cities in massive expansion
issues.summary: BermudAir announced 18 new routes and 10 new cities for its summer 2027 schedule, growing the airline in the North America-Caribbean leisure market.
issues.author: David Slotnick
issues.content_html:
BermudAir is making moves to be a major player in the booming market between the U.S. and the Caribbean.

The airline announced a plethora of new routes this past week, marking a major expansion across North American markets, including direct flights to Caribbean destinations.

BermudAir will add service from Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport (MSY), Nashville International Airport (BNA), Tweed New Haven Airport (HVN) in Connecticut, Burlington International Airport (BTV) in Vermont, Portland International Jetport (PWM) in Maine, San Antonio International Airport (SAT) and Fredericton International Airport (YFC) in New Brunswick, Canada.

Those seven join BermudAir's existing North American airports: Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR), Westchester County Airport (HPN) in New York, Boston Logan International Airport (BOS), Baltimore/Washington International Thurgood Marshall Airport (BWI), Raleigh-Durham International Airport (RDU), Orlando Sanford International Airport (SFB), St. Pete–Clearwater International Airport (PIE), Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport (FLL), Toronto Pearson International Airport (YYZ), Montréal-Pierre Elliott Trudeau International Airport (YUL) and Halifax Stanfield International Airport (YHZ).

The airline, meanwhile, is adding to its list of direct and nonstop destinations beyond L.F. Wade International Airport (BDA) in Bermuda, with flights to: Ian Fleming International Airport (OCJ) in Ocho Rios, Jamaica; El Salvador International Airport (SAL) in San Salvador, El Salvador; and Ramón Villeda Morales International Airport (SAP) in San Pedro Sula, Honduras.

The new airports join BermudAir's roster of previously announced destinations: Clayton J. Lloyd International Airport (AXA) in Anguilla; Philip S.W. Goldson International Airport (BZE) in Belize; Owen Roberts International Airport (GCM) in Grand Cayman; La Aurora International Airport (GUA) in Guatemala; and Providenciales International Airport (PLS) in Turks and Caicos. The airline also offers flights to and from its Bermuda hub.

"2027 represents an exciting new chapter for BermudAir," Adam Scott, BermudAir's founder and CEO, said in a statement. "We're bringing our distinctive brand of premium leisure travel to more cities and opening up more opportunities for travelers to experience Bermuda, the Caribbean and Central America."

While it is typically difficult for an airline to fly between two countries that are not the airline's home nation, BermudAir notes that it plans to operate the routes as fifth freedom flights originating in Bermuda, Turks and Caicos, Grand Cayman or Anguilla — all British Overseas Territories, which appears to satisfy regulatory statutes.

BermudAir launched in 2023 as a boutique carrier that planned to run flights between Bermuda and North America using small and efficient Embraer jets. It launched its first flights between North America and other destinations as part of its winter 2026-27 schedule.

The airline's expansion has been rapid, and if successful, the new routes would make BermudAir a regional force in the Caribbean leisure market.

issues.title: Black Friday special: Earn a Southwest Companion Pass by flying just 1 round trip
issues.summary: Southwest's Black Friday Companion Pass promotion lets you earn this valuable perk for a fraction of the usual cost.
issues.author: Summer Hull and Rachel Craft
issues.content_html:
Southwest Airlines' Companion Pass, which allows you to bring a friend nearly for free (you just have to pay the taxes and fees) on unlimited flights, is one of the most valuable assets in the world of points and miles.

It normally takes a whole lot of flying to unlock this pass — and one of the popular shortcuts that allows you to earn this pass with points from Southwest credit card bonuses is ending soon, which will only make it even harder to earn.

But if you'd rather spend your Black Friday weekend booking flights than buying discounted sweatpants, there is some good news. There's a new limited-time opportunity to earn a promotional Southwest Companion Pass if you book one round-trip or two one-way eligible Southwest flights by Sunday, Nov. 29, 2026, and travel on those flights by Jan. 5, 2027.

Your promotional Companion Pass would then be valid for unlimited use between Jan. 8, 2027, and March 3, 2027.

First, register for the promotion with your Southwest Rapid Rewards number. Then, book one qualifying round-trip flight or two one-way flights using your Rapid Rewards number by 11:59 p.m. CST on Sunday, Nov. 29. Flights must be completed sometime from Nov. 27 to Jan. 5, 2027.

Successfully complete the above steps, and you'll earn a promotional Companion Pass valid for use between Jan. 8 and March 3, 2027.

All fare classes, including the carrier's Basic option, are eligible for this promotion. And it doesn't matter how you pay for your flight, as there's no specific spending requirement. Rapid Rewards point redemptions and Cash + Points bookings qualify too, as long as you book through Southwest channels, such as the carrier's website or mobile app.

If you have existing flights on Southwest, they won't automatically count for this promotion. However, if you can cancel those reservations, register and rebook before the promotion ends on Sunday, that should work (provided you complete your travel within the qualifying travel window). Be sure to check for any fare differences before canceling.

Southwest's Companion Pass is almost legendary in the world of points and miles. It lets you bring a companion along on unlimited flights, whether you book with cash or points, for almost free. As long as there's an open seat on the plane, your companion can fly with you for just the cost of taxes and fees (which start at $5.60).

You must designate a companion in your Rapid Rewards account. However, you're allowed to change your designated companion up to three times per year, and this rule applies to promotional passes as well.

If you'd like to earn a Companion Pass for longer than just eight weeks or so this promotional pass is valid, there is still time to earn a Companion Pass for all of 2027 using the welcome bonuses from the Southwest credit cards as outlined here. You have to act quickly, though, since those rules are changing soon.

Related: Best Southwest Airlines credit cards

Bottom line

The Southwest Companion Pass can be extremely valuable for those who like to travel with a companion. Earning one is about to become a lot harder, so this is a great promotion for those who can register, book eligible travel by Sunday and travel between now and Jan. 5, 2027.

issues.title: These are some of my favorite travel experiences this year
issues.summary: From Grand Cayman to South Africa, Brian Kelly shares his most memorable trips from the past year.
issues.author: Brian Kelly
issues.content_html:
People often ask me about my favorite hotels or my most memorable travel experiences. But because I travel so frequently (and have been doing so for decades), it's difficult to pick those all-time favorites. I'll settle for recapping some of my top travel experiences and hotel stays this year.

More so than ever, I'm focusing on experiencing nature — for me, this is really the way to see the world and create lasting memories. Yes, I can fly in all the first-class cabins, but seeing the world's natural wonders and wildlife has been far more life-changing for me.

This year, I also focused on family travel with my kids and parents. My children will be school-age before I know it, so I want to take advantage of not being tied to school holidays to travel and enjoy shoulder-season and offseason escapes when fewer people are traveling.

These were my top hotel stays and travel experiences of 2026.

Swimming with orcas in Norway

I'm actually writing this as I return from an epic Norwegian adventure. I was just in Norway with my two sons and my parents, exploring the country in the blustery weather. I started off with a few days in Tromsø, taking my kids to the aquarium (they loved the seals!) and the library. Then, with my family by my side, I saw the northern lights. I've seen them before, but admiring them with my children was extra special.

Then we headed out on boat excursions to realize my dream of swimming with orcas, opting to book with Tromsø Pure because they focus on safety and on finding quieter spots away from other boats for a better experience.

At first, we spotted pods of humpbacks, and I was able to swim with them, which was one of the most out-of-body, exhilarating experiences I've ever had. There was even a brief moment when I thought I was about to be kicked and/or swallowed by a whale, which was terrifyingly thrilling (don't worry — I'm still here).

Even though a few of the days had rough seas and low visibility, I was able to swim with orcas later on during the trip, and I'll never forget it.

A safari in Tswalu Kalahari Reserve, South Africa

After taking nearly a dozen safaris over the years, I was ready for something different. I've done the bigger camps and seen the Big 5, so I wanted to try a more niche wildlife experience.

I stayed at Tswalu's Loapi Lodge in a two-bedroom villa, complete with a plunge pool and my own private chef. I much prefer a lodge to a tented camp, as hearing lions outside your tent at night and having no running water can be a lot to handle, and I'm done roughing it.

Unlike many safari destinations, Tswalu is unique because there aren't any elephants, but you can see meerkat colonies and observe them relatively up close. I also spotted many black and white rhinos and cheetahs.

I highly recommend Tswalu to experienced safari-goers, but if it's your first time, I'd suggest going to Cheetah Plains in Sabi Sands or Royal Malewane in Kruger National Park. You'll get to see the Big 5 and have the perfect introduction to a safari (and you might get addicted to safaris, like I am!).

Palm Heights in Grand Cayman

Many people skip the Caribbean in summer, but honestly, European summer heat can feel even more brutal, with beaches packed umbrella-to-umbrella in places like Spain, Italy and Portugal. This year, I canceled my summer trip to Portugal after a massive heat wave alert and went to Grand Cayman with my kids instead.

Yes, it was warm, but it didn't feel any hotter than Europe would have (or even a humid Midwest or East Coast summer), and the beach was uncrowded and uncomplicated — no stairs or rugged terrain, like I've had to traverse in Portugal. Plus, no jet lag!

My stay at Palm Heights was peaceful, and even though it's a boutique hotel, it felt very family-friendly. I loved that my suite overlooked the white sands of Seven Mile Beach, and the spa was absolutely gorgeous. I highly recommend it for families, couples, or any type of traveler.

Ritz Paris

In my opinion, the Ritz Paris represents true luxury. I used Chase Points Boost to book it, getting more than 2 cents per point.

The hotel is unapologetically over-the-top, with gorgeous rooms and lavish decor, but what I really love are the service and amenities. The hotel has a program that lets you check in early in the morning after landing from a transatlantic flight, and consumer-friendly options like this are what make it feel truly luxurious. After all, true luxury goes beyond a beautiful room or view — hotels should solve problems, reduce friction, and make traveling easier.

Did you have any special hotel stays or travel experiences this year? Feel free to drop me a comment below and share yours, and be sure to check out our full list for Where to Go in 2027.

issues.title: The best business credit cards for the bills behind Small Business Saturday
issues.summary: Restocking, shipping and ad costs add up fast. These business credit cards can help you earn more on the expenses behind Small Business Saturday.
issues.author: Becky Pokora
issues.content_html:
Small Business Saturday can bring the kind of rush every owner wants. Orders roll in, and sales climb.

issues.content_html:
Built in 1840, this one-room School House served as the educational center for all of the first to eighth grade children in the Hockanum area, later serving only up to sixth grade. This was one of several school houses serving small neighborhood communities around Hadley.

A 1647 Massachusetts law required all towns with 50 or more families to hire a teacher to instruct their children in reading and writing. Parents and students contributed to their school in the form of money, goods, supplies, and chores.

These were one-room schoolhouses, on land that was usually donated. Most schools had one book, the "New England Primer," that was used to teach the alphabet, syllables, and prayer.

The last class to go through this school was in 1933. By then, it was more economical to bus students to the center of town than to keep the neighborhood school houses open.

Along with the outhouse next to it, the Hockanum School House was, and still is, taken care of by the Hockanum community.

issues.content_html:
Spiegeltents were made to travel. These round wooden dance halls, lined with mirrors and stained glass, went from fair to fair. They went up fast and came down fast. The one on Randolph Street is not going anywhere. It was built indoors, on the 14th floor of a Loop building.

The building opened in 1926. Rapp & Rapp designed it, with the Oriental Theatre movie palace on the lower floors. The theater is now the James M. Nederlander Theatre. The whole building stands on the site of the Iroquois Theatre, where a fire in 1903 became one of the deadliest in American history.

High above the theater, the architects put a large hall for Masonic meetings. It sat empty for decades. Later it was turned into offices, and a dropped ceiling hid the room completely. When the building was converted into the Cambria Hotel, workers took that ceiling down and found the old hall again, steel bow trusses and all.

In 2019 the tent came over from Belgium in pieces, about 4,000 of them. Belgian tent builders put it together inside the hall, the traditional way, with no nails. It is about 72 feet across. From the hall, it looks like a small circus parked under factory trusses. Inside, there is carved wood, stained glass, velvet and mirrors everywhere. The mirrors are not just for looks. They let guests see around the posts that hold up the roof.

Since October 2026, the tent has been the home of Kermess by Circensia, which kept it right at the center of the room.

issues.summary: On the northwestern tip of France's Noirmoutier Island, behind the 19th-century Church of the Sacred Heart, a small cemetery overlooks the Atlantic Ocean. Beyond its stone walls stretch the waters of the Bay of Biscay, with the tiny island of Le Pilier visible on the horizon. Many of those buried here were sailors and fishermen whose lives were intimately connected to the sea. Among the traditiona
issues.content_html:
On the northwestern tip of France's Noirmoutier Island, behind the 19th-century Church of the Sacred Heart, a small cemetery overlooks the Atlantic Ocean. Beyond its stone walls stretch the waters of the Bay of Biscay, with the tiny island of Le Pilier visible on the horizon. Many of those buried here were sailors and fishermen whose lives were intimately connected to the sea.

Among the traditional graves stands a striking row of white Commonwealth headstones, commemorating the victims of a largely forgotten maritime tragedy.

On June 17, 1940, as British troops and civilians were being evacuated from France, German aircraft bombed the British troopship HMT Lancastria off the coast of Saint-Nazaire. The ship sank within minutes, taking thousands of lives in one of the deadliest maritime disasters of World War II.

In the following days, the Atlantic currents carried the bodies of victims onto the French coastline, including the shores of Noirmoutier.

Today, the cemetery contains 40 Commonwealth war burials, 22 of them unidentified. Most were victims of the Lancastria disaster.

Overlooking the very ocean that claimed so many lives, L'Herbaudière's marine cemetery remains a peaceful yet poignant reminder of the island's maritime heritage and the tragedies of war.

issues.title: Beguinage of Anderlecht in Anderlecht, Belgium
issues.summary: Tucked away in the historic centre of Anderlecht, just a stone's throw from the Collegiate Church of Saints Peter and Guido, lies one of Brussels' lesser-known historical treasures: the Beguinage of Anderlecht. Founded in 1252, it is considered the smallest beguinage in Belgium and once provided a home to a community of just eight women. Unlike traditional convents, beguinages offered women an opp
issues.content_html:
Tucked away in the historic centre of Anderlecht, just a stone's throw from the Collegiate Church of Saints Peter and Guido, lies one of Brussels' lesser-known historical treasures: the Beguinage of Anderlecht. Founded in 1252, it is considered the smallest beguinage in Belgium and once provided a home to a community of just eight women.

Unlike traditional convents, beguinages offered women an opportunity to live in a religious community without taking permanent monastic vows. The beguines were typically unmarried women or widows who chose a life of prayer, work and mutual support. They followed rules of chastity and obedience but remained free to leave the community whenever they wished. This offered women a degree of independence that was relatively unusual in medieval society.

The Anderlecht beguinage consists of two modest buildings surrounding an enclosed courtyard garden with an old well. The buildings date from different periods, with sections originating in the 16th and 18th centuries. From the garden, visitors can enjoy a view of the neighbouring Gothic collegiate church.

Interestingly, the beguinage was locally nicknamed the Klaphuis, meaning 'chatterbox' in Dutch, a playful reference to the conversations that supposedly took place among its residents.

Following the French Revolution, the religious community disappeared and the buildings were converted into a hospice for disadvantaged women. They continued serving this purpose until 1928. In 1930, the complex became a local history museum, displaying archaeological finds, religious art and objects illustrating Anderlecht's past.

After decades of use as a museum, the buildings underwent an extensive restoration, completed in 2022. The restoration aimed to recover the original appearance of the complex, allowing visitors to appreciate its historic architecture. Today, the beguinage offers a rare glimpse into the everyday lives of medieval women and the history of one of Brussels' oldest communities.

Despite being surrounded by the busy streets of Anderlecht, stepping through its entrance feels like discovering a little pocket of tranquillity that has survived for almost eight centuries.

issues.title: Share your instant camera photos to celebrate the first Polaroid camera sold in 1948
issues.summary: We're celebrating the launch of the Polaroid Land Camera Model 95 on November 26, 1948, by sharing your instant camera photos!
issues.author: Mathew Anderson
issues.content_html:
We’re celebrating the launch of the Polaroid Land Camera Model 95 on November 26, 1948, by showcasing your instant camera photos.

Attention photographers: Thursday, Nov. 26, marks the anniversary of the first Polaroid camera going on sale!

On Nov. 26, 1948, inventor Edwin Land’s Polaroid Land Camera Model 95 debuted at the Jordan Marsh department store in Boston. It cost $89.75 (in 1948 dollars), and it did something no camera had done for the public before: it produced a finished print in about a minute (as opposed to days or even weeks). The cameras reportedly sold out on the first day.

Land got the idea after his young daughter asked why she couldn’t see a photo he had just taken of her right away. Instant photography has been an epic win for photographers ever since, from the earliest sepia prints to today’s remarkably small instant cameras.

Share your instant cameras and photos

We’re marking the anniversary by rediscovering or shooting new instant cameras and photos, and we’re challenging you to do the same. Dust off that Polaroid, Instax or any other instant photo and camera.

  • Rediscover an old camera and photo and share it with a story about it and the era it was taken in. Or, take a new instant photo.
  • Any subject is welcome: your family, your pet, a favorite spot around town or whatever you have in front of you.
  • Submit your photo in a comment reply below (take a photo of the hard copy if necessary). Tell us something about it (preferably at least 25 words), along with the camera and film you used.
  • Please submit by 12 p.m. PT / 3 p.m. ET / 8 p.m. UTC on Monday, Dec. 7, to be considered for inclusion in our honorary article. New posts after that are welcome for general discussion.
  • Please only submit up to two photos.

That’s it! We’ll pick our favorites and publish a set of them in an exclusive article on the DPReview homepage on Dec. 8. The article will also be mentioned in an upcoming newsletter.

Any instant camera counts, but if you manage to shoot with an original Model 95 between now and then, we can pretty much guarantee your submission will be highlighted in a special section.

Bring on the instant photos!

The Nikon Z5IIC is an entry-level full-frame camera with a 24.5MP BSI CMOS sensor. As its name implies, that sensor, along with many of the camera’s other specs and features, are borrowed from the company’s larger, more expensive Z5II; Nikon has simply crammed it all into a smaller body, leaving off a few extras like the EVF, high-resolution screen and second card slot.

Key specifications

  • 24.5MP BSI full-frame CMOS sensor
  • IBIS up to 7.5EV
  • Full mechanical shutter
  • 3.2″ 1.04M dot fully-articulated display
  • 11fps mech. bursts, 30fps JPEG-only elec.
  • 4K/30 full-width, 60p w/ 1.5x crop

The Z5IIC costs $1400, coming in below even the Z5II’s launch price and representing a $450 discount compared to its current, increased MSRP. It’s available in black or silver, and can be kitted with a variety of lenses, including Nikon’s 24-50mm F4-6.3, 24-105mm F4-7.1 and 26mm F2.8 pancake.

What’s new

There isn’t much new about the Z5IIC, as it’s essentially an existing camera with some features removed, rather than added. This means that the main change is its design, which we’ll mostly cover in the Body and handling section. However, as a high-level overview, the camera has a squared-off body with a grip style similar to that of the Z5II (which ends up making it feel a bit chunky in the hand).

This design, and the EVF it omits, means it occupies a new position in Nikon’s full-frame mirrorless lineup. While the video-focused ZR may appear to fit that description, the Z5IIC’s ergonomics and user experience are much closer to that of a super-sized Z30, but even more focused on stills and hybrid use. This is the first EVF-less mirrorless camera that Nikon has made aimed as much at photographers as videographers.

Beyond the design, Nikon has introduced one minor upgrade to the camera’s autofocus system: in addition to the 9 types of subject the Z5II was trained to recognize, the Z5IIC gains an “aquatic life” mode, mainly designed for taking pictures in aquariums. The camera also gains the highly-customizable grain effect the company introduced on the Zf, which is likely a bigger deal than it seems in the age of social media feeds dominated by simulations of film.

How it compares

With its price and feature set, the Z5IIC doesn’t really have any direct competitors. The Panasonic S9, with its stabilized full-frame sensor and very similar price point may seem like one, but its single top-plate command dial and focus on shooting video, rather than stills, makes it a fundamentally different camera to use once you actually have it in your hand. We’re also comparing the Sony a7C II, since it has a similar form-factor (though a much higher price-point). Finally, we’ve included the Z5II to illustrate what you’re giving up for the C’s smaller size.

For video-first creators, the S9 is, in most ways, the better pick, thanks to its inclusion of open-gate modes, excellent IBIS performance and Panasonic’s unmatched toolbox of features that make shooting video easier (though all of this is slightly let down by its lack of a headphone jack, and somewhat limiting thermal performance). While stills shooters will likely appreciate the openness of the L-mount ecosystem compared to the relatively restricted Z-mount, none of our testers have really enjoyed using the S9 for photography and the lack of a mechanical shutter further cements this. It’s clearly not who the camera is aimed at.

Conversely, while the a7CII has a similarly open lens mount, it goes the opposite direction; it’s a better tool for stills than video, thanks to its quite slow readout speeds. We also appreciate the inclusion of a competent viewfinder, despite the small size and, while we miss having an AF joystick, that’s something the S9 and Z5IIC omit, too. The elephant in the room is price; the a7CII is a cut down version of an enthusiast camera, while the Z5IIC is based on an entry-level model, with the focus on more beginner-friendly scene and color modes that come with that positioning.

Body and handling

On its own, the Z5IIC’s body looks small for a full-frame camera, but once you pick it up and attach a lens it ends up feeling relatively substantial. It’s clearly still lighter than other models, but it’s dense, and our testers found the grip filled out even their relatively large hands.

We found the (very approximately) rangefinder-style design to be quite pleasing, and it’s nice that Nikon is providing a version with a silver top plate, even if there’s only a single own-brand lens matched to the color.

Controls

The Z5IIC comes equipped with plenty of controls. You get two configurable top-plate dials, a mode dial with two custom settings and most of the customizable buttons you’d find on the rest of the Z-series cameras, including two front-plate ones, next to the lens. Nikon has also included a button that lets you directly access its “Picture Controls” color modes (which you can add to by connecting the camera to Wi-Fi and the company’s Imaging Cloud service).

The one thing the camera doesn’t have is a joystick, so navigating through menus and controlling your autofocus point will have to be done using either the touchscreen or the multi-directional controller. While this isn’t our favorite way of controlling autofocus, it’s less of a concern on a camera where you’ll never be using an EVF.

The menus are, again, the standard Nikon fare that you’ll find across the rest of the company’s mirrorless lineup. We also appreciate another detail that Nikon kept the same: the dedicated stills/video switch, separate from the power-on switch.

Display

The Z5IIC’s display is large and fully articulated, but isn’t as high-resolution as the one found on the Z5II, nor is it the super-sized and super-bright model Nikon used for the similarly EVF-less ZR. We found that, in bright sunlight, it was a little too dim to see clearly, though it worked well in most other scenarios.

There will be those that complain that it articulates instead of tilts, and that there’s no EVF (despite Nikon already making essentially the same camera but with a viewfinder). While both are valid preferences to have, there are undeniable benefits to a fully-articulating screen; it’s much easier to preview shots or video of yourself using one, and it can work at odd angles that can be difficult to get with just a tilting one. Plus, if you’re putting the camera in a bag (something made much easier by its flat top and slightly smaller size), you can flip the screen inward towards the camera body to protect it.

Nikon says that its market research shows a strong contingent of users who are happy to use a screen-only camera. While they didn’t say it explicitly, it seems likely it’s mainly comprised of younger photographers who grew up using phones where the screen was the only option.

Ports and connectivity

The Z5IIC has a relatively robust selection of ports: there’s USB-C for charging and data transfer at 5 Gbps speeds, headphone and microphone jacks for audio monitoring and input and a microHDMI socket for video out. The latter isn’t our favorite connector ever, but it’s a reasonable choice on a camera at this size and price. It also has reasonable wireless connectivity, with 2.4/5Ghz Wi-Fi (the latter of which can power faster file transfers to Nikon’s app), and Bluetooth 5.0.

The camera’s single UHS-II card slot is located on the side of the grip, where it’s easy to get at even if you have your camera mounted on a tripod.

Battery

Like the standard Z5II, the Z5IIC uses Nikon’s standard 16Wh EN-EL15c battery, and is rated to get 350 shots out of a charge, extendable to 390 shots if you enable the power saving mode. The CIPA ratings under-represent the number of shots you’re likely to get under shooting conditions outside the lab, but work as a useful point of comparison amongst cameras. In our experience, it’s been good for a solid day of shooting, or a light weekend, but we’d recommend bringing a spare or USB-C power bank for the most intensive shooting sessions.

Image Quality

Our test scene is designed to simulate a variety of textures, colors and detail types you’ll encounter in the real world. It also has two illumination modes to see the effect of different lighting conditions.

In terms of detail captured, the Z5IIC is on par with its other 24MP peers, such as the Panasonic S9, Canon EOS R8 II and, of course, the regular Z5II, which uses the same sensor. The only camera that really stands out is the similarly-sized Sony a7C II, as it has a 33MP sensor (as well as a decidedly premium price, compared to the rest of the cameras in this lineup).

The Z5IIC’s JPEG noise reduction doesn’t do the best job at retaining detail at higher ISOs, but its Raws look as good as anyone else’s, so you can side-step that with your own processing if you wish. In good light its JPEG colors are characteristically pleasing, and you have some room to change the camera’s output using “Color Control” recipes downloaded from the internet. Like many of Nikon’s cameras aimed towards beginners, there’s a dedicated button for changing your JPEG color mode.

The Z5IIC also includes Nikon’s “pixel shift” mode to produce multi-shot high-resolution images, which let you get better tonal quality and noise performance when shooting a static subjects. However, as is the case for most vendors, you’ll have to merge them using desktop software, rather than the camera being able to do it automatically. Still, it gives you an option to get more image quality when shooting specific kinds of subjects.

One area where we’ve seen cameras struggle is shutter shock, where the opening of the mechanical shutter causes a bit of shake, blurring the image sightly, especially at lower shutter speed settings. While it’s possible to get the Z5IIC to exhibit shutter shock, most users won’t run into it, as Nikon has wisely set the camera’s shutter mode to “Auto” by default. This means it’ll use the electronic front curtain shutter at shutter speeds where shock is most likely to happen, and switch to the full mechanical shutter once you’re out of that range. We feel this is a great choice for a camera that will mainly be used by beginners, who may not know to watch out for shutter shock or how to avoid it.

Finally, there’s dynamic range. The sensor used in the Z5IIC has historically provided a lot of latitude, and it continues to do so here, letting you shoot to preserve highlights and pull up shadows in post without being limited by the camera’s read noise.

Autofocus

The Z5IIC adopts the same autofocus system that Nikon uses across its mirrorless lineup, so you have a range of AF modes to choose from, including a single point mode that focuses exactly where you tell it, larger points that can also take the area surrounding them into account, and both fixed and custom-sized zones that let you specify an area to focus on objects within. The camera lets you remove focus point types that you don’t use from the menu so you have a shorter list to scroll through.

There’s also a wide area mode, where the camera decides what to focus on, as well as an even more automatic AF-A mode where the camera tries to determine whether the subject is moving or static and switch between single and continuous focus acquisition (though we’ve found that, in modern cameras, the latter is reliable enough that this mode isn’t particularly useful). There’s also a “3D Tracking” mode, which gives you a small box that will attempt to stick to whatever you place it over, even as it or the camera moves. This is slightly distinct from what you’ll find on Sony or Canon cameras, which offer tracking across their focus point types.

The 3D Tracking, zone and wide-area AF modes, can be used in conjunction with the camera’s machine-learning derived subject recognition system, which can track 10 different kinds of subject (though they’re categorized into six categories, making the list less overwhelming list to scroll through). There’s also an auto subject recognition mode, which will look for any of the kinds of subjects that the camera can recognize in the scene, though there’s no option to narrow that mode down to just the kinds of subjects you expect to be shooting, like you can with some other brands’ systems.

By default, the camera uses Touch Shutter, which means that if you tap on the screen to select a focus point, the camera will take a photo after acquiring focus. This can be turned off via an on-screen button (which is easy to inadvertently reset into Touch Shutter mode, but can thankfully be completely removed), but means that the camera may not work exactly as most users expect the first time they turn it on.

Autofocus performance

The Z5IIC’s autofocus is typically responsive and accurate, and its subject recognition modes reliably pick out and track their intended targets. Importantly, we found that the human subject recognition mode was good at focusing on someone’s iris, rather than their nose, glasses, or eyelashes. While it wasn’t perfect in this regard, people who like taking portraits shouldn’t have to worry about pairing this camera with a relatively fast lens.

Nikon’s 3D Tracking system is also quite good at sticking with an arbitrary subject, even in challenging conditions. We were reliably able to track and recompose with this camera, and it was a rare occasion when we had to use another method. Those few times where tracking wasn’t cutting it, though, were made slightly more annoying by the camera’s lack of an autofocus joystick.

Overall, the Z5IIC doesn’t offer the absolute best autofocus you can get in a modern mirrorless camera – perhaps due in part to its sensor’s slower readout speeds – but its underlying algorithms are still in the top tier. Outside of the fastest-paced sports and action (which are far from this camera’s forte anyway), most shooters should find that they simply don’t need to spend much time worrying about the camera’s autofocus system, and can instead focus on composition, lighting and getting the most out of their subject.

In use

The Z5IIC does very little to change what has become a relatively classic Nikon formula at this point. If you’ve used one of the company’s recent cameras, or read one of our reviews of them, there’ll be little in this section that surprises you.

Overall, it’s pleasant to use, with enough customizable controls that you can largely avoid diving into the relatively complex though, thankfully, color-coded, menu system. There are benefits to this setup, which has a dedicated set of pages for core photo and video settings, then banks of Custom Settings covering different aspects of shooting, but it can take a while to get used to or remember where particular options live. This is exacerbated by the fact that those menus range from settings most users will never need to relatively vital functions; an issue that’s particularly acute in video.

It essentially feels like Nikon has used Custom Settings as a dumping ground for every new thing it comes up with, which could be overwhelming if you’re new to cameras (though no more so than other brands’). The upside is that, if you take the time to learn them, the Z5IIC offers a lot of room to grow, with features like pre-capture (unfortunately still JPEG-only), customizable burst rates and a highly customizable “i” menu that you can use to quickly access your most-used settings while remaining on the shooting screen.

Nikon’s Auto ISO system continues to be more annoying than it needs to be, as you can easily accidentally turn a dial and raise your minimum ISO setting (which should always be the camera’s base ISO) without necessarily realizing. Tuning whether the camera biases towards faster or slower shutter speeds when using auto ISO is also a bit of a chore, as it requires going several layers into the menu, and there’s no way to assign the setting to a button.

One thing worth delving into is the Z5IIC’s somewhat complicated connectivity. Nikon makes the SnapBridge app, which we’ve found to be generally competent at downloading images from your camera or remotely controlling it. While we’ve experienced issues connecting to Nikon cameras’ Wi-Fi in the past, we only ran into that issue a few times while testing this one.

Entirely separate from the app is Nikon’s Imaging Cloud service, which lets you directly connect the camera to a Wi-Fi network to upload your images to various cloud services, download firmware updates and new color mode profiles, which you select for syncing using Nikon’s web interface. While the latter is a bit of a clunkier experience than, say, using an app to select the profiles you want and sending them directly to the camera, there are helpfully little notification dots in the menu to let you know when your new profiles are available. The Z5IIC can’t be connected to both Imaging Cloud and your phone at the same time; you have to manually switch between the two modes.

The ability to easily sync color modes – both ones curated by Nikon and user-made ones – to the camera, made us a bit more likely to use the button dedicated to switching between them, even if it’s not in the easiest place to reach on the camera. Your downloaded profiles are also available via the relatively robust in-camera Raw reprocessing. Though, disappointingly, the in-camera film grain effect isn’t. It seems Nikon hasn’t updated the converter to account for the new feature, as the Raw processor can clearly handle it; if you reprocess an image that was taken using it, the effect is still applied to the resulting JPEG. This also means there’s no way to remove it in-camera.

Lens selection for the Z5IIC is pretty good. While Nikon only has a few lenses that are a good match for the camera’s size, many of its primes are priced sensibly for budget shooters, while remaining relatively nice to use. Both its F1.8 “S” series lenses and its two F1.4 primes deserve a special call-out here. There are also a variety of third party lenses available for Z mount, both officially licensed, such as Tamron’s lineup of reasonably affordable and compact zoom lenses, and ones Nikon hasn’t approved, including an array of primes available from Viltrox and others. However, companies going down the licensed route are subject to Nikon’s approval, which it has not extended to, most notably, any of Sigma’s full-frame options.

In Use – the auto experience

If the Z5IIC is your first camera, you may find yourself starting off in Auto mode, which largely hands the decisions of what to focus on and how to expose the image to the camera. While it does little to hide the underlying complexity of the camera or to teach you how photography works, we found that it generally produces satisfying images. Critically, it also still gives you a fair level of control; you can shoot Raw, use exposure compensation and manually specify what to focus on and what kind of subjects you want the camera’s AF system to recognize.

It also does a good job of separating settings from the manual modes. If you set the aperture priority mode up to use ISO 100 and manual focus, and then switch into Auto mode, it doesn’t carry over those settings (something we’ve seen other cameras do, leading to them having to make odd decisions that the user probably wouldn’t want). When you go back to one of the more manual modes, your settings are returned to where you left them.

There are a few quirks. In Auto mode, several settings are reset when you restart the camera, so any changes you make to ISO, color mode or autofocus selection aren’t retained. In some ways, this makes sense: if you accidentally set your camera to shoot in black and white and don’t know how to change it back, you have an easy escape route. However, it’s a bit annoying if you want to use the in a semi-automatic manner, and continue doing so, next time you turn the camera on. (Though at that point, it might be better to switch over to the Program mode). It’s also not entirely consistent: some settings, like film grain simulation, or which subject you want the camera’s autofocus system to recognize, will stay where you set them.

The Z5IIC is the first Nikon full-frame mirrorless to include “Scene” modes, which change various settings to match the specific subject you’ve told it you’re shooting. For example, if you set it to the “Sports” scene, it’ll use a large autofocus area and a high burst rate, whereas the “Sunset” scene switches off auto white balance so the camera doesn’t try to correct the very thing you’re trying to capture. We don’t find the interface for this to be particularly lovely – you have to scroll through the various scenes using the back dial until you get to the one you want – and we think beginner photographers are better served by learning the fundamentals of photography rather than using these modes. If you appreciate the additional hand-holding, though, this camera at least offers it as an option.

Video

We shot our first look video almost entirely with the Z5IIC.

Apologies if you’re tired of hearing this, but the Z5IIC’s video capabilities are again the same as you’d find on the Z5II. The top-level summary means that it ends up being very competent at videography, with 10-bit recording that uses the full width of the sensor up to 4K/30p, and a 1.5x crop to achieve 4K/60p that can be used for getting an unpleasantly soap-opera-like look or for slowing as slow-motion footage.

While those specs aren’t groundbreaking, Nikon has built a pretty extensive set of workflow tools around the camera’s core recording modes. It has a waveform monitor for more accurately judging exposure – especially handy if you’re recording in N-Log – HLG recording for HDR playback, a tally light to make it obvious when you’re recording and the ability to use its autofocus subject detection modes in video. It even supports recording in N-Raw, though it’s hard to imagine most of the Z5IIC’s target audience ever having a use for it or the SD card slot really enjoying the experience.

Video performance

The Z5IIC is a relatively capable camera for casually capturing video. It has generally reliable autofocus with the same subject recognition you’ll find in the stills mode, and produces footage with solid levels of detail. You can also use the camera’s different color modes in video if you’re going for a particular look, and there are some particularly nice ones developed in collaboration with Red available via Imaging Cloud.

We don’t find Nikon’s N-Log to be the nicest to grade, as there aren’t as many solid LUTs available for it as there are for other curves. However, you can make it work with a little effort, and you likely won’t need Log’s extra flexibility if your main goal with taking videos is just to record memories.

We also found the Z5IIC’s IBIS system isn’t as good as the best of its peers. While it doesn’t get in the way of intentional camera movements, it was a bit prone to wobbling around the edges with wide-angle lenses during static shots where the operator was trying to hold it still. This effect is more pronounced when shooting with wider-angle lenses, and you can see it in our overview video, which was largely shot with a Z5IIC.

Conclusion

The Z5IIC does almost everything that it aims to do well. As one of the least expensive full-frame cameras at launch, it provides great image quality for the price, with IBIS expanding the range of scenarios in which you can get the most out of its sensor. Its autofocus is among the best out there, and its ergonomics and user experience are good, though we would have liked an autofocus joystick.

In some ways, the corners that Nikon have cut to get this camera to its price are obvious; it used a lower-resolution, but still sufficient, rear display, and didn’t include an EVF. The latter omission is in common with most compacts ever sold: exactly like the ones that have become popular with the exact audience Nikon is trying to court. It’s understandable that Nikon chose to make this trade-off to get the price this low.

Photographers raised on smartphones will also likely appreciate Nikon’s approach to connectivity, slightly overcomplicated as it may be. I suspect many users will appreciate the convenience of their camera automatically uploading their photos to the cloud once they get home: no smartphone required. The easy access to new, community-sourced color modes is also a bonus.

The biggest problem for the Z5IIC, at least initially, is the existence of the Z5II, which, being older, is often available for a similar price. This situation, however, is great for consumers: you can decide exactly how much you value things like an EVF, autofocus joystick and redundant card slot, or the ease with which the lack of a viewfinder hump lets you slide the camera in and out of a bag, and go with whichever camera matches your budget and desires.

The second biggest problem is other formats. If size, cost and portability are priorities, you can get smaller, less expensive cameras in exchange for a fairly modest drop in image quality. And even staying with Z-mount can give a wider choice of well-priced, well-matched APS-C lenses.

Judged on its own merits, though, we think the Z5IIC is a very good camera at its price. Very few full-frame digital cameras in history have been this cheap, this capable and this agreeable to use. It won’t have the features that everyone wants, but for those who don’t feel they’re important, or who are willing to give them up if it can save them some money, the Z5IIC does its job well. We feel its usefulness as a way into cameras, or as a slightly smaller second body, comfortably earns it a Silver award.

Compared to its peers

There are few direct competitors to the competitors to the Z5IIC, which are both full-frame cameras focused on stills, while remaining as small as possible.

The camera it’ll likely be compared to the most is the Panasonic S9, as they’re around the same price point, feature very similar sensors with IBIS and lack viewfinders. We find the Z5IIC much nicer to use for most cases, largely thanks to its controls; it has two top-plate control dials and an autofocus joystick, both of which the S9 lacks. We also found the Nikon’s autofocus to be a fair bit easier to use and more reliable when it comes to tracking. For video shooters, the S9 offers better IBIS and more options, including open gate, but you also give up a headphone jack.

The Sony a7C II has a higher-resolution sensor, autofocus that’s on par or slightly better than the Nikon and even manages to squeeze in a corner viewfinder. In terms of usability there are a few trade-offs, as it doesn’t have an autofocus joystick and Sony’s menus still aren’t our favorites, but the biggest difference is price, with the a7C II retailing for over $1000 more than the Z5IIC.

If you’re mainly considering a Z5IIC for its size and price, it’s worth taking a look at the Fujifilm X-M5, which has a similar shape and the same focus on being great for stills and quite good for video. Its APS-C-sized sensor isn’t stabilized, so its image quality won’t be quite as good as the Z5IIC’s, but it and the lenses you can get for it are substantially lighter, smaller and cheaper. It’s autofocus isn’t quite as reliable, but its built-in color modes are well-judged, and very popular online.
