issues.title: Hoor Al Qasimi Named Curator of 2028 Venice Biennale, Report Details Limited Damage to Bayeux Tapestry Following Transport to the British Museum, and More: Morning Links for November 27, 2026
issues.summary: Here's what we're reading this morning.
issues.author: Hikmat Mohammed
issues.content_html:
To receive Morning Links in your inbox every weekday, sign up for our Breakfast with ARTnews newsletter.

Good Morning!

  • Sheikha Hoor Al Qasimi has been named curator of the 2028 edition of the Venice Biennale.
  • In a report, France’s ministry of culture details where the Bayeux Tapestry sustained damage during the course of its transfer from Normandy to the British Museum.
  • A painting recently attributed to Titian, thought to be a self-portrait and purchased for nearly $70,000 in 2024, is on sale in a London gallery for $1.97 million.

The Headlines

THE PRINCESS AND THE VENICE BIENNALE. Sheikha Hoor Al Qasimi has been named curator of the 2028 edition of the Venice Biennale, the world’s largest recurring art exhibition, which runs from April 8 to November 26, 2028, ARTnews reports. Al Qasimi is also president and director of the Sharjah Art Foundation, a member of the United Arab Emirates’s Sharjawi royal family and president of the Sharjah Museums Authority. She will be the first Arab curator of the Venice Biennale, and was selected upon the recommendation of its president, Pietrangelo Buttafuoco. In a statement, Al Qasimi said: “For me, La Biennale continues to be a critical space to engage with the work of influential artists and curators. I am honored to have been invited to curate this exhibition and grateful to President Pietrangelo Buttafuoco and the board for their confidence and trust.”

DAMAGE REPORT. A report made public yesterday by France’s ministry of culture details where the Bayeux Tapestry sustained damage during the course of its transfer from Normandy to the British Museum, Le Figaro reports. While the overall state of the 950-year-old tapestry was deemed “satisfactory” by the eight conservationists and experts working in France and England, they found there were “two zones of fiber breakage,” new folds and tensions, as well as “very small” damage that appeared in areas that were already weakened before the voyage. The loan of the fragile tapestry was heavily criticized for risking damage to the artifact, but was ultimately made possible in part thanks to carefully controlled ground transport that was designed to eliminate almost all vibrations. The artifact has since become the hottest museum show in London, attracting long lines and selling out tickets within minutes.

The Digest

A painting recently attributed to Titian, thought to be a self-portrait and purchased for nearly $70,000 in 2024, is on sale in a London gallery for £1.5 million ($1.97 million), and it is among several rediscovered paintings in an exhibition titled Titian, Rubens, Van Dyck, open until December 18. [The Art Newspaper]

Two illuminated manuscripts and three crosses from the 15th century were returned from the American collection of Robert McCarthy to Ethiopia, as part of a unique new partnership between the Ethiopian Heritage Authority (EHA), the Toledo Museum of Art (TMA) and McCarthy. [The Voice]

Veruschka, the German supermodel, who became an iconic muse to the fashion, arts and cultural world of the 1960s and 70s, has died at 87. [WWD]

Neil Simmons, a sculptor whose famous marble piece depicting Margaret Thatcher was decapitated by a protester, has died at 73. [The Times of London]

A rare “Breast Bowl,” or “jatte-téton,” that belonged to French Queen Marie Antoinette and was used in her royal “pleasure dairy,” hammered in Paris for $3.23 million with fees, beating its high estimate of $2.19 million. [ARTnews]

The Princess of Wales, spent time at the Hugo Burge Foundation in Berwickshire, which supports the arts in the UK, and she spoke about the healing qualities of art-making with painter Siobhan McLaughlin, who makes her own pigment and works with stone and earth. [Times of London]

The Kicker

KANALIZING. On Saturday, Kanal or Kanal-Centre Pompidou, Brussels’ nearly 10-acre “city-museum,” opens to the public, heralding the Belgian capital’s first major modern and contemporary art museum organized in collaboration with the Centre Pompidou. As ARTnews reported in September, the mega-project of free and ticketed spaces has been met with controversy over the course of its decade in the making, notably because of ongoing uncertainty about its financial survival, its cost, as well as its dependence on the Pompidou in Paris. Unless there is a political turnabout, Kanal’s publicly funded budget allocated by the Brussels-Capital Region is expected to drop from its current €28 million to €10 million by 2029, which is not enough to keep the project running, according to its leaders. This week, at a large press conference attended by ARTnews, Boris Dilliès, the minister-president of the Brussels region, was on the defensive about the initiative, he said he has faith, while admitting to heavy criticism. The story of Kanal’s rocky road to becoming reality has been widely reported in stories pegged to this week’s opening, but few have offered their thoughts on the 10 exhibitions debuting with it, and what it’s like to wander the vast halls of this new cultural phenomenon. ARTnews stayed on to more fully experience the myriad of shows open to previewing guests, which, over the course of two days, included artists and about 5,000 local schoolchildren. Watch this space to hear our take on Europe’s latest, highly ambitious cultural endeavor, including where it already shines, and where there is room – literally, a whole lot of space – for much more still to come.

issues.title: Russia Is Erasing Memories of the Gulag and Reframing Stalin’s History
issues.summary: Since 2022, at least 26 memorials dedicated to Gulag victims have disappeared.
issues.author: Hikmat Mohammed
issues.content_html:
All over Russia, memories of the Soviet Union and its former dictator Joseph Stalin are being manipulated to tell a new story by the government of President Vladimir V. Putin. An investigative report by The New York Times details how the horrors of Gulag camps are being reframed to depict the Soviets as the victors of World War II and the fight against Nazism. Russia is also using the memory of WWII to act as an extension of its fight against Ukraine.

Efforts to rewrite the story of Russia were already in play before the country’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022. Notably, Memorial, an organization dedicated to memorializing the camps, was dissolved and labelled an “extremist organization” by Russia’s Supreme Court, forcing the group to move its operations abroad. Memorial was also awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2022.

The Gulag was established by Vladimir Lenin in the late 1910s and early 1920s, but Stalin was the one who expanded the operation from the 1920s to the early 1950s. Nearly 1.5 million people were imprisoned in the Gulag and died from extreme cold, starvation, disease, and intense labor. Monuments that preserved its painful history are now being erased or censored. Examples include the shuttering of Moscow’s Gulag Museum earlier this year and the disappearance of at least 26 memorials dedicated to Gulag victims since 2022.

Additionally, in the summer, a Gulag memorial plaque was removed from the Arctic village Yur-Shor, and more symbols of the Gulag are starting to vanish. Under the power of the Kremlin, Russia is undergoing its own modern-day “digital gulag,” according to the Independent. To wit, a mandate now requires that all new digital devices be equipped with the messenger app Max, launched last year by the Russian tech company VK, which allows Russia’s Federal Security Service access to materials from the app.

issues.title: German Museum Transforms Permanent Collection Galleries into Gym to Attract Youth
issues.summary: "Gym. Fit with Art" unfolds in galleries at Düsseldorf's Kunstpalast museum displaying historic and contemporary art.
issues.author: Devorah Lauter
issues.content_html:
We’ve seen dance and musical performances in museums, as well as yoga classes, but a full array of gym equipment and gear? Beginning earlier this month and running through February 21, 2027, the Kunstpalast in Düsseldorf, Germany, has set up weight machines, mats, treadmills, ellipticals, and all manner of gym equipment in its permanent exhibition galleries, so that visitors can work out beside the historic and contemporary artworks, reported the Times of London. Whether or not participants are able to take in the art hanging in front of them while bench pressing, is anyone’s guess, but the idea has its fans, some of whom show up to the museum appropriately dressed in workout clothes.

What artworks do these health-conscious visitors get to enjoy while sweating away? The program titled “Gym. Fit with Art” unfolds across 20 stations beside the museum’s collection of over 800 works, which span pieces by Peter Paul Rubens to Gerhard Richter. It was conceived as a tribute marking the centenary of the GeSoLei, which was the largest trade fair held during the Weimar Republic, which was also dedicated to health.

“We want to target people who might prefer going to the gym rather than a museum on weekends,” and this particularly includes younger audiences, said Alina Fuchte, who has led the project. To wit, “the museum is transforming its collection into an extraordinary fitness circuit,” states the museum website. “Instead of just strolling from painting to painting and admiring the art, visitors will soon be able to get active,” it adds. The endeavor is sponsored by TARGOBANK in cooperation with Technogym, which makes fitness equipment, according to the website.

“Anyone who would rather simply take in the art is equally welcome,” continues the website. This, however, begs the question of whether that simple act may be tough to do while standing beside someone jogging on a treadmill in front of large busts of Johann Wilhelm, Elector Palatine, and his wife, Anna Maria Luisa de’Medici, per just a few examples of the works on view.

One visitor, Kai Heimes, 25, tells the Timesof London, “It’s cool to work out in the collection,” and if it feels “awkward” for some, “I don’t think it’s a big deal,” he added.

However, another, Moritz Rossmanith, 40, admitted to being “a bit confused by it all.” Rossmanith was visiting from Rome, and thought it was “very strange to see kids holding thick barbells while there’s old Italian art on the wall.” Children are reportedly the biggest fans of the gym gear.

As for bringing water bottles to the museum-gym, given that many other museums sternly scold visitors for taking covert sips of water inside art galleries, that rule doesn’t seem to apply here.

“Coming here and realizing this is also a space for me, I can feel comfortable here, I can be free here, I can try new things—that, for me, is the first step,” said Fuchte.

Did we mention there is also a range of scheduled fitness classes at the museum? You can sign up here.

issues.title: ‘The Book of the Human Body’ Surveys 2,000 Years of Remarkable Anatomical Inquiry
issues.summary: We've long wanted to understand our innards. Do stories and artists like this matter to you? Become a Colossal Member today and support independent arts publishing for as little as $7 per month. The article ‘The Book of the Human Body’ Surveys 2,000 Years of Remarkable Anatomical Inquiry appeared first on Colossal .
issues.author: Kate Mothes
issues.content_html:
As long as humans have been around, we’ve been curious about existential questions like, Why are we here? And how do things work? That goes for our own bodies, too. But in our era of modern science and medicine, it’s difficult to imagine a time when physicians weren’t familiar with all of the bones in the skeleton, how a baby grows inside a womb, or how the cardiovascular system works. Even the profession that comes to mind when we think of a doctor didn’t really emerge until the past few centuries. During the medieval period, barber-surgeons were the primary medical practitioners (yes, the people who cut hair also conducted surgeries).

As medicine morphed into a scientific and intellectual pursuit, academies cropped up starting in the late 1700s, such as the College of Philadelphia—the first medical school in the U.S.—and the Edinburgh School of Surgery in Scotland. Ethics were, let’s say, malleable. In Edinburgh, a legal shortage of fresh cadavers used for study in the early 1800s spawned a shady underground trade in bodies, many of which were dug up from new burials in the dead of night. And then there were the famous serial murders committed by William Burke and William Hare, who cashed in by selling well over a dozen of their victims’ corpses to anatomist Robert Knox for use during his lectures. Suffice it to say, some scholars really wanted to understand our innards.

Slated for release in January, The Book of the Human Body delves into the art and science of anatomy, disease, reproduction, and more. Published by TASCHEN, the two-volume set compiles more than 950 images from over 75 rare books and manuscripts from around the world. From ancient analyses to medieval studies to modern diagrams, the anthology surveys the breadth of eras and cultural influences that have shaped our understanding of our physical selves.

Authored by medical historian Richard Barnett, the book celebrates universality and unquenched curiosity. Despite sleeping, breathing, and walking around in our bodies every day, we are often still mystified by much of what makes them work. Throughout history, that sense of wonder has remained constant. Barnett says, “Whatever they might represent, whatever they might express, these extraordinary images have lost none of their power to shock or captivate, to teach or inspire.”

Illustrations include a silk manuscript dated to 168 B.C.E., discovered in a tomb in southern China, which features 44 figures engaged in exercises of “self-cultivation,” plus excerpts from Andreas Vesalius’s anatomical atlas, Fabrica, published in 1543. “In all of these examples, the illustrations stand out not only as objects of medical understanding, but as conspicuous works of art in their own right,” the publisher says.

Pre-order your copy on Bookshop.

issues.author: Colossal
issues.content_html:
Every month, we share opportunities for artists and designers, including open calls, grants, fellowships, and residencies. Make sure you never miss out by joining our monthly Opportunities Newsletter.

Fall $1,800 Innovate Grants for Art + PhotoFeatured
Innovate Grant awards two $1,800 grants each quarter to one visual artist and one photographer. Nine honorable mentions in each category are also featured on the Innovate Grant platform and join a growing creative community of esteemed artists. Applicants must be 18 years and older, and all media and genres are accepted. All applicants retain the right to the work they submit.
Deadline: 11:59 p.m. PST on December 15, 2026.

Bryson County RetreatFeatured
Practicing artists of any background and at any stage of their career are encouraged to apply for a 2027 residency at Bryson County Retreat. Residency periods can be flexible, but month-long stays are suggested. Bryson County is designed to provide ample living and working space and inspirational settings where an artist may work free from the distractions and responsibilities of day-to-day life. The program includes free lodging near tannic dark water lakes, sprawling live oaks, and drooping Spanish moss at the headwaters of the Santa Fe River in north central Florida.
Deadline: Rolling.

Open Calls

Wildlife Photographer of the Year (International)
Alongside its conservation message, this prestigious global competition is hosted by London’s Natural History Museum to champion the work of photographers, whether professional or amateur, young or older, or using top-of-the-range equipment or smartphones. Photographers are eligible for myriad awards, with a Grand Title prize of £15,000. The entry fee is £35 (free for Young WPY contest).
Deadline: 11:30 p.m. GMT on December 3, 2026.

Responsa Foundation Open Call for Textile Art (International)
The Responsa Foundation champions projects that create meaningful social impact and foster public engagement. The organization is seeking textile artists to submit work for This Memory, a group exhibition taking place from September 22 to October 3, 2027, at Burgh House in Hampstead.
Deadline: December 4, 2026.

Open Call for Public Art Proposals in Moab (Utah, National)
Moab Arts is accepting proposals for 2027 public art projects. Proposals are welcome for sculpture, murals, three crosswalks, and sticker designs but may include other ideas for different media or locations around the city. Preference is given to local and regional artists.
Deadline: 11:59 p.m. MST on December 6, 2026.

Material Works Art Award 2026 (International)
Material Works supports artists through one-time $2,500 awards in exchange for original pieces added to its growing contemporary art collection. The award recognizes artistic excellence and aims to promote career advancement through increasing visibility and exposure. There is a €40 application fee.
Deadline: December 6, 2026, or when the first 300 artworks submitted, whichever comes first.

Call for Mail Art (International)
Hive Center for the Book Arts in Evanston, Illinois, welcomes mail art for the exhibition love|mark, which runs from January 1 to February 27. All submissions must arrive at at the center by December 15 for inclusion in the show.
Deadline: December 15, 2026.

Sony Future Filmmaker Awards (International)
The Sony Future Filmmaker Awards is a major program providing opportunities for creators and filmmakers. The shortlisted filmmakers are flown to Sony Pictures Studios in Culver City, California, to attend an awards ceremony and an industry immersion program. Categories include fiction, nonfiction, animation, immersive, student, and vertical format.
Deadline: 7 a.m. CST on December 15, 2026.

GLEAM 2027 Request for Proposals (International)
Olbrich Botanical Gardens in Madison, Wisconsin, invites proposals for temporary, large-scale, light-based artwork for GLEAM, a public art exhibition. The show will be open to the public from August 28 to October 23, 2027.
Deadline: 11:59 p.m. CST on January 6, 2027.

Visual Arts Prize IDEA – Vila d’Amer (International)
Apply for this inaugural prize open to artists working in all visual arts media. Two winning artworks, with prizes of €3,500 and €1,500, will become part of the permanent International Visual Arts Collection IDEA – Vila d’Amer.
Deadline: January 10, 2027.

360 CHICAGO: CloudWalk Call for Artists (Chicago)
One artist will be selected for this major installation in the CloudWalk gallery atop 875 N. Michigan Ave. The selected artist receives a $10,000 commission, and the winning installation will go on view starting April 2027.
Deadline: January 18, 2027.

World of WearableArt 2027 Competition (International)
Entries are now open for the 2027 WOW Competition in Wellington, New Zealand. Awards consist of NZ$200,000 in prizes, including the Supreme WOW Award of NZ$30,000.
Deadline: February 11, 2027 (international), March 31, 2027 (New Zealand).

Grants

The Filmed in Nevada County Grant (International)
To support filmmakers in the production of work in Nevada County, California, Nevada City Film Festival offers grants between $1,000 and $20,000.
Deadline: December 1, 2026.

Southern Prize and State Fellowships for Visual Arts (U.S. South)
The South Arts Southern Prize and State Fellowships acknowledge the highest quality artistic work being created in the American South. The program is open to individual artists living in Alabama, Florida, Georgia, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, North Carolina, South Carolina, and Tennessee. State Fellowships are $5,000, with one awarded per state. These then compete for two Southern Prize tiers of $25,000 and $10,000.
Deadline: January 15, 2027 (fee waiver request by December 18, 2026).

The Virigina A. Groot Foundation Grants (International)
Each year, the Virginia A. Groot Foundation offers three grants to artists who have exceptional talent and a demonstrated ability in ceramic sculpture or sculpture of diverse mediums. The grants are organized into tiers, with the top award providing $60,000, the second award offering $30,000, and the third awarding $20,000.
Deadline: January 9, 2027.

Foundation for Contemporary ArtsEmergency Grants(U.S.)
Emergency Grants provide urgent funding for visual and performing artists and poets who have sudden, unanticipated opportunities to present their work to the public, but there is insufficient time to seek other sources of funding or unexpected expenses are incurred for projects close to completion. Each month, the organization makes approximately 15 to 20 grants in the range of $500 to $3,000 each.
Deadline: Rolling.

National Lottery Project Grants(U.K.)
Both individuals and organizations can apply to Arts Council National Lottery Project Grants. These awards are designed to focus on specific projects with starting and ending dates including festivals and carnivals, dance, libraries, literature, museums, music, theater, or visual arts programs. There is no maximum threshold for the fund.
Deadline: Rolling.

Black Artists Grant(U.K.)
The Black Artists Grant offered by Creative Debuts is no-strings-attached financial support to help Black artists. Selected applicants receive £500, and applications are reviewed monthly.
Deadline: Rolling.

The Adolf and Esther Gottlieb Emergency Grant (International)
This program provides one-time financial assistance to qualified painters, printmakers, and sculptors whose needs resulted from an unforeseen catastrophic incident and who lack the resources to meet that situation. Awardees typically receive $5,000 and up to $15,000.
Deadline: Rolling.

Pollock-Krasner Foundation Grant (International)
The foundation welcomes applications from painters, sculptors, and artists working on paper, including printmakers. Grants are intended for one year and range up to $50,000. The artist’s circumstances determine the size of the grant, and professional exhibition history will be considered.
Deadline: Rolling.

Residencies, Fellowships, & More

Kent Cultural Alliance Spring 2027 SERVICE Residency (U.S.)
Artists are invited to apply for a six-week residency session in Chestertown, Maryland, devoted to the theme of service. Each selected artist will receive a $7,500 stipend for the six-week session, a travel reimbursement up to $1,000, and studio and gallery expense reimbursement up to $1,500.
Deadline: 5 p.m. EST on December 1, 2026.

Charles Allis Art Museum Artist in Residence (International)
Located in Milwaukee’s Lower East Side neighborhood, the Charles Allis Art Museum residency program gives one artist the opportunity to engage with the Allis’ collection of more than 800 historic pieces from the early 20th century. The participant receives an $1,800 honorarium and up to a $400 travel stipend.
Deadline: December 4, 2026.

2026 McKnight Fellowships for Fiber Artists (Minnesota)
Each year, the Textile Center awards two unrestricted $25,000 fellowships to post-emerging Minnesota fiber artists who demonstrate exceptional proficiency, sustained practice, and commitment to the field. Fellowship dates are March 1, 2027, to February 28, 2028.
Deadline: December 7, 2026.

Open AIR Residencies (International)
Open AIR is a Missoula-based nonprofit that brings artists and communities together through place-based residencies and public arts programs across Montana. Sessions currently accepting applications include summer 2027, fall 2027, and spring 2028.
Deadline: December 7, 2026.

Cove Park Awarded Residencies for 2027-28 (International)
Located in beautiful Argyll & Bute, Scotland, Cove Park awards funded residencies, in addition to travel, visa, materials, and access allowances when required. (Self-funded Open Residencies and subsidized winter residencies are open on a rolling basis.)
Deadline: December 11, 2026.

An Talla Solais Càirdeas/The Kinship Residency (International)
BIPOC artists working in any medium are invited to apply to this fully funded residency in Ullapool in the Scottish Highlands. The program runs throughout January, February, and March 2027. The residency covers all work space, housing, mentoring, and exhibition costs in addition to a £750 weekly stipend.
Deadline: December 14, 2026.

Joshua Tree Highlands Artist Residency 2027-28 (International)
Joshua Tree Highlands Artist Residency offers time and space amidst the natural beauty of Joshua Tree National Park. Seven-week residencies include scholarship funds, housing, and studio space designed to accommodate a broad range of artistic activity and open studio events. There is a $45 application fee.
Deadline: December 15, 2026.

ren AiR (International)
ren is a discovery platform where you share everything that goes into your artistic practice. For its residency, four selected artists will each receive $5,000 to develop and realize a project of their choice, wherever they are based, while sharing their creative journey with the ren community. In addition, eight artists will receive $2,000 prizes.
Deadline: December 31, 2026.

Ox-Bow Summer Fellowship (International)
The Ox-Bow Summer Fellowship offers twelve weeks to slow down and deepen your practice within a creative community. The program will welcome 18 fellows and is open to senior BFA students, MFA students, postgraduates, and artists with comparable professional experience.
Deadline: January 7, 2027.

Fine Arts Work Center Seven-Month Residency (International)
The Fine Arts Work Center in Provincetown grants 10 annual fellowships each to visual artists and writers for a seven-month residency that runs from October 1 to April 30. Visual arts fellows are provided with a private furnished apartment and a separate studio, a $1,300 monthly stipend, plus a $1,000 exit stipend to support relocation at the end of the fellowship. There is a $55 application fee until midday on December 1, then $65 until the opportunity closes.
Deadline: February 6, 2027.

Smithereen Farm Winter Residency (International)
Smithereen Farm offers affordable, shared, winter housing to farmers and agrarian-adjacent people and creatives. In the winter, its studio spaces and rooms in shared houses are generally rented for $350 per month, which includes access to common rooms, space for studio work or desks, utilities, fast Wi-Fi at Reversing Hall, a carpenter shop, sewing machines, video projection space, and access to the farm’s agricultural library.
Deadline: Rolling.

Jackrabbit Studios Residency (International)
Jackrabbit Studios is a creative sanctuary and retreat space in the Southern California High Desert that welcomes creatives, healing arts practitioners, and facilitators at any stage of practice to our five acres of secluded and sublime desert expanse to craft a residency tailored to your season of practice. Fees range from $450 per week to $2,000 per week, and pets are welcome for an additional fee.
Deadline: Rolling.

issues.title: Run with the Semi-Wild Yilki Horses of Anatolia in Nur Tucker’s Captivating Photos
issues.summary: In 'The Untold Story of the Yilki Horse,' the British-Turkish photographer captures a portrait of the region's living heritage. Do stories and artists like this matter to you? Become a Colossal Member today and support independent arts publishing for as little as $7 per month. The article Run with the Semi-Wild Yilki Horses of Anatolia in Nur Tucker’s Captivating Photos appeared first on Colossal
issues.author: Kate Mothes
issues.content_html:
Around the dusty plains and otherworldly volcanic rock formations of the historical region of Cappadocia, a millennia-old tradition continues. Here in Central Anatolia, Turkey, horses have been a part of daily life, civic programs, and military campaigns since prehistory. In The Untold Story of the Yilki Horse, photographer Nur Tucker captures a portrait of the region’s living heritage.

Published by Hemeria, the title delves into the beauty and tenacity of the semi-wild horses while also highlighting the lifestyles of those who herd them through rugged landscapes. Tucker, who is a British-Turkish photographer based in the U.K., has long been drawn to the vigor and elegance of horses, and the yilki breed that populates Anatolia have a particularly resonant history.

“Yilki” comes from the Turkish verb yılmak, which means “to flee” or “to be set loose.” The name “has come to describe the condition of these herds that live between liberation and loss, between domestic heritage and wild abandon,” says a statement.

In a place where horses have been bred for agriculture, transportation, battle, and more for thousands of years, their role forever changed within just the past century due to mechanization and industrialization. With motorized tractors, trucks, and cars to work the fields and provide transportation, horses essentially became redundant. Released to fend for themselves, they survived harsh winters, bred on their own, and grew into sizable herds. In The Untold Story of the Yilki Horse, Tucker composes a love letter to these striking animals, celebrating their resilience through more than 100 images.

The book is now available for purchase directly from Hemeria, and it’s slated for worldwide release next October. See more on Tucker’s Instagram.

The article A Sculptural Playground in Shanghai Is Designed for Human-Powered Play appeared first on Colossal .
issues.author: Grace Ebert
issues.content_html:
In Shanghai’s Jing’an Sculpture Park, a monumental new installation by Brooklyn’s Wade and Leta has a clear goal: to get people up and moving in the same space. Titled “Catching Feelings,” the interactive artwork doubles as an all-ages playground with the artists’ signature sculptures and geometric forms. A central tower holds a quartet of slides, while other spinning and writhing elements are designed for more unstructured interaction.

“Catching Feelings” is one of 36 projects in the ninth edition of the Jing’an International Sculpture Project, an annual project helmed by the UCCA Center for Contemporary Art. In comparison to the artists’ earlier works, the bold, kinetic playground is decidedly analog, with any movement powered by the people interacting with its components rather than embedded motors or motion generated by the wind.

“We’re interested in the life and activity around our work—the behaviors it causes, the elations it brings,” the artists say in a statement. “We watched the same grandfather return with his granddaughter to play hide and seek; an 84-year-old and his partner used the space as the backdrop for their video recordings; new friends were made on our ground spinners; we even glimpsed a man in a business suit having a go on the slide.”

“Catching Feelings” is presented alongside monumental works by Olafur Eliasson, Marshmallow Laser Feast, and many others on view through December 31. Find more from Wade and Leta on their Instagram.

issues.title: Artist Rachel Whiteread to design trophy for the 2027 BRIT Awards.
issues.summary: British artist Rachel Whiteread has been commissioned to design the trophy for the 2027 BRIT Awards, the annual awards for British and international music. The artist’s design will be presented to winners at the annual music awards ceremony, which will take place at Manchester’s Co-op Live arena on February 27, 2027. Whiteread follows a succession of prominent artists and designers who have reimag
issues.author: Arun Kakar
issues.content_html:
British artist Rachel Whiteread has been commissioned to design the trophy for the 2027 BRIT Awards, the annual awards for British and international music. The artist’s design will be presented to winners at the annual music awards ceremony, which will take place at Manchester’s Co-op Live arena on February 27, 2027.

Whiteread follows a succession of prominent artists and designers who have reimagined the trophy, which takes its form from Britannia, the female personification of Britain. Previous designers include Tracey Emin, Peter Blake, Vivienne Westwood, Zaha Hadid, Rachel Jones, and Slawn.

For her design, Whiteread has drawn on her signature artistic approach of making negative space visible. Throughout her career, the artist has used materials such as plaster, resin, and concrete to cast the spaces within and around everyday objects, from furniture to entire buildings.

“I used the moti of the BRIT Award and tried to change it in some way,” Whiteread said in a statement. “I exposed the interior of the statue—as an artist would do with their music.”

In 1993, Whiteread became the first woman to win the Turner Prize, the same year she unveiled House (1993), a life-sized concrete cast of the interior of a Victorian terraced house in East London. In 1997, she became the first woman to represent Britain at the Venice Biennale in a solo presentation.

Among her most significant public commissions is the Judenplatz Holocaust Memorial (2000) in Vienna, a concrete sculpture resembling an inverted library that commemorates the 65,000 Austrian Jews murdered in the Holocaust. She was awarded a damehood in 2019 for her services to art.

“Art and culture are under very real threat, so I was grateful to be able to take a tangible role in highlighting the importance of safeguarding creativity through the design of this year’s trophy and standing together as artists—whether from music or the visual arts,” Whiteread added.

Last year’s trophy was designed by British fashion designer Matthew Williamson, and awards were won by musicians including Olivia Dean, Wolf Alice, and Sam Fender. The 2027 ceremony will be broadcast on ITV1 and ITVX in the U.K.

The 62nd International Art Exhibition will run from April 8 to November 26, 2028, with pr
issues.author: Josie Thaddeus-Johns
issues.content_html:
Hoor Al Qasimi, president and director of the Sharjah Art Foundation, will curate the 2028 Venice Biennale, La Biennale di Venezia announced on Thursday. The board had appointed her on November 20 as director of the Visual Arts Department, after the biennale’s president Pietrangelo Buttafuoco recommended her.

The 62nd International Art Exhibition will run from April 8 to November 26, 2028, with pre-opening days on April 5, 6, and 7. The title and theme of the exhibition are not yet announced.

Al Qasimi will take on the show two years after the 2026 edition, whose curator, Koyo Kouoh, was announced in December 2024. Kouoh died in May 2025, and the exhibition, "In Minor Keys," went ahead as planned under the team she had assembled.

Buttafuoco praised Al Qasimi's “rare ability to listen to places and their people.” He linked her “balance and composure” to mīzān, or inner harmony. “We entrust her with the 62nd International Art Exhibition with great confidence,” he said.

Al Qasimi said she first visited the Biennale's 50th edition in 2003, soon after she began curating the Sharjah Biennial, and called Venice “a critical space” for engaging with artists and curators. “I am honoured to have been invited to curate this exhibition,” she said, and thanked the board and Buttafuoco for their trust.

She has run the Sharjah Biennial since 2003 and founded the Sharjah Art Foundation in 2009. In 2023, she curated the biennial’s 15th edition, a show Okwui Enwezor conceived before his death in 2019. She was artistic director of the 2025 Aichi Triennale in Japan, the first curator from outside the country to lead it, and curated the 2026 Biennale of Sydney. She also curated the United Arab Emirates pavilion at the 2015 Venice Biennale.

ArtReview named her the most influential person in the art world on its 2024 Power 100 list, up from 36th place the year before. In 2025, she ranked third.

issues.title: Is Your Class Worth It?: Connecting Classes to Workforce Skills
issues.summary: It’s no secret that college tuition is rising rapidly causing students to rethink the value of a college degree and consider alternative paths to a career. But they might also question the value of your class and wonder if it is worth their money, time, and effort. How will your class help them meet their […] The post Is Your Class Worth It?: Connecting Classes to Workforce Skills appeared first o
issues.author: Stephanie Reese Masson
issues.content_html:
It’s no secret that college tuition is rising rapidly causing students to rethink the value of a college degree and consider alternative paths to a career. But they might also question the value of your class and wonder if it is worth their money, time, and effort. How will your class help them meet their career goals and improve their job skills? Addressing those questions in course planning and design can yield impressive results including increased focus and motivation, a positive effect on students’ approach to assignments, and changing viewpoints on homework assignments as valuable learning experiences.

These outcomes can be achieved with three simple steps: a first day discussion, homework that asks students to read about classroom skills in action and reflect on how they will use the same skills in their careers, and TILTed (Transparency in Learning and Teaching) assignments that show students the purpose for homework and/or major assignments.

1. The First Day Discussion

Instead of starting class with introductions or discussing the syllabus, start by asking students how they think your class will help them. In my freshman English classes I ask, “Why do you think NSU requires this class? Why do you think it might be important?” Prompt them to brainstorm why the class is part of their degree program. What skills will they learn that will help them in other classes, their lives, and careers? Write the answers on the board or type them and project them onto a screen. Put added emphasis on career skills learned and give examples of how they will be used.

For example, in my English course I might mention using narrative writing skills when preparing an accident report for a police officer or a client progress report for a physical therapist or using argument essay skills to write a proposal for new equipment at work.

2. Homework About Skills In Action

Use interviews or case studies of the skills in action in the workplace for each unit. In my English 1010 course I have students read an interview with a working professional discussing narrative writing, evaluations, and argument essay skills and how they use them on the job. Once students read the interviews, I ask them to write one or two paragraphs discussing how they will use this skill or skills in their daily lives, in classes, and/or in their future careers.

Good interviews are provided in The McGraw Hill Guide, 5 th edition and Business Communication Today, 16 th edition. Interviews are also available online or a guest speaker could be invited to the class.

If you only have time to make one change, this one generated the most positive feedback on student surveys.

3. TILTed (Transparency in Learning and Teaching) Assignments

TILTed assignments are constructed around a Purpose, Task, and Criteria. I reworked each major assignment in my freshman English classes to meet the TILTed framework for Spring 2026, focusing especially on the purpose section. This strongly connects the writing task with the reasons for doing it such as meeting objectives of the class and future workforce duties.

For example, for a narrative writing assignment, the purpose was as follows: “This assignment eases you into the types of academic writing expected in a college setting while also letting you express yourself creatively by writing your own story. It helps you meet the goals and objectives of the class by demonstrating writing as a purpose-driven process of communication and demonstrating writing to diverse audiences, for a specific purpose, in a specific context. It also enhances skills needed for the workplace where narrative is part of many different writing tasks such as writing an incident report for a police officer, writing a patient progress report for a physical therapist, or writing a pupil progress report as a teacher.

More information about TILTed assignments is available at https://www.tilthighered.com/resources or https://www.uwidocs.org/2020/03/31/tilt-your-assignment-prompts/.

Results—What Did Students Think?

Throughout the Spring 2026 semester, through talking to students and grading homework submissions, I knew the new framework was helpful, but I also gathered data for the TILTed versus unTILTed assignments in my online literature course and the overall framework using all three moves in my freshman English courses. Students were given a Microsoft Forms survey to complete with extra credit points given for participation.

When rating the workforce skills homework assignments where they read an interview with a working professional discussing using the learned skills and then reflected on how they would use them in their own lives, 81% of the students said the homework helped them see the essays “as a valuable learning experience rather than just ‘busy’ work.”

Further, 95% of students said the homework assignments helped them to understand the relevance of each essay type for their future careers.

Ranking from 1 to 5, with 5 being the highest level, students ranked reflecting on the practical applications of these essay types as affecting their focus and motivation while writing the essays at a 4.24 level overall. Since focus and motivation are often lacking in English courses, I was happy to see such positive results in this area.

Students were also asked “if the homework assignments about workplace skills helped you improve focus and motivation when writing the essays, explain how and why.”

Among the more positive comments were, “[It] helped me see a point to the writing,” “It allowed me to put in perspective how important it is to learn how to write correctly and how I will use this in my future career,” and “When doing these homeworks they were not just busy work they were a way to help reflect on what we would be doing and how we should go about writing these essays in an appropriate way.”

Students were also asked how the homework assignments about workplace writing impacted their approach to the assignments. Among comments were, “The homework assignments about workplace writing helped me approach the class assignments with a more practical mindset. Instead of seeing each task as just another school requirement, I started thinking about how the skills could translate into real communication I might use in a job—like organizing information clearly, choosing the right tone, and writing with a specific audience in mind. Understanding how writing functions in professional settings made me pay more attention to clarity, purpose, and conciseness in my essays. It also helped me realize that the techniques we practice in class aren’t just academic—they’re tools I’ll actually need in the workplace.”

Another student wrote,” It made me more careful about what I was writing and honestly made me more passionate. Those smaller writing assignments concerning the workplace made me remember that writing isn’t just a temporary thing and it is a valuable skill to know.” Yet another reflected, “These assignments about the workplace impacted my approach to them because I was more interested in talking about something I wanted to do in the future.”

In a separate survey, students in my sophomore required literature course viewed both the TILTed and unTILTed versions of two major assignments. Results showed 75% preferred the TILTed version. Overall, they felt the TILTed version was more specific, gave examples, and answered more questions students might have. Some liked the TILT format of showing the purpose, task, and criteria better; and most students said the TILTed versions were more transparent and clearer overall when specifically asked to comment on that aspect.

On an even more positive note, 75% said the TILTed assignments increased their motivation.

And those are the reasons I’m doubling down on these strategies for future courses.

If you have comments or ideas for other techniques to increase connections to workforce skills, let me know in the comments.

Stephanie Reese Masson is an instructor of English, social media manager, and department internship coordinator at Northwestern State University of Louisiana. Her work has appeared in Prime Number Magazine, Word Catalyst, Peacock Journal, and The Battered Suitcase. She has authored academic articles for the MERLOT Journal of Online Learning and Teaching, The Chronicle of Higher Education, and Louisiana English Journal.

issues.title: Writing Is Not a Checkpoint: Teaching Contextual Judgment in the AI Era
issues.summary: At the public library desk, questions about writing often arrive as requests for technical help. Patrons drafting personal statements need to decide which details about their experience to include; people completing online forms need to interpret questions before answering them. Helping patrons make writing decisions has been as much a part of my library work […] The post Writing Is Not a Checkpoi
issues.author: Witt Salley
issues.content_html:
At the public library desk, questions about writing often arrive as requests for technical help. Patrons drafting personal statements need to decide which details about their experience to include; people completing online forms need to interpret questions before answering them. Helping patrons make writing decisions has been as much a part of my library work as explaining where to click.

I encounter similar questions in online writing courses. Students bring rules such as “never use I,” “always write five paragraphs,” and “never use artificial intelligence.” Some rules are assignment requirements; others are writing conventions students have learned to apply everywhere. Contextual judgment requires understanding what a rule accomplishes and when it applies. Students need opportunities to explain their choices within course requirements and ask for clarification when an expectation is unclear.

Rhetoric and composition scholar Sharon Crowley described required freshman English as a “border checkpoint,” where students had to establish their right to belong in higher education (1991, 160). She argued for ending the universal requirement while retaining the course as an elective (170). I draw on her account of gatekeeping to ask a narrower classroom question: How can instructors teach judgment while assessing compliance with assignment requirements? AI policies establish what is permitted; instruction must help students judge whether a permitted use serves the assignment’s purpose. The following examples illustrate ways to teach contextual judgment through activities and feedback you can adapt to your own courses.

Start with the Rules Students Bring

Nancy Walker, who helped me learn to teach writing, was an English professor and director of freshman English at what was then Southwest Missouri State University. In her 1987 statement, “Thoughts About Teaching,” she described how students could move from rigid right-or-wrong thinking to the belief that every judgment was a matter of personal preference. She called for “contextual deciding,” in which students evaluate ideas in context, commit to a choice, and remain willing to reconsider it (2).

A writing rules inventory offers one way to practice contextual deciding. Early in the course, ask students to list three rules they have learned. Have them choose one and explain where they learned it, what purpose it might serve, and when it might be useful. Follow the inventory with examples that test the rule’s limits.

To test “never use I,” compare two sentences. “I interviewed three residents” identifies who gathered the evidence. If a writer has verified a survey’s respondent count, adding “I believe” to “The survey had 40 respondents” makes the count sound uncertain. In this example, the qualification is unnecessary; the first-person pronoun is not the problem. Ask students to explain the difference, revise the rule, and test it on a sentence from a draft. Discuss how the revised rule accounts for the writer’s purpose.

Make Transfer Explicit

Walker urged teachers to plan activities that make discovery possible (1987, 1–2). Students who have already written a research paper may need help identifying what a new research task asks them to do differently.

The Elon Statement on Writing Transfer emphasizes reflection on how writers adapt prior learning to new tasks (Center for Engaged Learning 2015). For a memo recommending a course of action to a busy supervisor, ask students to write a brief transfer note before they draft the memo. Which practices from an earlier research essay can they reuse? What will they need to change for this reader and purpose?

Ask students to identify one adjustment, such as placing a recommendation before its supporting explanation. After students draft the memo, have them revisit the note and explain how a specific passage addresses the supervisor’s needs. Compare the passage with the explanation and give feedback on any needed revision. Students can consult the note when deciding whether the same strategy fits a later assignment.

Use the Problem as Material

Walker described a student who was stuck writing about his father. She helped him notice that his draft expressed affection as well as criticism (1987, 3–4). When students hesitate over an AI revision, ask them to compare the original and suggested wording and explain how the change affects the claim. The Association for Writing Across the Curriculum recommends reflection on whether and how AI serves a writing task (AWAC Working Group on AI in WAC 2025).

Explain permitted uses of AI before students begin an assignment. A process note does not authorize prohibited assistance. After major assignments in my online writing courses, I ask for an AI Use Note or process note that acknowledges assistance and examines the writer’s decisions:

  • What tools or other assistance did you use, and for which parts of the assignment?
  • Which suggestions did you accept, change, or reject, and why?
  • How did you check the claims and sources you used?
  • What alternatives did you consider for one writing decision, and why did you choose your approach?

Students who worked without AI can describe research and revision decisions. For students who used AI, the note should address how they evaluated AI suggestions and whether their use met the assignment’s rules. Instructors can collect the note with a draft and give feedback students can use during revision.

If students cite a source without reading it, ask them to read it and check whether it supports the claim. Have students correct any unsupported claim or inaccurate citation. Read the note alongside the draft to discuss whether the explanation matches the writing. A plausible explanation alone does not establish authorship or compliance.

Instructors in other disciplines can adapt the note to the decisions their assignments require. In a nursing assignment based on a fictional case, students could explain how they checked a patient education handout against assigned sources. In business, students could explain why they revised a message for a particular audience or kept confidential information out of an AI prompt.

Walker asked teachers to do the work they assign and share their writing with students (1987, 4). If I use AI to help draft an example, I can name the tool, show the suggestion beside my final wording, and explain my decision. Students can use the process-note prompts to question my reasoning.

Make Authority Usable

In my college courses, I invite students to call me Witt or Dr. Salley. Offering my first name is a deliberate invitation to approach me with unfinished ideas or questions they may hesitate to ask. I want students to feel comfortable reconsidering a claim or asking what assistance they should acknowledge while they still have time to revise. My responsibility for teaching and assessment remains the same whichever name they choose.

I offered the same choice in public library programs. Some younger participants told me that calling me Witt felt uncomfortable because of the age difference. I respect a preference for Dr. Salley in either setting. Whatever form of address students use, I need to respond to the substance of their questions. When a student asks whether a source fits an assignment, I explain the relevant criteria and how to apply them to the proposed claim.

A Course in Public Literacy

I think of public literacy as using writing to participate in decisions beyond the classroom. A course can give students practice evaluating a claim intended for public circulation or explaining a recommendation to someone who may act on it. The personal statements and forms patrons bring to the library require similar attention to what a reader needs to know.

Begin with an assignment you already teach. Specify a new reader or purpose, and ask students to revise a passage and explain why the changes suit the new context. Read each explanation alongside the revised passage. Students may understand what readers need yet struggle to revise accordingly; feedback should address both the reasoning and the writing.

Witt Salley is Director of Digital Learning and Instructional Innovation at Carroll Community College, where he also teaches writing online. A former public librarian, he writes about online education and the judgment involved in using information and emerging technologies.

References

AWAC Working Group on AI in WAC. 2025. “AWAC Statement on AI and Writing Across the Curriculum.” Version 2.0. Association for Writing Across the Curriculum. https://wacassociation.org/ai-statement/

Center for Engaged Learning. 2015. Elon Statement on Writing Transfer. Center for Engaged Learning, Elon University. https://doi.org/10.36284/celelon.statement1

Crowley, Sharon. 1991. “A Personal Essay on Freshman English.” PRE/TEXT 12 (3–4): 155–76.

Walker, Nancy. 1987. “Thoughts About Teaching.” Unpublished teaching statement, Department of English, Southwest Missouri State University. 5 pp.

issues.title: End With the Heart: Sustaining Compassionate Connections
issues.summary: As the semester begins to come to a close, something shifts in the room. The energy changes. There is a quiet mixture of fatigue, anticipation, pressure, and, at times, disconnection. Students are holding many things at once. Deadlines, uncertainty, personal responsibilities, and hopes for what comes next. As faculty, we are often holding just as […] The post End With the Heart: Sustaining Compass
issues.author: Dr. Mindith R. Rahmat, PsyD
issues.content_html:
As the semester begins to come to a close, something shifts in the room. The energy changes. There is a quiet mixture of fatigue, anticipation, pressure, and, at times, disconnection. Students are holding many things at once. Deadlines, uncertainty, personal responsibilities, and hopes for what comes next. As faculty, we are often holding just as much.

If we begin our courses with the heart, then we are called to end them the same way.

The final weeks of a course are not simply about finishing content or assigning final grades. They are about how we accompany our students through a meaningful transition. They are about how we hold the learning, the relationships, and the lived experiences that have unfolded over time. Ending with the heart invites us to remain present, to stay relational, and to approach closure with the same compassion that grounded the beginning. This relational approach to teaching echoes hooks’ (1994) vision of education as a practice rooted in connection, presence, and shared humanity.

Returning to Compassion in the Closing Weeks

Compassion, as Gilbert (2009) reminds us, involves an attunement to suffering with a commitment to respond to it. Neff (2003, 2023) expands this understanding by emphasizing self-compassion as the practice of relating to ourselves with kindness, recognizing our shared humanity, and remaining mindfully present with our experiences. Germer (2009) further describes compassion as a moment-to-moment process of turning toward difficulty with care rather than avoidance, allowing us to meet challenges with warmth and understanding.

In the final weeks of a course, this attunement becomes especially important. Students may not always name what they are carrying, but we can often feel it. Increased anxiety. Self-doubt. Exhaustion. A sense of urgency. A feeling of being overwhelmed and overextended.

Ending with the heart means softening into self-kindness, remembering our shared humanity, and staying present with what is, rather than what we wish had been. It is not about removing the challenge but about holding it with care.

Holding the Home Stretch with Intention

The final weeks benefit from clarity and steadiness. When expectations are clearly communicated and thoughtfully organized, students can exhale, even if just a little. A simple roadmap of what remains, paired with reassurance, can reduce uncertainty and support focus.

At the same time, compassion invites us to ask ourselves: What truly matters now? What are the essential learning experiences we want students to carry with them?

When we align our expectations with what is meaningful rather than excessive, we create space for deeper engagement rather than overwhelm. This is not about lowering standards. It is about teaching with intention and discernment.

Staying Connected as Energy Shifts

It is natural for engagement to change as the semester winds down. Students may feel pulled in many directions. Rather than interpreting this as disengagement, we can approach it with curiosity and care.

Inviting students to reflect on their learning can gently reawaken connection. What has stayed with you? What challenged you? Where have you grown?

One simple practice I often use is inviting students into a brief “glow and grow” reflection—naming something they are proud of and something they are continuing to develop. This creates space for both celebration and self-compassion, allowing students to hold their learning with balance and care.

These moments do not need to be complex. Sometimes a brief reflection, a shared conversation, or a pause to acknowledge the collective experience of the semester can bring the room back together.

Naming what is present matters. When we say, “This is a full time for many of us,” we remind students that they are not alone. That sense of shared humanity can be grounding in ways that are often understated but deeply felt.

Tending to Stress with Compassion

The end of the semester can be one of the most stressful periods for students and faculty alike. Bringing small moments of care into our classrooms can make a meaningful difference.

This might look like a brief pause for a breath. A moment to check in. A gentle reminder that it is okay to feel overwhelmed. These practices do not take away from learning. They support it.

Encouraging self-compassion during this time can help students shift how they relate to their own struggles. Rather than moving into cycles of self-criticism, they can begin to meet themselves with kindness and understanding. Research suggests that self-compassion supports emotional resilience and reduces distress (Neff, 2003).

When we model this ourselves, even in small ways, we offer students permission to do the same.

Creating Meaningful Last-Day Experiences

The final class session holds a particular kind of significance. It is a moment of closure, but also of integration.

Rather than filling this time with only final logistics, we can create space for reflection. Inviting students to share what they are taking with them, what mattered, or what they are proud of can be deeply grounding.

There is something powerful about being witnessed at the end of a journey.

Expressions of gratitude can also be meaningful. When we take a moment to acknowledge our students, not only for what they have done but for who they have been in the space, it reinforces their sense of belonging and worth.

Extending Connection Beyond the Final Class

Ending with the heart does not have to stop when the final class session ends.

One practice I have found deeply meaningful is sending a follow-up email to students after the course concludes. In this message, I gently recap our shared journey. I reflect on moments of growth I witnessed, themes that emerged, and the ways students showed up for one another and for themselves.

This is not an evaluation. It is a continuation of the relational space we built together.

Students often carry these reflections with them. Being reminded of their growth, especially in their own words or through moments they may have overlooked, can support their sense of competence, belonging, and self-trust as they move forward.

In many ways, this final outreach becomes a quiet closing circle. A way of saying, “I saw you. Your presence mattered here.”

Holding Imperfection with Care

Not every course unfolds in the way we imagined. There may be moments we wish we could revisit. Times when connection felt harder to access. Endings that feel incomplete.

Ending with the heart includes making space for this.

We can acknowledge what was challenging while also honoring what was meaningful. We can reflect on our own learning alongside our students. This kind of honesty, held with care, models growth, humility, and compassion.

It reminds students that learning is not about perfection. It is about presence, effort, and continued becoming.

Closing the Relational Space

A course is more than a series of assignments. It is a shared relational experience.

As we close, we have the opportunity to affirm each student’s presence in that experience. Sometimes this happens through feedback. Sometimes through a brief note or class announcement. Sometimes through a simple, genuine acknowledgment in real time.

These moments stay with students.

Ending with the heart means recognizing that how we close matters just as much as how we begin. It is an opportunity to leave students with a felt sense of being seen, valued, and capable of continuing forward.

Ending With the Heart

When we approach the final weeks of a course with compassion, we shift the experience from one of completion to one of integration.

We are not simply finishing. We are honoring.

We are honoring the learning, the effort, the challenges, and the relationships that have unfolded. We are holding space for transition with care and intention.

And in doing so, we remind our students, and ourselves, that education at its best is not only about what we know, but about how we show up for one another along the way.

Dr. Mindith R. Rahmat, PsyD, is a core faculty member at Antioch University, where she specializes in compassion-focused pedagogy, trauma-sensitive mindfulness, and mindful self-compassion. With over 25 years of experience teaching yoga, meditation, and holistic wellness practices, she integrates these methodologies into her classroom, fostering equitable, intentional learning environments that promote well-being, resilience, and flourishing.

issues.title: Be the Driver: Keeping Generative AI in the Backseat by Supporting Students’ Use of AI
issues.summary: Navigating the ever-evolving world of generative AI can be daunting for some, exhilarating for others and unsettling for even more. Grounding a course expectation that AI can be a supporting tool, rather than a driver of course work, can set students (and instructors) up for a smooth semester. In an effort to provide an equitable […] The post Be the Driver: Keeping Generative AI in the Backseat by
issues.author: Melissa Parks, PhD
issues.content_html:
Navigating the ever-evolving world of generative AI can be daunting for some, exhilarating for others and unsettling for even more. Grounding a course expectation that AI can be a supporting tool, rather than a driver of course work, can set students (and instructors) up for a smooth semester. In an effort to provide an equitable learning experience for all students, I’ve employed several strategies to help students learn to use AI to enhance, not replace, their learning. Suggestions for course strategies intentionally begin broad so faculty from any disciple can adapt the ideas into their field. For additional context, several examples are offered as they were applied in education courses.

The Driver

Using the image of a driver of a car with a computer as a backseat driver (Image 1: AI Brainstorm) can be useful to frame classroom conversation and situate the instructor’s expectations around AI use in student work.

Image 1: AI Brainstorm

During the second course meeting (intentionally not the first to allow for late-comers to hear the same information), I asked students to collaborate with me and generate a class AI policy. Applying the education principle of buy-in (Academic Outreach and Innovation Learning Innovations, 2019) the intention was to use students’ ideas to shape expectations for the semester.

By acknowledging AI as a useful tool, not something to be used in secret, instructors can invite open conversation about how AI can be used to support student learning in a particular course. Instructors can ask students which AI tool they prefer to use and place students in the driver’s seat to lead the conversation about how AI sites are selected and how they evaluate the quality of the output generated. The image of a car (Image 1) can serve as a brainstorm frame on which students capture their experiences with AI. Depending on the size of the class, this can be done anonymously and submitted to the instructor for review or brainstorms can be shared in small groups in class. The latter was most effective for my students. From the small group conversation, students were asked to create a collaborative list that captured sites used regularly with the pros and cons of each site. Each list was then shared with the whole class. This conversation opened the door for students to also share sites they have heard of but not yet tried. From this exchange of ideas, the instructor can generate a list of most used sites and sites most thought about but not used.

Teaching Students to be Cautious Drivers

Using the students’ ideas as a spring board, the instructor determines which sites are appropriate to the course objectives and explains how using those generative AI sites can enhance students’ learning in the course. For example, in education course, sites like ChatGPT may not be as effective as sites like eduaide.ai. or magicschool.ai. After selecting the most appropriate tool the instructor can model, while sharing the potential benefits and challenges, how to appropriately use AI in the course. In education courses, that included showing how to use precise verbs, direct, specific commands and quantifying expected results to generate the desired output.

Instructors can model think-alouds (Green, 2025), practices where instructors verbalize their thoughts, reasoning and decision in real time to explain the strengths and weaknesses of the output to show students how to evaluate and revise output based on course content and assignment specifications.

During this modeling, instructors can demonstrate how to direct the site to generate content that is relevant and appropriate to the course and the task. In some cases, students are unaware of the drawbacks and strengths of particular AI sites. Instructors can discuss, then lead a class exploration of selected generative AI sites reviewing the quality of output in terms of biases and hallucinations (MIT Sloan Teaching & Learning Technologies, 2026a). This process can also support previous conversation about the required quality of the input. To get better outputs, students must be thorough and precise with their input (Valliani, 2023; MIT Sloan Teaching & Learning Technologies, 2026b). Using a subject specific prompt, the instructor can model high quality inputs and critically review the AI output.

It is important to note, this critical review requires students to have an understanding of course content to support their analysis of the output. A handout with some pertinent questions to guide students review of output may be helpful (Image 2: Evaluative Questions). Students can also be encouraged to add their own ideas to the list.

Image 2: Evaluative Questions

Instructors can offer students the chance to begin to evaluate the effectiveness of several sites by modeling a side-by-side split screen comparison of two (or more) sites. This can also be the time for instructors to model how to adjust the setting on the AI site to make usage more efficient. For example, in ChatGPT, settings can be adjusted to instruct the site to stop complimenting your questions and adjust response style and tone.

Moving students to real-time hands-on practice, instructors can assign practice prompts for students to further guide the experience and support students’ developing understanding about how to use AI and how to balance the AI output with their personal learning toward course objectives.

Guardrails: Discussing AI Data & Privacy Policies

Spending a few moments of class time reviewing terms and conditions of the site(s) selected as the backseat driver in a course is important. Students must be taught to consider ownership of data entered into generative AI sites. Students must also be explicitly taught to not upload any personal information or images of people without their consent. Further, uploading copyrighted information, such as journal articles or pages from a textbook, may infringe on copyright. Hosting a copyright expert guest lecturer from the university faculty may be helpful. Universities may have Library Guides already created for students (see Syracuse University Libraries, 2026). Terms and conditions of generative AI sites are updated regularly and the storing of data entered changes regularly.

Transparency in Practice

Rather than fight the AI surge, faculty can elect to show students how to use AI effectively to support course content. After taking class time to establish course AI policies, instructors may create a course AI statement, based on the ideas generated in class conversations and practice with students. The AI Policy, or AI Contract, can outline which sites can be used for select purposes and to what degree they should be used (Image 3: AI in This Course Contract).

Image 3: AI in This Course Contract

A general AI contract can be posted on the course LMS or on individual assignments. Instructors can also require students share their thinking by submitting an AI Statement with each assignment (Image 4. AI Statement).

Image 4: AI Statement

With students collaborating in what types and to what degree AI can be used to enhance their learning, AI serves as a supporting tool, rather than a secret intended to be concealed. By articulating ways in which AI was successful, or unsuccessful, students can have the ability to work toward mastering course content by critically examining and refining output and having open and transparent conversations about their learning.

Melissa Parks, PhD. is an associate professor of elementary education at Stetson University in Deland, Florida. Dr. Parks is an active member of the National Science Teaching Association (NSTA) and is currently a member of the NSTA Early Childhood-Elementary Science Teaching and Postsecondary Science Teaching Committees. Her research interests include elementary pedagogies & curriculum and environmental stewardship.

References

Green, Jennifer (2025, March 15). How to Plan a Think Aloud. https://researchschool.org.uk/bradford/news/how-to-plan-a-think-aloud

MIT Sloan Teaching & Learning Technologies. (2026a). When AI Gets It Wrong: Addressing AI Hallucinations and Bias.https://mitsloanedtech.mit.edu/ai/basics/addressing-ai-hallucinations-and-bias/

MIT Sloan Teaching & Learning Technologies. (2026b). Effective Prompts for AI: The Essentials.https://mitsloanedtech.mit.edu/ai/basics/effective-prompts
