issues.title: Bringing Whole Books Back to the Classroom
issues.summary: Somewhere along the way, we stopped reading books in a lot of schools. Let's get them back. The post Bringing Whole Books Back to the Classroom first appeared on Cult of Pedagogy .
issues.author: Jennifer Gonzalez
issues.content_html:
Listen to the interview with Jen Serravallo (transcript):

Sponsored by Highfive and SimpleK12

This page contains Bookshop.org links. When you make a purchase through these links, Cult of Pedagogy gets a small percentage of the sale at no extra cost to you. What’s the difference between Amazon and Bookshop.org?

I was fortunate to grow up in a house full of books. From birth, my parents read to me and my siblings, read on their own, and even did the most cringe things to encourage reading, like the day when I was fourteen — fourteen — and they announced in front of my friend Adam, whose primary hobby was making fun of me, that we were going to start doing FAMILY READING NIGHT once a week.

Adam NEVER let me live that one down.

My point is, I didn’t really need school to support my love of reading. But growing up in the 70s and 80s, I did get that support. There were lots of library visits and SSR periods and book reports and so on. I don’t think we were assigned a ton of whole books, but we were definitely reading real writing, written by people who had stories to tell and things to say.

Years later, as a middle school ELA teacher, I got to share that experience with my students. I have especially fond memories of our school book room, where we stored class sets of novels. I can still picture them: Tuck Everlasting; Holes; Freak the Mighty; Roll of Thunder, Hear My Cry; and of course, The Outsiders. About 150 copies of each, stacked on floor-to-ceiling shelves, waiting for us to choose them. It was a delicious feeling, moving them into crates, bringing them into my classroom, then signing out one copy per student, knowing we’d be going on a little journey together.

We would always do the first chapter together in class. I would read most of it myself, out loud, stopping to think aloud, get their reactions, maybe jot a few names down on the board to make sure we were all clear about who was talking and what was going on. I might have them read a little more silently, then touch base again as a group. I knew it took a while to get really sunk into a book, to have it grab you, so I never wanted to leave it to chance that they’d be able to do this on their own, at home. We had to get anchored together.

Those are good memories. Not all of my students did the reading like they were supposed to, and not everyone liked every book. There were days when kids were bored or hadn’t read or pretended to read. But we were sharing something: a piece of art, someone’s vision brought to life, a complete experience carefully crafted and shaped, then laid out on paper, wrapped in a cover, and packaged so you could literally carry it around in your backpack. With every book, we got to have conversations about people and life and why people do the things they do. Apart from the academic value, it felt like we were doing something real, participating in a long, long tradition of people capturing their thoughts and experiences and passing them down through the years.

The first time I encountered the idea of “passages” was around 2010, when I was supervising preservice teachers at the university level. I was helping one of my student teachers create an assessment aligned with our required ELA standards, and she told me she had to use the assessment issued by the school where she was placed. The assessment was all multiple-choice and it was all based on short reading passages. After going back and forth with her for a while, it finally dawned on me that her students weren’t reading actual books. They weren’t even reading complete stories or articles. Just “passages.”

At the time, I thought this was an isolated situation. I didn’t realize it was a sign of where reading instruction was headed.

In the years since, I’ve heard more and more about classrooms where students spend most of their reading time working with short texts and excerpts, while whole books have become an occasional extra, if they’re included at all. And although I understand the value of teaching students specific reading skills and strategies, I have to wonder what gets lost when we spend so little time actually reading books.

That’s what we explore on the podcast with literacy expert Jennifer Serravallo. We looked at how whole books lost their place in many classrooms, why reading them matters, and how teachers can make room for them again, even within a packed curriculum. Her new classroom kits — Whole Book Comprehension, Grades 1–6, are a ready-to-use resource that can be added to any literacy program or core curriculum.

Why Books Are Disappearing from Some Classrooms

Whole-book reading has gradually lost its place in many classrooms, a shift that likely has several contributing factors, including increased emphasis on standardized testing and changes in how reading is taught. More recently, science of reading legislation has prompted another wave of curriculum changes, with many schools adopting new core literacy programs. Serravallo has observed that some core literacy programs leave little room for whole books.

“Many of these core programs rely on short excerpts, short stories, articles,” she says.

Shorter texts certainly have instructional value. As Serravallo explains, “They help kids to connect across texts. You could build text sets to develop concept knowledge. You can get through a lot of different texts together in a short period of time.” The problem is that with so much material packed into some of these programs, teachers often have little time left for anything else; something has to give.

“I’ve been in schools where they used to have a classroom library filled with books that kids could select from,” Serravallo says. “And they’ve put them in the closet. They’ve put them away. Because, ‘Oh, we don’t have time for that anymore.’” She has also seen school libraries converted into technology centers, reducing opportunities for students to browse and select books.

Why Whole-Book Reading is Important, Especially Now

There’s something about getting lost in a good book that you just can’t replicate by reading a collection of shorter texts. Serravallo points to the work of researcher Maryanne Wolf, author of Reader, Come Home, who describes a “deep reading state” that happens when we become fully immersed in a text. “It’s an opportunity to build empathy, take different perspectives on, do deeper inferential and critical work,” Serravallo explains. These are especially important skills in an age when AI makes it so easy to outsource our thinking.

Reading whole books also helps students build executive functioning skills like sustaining attention, keeping track of information over time, and connecting ideas across chapters. These days, with so much of our time spent scrolling through short bursts of content, many of us have gotten out of the habit of sitting down with a book for any length of time. Serravallo admits that even she struggles to get back into reading novels after spending long stretches working on other projects. The good news is that we can rebuild that reading stamina with practice, and teachers can help students do the same.

And there’s some evidence that whole-book reading can lead to significant improvements in comprehension. In a 2019 study, teachers set aside their usual approach to reading instruction and spent 12 weeks reading two challenging novels at a fast pace with their students, providing support along the way. By the end, students made gains equivalent to an average of 8.5 months of progress in reading comprehension, while struggling readers gained an average of 16 months.

So bringing whole books back isn’t just about helping students enjoy reading again. It’s about giving them the time and support to become stronger, more thoughtful, more capable readers.

Looking for books to build your classroom library? Our 2024 interview with three award-winning librarians offers some outstanding titles to consider: Curating a More Inclusive Library

How To Make Space for Whole Books Again

Even teachers who want to bring back whole-book reading may struggle to find time for it in an already packed curriculum. But the goal isn’t to return to the days when novels dominated reading instruction. Instead, Serravallo suggests finding ways to work whole books into what’s already being taught:

  • Take a break between units or modules. Look for places where you can tighten your existing curriculum a little bit, especially lessons that repeat skills students have already mastered. Then use that time for a short, focused whole-class book study. Rather than stretching a novel out over six or eight weeks, Serravallo suggests moving through it at a brisk pace, possibly in just one week.
  • Connect books to content studies. Look for whole books, especially nonfiction, that align with topics students are studying in science or social studies. Reading these books can become part of the content instruction rather than something you have to find additional time for.
  • Use small-group time or book clubs. If students already have time set aside for centers, independent work, or small-group instruction, some of that time could be devoted to reading and discussing whole books. Teachers can provide vocabulary support or teach a reading strategy, then have students read independently or with partners before coming together to discuss.
  • Make use of intervention or enrichment blocks. If your school has these in place, some of that time might be used for whole-book reading.
  • Try whole-book reading in summer school. Summer programs can offer an opportunity to build reading stamina and engagement through book clubs, especially when teachers have more flexibility to organize instruction around complete books.

Ultimately, the goal is to find a consistent place for whole-book reading in the schedule, whether that’s a regular block of time or a recurring break between units. For teachers working within required curricula, making that space may require conversations with administrators about what can be adjusted or scaled back.

Finding the time is worth the effort. Students need opportunities to develop the stamina and confidence that come from working their way through an entire book, especially if they’re not accustomed to doing so. With the right support and enough practice, they can begin to see themselves differently as readers. As Serravallo puts it, we want students to develop the confidence to say, “Yes, I’m a reader. I can do this. And I want to.”

Everything You Need to Bring Books Back

Whole Book Comprehension, Grades 1–6 is Serravallo’s low-prep, high-impact resource that can be added to any literacy program or core curriculum. Each grade-level kit provides everything a teacher needs to thoughtfully implement more whole-book reading in their classroom, including a curated class set of eight books. Learn more about the kits here.

Come back for more.
Join our mailing list and get weekly tips, tools, and inspiration that will make your teaching more effective and fun. You’ll get access to our members-only library of free downloads, including 20 Ways to Cut Your Grading Time in Half, the e-booklet that has helped thousands of teachers save time on grading. Over 50,000 teachers have already joined—come on in.

issues.title: Rethinking Performance Assessment
issues.summary: Knowing the content and mastering the skills is one thing. Putting them to use is another. The post Rethinking Performance Assessment first appeared on Cult of Pedagogy .
issues.author: Jennifer Gonzalez
issues.content_html:
Listen to the interview with Jay McTighe (transcript):

Sponsored by Highfive and Mastering the Lesson Plan

This page contains Bookshop.org links. When you make a purchase through these links, Cult of Pedagogy gets a small percentage of the sale at no extra cost to you. What’s the difference between Amazon and Bookshop.org?

Imagine a basketball coach spending an entire season teaching players how to dribble, pass, and shoot, but never letting them play an actual game. Instead, at the end of the season, the coach gives them a written test about basketball.

Or what about a theater teacher spending a whole semester teaching students how to memorize lines, project their voices, and move around a stage. Then, rather than performing in an actual play, their final assignment is to create a video explaining the techniques of good acting.

Both scenarios sound ridiculous. But in classrooms, we sometimes do the equivalent. We teach students individual skills and chunks of knowledge, then assess how well they’ve learned them without ever asking them to put everything together in a meaningful performance.

When we want to find out what students have learned, a traditional test can tell us quite a bit. But if we want to know whether students can actually apply their knowledge and skills to solve problems, make decisions, or create something meaningful, we need a different kind of assessment.

That’s where performance assessments, or performance tasks, come in. These are projects and other assignments where students demonstrate their learning by doing something with it, like designing a solution to a problem, developing a proposal, or creating something for a real audience. When designed well, they can give us a much richer picture of what students know and can do. And while many teachers already use projects and other performance-based assessments in their classrooms, a few common design mistakes can prevent these tasks from giving us the evidence of learning we’re really looking for.

This is the problem Jay McTighe addresses in his book, co-authored with Kristina Doubet and Eric Carbaugh, Designing Authentic Performance Tasks and Projects: Tools for Meaningful Learning and Assessment. An educator, author, and curriculum and assessment expert best known for his influential work on backward design in the book he co-wrote with Grant Wiggins, Understanding by Design, McTighe offers practical guidance for creating performance tasks that give students meaningful opportunities to apply what they’ve learned.

On the podcast, McTighe walks us through three examples of effective performance tasks, explains what makes them work, and shares practical guidance for designing our own while avoiding common mistakes. You can listen to the full interview above, read the full transcript here, or get the highlights below.

Performance Tasks Are More Than Just Assessments

McTighe prefers the term performance tasks over performance assessments because he doesn’t want teachers to think of them as something they simply add at the end of a unit to get a grade. Instead, he encourages teachers to plan these tasks from the beginning, asking not just what content they need to cover, but what they want students to be able to do with what they’ve learned.

This also means letting students know early on what they’re working toward. Just as athletes know what game they’re preparing for and actors know what play they’ll perform, students should understand how the skills and knowledge they’re learning will eventually come together.

McTighe wants teachers to think of performance tasks as “rich learning activities and experiences that can build and deepen student learning.” Although they can certainly be used for assessment, he emphasizes that they’re “not simply an end of teaching episode or experience.”

Three Examples of Performance Tasks

To illustrate what effective performance tasks can look like, McTighe shares three examples from different subject areas and grade levels.

State Tour (History and Geography)

Students take on the role of a state tourism advisor, designing a four-day tour that highlights their state’s history, geography, and economic assets. They create an itinerary and justify their choices.

This task places students in a realistic (although simulated) situation, requiring them to apply what they’ve learned rather than simply recall facts. McTighe also recommends introducing the task at the beginning of the unit so students can think about their tour as they learn about the state. “In other words, it will enhance their learning.”

Responsible Citizen (Civics)

Students identify a problem or need in their school or community, propose a solution, and make a persuasive case to someone with the authority to act, such as a principal or city council. They might communicate their proposal through a letter, presentation, or other appropriate format.

This task requires students to apply their understanding of civic participation while also using communication and argumentation skills. It also offers meaningful choices: Students can select an issue they care about, identify their audience, and potentially choose how to present their proposal. As McTighe points out, “One of the factors that motivates students is not only relevance, but the opportunity to work toward their strengths and have some choice.”

Making the Grade (Math)

When studying measures of central tendency, students analyze their own grades and determine whether the mean, median, or mode would produce the most favorable quarterly grade. They write a note to their teacher explaining and defending their choice.

McTighe especially loves this example because it makes an abstract mathematical concept immediately relevant to students. The teacher who developed it reported that students became more interested in understanding mean, median, and mode once they saw how the concepts could affect their own grades. And unlike a lengthy project, this task is relatively quick. As McTighe explains, “You can have authentic — but short nonetheless — rich, relevant tasks that engage learners and can provide evidence of understanding.”

What Makes a Good Performance Task?

Looking at these three examples, McTighe identifies several characteristics that make performance tasks especially effective.

Application and Explanation

According to McTighe, these are the two essential ingredients of a strong performance task: Students need to apply what they’ve learned and explain their thinking. In the Making the Grade task, for example, students don’t just calculate the mean, median, and mode of their grades. They have to decide which measure works best for their situation and defend their choice. Together, application and explanation provide much stronger evidence of understanding than simply recalling information.

Authenticity

Whenever possible, performance tasks should place students in realistic situations where they can see a purpose for what they’re learning. The situation doesn’t have to be real: In the State Tour task, students aren’t actually employed by a tourism agency, but they’re doing the kind of work a tourism advisor might do. This kind of authenticity helps students see the relevance of what they’re learning.

Open-Endedness

Good performance tasks allow for multiple possible responses rather than a single correct answer. In the Responsible Citizen task, students might identify very different community problems and propose very different solutions. What matters is how well they use their knowledge and skills to develop and support their proposals.

Higher-Order Thinking

Performance tasks should also require students to think beyond basic recall and comprehension. Look for verbs like apply, design, analyze, evaluate, defend, and critique.

McTighe prefers Webb’s Depth of Knowledge (DOK) framework over Bloom’s Taxonomy for evaluating the thinking required by a task. He recommends aiming for DOK Level 3, which involves multistep thinking, application, and justification. More complex, student-directed projects may reach Level 4.

There are exceptions: For very young students or beginners learning a new language, Level 1 or 2 tasks may be more appropriate initially. As their knowledge and skills develop, teachers can gradually introduce more cognitively demanding tasks.

Designing Your Own Performance Tasks

Once you’ve identified what you want students to understand and be able to do, how do you turn those goals into a meaningful performance task?

McTighe recommends a framework called GRASPS, which he developed with Grant Wiggins. It helps teachers build a realistic context around the learning they want students to demonstrate:

  • Goal: What is the student trying to accomplish?
  • Role: What real or simulated role will the student take on?
  • Audience: Who is the work intended for?
  • Situation: What problem, challenge, or context gives the task its purpose?
  • Product or Performance: What will the student create or do?
  • Success Criteria: How will the quality of the work be evaluated?

In the State Tour example, students take on the role of tourism advisors (Role), creating an itinerary (Product) to help visitors (Audience) learn about their state (Goal). The GRASPS framework helps turn what could have been a straightforward report into a more purposeful task.

But the realistic scenario is only part of the design. The task and its assessment criteria also need to align with the intended learning goals. A rubric should focus on what students are supposed to demonstrate, not just the appearance or polish of the final product.

One practical way to check that alignment is to give a colleague your task and rubric without showing them the learning objectives. Ask them to identify what students are supposed to learn. If they can’t tell, you may need to revise the task, the rubric, or both.

Common Mistakes When Designing Performance Tasks

Even experienced teachers can run into problems when designing performance tasks. McTighe points to three common mistakes to watch out for.

1. Making the Task Too Big

Performance tasks don’t have to be elaborate, weeks-long projects. In fact, McTighe recommends starting with smaller, more manageable tasks, especially when students are new to this kind of learning. As teachers and students gain experience, they can gradually increase the complexity, duration, and level of student independence.

2. Assessing the Wrong Things

Sometimes the rubric for a performance task focuses more on the finished product than on the learning it’s supposed to demonstrate. A beautifully designed presentation, for example, doesn’t necessarily show that a student understands the content.

McTighe recommends focusing assessment criteria on the intended learning goals. For things like spelling, grammar, or presentation quality, he suggests using impact criteria: Rather than simply counting errors, consider how much those errors interfere with the effectiveness of the student’s work.

3. Prioritizing the Playbook Over the Game

McTighe compares teaching to coaching a sports team. A coach wouldn’t spend the entire season covering the playbook without giving players opportunities to practice in scrimmages and ultimately play the game. Yet teachers sometimes focus so heavily on covering standards and content that students get few opportunities to apply what they’ve learned. Rich performance tasks may even be scrapped to make room for more content coverage.

Even when a final performance task is planned, teaching individual skills isn’t enough preparation. Students also need formative assessments that function like scrimmages: smaller, similar tasks where they can practice putting their learning together and receive feedback before performing independently.

As McTighe puts it, “Our job is not to cover the playbook. The playbook is a resource. The game is what we’re preparing for.”

issues.title: When Teachers Push Back: What Are We Missing?
issues.summary: When teachers push back against change, they often get labeled as "resistant." But that label can keep us from seeing what’s really going on. The post When Teachers Push Back: What Are We Missing? first appeared on Cult of Pedagogy .
issues.author: Jennifer Gonzalez
issues.content_html:
Listen to the interview with Elena Aguilar (transcript):

Sponsored by Highfive and Mastering the Lesson Plan

When an instructional coach or school leader is trying to help a teacher improve their practice, they’re usually asking that teacher to change something. And while those changes are intended to improve teaching and learning, teachers aren’t always eager to make them; sometimes they push back pretty hard.

When that happens, it’s easy for the person doing the coaching to assume the problem lies with the teacher. They’re resistant to change. They’re set in their ways. They just don’t want to try something new.

But what if the coach, or the PD provider, or the team leader is contributing to that resistance, too?

That’s one of the central ideas in Elena Aguilar’s new book, How to Coach Resistance: Turning Pushback Into Possibility, her ninth book on teaching. In the book, she argues that resistance isn’t simply something one person does; it’s a dynamic between two people, and the way a coach responds to pushback can actually make it worse. But this is also good news: It means coaches have more control over these interactions than they might think, and by changing their own approach, they can create the conditions for real growth.

On the podcast, Aguilar draws on her years of experience as an instructional coach and her deep knowledge of adult learning to help us look at resistance differently. We talk about the emotions that often lie beneath pushback, how to identify the gaps that keep teachers from moving forward, and what to do when a teacher has legitimate reasons for questioning what’s being asked of them. Although her book is written primarily for instructional coaches and school leaders, these insights are valuable for anyone who works with other people — whether they’re mentoring a new teacher, collaborating with colleagues, or navigating difficult conversations in their personal lives.

You can read the full transcript here, listen to our interview in the player above, or get the highlights of our conversation below.

1. We May Be Contributing to the Pushback

Instead of viewing resistance as a teacher’s problem, Aguilar sees it as something that happens between two people. A teacher pushes back against a proposed change, and the person coaching them pushes back in return. “What we experience as resistance is actually the dynamic between two people,” she says.

Both sides of that interaction are often fueled by fear. A teacher may worry about making a change, while the coach may worry about being unable to help them move forward. The teacher gets defensive; the coach gets defensive. The teacher says students can’t do something; the coach insists they can. Each person’s response adds to the pressure.

Aguilar uses the image of two hands pushing against each other. The pressure comes from both people. To change the dynamic, the coach can lower their own hand.

“If you don’t want to experience resistance, drop your hand. Stop exerting your own pressure against their pressure.”

In practice, that means getting curious. Instead of arguing for the curriculum, a coach might ask what concerns the teacher has about using it. That shift creates room to learn what is actually happening.

“This doesn’t mean that we have to agree with them,” Aguilar says. “It doesn’t mean we have to try to adopt their mindset, but it means we can get curious and we can build a relationship and we can stop pushing.”

The idea that coaches contribute to resistance may be uncomfortable at first, but Aguilar sees it as a source of hope. “This is not to blame you,” she writes in the book. “It is the most hopeful thing I can tell you, because it means resistance is not fixed. It is determined at least in part by what you bring into the room, and what you bring is something you can change.”

2. We May Be Overlooking the Emotions Underneath

When a coach drops their own resistance and gets curious, what they’re likely to discover are strong emotions underneath. Knowing how to approach these is key to moving forward.

Aguilar’s ACE framework gives coaches a three-step process for doing this: Acknowledge emotions, Cultivate compassion, and Expand the story.

Acknowledge Emotions

Before moving into problem-solving, it helps to pause to acknowledge what the teacher is feeling. This doesn’t require a lengthy conversation or a background in therapy.

“We don’t have to be therapists,” Aguilar says. “We don’t have to probe into their past. We don’t have to do much more than acknowledge them. And through acknowledging them, we’re also communicating acceptance.”

The approach should be more exploratory than prescriptive. Aguilar recommends leaving room for the teacher to participate in naming the emotion. Rather than declaring that someone is angry or scared, a coach might say that it sounds like there is some fear present and ask whether that seems accurate.

Another option is to use her Core Emotions tool, a list that helps people find words for their feelings. A teacher might initially identify nervousness or distress, then recognize fear or shame underneath. Naming those emotions can make it possible to talk about the support they need.

Cultivate Compassion

A struggling teacher may be judging themselves harshly, making it harder to consider another perspective; this is where it helps to cultivate compassion for them.

To help someone access self-compassion, Aguilar might ask what they would say to a best friend going through the same experience. Often, the answer is something much kinder than what they’re telling themselves. From there, they may be more able to extend compassion to students, administrators, or others they’re blaming.

In the book, Aguilar emphasizes that for this step to work, it’s essential for coaches to have compassion for themselves. “You are inviting them to speak kindly to themselves about hard days and hard classrooms and hard years. If the person doing the inviting has not practiced this on themself, the invitation is hollow.”

Expand the Story

The final step examines the beliefs attached to the experience: what is possible, what a situation means, or what another person’s behavior tells us about them.

“We want to begin to unpack the belief,” Aguilar explains, so that people can recognize the story they’re holding and choose whether to expand it. A coach can invite the teacher to consider another explanation or try a different approach, opening a path back to instruction.

3. We May Be Misinterpreting What’s Getting in the Way

Once we’re ready to talk about instruction, we still need to identify what support would help. Aguilar’s Gaps Framework offers a way to explore that question.

“Anytime we want to do something and we’re not able to, there’s a gap,” she says. “And it’s an area for growth. It’s not a deficit. It’s an area for growth.”

The framework identifies six categories: skill, knowledge, capacity, will, emotional intelligence, and cultural competence. Teachers labeled resistant are often assumed to have a will gap: They simply don’t want to do what is being asked. But a closer look may reveal a different need.

Aguilar offers the example of a secondary math teacher objecting to a curriculum that requires substantial reading. Asking about the teacher’s training might reveal that they were never taught how to teach reading. What initially sounded like unwillingness turns out to involve knowledge and skills.

“We need to know what is the gap or where is the area for growth before we start offering the interventions or the coaching.”

One way to introduce the framework, Aguilar says, is through the lens of a problem with students.

Suppose a teacher says students won’t turn in homework. Looking through the categories together might reveal that some students haven’t mastered the skills the homework requires, while others have jobs or caregiving responsibilities that limit their capacity. Once the teacher sees those possibilities, the coach can invite them to examine their own needs. Do they know how to design homework for students at different levels of mastery? That opens a conversation about differentiated assignments and allows the teacher to identify the support they need.

4. We May Be Overlooking Legitimate Reasons for Pushing Back

Sometimes teachers push back because they feel what they are being asked to do is simply wrong. Coaches need to make space for this possibility.

“There are times when resistance is righteous, and there needs to be resistance,” Aguilar says. “Resistance in and of itself is not a bad thing.”

She offers an intentionally extreme example: a kindergarten teacher being told to have students sit still on the carpet for an hour of instruction. The teacher knows the expectation is developmentally inappropriate. That objection deserves to be heard.

Even when a coach can’t change the requirement, they can explore the teacher’s options: What opportunities exist to say no? What consequences might follow? How could the concern reach someone with the authority to act?

This also calls for coaches and leaders to examine their own values. If they’re being asked to enforce something they believe is wrong, they may need to acknowledge that conflict and speak up.

The core of Aguilar’s approach is curiosity, a willingness to learn what’s happening for a teacher before deciding what they need. The message she wants teachers to hear is simple: “I’m not here to judge you. I’m not going to tell you what to do. I want to be a partner. I want to help you work through this.”

When a teacher trusts that this is the coach’s intention, there’s room for a different conversation — one where they can name what’s hard, question what’s being asked, and help determine what comes next. That’s where the possibility for growth begins.

issues.title: Why School Improvement Fails So Often
issues.summary: Meaningful change takes more than a good program or process. Here’s what helps educators solve problems together and make real progress. The post Why School Improvement Fails So Often first appeared on Cult of Pedagogy .
issues.author: Jennifer Gonzalez
issues.content_html:
Listen to the interview with Max Yurkofsky and Jal Mehta (transcript):

Sponsored by Brilliant and Listenwise

This page contains Bookshop.org links. When you make a purchase through these links, Cult of Pedagogy gets a small percentage of the sale at no extra cost to you. What’s the difference between Amazon and Bookshop.org?

Imagine this: You go to your first faculty meeting of the school year, and after a few welcoming remarks, your principal says, “This year, I just want you to keep doing what you’re doing. No changes.”

If that has ever happened anywhere, at any time, I’d love to hear about it, because as far as I can tell, every school for all of eternity has been trying to improve in some way. It’s part of our nature as humans to keep looking for ways to make things better. And schools are such complex ecosystems that there’s always going to be room for improvement.

These efforts vary in size and scope. Sometimes we’re just fine-tuning, on our own or with a group of colleagues, reflecting on our practice and making things a little better by degree. This kind of improvement tends to be pretty organic; we identify a need, make an adjustment, see how it goes, and keep refining.

Then there are the big, school-wide or district-wide efforts: a new curriculum, a branded leadership program, a whole new set of practices everyone is expected to start using. These often follow a familiar pattern. The initiative rolls out, everyone invests time and energy into it, and a few years later it’s replaced by something else. The churn can be exhausting.

Some of that is inevitable. We’re working with complex problems, the solutions aren’t always obvious, and there’s bound to be some trial and error. But a big reason these initiatives keep getting replaced is that they often don’t get the results people hoped for.

In recent years, schools have turned to improvement models that work differently. Rather than bringing in a prepackaged solution and asking teachers to just implement it, these frameworks give the people closest to the problem a process for studying it, trying possible solutions, seeing what happens, and adjusting from there. In theory, these approaches should get better results: The people doing the work have a hand in figuring out what needs to change, and the solution develops through a process of learning and adjustment.

But they don’t always work that way in practice. Sometimes the framework itself becomes just another thing handed down from above, another set of steps people are trained to follow, with more attention paid to following the process than to creating the conditions that make real problem-solving possible.

And yet, in some places, they really do work the way they should, leading to the kinds of improvements people were hoping for.

So what’s happening in the places where it’s working? What allows this kind of improvement work to actually become a way for people in schools to solve problems together, rather than just another program that eventually gets replaced?

Jal Mehta and Max Yurkofsky have an answer to that question. In their new book, A Chance to Solve Their Own Problems, they take a close look at how these kinds of problem-solving approaches play out in real schools and districts, examining why they succeed in some places and falter in others. Through that research, Mehta and Yurkofsky identified a set of conditions that seem to make the difference.

On the podcast, they explained what those conditions are, why so many well-intentioned improvement efforts fail to create those conditions, and what schools can do differently if they want improvement to become something people actually do, rather than another initiative they’re asked to implement. You can listen to the full interview above, read the full transcript here, or get the highlights below.

Why School Improvement Efforts Go Wrong

In their research, Mehta and Yurkofsky saw a few patterns that repeatedly got in the way of successful improvement efforts. Here are four of the most common.

The People Closest to the Problem Are Left Out

In many school improvement efforts, the problems to be solved are identified by people at the top, then handed down to educators to work on. Mehta argues that this leaves out the people who are in the best position to see what needs attention in the first place. “We’re not actually trusting the people who are closest to the ground to sort of say, ‘Hey, I have an inquiry question.’”

That trust matters because people are far more likely to engage in improvement work when it addresses a problem they actually experience. “Are you addressing a problem that teachers think that they have,” Mehta says, “or are you addressing a problem that you think teachers have? Because if ultimately this is a process that’s going to be taken up by educators, educators need to feel really connected to the problem.”

We Focus on People Instead of Systems

Schools often use data to identify which teachers, students, or teams are struggling, then focus their attention there. Yurkofsky argues that it’s more useful to look beyond the individual and examine the system around them.

“What’s more helpful is to go one layer deeper and think about, why is this particular teacher struggling with those standards? What part of the system is contributing to that outcome continuing to happen? . . . How is our instruction set up to support this teacher? How are we coaching and onboarding? What kinds of curriculum are we using? Where might that be falling short? When you address that, you’re not just helping that one teacher, but you’re trying to make an improvement for anyone who’s impacted by that system.”

Shifting our focus to systems can also make it safer for people to be honest about what isn’t working. “It kind of liberates folks to share where they’re having trouble, to say, hey, I’m struggling with this, our curriculum is actually not that strong here, the activities we’re using could be improved here.”

We Focus on Fidelity Instead of Learning

When schools adopt a new curriculum, program, or initiative, a lot of attention can go toward whether people are implementing it the way it was designed. Yurkofsky says this emphasis on fidelity can get in the way of something more important: learning from what happens when we actually put it into practice.

A program that wasn’t written for a specific context will never be perfect, he says, so making it work requires iteration. “The only way we’re going to make [it] better is by trying to do what we can, hollering when something’s not working, … and then adjusting and revising it so that it can be better tailored to our system.”

That means making a real commitment to trying something, but continuing to share where it falls short and adjusting it along the way. “Fidelity is never the point,” Yurkofsky says. “Fidelity means we’re not learning.” Instead, he prefers the term adaptive integration: “You’re integrating something adaptively into your system to make it work for your system. And that’s a continuous process.”

We Jump to Solutions Before Fully Understanding the Problem

Sometimes schools commit to a program, curriculum, or improvement method before they’ve fully defined the problem they’re trying to solve. Once that investment has been made, it’s easy to start shaping the problem around the solution instead of asking whether that solution is actually the right fit.

Mehta illustrates this with an example from a design thinking exercise he did with his students. Their task was to look for ways to improve the physical space in their education school, so they interviewed people who used different parts of the building to find out what was and wasn’t working. When they came back, one group reported that the school needed phone booths or small rooms where people could take Zoom calls. Mehta pointed out that they had already jumped from the problem to a solution: The actual problem was that people needed private spaces for Zoom calls.

Once the problem was framed that way, many more solutions became possible. “You want to define the problem in a way that opens up enough space that there are different solutions,” Mehta says, “ then see which one actually helps you move forward.”

The Building Blocks of Effective Improvement

So when school improvement initiatives do work, what does it look like? Across the different approaches they studied, Mehta and Yurkofsky found that three elements need to work together: mindsets, routines, and practices. Having one or two isn’t enough; successful improvement efforts depend on all three.

Mindsets

Mindsets are the beliefs and assumptions people bring to improvement work, and they can have a big impact on whether that work goes anywhere. Yurkofsky gives the example of a school trying to improve literacy: Even with a strong curriculum and good supports in place, progress will be difficult if teachers believe that teaching literacy isn’t part of their job.

“You might have secondary teachers who say, ‘It’s not my job to teach literacy. They should have learned this in elementary school,’” he says. If that mindset stays in place, simply giving teachers new practices or routines won’t be enough. For the work to be successful, the people involved need to believe in the problem they’re working on and see themselves as capable of helping to solve it.

Routines

Routines are the structures that allow educators to work together on a regular basis. These might include regularly looking at student work or other data together, observing one another’s classrooms, or meeting to decide how students should be grouped and regrouped.

Without these routines, improvement can become something people pursue on their own rather than something they learn about together. In one district Mehta studied, people were encouraged to experiment and innovate, but without clear routines, “people who were innovating felt like they were a little bit on an island and that they weren’t in common conversation with other people in the system.”

Practices

Practices are the actual strategies, methods, and resources educators use to make the improvement happen. If a school is working on literacy, for example, teachers need a clear picture of what good literacy instruction looks like, along with strong instructional materials and people with the expertise to help them use those materials well.

This piece can easily be overlooked when a school is focused on getting the improvement process right. Mehta points out that if you’re trying to make a significant change in instruction, “you’re not gonna, like, PDSA cycle your way” from one kind of teaching to another. At some point, he says, you need “some infusion of . . . disciplinary expertise.”

That expertise might already exist within the school, or it might need to come from somewhere else. The important thing is that educators have access to knowledge and practices that can actually help them solve the problem they’ve identified. As Mehta puts it, “the ideas have to come from somewhere.”

Cultivating the Right Environment for the Work

Having the right mindsets, routines, and practices isn’t enough on its own. For those pieces to actually work together, they need to exist in an environment that supports them. That means school and district leaders need to create and protect the conditions that allow people to take risks, learn from one another, and stay focused on meaningful improvement over time. Mehta and Yurkofsky point to three ways they can make that happen.

Protect Time and Space

“The first thing to recognize is that teachers are time-starved,” Mehta says. “There is no greater scarcity in our system than time for teachers.” Real improvement work requires time to step back from the immediate demands of getting ready for tomorrow and look for larger patterns in what’s happening. “Somebody with some authority has to protect the space and time to really do this kind of work.”

Make It Safe to Learn

Improvement also requires people to feel safe admitting when something isn’t working. “Learning requires trying things and sometimes failing,” Mehta says, but in some of the schools they studied, people felt that “it’s just not safe to fail here.”

If teachers are expected to have everything working perfectly, they can’t openly examine mistakes, experiment with new approaches, and learn from the results. As Mehta puts it, “That’s not the kind of environment that will produce learning.”

Make Improvement Part of a Larger Strategy

Finally, improvement methods shouldn’t become ends in themselves. Mehta says the most successful efforts are part of a larger strategy with “some direction and purpose” and the resources needed to achieve it. Instead of deciding, for example, “we’re gonna do rounds,” schools should start with a clear goal, then use improvement processes as one part of a larger plan for reaching it.

If all of this feels like a lot, that’s because it is. None of these changes can be made overnight, and trying to tackle all of them at once would probably be overwhelming. So where can a school leader start?

Yurkofsky suggested reframing the way we think about problems.

“We can’t learn if we’re not raising problems,” he says. “That’s what drives improvement.” In fact, he encourages leaders to “view problems as a gift.” When teachers are willing to say what isn’t working, it’s a sign of trust. And how leaders respond in those moments, with curiosity rather than defensiveness, can determine whether people will keep bringing problems forward.

Maybe that’s the simplest place to start: Make it safer for people to tell the truth about what isn’t working, listen carefully when they do, and give them a real chance to help solve the problems they see.

You can read more of Max Yurkofsky‘s writing about education on his Substack and explore Jal Mehta‘s work through Harvard’s Deeper Learning Institute, including its annual Deeper Learning Educator Camp.

issues.title: The Perfect Attendance Paradox: When Showing Up Isn’t Enough
issues.summary: Perfect attendance in school is often seen as the ultimate prize. You show up every single day, and you may get your name on the morning announcements or a perfect attendance award certificate at the end of the year assembly. It’s viewed as proof that a student is responsible and dedicated. But here is the... The post The Perfect Attendance Paradox: When Showing Up Isn’t Enough appeared first on T
issues.author: Janelle Cox
issues.content_html:
Perfect attendance in school is often seen as the ultimate prize. You show up every single day, and you may get your name on the morning announcements or a perfect attendance award certificate at the end of the year assembly. It’s viewed as proof that a student is responsible and dedicated.

But here is the problem: what if that message doesn’t tell the whole story? Some kids may push themselves to come to school even when they are sick for fear of losing this coveted award. Others may miss because of family issues or chronic health problems. Then there are the students who never miss a day but are not engaged at all.

The perfect attendance paradox challenges the belief that showing up to school is enough. Here we’ll take a look at why serving students is more than just tracking the days they show up.

The Pressure to Power Through

One of the most obvious downsides of perfect attendance is the pressure a student or their parent may put on them to power through not feeling well and coming to school. By staying home, a student may feel like they are being left out or may lose recognition as the kid with perfect attendance.

Think about the risks a student is taking by coming to school when they are sick. It also teaches them the wrong lesson. Instead of listening to their bodies and resting up, they think that their worth is tied to never missing a day of school. This mindset can follow them into adulthood and lead to unhealthy habits.

Overlooking Students with Chronic Health Needs

Imagine being a student with a chronic health condition, a disability, or a medical condition that makes it hard to attend school every day. Perfect attendance programs can unintentionally leave these students behind. These students may feel less valued than their classmates who don’t face the same obstacles as they do.

Let’s take the example of a student who has diabetes. They may do everything they can to stay engaged when they are in the classroom, but their efforts may go unnoticed because they don’t have a perfect attendance record. Instead of noticing their resilience, the focus lands on the days they are missing. This creates a space that feels unfair. The focus moves away from supporting a student and instead lands on enforcing a rule.

Family Realities That Interfere

Health issues are not the only thing that affects attendance. Family circumstances can also play a big role in whether a student attends school or not. Students who may have a death in the family, a crisis at home, unstable housing, or family responsibilities may miss school and be completely outside of their control. Perfect attendance awards and certificates rarely take these realities into account.

A child who may be late to school every day or misses class due to taking care of their siblings or because they have to work may be less committed to learning than other classmates. Yet the system values perfect attendance over responsibilities that may be out of a child’s control. Instead of making these students feel excluded, schools could support families in ways that address the root cause of their absences.

Missed Opportunities for Root Causes

If schools are focusing on perfect attendance records, they risk ignoring the root causes of why some students are not attending classes. Is a student getting bullied? Do they have a ride to school? Is their mental health keeping them from coming to class? Oftentimes, these issues get ignored, leaving larger issues unaddressed.

Instead of tallying absences, schools should consider looking at attendance patterns. Patterns can reveal a lot of information and can be a starting point for deeper conversations. Looking at the root causes of absences can help educators find meaningful solutions.

Attendance Does Not Equal Engagement

Perfect attendance programs focus on whether a student is in attendance, not how engaged they are when they are in the classroom. Being in the classroom doesn’t guarantee a child is engaged or motivated to learn. Some students may show up but struggle silently, while others may lack the support they need to thrive academically.

Awarding attendance based solely on whether a student is present overlooks building a sense of belonging or sparking curiosity. Attendance is just the starting point. The real question we should be asking is, are students connected and participating while they are here?

Rethinking How We Celebrate Attendance

Being in school regularly is important. It helps kids build routines and supports learning. But trying to get perfect attendance shouldn’t be the ultimate goal, and it doesn’t always send the right message. Consider celebrating effort, growth, and resilience. Students who have made progress in coming to school may receive the “improved attendance certificate.”

Students who have missed school because of an illness or struggle but stayed connected and kept learning may get the “resilience award.” When schools pair attendance with also taking care of themselves, it will show students that being present matters, but so does taking care of their well-being.

Practical Shifts Schools Can Make

Here are a few shifts schools can make to rethink the perfect attendance paradox.

  • Create recognition awards that move away from “perfect attendance” and towards growth and persistence.
  • Teach students that staying home when they are sick is a responsible choice.
  • Create flexible policies for students with chronic illness or unique challenges.
  • Look at attendance patterns as ways to get to the root cause of absences.
  • Partner with parents and guardians to address barriers to student absences.

Attendance is important, but it’s not the most important thing. By shifting focus from perfection to progress, schools are sending the message that effort and growth are more important than perfect attendance.

issues.author: Janelle Cox
issues.content_html:
Classrooms today are heavily reliant on technology. From Chromebooks and iPads to interactive whiteboards, technology has become a part of everyday teaching and learning. As classrooms become more and more dependent on devices, the question many are asking is whether the shift is equitable for all students.

Equity in a tech-driven classroom isn’t just about making sure that every child has a laptop; it’s ensuring that all students, regardless of their race, gender, ability, or circumstance, have access to technology. It also means being aware of the challenges that come with digital tools and finding ways to tackle those challenges.

Here are some key areas to focus on when creating a tech-driven classroom that supports all learners.

Addressing the Digital Divide

When you hear the term “digital divide,” you’re probably thinking about students who have access to technology and those who don’t. While this is mostly true, it’s actually a bit more complicated than that. A student may have a school-issued device, but may lack the internet, or some students may share a computer with their siblings or not have a quiet place to use it. The divide isn’t just about having the technology; it’s about whether the student can use it in a meaningful way to learn.

To address these challenges, school districts can partner with local internet providers to offer low-cost or even free internet services. Keep school libraries or student services open later to help students who need access to the internet. Or allow students to utilize WIFI hotspots on their school-issued devices.

To truly address the gap, consider sending out a survey to parents to find out what technology and internet services their child has access to. This can help you identify families that need extra support.

Training for Both Students and Teachers

It’s easy to assume that today’s students know how to use all digital devices and online tools. However, while most students are comfortable navigating social media, they may need more support with digital literacy and evaluating and formatting resources.

Teachers also may feel confident with some programs or trying new platforms, but others may need more support. Providing professional development that is specific to classroom needs, as well as giving teachers time to practice, is essential.

When both students and teachers receive training, technology becomes less of a challenge and more of a tool to support learning.

Meeting Diverse Learning Needs

One of the greatest uses of technology in the classroom is that it can support different learning styles and abilities. With the right digital tool, technology can meet the needs of all students. For example, students struggling with reading can use the Natural Reader tool that turns text to audio, while visual learners can use the Canva app to help organize and present information.

English Language Learners can be supported through apps like Google Translate, while students who learn better through hands-on learning can utilize apps like Kahoot. Technology can be a powerful tool that can help every student learn in a way that is best for them.

Watching Out for Algorithmic Bias

Many of the digital tools schools use rely on algorithms. These are systems that decide on what content a student sees or how their work is scored. While it’s a great time-saver for teachers, it can also create problems.

For example, predictive text may not recognize certain names or phrases, which can leave some students feeling left out, or some programs may grade one student more harshly than another based on a certain preferred writing style. Even some facial recognition software used for student attendance or security has been shown to be biased against darker skin tones.

This is why it’s so important not to solely rely on technology for all decision-making regarding students. Educators need to look closely at how these programs affect students and use the data along with their own personal judgment.

Ensuring All Students are Heard

One of the great things about technology is that it gives all students a platform to be heard. In traditional classrooms, students raise their hands when they have something to say, and the teacher takes turns allowing students to talk. Technology changes that. Collaborative tools like Google Docs make it easy for all students to contribute.

Podcasts and videos allow students to share their voices in creative ways that teachers would never see if they were to just raise their hands or write it down. When tools like these are intentionally used, they do more than just increase participation; they give students a voice and allow everyone to be part of the conversation.

Practical Steps for Teachers

Making technology work for every student can be a challenge, so here are a few practical steps that can help make a difference.

Review Student Resources

Survey students and parents to see what technology resources are accessible at home. Once you know the situation, you can connect families to after-school lab hours or internet hotspots.

Offer Student Choice

Not all students learn the same way. Offer students choices on how they learn best, using different formats, such as creating videos, using apps, etc. This flexibility levels the playing field for students.

Rotate Tools

Offer students different tools and platforms throughout the year so they can see what works best for their specific learning style.

Check for Bias

Think critically about the tools that you use and ask yourself if the program works well for all groups of students. Use the data from your apps as well as your own observations.

Encourage Student Feedback

Ask students for feedback on the tech they are using. Use this information to help guide your choices and adapt your instruction to meet the needs of all students.

Prioritize Balance

Equity means using technology in a meaningful way. Pair technology with offline activities to give all students the chance to shine.

Equity in a tech-driven classroom is not just about ensuring all students have access to technology, but also can use these tools in a way that supports learning. It’s about making sure that all students can thrive in a digital world.

issues.title: Memory Games for Kids in the Classroom
issues.summary: Memory plays an essential role in almost everything students do in the classroom. Whether it’s recalling math facts or following directions, having a strong memory makes learning easier. While rote memorization and traditional worksheets have their place, incorporating memory games for kids is a great way to help students strengthen their memory. Adding memory games... The post Memory Games for Ki
issues.author: Janelle Cox
issues.content_html:
Memory plays an essential role in almost everything students do in the classroom. Whether it’s recalling math facts or following directions, having a strong memory makes learning easier. While rote memorization and traditional worksheets have their place, incorporating memory games for kids is a great way to help students strengthen their memory.

Adding memory games for kids to your classroom routine can help students’ working memory in a fun and engaging way. The great thing about adding these games to your routine is that they not only help students build recall, but they also can be adjusted to fit any grade level.

The Games: Practical Activities to Strengthen Student Recall

  1. What’s on the Tray?

  • Best for: Grade 1-5
  • Activity: This classic memory game is a great warm-up activity. Place 10-15 objects on a tray (pencil, eraser, piece of candy, small toy, a block). Give students about one minute to study the tray, then cover it up with a cloth. Challenge students to write down as many objects as they can remember.
  • Variation: For younger students, you can have a printout of the objects they can circle, and for older students, you can add more objects to the tray.
  • Learning Outcome: Strengthens recall and attention to detail. Supports reading comprehension and observation skills.

  1. Memory Story Chain

  • Best for: Grades 2-8
  • Activity: This is a verbal game; one student begins a sentence such as, “I went to the park and saw a bird.” The next student repeats the sentence and adds on to it, “I went to the park and saw a bird and tripped over a rock.” This chain continues around the room until everyone has a turn, or someone messes up, and it starts again.
  • Tip: Instruct students to keep sentences short so it doesn’t become overwhelming.
  • Learning Outcome: Builds auditory memory, sequencing, and language skills. Also great for strengthening listening comprehension.

  1. Number Pattern Recall

  • Best for: Grades 3-8
  • Activity: Write a sequence of numbers on the board, then give students about 30 seconds to look at it, and then erase it. Ask students to write down the sequence of numbers from memory. Gradually increase the number of digits as students get better at it.
  • Variation: For older students or an extra challenge, include patterns (2,4,6,8…) and ask students to extend the sequence.
  • Learning Outcome: Builds memory, mental math, and pattern recognition.

  1. Sound Match Recall

  • Best for: Grades K-3
  • Activity: Challenge students to listen to simple sounds (bells, chimes, clapping), then have them match the sound that they hear.
  • Variation: Use instruments for younger students or create sound cards with written cues for older students.
  • Learning Outcome: Strengthens auditory memory.

  1. What’s Changed?

  • Best for: Grades K-4
  • Activity: Select a student volunteer and have them stand in front of the classroom for about 30 seconds. Instruct the student to leave the classroom and have them take off one thing (glasses, bracelets, or switch shoes). When they return, have the classmates try and figure out what has changed.
  • Learning Outcome: Sharpens observation skills and memory of visual details, which is essential to focus and attention.

  1. Recall Words

  • Best for: Grades 2-8
  • Activity: Write 5-10 words on the board and give students one minute to study them. Erase the list and challenge students to write down as many words as they can remember. Connect words to topics you are studying or vocabulary words.
  • Variation: Challenge students to use the words in a sentence for a bonus.
  • Learning Outcome: Improves short-term memory and reinforces vocabulary.

  1. Memory Match-Up

  • Best for: Grades 1-6
  • Activity: This game may remind you of the classic concentration matching game. Create cards with vocabulary words on one side and their meaning on the back, or math facts on one side and the answers on the back. Instruct students to flip two cards at one time, trying to match a pair.
  • Variation: Have students create the cards.
  • Learning Outcome: Reinforces content while strengthening memory.

  1. Memory Map

  • Best for: Grades 6-12
  • Activity: Show students a simple map (neighborhood labeled, state with cities labeled). Give them a few minutes to study it. Take it away and challenge them to recreate it from memory by filling in as many details as possible.
  • Variation: Use diagrams (water cycle, plants, etc.)
  • Learning Outcome: Enhances spatial memory and visual recall.

  1. Picture Recall

  • Best for: Grades 2-8
  • Activity: Display a picture for about 30 seconds. This can be a photograph, a poster, or even a classroom photo. After 30 seconds, cover it and challenge students to list everything they can remember.
  • Variation: Split students into teams and have them race to see which group can write down the most things in the picture.
  • Learning Outcome: Strengthens visual memory, attention to detail, and teamwork.

  1. The Name Game

  • Best for: Grades 2-8
  • Activity: Start with one student and have them say their name along with an adjective that starts with the same letter as their name (Brave Brady, Joyful Jenny, Funny Frankie). The next student repeats the name before them, adding their own. By the end of the game, the class knows everyone’s name.
  • Learning Outcome: Boosts memory while encouraging peer bonding.

Why Memory Games are Important

A strong working memory helps students retain key concepts. It also helps them to follow directions and apply knowledge to new situations. Not to mention, they are fun! Who doesn’t like to play games?

By adding memory games for kids to your routine, you are helping students build the cognitive skills they need to focus and retain information.

issues.title: 5 Benefits of Science Journaling for Student Learning
issues.summary: Journaling has been around for decades and can be a powerful tool to enhance learning. Science journaling is more than just a place to jot down terms or lab results. It gives students the chance to express their understanding of key concepts in ways that worksheets or tests cannot. It also encourages them to explore... The post 5 Benefits of Science Journaling for Student Learning appeared first o
issues.author: Janelle Cox
issues.content_html:
Journaling has been around for decades and can be a powerful tool to enhance learning. Science journaling is more than just a place to jot down terms or lab results. It gives students the chance to express their understanding of key concepts in ways that worksheets or tests cannot. It also encourages them to explore ideas, sharpen observation skills, and think critically.

Here’s a closer look at the benefits that make science journaling worth your time.

Fosters Critical Thinking

Science is based on curiosity, such as asking questions, testing ideas, and making sense of evidence. Journaling allows students to think more deeply about what they are observing. Rather than simply writing down answers, they can use their journals to explain their observations, make connections, and reflect on what they’re learning.

For example, during a unit on plants, students might predict what happens during different stages of growth, record their observations of the changes, and then compare their predictions to what actually happens. They even use their journals to sketch, add diagrams, or add new information. By engaging with questions, students develop and use their problem-solving skills, which not only benefits them in science class but also throughout their lives.

Enhances Observation Skills

Observation skills are the foundation of science class. They help students notice details and gather the information and evidence needed to understand what they are learning. Journaling helps students pay attention and notice the small details they may not have seen if they weren’t writing them down.

Take the lesson mentioned earlier on plants. Instead of just writing down that the plant has sprouted, a science journal ensures students measure the height of the plant, the number of leaves it has, or how it changes over time. Writing down these details helps to sharpen their ability to notice patterns.

Improves Scientific Communication and Literacy

Having the ability to communicate clearly is another key component of science class. Journaling helps students practice using scientific vocabulary, writing explanations, and supporting data. This helps students with their scientific terminology as well as prepares them to write any formal reports or presentations.

For example, when upper elementary students are experimenting with different soils to help their plants grow, they can include key terms like “nutrients” and “retention” instead of saying the soil is “good” or “bad.” For middle and high school students, journaling can be paired with peer reviews to help with feedback and accuracy. This helps to build solid communication skills.

Promotes Creativity and Curiosity

Science journaling is not just about writing key terms and data. When students are encouraged to draw, sketch diagrams, and ask questions, it gives them a space to be curious and use their imagination. An elementary student may sketch a plant and label it, while a high school student may use their journal to draw the life cycle of a plant and explain the process. These approaches are creative and personal. They provide a place for students to imagine and explore without the fear of being graded or having the right answer.

Serving as an Authentic Form of Assessment

One of the best benefits of a science journal is using it as a means of assessment. While science journals typically are not graded, they can be a great resource for teachers to show a student’s learning process. Teachers can use the journal to see how students’ understanding has evolved. By tracking entries, teachers can see not only the students’ progress, but also the effectiveness of their own instruction.

Older students can also use their journals as portfolios. They can look back at them to reflect or use them as a study tool, reminding them of key terms they’ve forgotten about or previous experiments.

How to Bring Science Journaling into Your Classroom

To start integrating science journaling into your classroom, start small with just a few minutes at the end of each lesson. Be flexible and allow students to choose whether they want to record observations, write questions they may have, or sketch diagrams. Over time, students will begin to see that their journals are a valuable tool.

To get students into science journaling, consider using simple prompts like “What surprised you the most during the experiment?” or “What are you still curious about?” This will help students think beyond the data and facts and dive more into their curiosity.

It’s also important to note that students need to be aware that there is no “correct” way to use their journals. Based on their own learning style and preferences, each student’s journal will look different. Some students may have their notebooks filled with sketches and diagrams, while others may just have key terms and explanations.

Science journaling can be so much more than just recording information in a notebook; it can be a place where students can explore their creativity, sharpen their observation skills, and deepen their learning. By using this strategy in your classroom, you’re allowing students to learn ways to wonder, question, and explain concepts.
