issues.title: Michigan just hit pause on a plan to update the controversial Line 5 oil pipeline
issues.summary: Outgoing Governor Gretchen Whitmer froze state permits for a proposal to replace an underwater segment of the aging pipeline.
issues.author: Vivian La
issues.content_html:
Michigan Governor Gretchen Whitmer said Tuesday that she’s pausing both pending and issued state permits for the plan to replace a segment of the Line 5 oil pipeline beneath the Straits of Mackinac.

Whitmer said regulators at the Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy, or EGLE, need to answer questions about the full scope of the plan’s threats to the environment.

Those questions, according to Whitmer, were raised by a Michigan Supreme Court ruling this summer on a related Line 5 tunnel permit. Justices tossed out a permit issued by a separate state agency, saying their review of environmental harms was too narrow.

Line 5 has been transporting oil and natural gas liquids 645 miles between Ontario and Wisconsin since 1954. A 4-mile segment passes through the Straits of Mackinac, the narrow waterways that connect Lake Michigan to Lake Huron, separating Michigan’s Lower and Upper peninsulas. Sensitive coastal and wetlands habitats are found in the straits, and the area is sacred to Anishinaabe peoples, featuring prominently in their creation story and serving as burial grounds for their ancestors.

“I have always said my ultimate goal is to get Line 5 out of the water,” Whitmer, whose second and final term will end January 1, said in the announcement. “Just one spill threatens irreparable damage to our water, our economy, and our way of life.” The permit pause comes weeks after regulators in Wisconsin had been dealing with a spill on the portion of Line 5 that crosses that state.

It’s the latest setback for pipeline owner Enbridge Energy, which first proposed the plan to replace an aging portion of the pipeline with a new one, buried in a tunnel beneath the straits, almost a decade ago.

Enbridge maintains that the pipeline is safe. In a statement, spokesperson Ryan Duffy pointed to the company’s record of permit approvals — including the pending EGLE permit, which would have been a renewal of one it received in 2021.

Line 5 delivers the energy people depend on every day, Duffy said. “At Enbridge, we remain committed to that purpose and equally committed to safeguarding the Great Lakes,” he said.

The permit freeze is a win for Line 5 opponents who have protested for years against the tunnel project and have fought to shut down the entire pipeline.

“I think this is a really, really excellent step in the right direction,” said Ashley Rudzinski, climate and environment program director for the nonprofit Groundwork Center for Resilient Communities. “We’re seeing the Whitmer administration, finally, putting some real strength behind the words that she had already spoken.”

The Line 5 tunnel project has received federal approval, but with the remaining state permits in question, it’s unclear what its future looks like. Separately, Line 5 faces legal challenges from groups that have fought to shut down the entire pipeline for years, including the Whitmer administration.

Lawyers representing Michigan tribes in their fight to shut down Line 5 said they hope this momentum continues into the administration of Governor-elect Jocelyn Benson, who, like Whitmer, is a Democrat. All 12 federally recognized tribes in Michigan oppose the pipeline.

“No matter who the governor is, it’s in all of our interests to keep the Great Lakes free of oil and to transition away from Line 5,” said Laura Berglan, senior attorney with the legal nonprofit Earthjustice, which represents the Bay Mills Indian Community, the Sault Ste. Marie Tribe of Chippewa Indians, and the Little Traverse Bay Bands of Odawa Indians. “We need to protect our shared resources and our tribal resources for the future.”

This story was originally published by Grist with the headline Michigan just hit pause on a plan to update the controversial Line 5 oil pipeline on Nov 25, 2026.

issues.title: As food prices rise, do shoppers still care about sustainability?
issues.summary: Consumer spending drives the U.S. economy, but voting with your dollars has its limits.
issues.author: Frida Garza
issues.content_html:
The headlines say what people already know: Food is getting more expensive. Consumers have been feeling an uptick in the overall price of both dining out and preparing meals at home this year, according to numbers from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.

And just in time for the holidays, things seem to be getting worse. The American Farm Bureau Federation found that the price of goods usually found in a Thanksgiving dinner increased this year for the first time since 2022. One economist told Bloomberg that Americans should expect food prices to keep creeping up into next year.

The high price of fuel, driven by the war in Iran, has contributed to the sticker shock Americans are feeling at the grocery store. Farmers need diesel to harvest, process, store, and transport produce and other crops from the field to retailers. Climate change, as well as El Niño spurring extreme weather globally, is also at play.

And yet, however flummoxed U.S. consumers may be about the high costs of living — a major driver of the midterms’ “blue wave” — consumer spending has only gone up. In fact, consumer spending, which makes up about two-thirds of the U.S. gross domestic product, or GDP, and has driven the economy for some time, increased by 3.8 percent in the third quarter of this year.

At the same time, food systems are still responsible for somewhere between a quarter and a third of global greenhouse gas emissions. With food prices creeping up, it’s worth asking whatever happened to the idea of consumers as climate or environmental activists. The concept of “voting with your dollars” is often described as a meaningful tool for combating carbon-intensive practices in the food supply chain, such as deforestation. But do today’s shoppers still care about where their food comes from and how it’s grown when they’re worried about their supermarket bill (and all the other ones)?

The research is mixed. Some studies suggest that shoppers are comfortable springing for the more eco-friendly option, such as climate-proof wine, even if it costs a premium. But buyer motivations are complex: When it comes to food, even when consumers are paying for more sustainable options, some research shows that they’re more likely to have made that choice for other reasons, such as its taste or health claims.

If the question is whether consumers are motivated by sustainability or by price, the answer may be both, said Sandra Goldmark, a professor at the Columbia Climate School focused on circular economies. “People want a sustainable option. They want it to be healthy for their body and the planet,” said Goldmark. “And they have a price factor,” she added.

The practice of voting with your dollar “has limits,” said David Ortega, an agricultural economist and professor at Michigan State University. Such a practice works when “the sustainable option costs about the same [as the standard option] — less so when there’s a real premium and budgets are tight.”

Eggs, Ortega said, are a good example. When the price of eggs ballooned last year, higher-income households were more likely to be able to afford the more expensive, more sustainable options like cage-free eggs. “Most shoppers can’t, so they reach for the cheapest eggs or conventional products at the supermarket,” he said.

Additionally, the share of GDP that comes from consumer spending may overstate shoppers’ leverage in the food sector, said Ortega, as the bulk of that spending currently goes toward housing costs. What’s more, Ortega noted that the way cage-free eggs have become the industry standard had more to do with shifting state laws and retailer commitments than just “shoppers choosing to pay more.”

Read Next The American Dream wasn’t built for climate change Kate Yoder

Still, history shows that public pressure campaigns can still push companies to flip their supply chains. This works best when the campaigns are targeted and sustained — like when the Coalition of Immokalee Workers, a worker-led human rights group, led boycotts of Taco Bell across the U.S. over its supply chain agreements with tomato farms that mistreated workers. After four years, Taco Bell’s parent company agreed to only work with suppliers that are compliant with a code of conduct developed by farmworkers.

Companies gain something when they respond to consumer demands for change — they avoid reputational harm. In the early 2000s, outrage over a Greenpeace report on deforestation in the Amazon led to soy traders agreeing not to purchase soy from newly deforested lands. Although it fell apart earlier this year, that agreement lasted for nearly two decades — and it was considered widely successful.

The end of the Amazon soy moratorium presented a major blow to conservation efforts in Brazil — but that doesn’t mean consumers today have no say in where their food comes from. The growing influence of the Make America Healthy Again, or MAHA, movement shows that these concerns matter more than ever to many households.

Real change may come when policy changes and public investment in sustainable food systems matches consumer desires, said Jody Kirchner, director of market insights at Good Food Institute, a think tank focused on the alternative protein economy. When the option that’s better for the environment and the planet costs more than the status quo, “shoppers can’t break that loop on their own,” Kirchner added. But maybe they can do it together.

This story was originally published by Grist with the headline As food prices rise, do shoppers still care about sustainability? on Nov 25, 2026.

issues.title: The ‘drill, baby, drill’ Democrat who will soon help oversee Texas’ oil industry
issues.summary: He’s the first Democrat elected to the Texas Railroad Commission since 1990. What can Jon Rosenthal accomplish?
issues.author: Celeste Guajardo
issues.content_html:
This coverage is made possible through a partnership between Grist and KERA, a public media organization serving the Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex.

This month’s midterm elections featured a previously unthinkable result in Texas: Democrats won every single statewide race in the Lone Star State. Some of those newly elected Democrats have become household names, like Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa and Senator-elect James Talarico. But the list of Democratic victors also includes a centrist set to occupy a little-known office with outsize influence over the country’s oil and gas industry.

Jon Rosenthal won a contentious race for a seat on the Texas Railroad Commission against Republican Bo French, whose racist social media posts drew national bipartisan backlash. Rosenthal, the first Democrat elected to the commission since 1990, isn’t trying to usher in radical change, and his influence will be limited by the two Republicans already sitting on the commission. But he’s aiming to bring transparency, accountability, and a bigger budget to the regulatory board.

“Voters have delivered a mandate for a change,” said Rosenthal at a post-election press conference. “My top priority … is doubling the Railroad Commission’s budget. I believe the commission needs more resources to do the work they are [tasked] to do.”

The Railroad Commission was established in 1891 to regulate the rail industry. Over the years, the agency’s focus shifted to overseeing the state’s booming oil and gas industry. In 2024, Texas accounted for almost half of the country’s crude oil production. This fact makes the Railroad Commission one of the most powerful state-level regulatory agencies in the country. The commission generally takes a deregulatory approach and is widely considered friendly to the industry it regulates, especially with oil companies donating generously to the campaigns of commissioners they support.

Rosenthal describes himself as a “drill, baby, drill” Democrat, arguing a clean environment and good jobs can coexist. He worked in the oil and gas industry for over 25 years as a mechanical engineer. In 2018, he was elected to the Texas House of Representatives, representing parts of Houston, and was reelected three times before running for the Railroad Commission.

His victory likely has much to do with the unpopularity of his opponent. French, a former local Republican Party chair, prompted widespread criticism when he made a racist social media post in September about South Asian students celebrating at a University of Texas football game. The race also drew attention to French’s previous offensive remarks, like posting a since-deleted online poll in 2025 asking whether “Jews” or “Muslims” pose a bigger threat to the United States. Several prominent Republican politicians denounced French’s bigoted comments, which led to a fundraising boost for Rosenthal.

Rosenthal will join Republicans Wayne Christian and Christi Craddick on a commission that has recently attempted to shield itself from public scrutiny. In August, the agency adopted a new public participation policy that does not guarantee public comments at its monthly meetings. A public comment period is now included only if a commissioner requests it on the agenda.

Christian, a far-right conservative, championed the new policy, while the more moderate Craddick voted against it. Christian faced criticism from Democratic state lawmakers for not showing up to a legislative hearing that would have included discussion of that decision, and he used profanity when defending the vote from Commission Shift, a nonprofit watchdog group.

In a social media post, Rosenthal called the new policy “shameful.” He campaigned on making hearings more accessible. Virginia Palacios, the executive director of Commission Shift, expressed optimism that the new commissioner can help increase transparency.

“It’s a possibility that if we have someone like Jon Rosenthal who ran his campaign on the idea that open meetings should be open, you could potentially have two commissioners that would vote for open public meeting policy,” she said.

Rosenthal could occasionally team up with Craddick to neutralize Christian on other policy questions as well. “There are times when [Craddick and Christian] vote differently on some of these permit … or policy approvals, even though the vast majority of their votes tend to be the same,” Palacios explained.

Palacios does not expect “drastic changes” with Rosenthal’s election, but she does believe there will be greater opportunity for public engagement. According to his campaign website, Rosenthal wants the commission to hire regional community liaisons to make it easier for Texans to offer input.

“We’ve recently heard of communities that requested the Railroad Commission to go out and visit them in person … and the Railroad Commission denied those requests,” said Palacios. “We would hope to see that this new sitting commissioner would be more responsive to the public and try to show up in person where others haven’t.”

Apart from improving transparency and community relations, Rosenthal’s biggest ambition is to double the agency’s biennial budget from approximately $500 million to $1 billion. He argues this will help “turbo-charge” the plugging of orphaned oil wells, those that have been inactive for at least 12 months, and zombie wells, those whose plugs are failing.

Thousands of these wells across Texas are leaking methane , a potent greenhouse gas that contributes to trapping heat in the atmosphere. The Railroad Commission plugged over 2,000 orphaned wells during its last fiscal year — a record number — but still ended up with more of them at the end of the year than they started off with. That’s because a large number of low-producing and inactive wells become orphaned.

“We want to enable this agency to further ramp up well-plugging operations … but also get proactive in helping to prevent future wells from being orphaned,” said Rosenthal at his post-election press conference. “If we don’t go after what causes this … we’re going to be chasing our tail forever.”

Notably, Rosenthal’s ambition to double the commission’s budget is not something the board can accomplish on its own. The Texas Legislature would have to approve such a budget increase, and Governor-elect Hinojosa would have to sign it. Democrats will have a majority in the Texas House come January, and although the Texas Senate remains in Republican hands, the Democratic lieutenant governor-elect will wield significant power in the upper chamber.

Hinojosa and the new class of Democratic state lawmakers haven’t spoken publicly on whether they’ll prioritize the Railroad Commission’s budget, but Rosenthal expressed confidence that his history as a state representative will come in handy as he seeks more money for the agency’s operations.

“In this new environment, I might be one of the Railroad Commission’s more valuable players,” said Rosenthal at the press conference. “Because some … lobbyists or agency personnel are not used to walking into a Legislature controlled by the Democrats.” Meanwhile, “I know how to talk to Democrats because I am one. And it will be my job to help educate my former colleagues about how important this is.”

This story was originally published by Grist with the headline The ‘drill, baby, drill’ Democrat who will soon help oversee Texas’ oil industry on Nov 25, 2026.

issues.title: What to know about the Army’s lead detonation in Iowa
issues.summary: Two quick blasts destroyed nearly 5 tons of unstable lead azide. Early monitoring detected no airborne lead, but officials are still testing southeastern Iowa for contamination.
issues.author: Juanpablo Ramirez-Franco
issues.content_html:
After months of planning, days of warnings, and the fear of a plume of lead dust, the destruction of nearly 5 tons of unstable explosives in southeastern Iowa was over in seconds.

For all the concern about what might happen when the U.S. Army blew up 68 drums of lead azide on Wednesday, the detonation itself proved remarkably uneventful. Two booms sounded across a clear, cold winter morning just after 9 a.m., each creating a wispy white plume that quickly dissipated. State and federal officials said the operation appeared to have gone as planned, and more than an hour later, the Environmental Protection Agency’s real-time air monitors had detected no airborne lead.

Officials had warned that the detonation could send lead-laden dust over homes and farmland for miles around. The EPA deployed 300 employees and contractors and collected more than 1,200 air, soil, dust, and water samples before the blast to establish a baseline. Early air-monitoring results suggest the elaborate precautions the Army took may have limited the amount of airborne lead. Post-blast sampling is now underway to determine where lead was deposited and whether cleanup is necessary.

The operation followed days of controversy, evacuations, and shelter-in-place warnings, as well as objections from elected officials in Iowa and Illinois and an unsuccessful legal effort by environmental groups to stop it. Here’s what to know about why the Army undertook the unusual operation, the risks it posed, and what officials are watching for now.

Why did the army detonate old munitions?

Army inspectors discovered in March that 68 drums of decades-old lead azide had begun to crystallize, making it increasingly sensitive to friction, vibration, and temperature changes. Even the slightest movement could trigger an explosion.

“The lead azide has aged. It’s become unstable to the point where moving it or even allowing it to sit on the odd chance that it receives some sort of shock or friction could lead to a spontaneous explosion,” said Greg Domski, associate provost and professor of chemistry and biochemistry at Augustana College in Rock Island, Illinois.

After consulting with the Environmental Protection Agency, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, and Firearms, and other agencies, the Army decided the best option was to detonate the material where it sat. The plan to do so had been ongoing in the months since.

What is lead azide?

Lead azide is a compound of lead and nitrogen, commonly used in detonators to set off other explosives. About 9,700 pounds of the material was detonated.

Has the Army blown up lead azide before?

While the Army has destroyed weapons and materials in the past, it has never destroyed so large an amount of lead azide. This operation required detonating 9,700 pounds of the material stored in 68 drums.

“We detonate all the time, but we have not detonated lead azide at this quantity,” said Lori McFate, public affairs specialist with the Army Sustainment Command in Bettendorf, Iowa.

The operation followed months of planning and review by the EPA’s regional office in Kansas City, Missouri. The agency issued an emergency permit for operation on November 16; a federal appeals court ruled Monday that the detonation could proceed.

When did the detonation happen?

The detonation occurred at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa at about 9 a.m. Wednesday. The plant is about 160 miles southeast of Des Moines, Iowa, and about 230 miles west of Chicago. The nearest communities lie just 10 miles to the west across the Mississippi River.

The Army delayed the operation after elected officials in both states raised concerns about safety. Iowa Governor Kim Reynolds and Governor-elect Rob Sand were joined by other politicians in calling for a delay. The environmental organization Earthjustice also sued to try to pause the detonation.

Where will the plume go?

The Army had projected that the plume would travel southwest from the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, away from Illinois. When the detonation occurred Wednesday morning, two small white plumes rose above the site and quickly dissipated.

More than an hour after the blast, the EPA said all of its real-time air monitors throughout the region were detecting no airborne lead. The monitors continued collecting data throughout the detonation and afterward.

But those readings do not yet establish where lead from the blast may have settled. The Army had warned that lead-containing dust could be deposited downwind. Army and EPA crews are now collecting soil, water, and surface samples along the projected plume path to determine where lead was deposited and whether cleanup is necessary.

What are the health risks?

There is no safe level of lead exposure. The neurotoxin can damage the brain and central nervous system and is particularly dangerous to children and pregnant women. Exposure is associated with cognitive delays, heart problems, and reproductive issues.

People in the plume’s path could be exposed by inhaling airborne lead particles or coming into contact with lead dust. The Army said it would test air, soil, and water before and after the detonation to determine where lead has been deposited and guide any necessary cleanup.

“Lead is an element, and doesn’t break down,” said Robert Hirschfeld, director of water policy at the Prairie River Network. “Those health risks persist as long as the lead does.”

Will this affect crops or animals?

The Department of Agriculture said earlier this week that 350 farms lie in the projected path of the plume, according to the Associated Press. The agency also said it will work to keep lead and other heavy metals out of the food supply. Farmers were advised to move livestock indoors and protect hay and water supplies.

It is not yet clear whether agricultural land or livestock were exposed. Iowa agriculture officials are advising farmers to have soil and forage tested after the detonation and to monitor livestock for signs of lead poisoning. EPA and Army crews are also conducting post-blast sampling to determine where lead was deposited.

What can people do to limit their exposure?

The Illinois Department of Public Health recommends the following safety tips:

  • Stay indoors and keep windows closed for 24 to 48 hours after the detonation.
  • If you have a heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning system that actively draws in outside air, like in a school or commercial building, then you may want to temporarily close the intake and switch to recirculate.
  • Use a portable air cleaner to supplement your furnace filter.
  • Once the U.S. Army determines the airborne exposure period has ended, wet-clean potentially affected surfaces, including playground equipment, toys, and windowsills, using soap and water. Avoid sweeping, which may redistribute dust.
  • If you need to drive through an area impacted by dust, set your car’s AC/heater to recirculate. Afterward, you can take your car to the car wash and replace the cabin filter, if needed. A high-efficiency cabin filter will capture fine particulate matter.
  • Wash your hands before eating and drinking and take your shoes off when you enter your home.
  • Visit your doctor if you have health concerns.

Chicago Public Media reporters Isabela Nieto and Misha Manjuran Oberoi contributed to this report.

UPDATE: This story and its headline have been updated to reflect the latest news.

This story was originally published by Grist with the headline What to know about the Army’s lead detonation in Iowa on Nov 24, 2026.

issues.author: Mongabay.com
issues.content_html: International Jaguar Day has been marked every Nov. 29 since 2018, to raise awareness of the threats faced by the Americas’ biggest cats and the efforts to protect them. Jaguars (Panthera onca) were once found across some 19 million square kilometers (7.3 million square miles), from what is today the southwestern U.S. to central Argentina. But their range has shrunk by more than half, and today spans about 9 million km² (3.5 million mi²). Most jaguars live in a stronghold ranging from the Amazon Rainforest and stretching into the Pantanal wetlands, the Chaco dry forest and the Llanos grasslands of Colombia and Venezuela. However, recent sightings and reports from outside these core areas highlight that many jaguars are still holding on at the edges of their historical territory. For example, in Brazil’s eastern Atlantic Forest and dry Caatinga, fewer than 250 adult jaguars survive, and researchers have begun banking their genes in an effort to save them through cloning. At the northern edge of the species’ range, a male nicknamed Cinco showed up on camera footage in southern Arizona state in late 2025, becoming the fifth jaguar recorded there in 15 years. Meanwhile, in Honduras’s Sierra del Merendón, a mountain range in the country’s northwest, camera traps recorded a young male at an altitude of about 2,200 meters (7,200 feet) for the first time in a decade. “The fact that they’re able to travel through these high elevation areas also shows how resilient they are,” Allison Devlin, who directs the…This article was originally published on Mongabay

It is far from the farmland where he used to live in Myanmar, before he and thousands of Rohingya people like him fled […]
issues.author: Ata Ullah
issues.content_html: KUTUPALONG REFUGEE CAMP, Bangladesh —”It is like a jail, but it isn’t a jail,” says Roshid Ahamed Bin, a 47-year-old Rohingya farmer, living in what is now a refugee camp in Bangladesh. It is far from the farmland where he used to live in Myanmar, before he and thousands of Rohingya people like him fled persecution eight years ago. Here, amid the world’s largest refugee settlement with over 1.1 million refugees, space is tight and evergreen forests have paid the price. But families are combining NGO-funded farming projects with traditional Rohingya agroecology techniques to create agroforestry plots that are restoring land while helping refugees become self-sufficient in response to deep cuts in international food aid. “I feel so bad here as I have no land, but I am keeping my ancestors’ heritage alive. Growing these crops reminds me of the life we had in Myanmar. Here, life is difficult,” said Amina Khatun, a 58-year-old refugee living in Camp 1W, a sector of the sprawling settlement. Before the 2017 influx, Kutupalong refugee camp in Cox’s Bazar was a tropical evergreen forest, dominated by Dipterocarpus species, and sanctuary for endangered Asian elephants (Elephas maximus). To make way for the massive refugee settlements, the Bangladeshi government allocated roughly 2,500 hectares (6,100 acres) of protected forest land, and refugees and aid agencies cleared the vegetation to build shelters and provide firewood. Over 1,500 hectares of forest were cleared in total. The rain, with nowhere to soak in, ran straight down the slopes. Landslides became…This article was originally published on Mongabay

issues.summary: Nearly 120 residents of Vindoulou, a neighborhood in Pointe-Noire, Republic of Congo, have filed a civil claim before the city’s High Court in relation to pollution allegedly caused by a foundry. “We want tests, but also compensation for damages and losses,” Cyrille Traoré Ndembi, a plaintiff and president of the Vindoulou Residents’ Collective, which represents […]
issues.author: Elodie Toto
issues.content_html: Nearly 120 residents of Vindoulou, a neighborhood in Pointe-Noire, Republic of Congo, have filed a civil claim before the city’s High Court in relation to pollution allegedly caused by a foundry. “We want tests, but also compensation for damages and losses,” Cyrille Traoré Ndembi, a plaintiff and president of the Vindoulou Residents’ Collective, which represents people living in the working-class neighborhood, told Mongabay on the phone. The civil case, filed in October, is the latest in a series of actions taken against Metssa Congo, a foundry that opened in the neighborhood in 2013.The facility recycled, among other things, car batteries, extracting lead and turning it into lead bars for export. The plant is part of the Metssa Group, an industrial metals trading company based in the United Arab Emirates. The battery recycling process can pose serious health risks. According to the WHO, lead can be released in the form of fumes, particles and dust at every stage of the process, from draining and dismantling to smelting and refining. Environmental contamination from recycling can be substantial, exposing workers and nearby communities to significant levels of lead, the health agency says on its website. According to Traore Ndembi, residents of Vindoulou soon experienced this reality first-hand, complaining about toxic fumes coming from the plant. But for the Indigenous communities who call the Malaysian Borneo home—its forests, rivers and mountains hold a different kind of value. These forests are interconnected ecosystems that sustain communities with food, medicine […]
issues.author: Izzy Sasada
issues.content_html: What kind of wealth do Borneo’s ancient rainforests hold? Industries such as logging and palm oil have generated vast monetary wealth for some. But for the Indigenous communities who call the Malaysian Borneo home—its forests, rivers and mountains hold a different kind of value. These forests are interconnected ecosystems that sustain communities with food, medicine and livelihoods, while holding generations of knowledge, traditions and culture. But as industrial pressures continue to pressure these landscapes, some communities are working harder than ever to defend their homes and protect the ecological wealth that exists in these forests. issues.title: ‘Absolute fixing,' ‘understandable mistake’: Fans debate Sikandar Raza's controversial missed run-out in ILT20
issues.summary: Fans are split between "absolute fixing" and an "understandable mistake" after Sikandar Raza botched an easy run-out of Faf du Plessis in ILT20 2026.
issues.content_html:
‘Absolute fixing,' ‘understandable mistake’: Fans debate Sikandar Raza's controversial missed run-out in ILT20 originally appeared on Cricket News. Add Cricket News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

KEY TAKEAWAYS:

  • Sikandar Raza fumbled a simple run-out of Faf du Plessis in the ILT20 clash between Sharjah Warriorz and Dubai Capitals, and the clip quickly went viral.
  • Some fans called the sequence "absolute fixing" and tagged the ICC, while others argued Raza simply misjudged where the batter was.
  • Sharjah Warriorz won by seven wickets with 42 balls left, and the league has a history of viral moments that trigger fixing talk.

MORE: Pant record in away Tests: Is he India's best bet in SENA and overseas?

Viral video of Sikandar Raza botching easy Faf du Plessis run-out sparks fierce fan debate in ILT20

Sikandar Raza somehow failed to run out a stranded Faf du Plessis, and the fumble has divided cricket fans. The Sharjah Warriorz captain had plenty of time and the bails in front of him, yet the batter slid back to safety, and social media was soon arguing over whether it was a blunder or something more sinister.

The incident took place on the third ball of the sixth over of Dubai Capitals' innings, with Raza himself bowling to Max Holden. He delivered a slightly short ball outside off stump, and Holden pushed it towards cover. Du Plessis, the non-striker, had wandered well out of his crease at the bowler's end before he was sent back.

The fielder at cover threw the ball to Raza, who was standing at the non-striker's end, and Du Plessis was still far short of his ground. Raza gathered the throw cleanly and had ample time, but he didn't seem to notice the batter at first.

He then fumbled twice while trying to remove the bails, and only broke the stumps after du Plessis had dived back in. Holden also made a desperate dive at the other end and appeared to hurt his shoulder.

MORE: Bumrah goes wicketless: India pacer's third-longest drought by overs has fans worried

Fans split over Sikandar Raza's missed run-out in ILT20

A few fans described it as "pathetic and shameful" and tagged the ICC, asking how an experienced international captain could take so long with the ball in hand and miss the stumps twice.

"Absolute Fixing by Sikandar Raza." – @theFaizFazel

@ILT20Official Absolute Fixing by Sikandar Raza.

— Faiz Fazel (@theFaizFazel) November 27, 2026

Another account went further and suggested the governing body should step in.

"Please ban the whole league @ICC" – @_StrangerMan7

@ILT20Official Please ban the whole league @ICC

— StrangerMan (@_StrangerMan7) November 27, 2026

A third user chose to criticise the tournament itself rather than the player.

"Already this league standards questionable" – @Cric_Venky.

@ILT20Official Already this league standards questionable

— Venky. (@Cric_Venky) November 27, 2026

Plenty of supporters took the opposite view and pointed to Raza's body language. Their argument was that he had his back turned and his eyes on the striker's end, expecting the throw to go there, so he realised only a split second later that du Plessis was stranded at his end.

"Everyone saying this is fixing, I don't think Soo , there's clearly visible that Skindar Raza is not watching the batsman he thinks batter will reach the ground . It's just a mistake happen with everyone." – @cricket__room.

Everyone saying this is fixing, I don't think Soo , there's clearly visible that Skindar Raza is not watching the batsman he thinks batter will reach the ground . It's just a mistake happen with everyone. #ILT20 https://t.co/hCfukRxrU5

— Cricket Room (@cricket__room) November 27, 2026

Another user made a similar case, saying no bowler in that position would keep watching the batter.

"People calling this match fixing. He very obviously sensed that the batsman had already dived and did not see that the dive was short of the crease. No bowler in his place will ever watch the batsman. Very understandable mistake." – @bhavapuritwink.

@ILT20Official People calling this match fixing. He very obviously sensed that the batsman had already dived and did not see that the dive was short of the crease. No bowler in his place will ever watch the batsman. Very understandable mistake.

— ENE Repeat’s greatest hypeman (@bhavapuritwink) November 28, 2026

Previous ILT20 controversies that fuel fixing talk

Raza’s run-out fumble is hardly the first viral ILT20 moment to send social media into overdrive. In December 2025, Nicholas Pooran of MI Emirates deliberately declined to stump a struggling Max Holden, who was on 42 off 36 balls, and Desert Vipers retired Holden out on the next delivery before winning by one run. Both moves were legal, but fans still cried match-fixing.

In January 2025, Gulf Giants coach Andy Flower gestured angrily from the dugout after Tom Curran was given out in a dead-ball run-out dispute, which pushed Pooran into withdrawing his appeal in a match Gulf Giants won off the last ball.

MORE: 'He was off balance' - Ashwin criticises Pant for dropping Mitchell

In January 2026, Abu Dhabi Knight Riders captain Jason Holder slipped in his delivery stride and sent a ball sailing over the batter's head to near fourth slip. It was ruled a height no-ball caused by sweaty hands, yet it drew heavy mockery.

Just a day before Raza's miss, Sunil Narine walked off retired out after a 17th-over maiden against Rashid Khan, without consulting his partner or the dugout, while chasing 208.

Part of the reason social media jumps to corruption claims is that the UAE also hosts lower-tier events such as the Abu Dhabi T10, which has faced several ICC Anti-Corruption Unit investigations and bans. Fans often lump viral fielding lapses, strange no-balls and tactical retirements in the ILT20 together with those cases, even when there's no sign of an integrity breach.

issues.title: POSTGAME THOUGHTS: Despite defensive showing, Aggies come up short in season finale vs Texas
issues.summary: Half of a team simply isn’t enough
issues.content_html:
I’ll give them this: This version of Texas A&M was much more watchable than what we saw for the vast majority of the season. But ultimately, the result was the same, as Texas did just enough to stave off the Aggies and secure a 16-6 win over the Aggies Saturday night in College Station.

The Aggie defense came to play, refusing to surrender a first down on each of the first two drives, but a muffed punt meant that Texas still struck first with a long field goal to go up 3-0. The Aggies would then somewhat inexplicably choose to punt when they had a 4th and 3 in Texas territory, then watch the Longhorns go on an 88-yard touchdown drive to take a 10-0 lead early in the second quarter. You’d be forgiven if you assumed at that point that this game was gonna get really ugly. It certainly felt like it could have gone that way. But the Aggie defense continued to be stingy, and Brady Hart and the A&M offense put together a couple chunk plays to set up a long David Olano field goal just before halftime.

Both offenses would struggle in the second half, with the only real TD threat from either side being foiled by Arch Manning throwing a goal line interception to A&M S Tawfiq Byard. But Texas would finally kick a field goal to go up 16-6, and once that happened, it was church. Despite it staying a one-score game until halfway though the fourth quarter, it never really felt like A&M was a serious threat to win this game. That’s what happens when you have a historically bad offense.

What was good?

To his credit, A&M QB Brady Hart looked solid, if unspectacular, in his second career start. He didn’t turn the ball over, and was able to find open receivers (and deliver the ball to them) on a consistent basis. In both completion percentage and yardage, he outdid his debut in Norman a week ago. It wasn’t enough to win, but it was enough that we never really saw much of Marcel Reed in a game where both were expected to play. It was also enough to continue to wonder why it took so long for Hart to get a look when Marcel looked so utterly lost this entire season. There’s a good chance neither of them are taking snaps for A&M next season, but that’s a conversation for another day.

The defense, like it had for a good chunk of the season, looked good. At times great. But it’s hard when the offense refuses to play any semblance of complementary football. Texas had 2.9 yards per carry. Arch Manning had only 4.2 yards per attempt. Texas finished 15.5 points below their season average. It’s hard to have any particular critique of the defense, other than that they weren’t capable of winning the game all by themselves.

This sounds like a cope, but the environment and the interactions between these fanbases is so great to have back in our lives, even in a losing effort. I hate losing to Texas, but I hated not playing them for over a decade even more. It’s part of the fabric of college football, and it never should have gone away to begin with.

What’s next?

Heck if I know, but I sure hope Mike Elko does. Obviously you assume that staff changes are coming on the offensive side of the ball. Likely massive ones. And it certainly seems like QB is a position you will need to solve in the transfer portal. After an exceedingly frustrating season, that should at least make for a very entertaining December.

But man, what a slog this season proved to be. Pound for pound, maybe the most disappointing season in my time as an A&M fan, when you look at what they did relative to the preseason expectations. Which is really saying something, considering how many times we’ve failed to meet preseason expectations. The catastrophic failure of this season’s team is a huge chink in Mike Elko’s armor, so now it’s his job to fix it. Whether it’s coaches, players, processes, culture, or some combination of all of it, is something that only those inside that building truly know. But we certainly now enter a pivotal time in his tenure. Let’s hope he has what it takes to right the ship, because this year’s ship was oh so wrong.

#BTHOoffseason (sobs into a maroon pillow)

issues.title: Jay football heading to FHSAA Independent League championship
issues.summary: Jay football will play for its first FHSAA championship next week after beating Mount Dora Christian in the Independent League semifinals.
issues.content_html:
For the first time in school history, Jay football will play for an FHSAA championship.

The Royals will play for the Independent League B championship after stomping Mount Dora Christian 37-12 in Mount Dora on Nov. 27.

Jay (10-2) will play South regional champion Melbourne Holy Trinity (10-2) in the Independent League B Championship on Dec. 4 at 6 p.m. CT at The Range at H.G. Morse Stadium at the Villages Charter School in Sumterville.

Holy Trinity Episcopal Academy beat Lakeland Santa Fe Catholic 38-14 in the South regional final.

The Royals traveled over 400 miles for this Final Four game but didn't appear to be hindered by the long road trip.

Jaylen Youngblood ran for a touchdown in the first quarter, then Jaymes Youngblood ran for the two-point conversion. Jaylen Youngblood found Tanner Mandell for a 35-yard touchdown in the second quarter, then Jaymes Youngblood ran in the two-point conversion again for a 16-0 lead.

Jaymes Youngblood ran for his lone touchdown of the night in the third quarter for a 22-0 lead before Mount Dora Christian answered with its only touchdown of the night to get on the board.

Submit your athlete's top plays for our new Play of the Month series

Cam Pierce ran for a four-yard touchdown followed by a Jaymes Youngblood two-point conversion later in the quarter, then Bryson Morris added an exclamation point with a pick-6 in the final frame.

The win continued Jay's dominant postseason run, having outscored its three postseason opponents by a combined score of 128-24. The Royals nine non-forfeit wins have all been by double digits and they've outscored at least 24 points and given up 14 points or less in every one.

When Jay decided to opt out of playing in the FHSAA State Championship Series in January, the Royals did so because they were tired of the perceived inequities between Rural division schools, believing the top teams in the class were recruiting and bring in transfers to create an unfair playing field.

They initially want to move into the Sunshine State Athletic Association Atlantic League, but decided to go back to the FHSAA and join the inaugural Independent League after concerns about the former's playoff structure.

Now after an uncertain offseason, Jay will get the chance to compete for a championship next week.

issues.title: Grizzlies top Timberwolves 114-109 to win NBA Cup West Group B
issues.summary: MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — Cedric Coward scored 22 points, Javon Small tied a season high with 19 points off the bench, and the Memphis Grizzlies won the NBA Cup West Group B on Friday with a 114-109 win over the Minnesota Timberwolves.Ty Jerome added 18 points and Cam Spencer 16 for the Grizzlies, winners in eight of their past nine games.
issues.author: MIKE COOK
issues.content_html:
MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — Cedric Coward scored 22 points, Javon Small tied a season high with 19 points off the bench, and the Memphis Grizzlies won the NBA Cup West Group B on Friday with a 114-109 win over the Minnesota Timberwolves.

Ty Jerome added 18 points and Cam Spencer 16 for the Grizzlies, winners in eight of their past nine games.

Ayo Dosunmu led Minnesota with 27 points and eight assists.

Jonathan Kuminga scored 19 points and Bones Hyland had 16 off the bench for the Timberwolves, whoh made just 14 of 23 free throws. Minnesota entered the game shooting a league-worst 69.6% from the line.

Already without the injured Anthony Edwards, Minnesota played without top guard LaMelo Ball, who sprained his left ankle in Wednesday’s win at Oklahoma City and is considered day to day. Ball is averaging 17.3 points per game and a team-high 5.7 assists.

Coward and Spencer scored seven points in a 21-6 Memphis surge to start the fourth quarter for a 99-87 lead with less than seven minutes to play.

A pair of steals and layups by Dosunmu cut the deficit to 109-105 with 31 seconds left, but the Timberwolves got no closer.

Memphis center Zach Edey, who left Wednesday’s game in the first half due to left ankle soreness, started and scored five points in 12 minutes before fouling out.

Down by 14 late in the first half, Minnesota started the third quarter on a 26-11 run for a 76-72 lead, capped by Kuminga's transition dunk after a block by Joan Beringer of a Small drive.

Jaden McDaniels scored 13 points for Minnesota before fouling out. He scored 91 points combined in his previous three games.

Up Next

Grizzlies: Home against the Los Angeles Lakers on Sunday.

Timberwolves: At Sacramento on Sunday to start a three-game road trip.

issues.title: 'It's always sour to lose' admits Tibor Del Grosso after going second to Thibau Nys in Ostrava at World Cup opener
issues.summary: Former U23 Cyclo-cross World Champion confirms he will compete on a full schedule of 12 CX World Cup races for another try at elite world title in Oostende
issues.author: Ben Goddard
issues.content_html:
Tibor Del Grosso (Alpecin-Premier Tech) continued his search for a maiden elite World Cup victory, finishing a close runner-up on his cyclo-cross return on Friday at Ostrava in the Czech Republic.

The 23-year-old was battling for victory on the last lap with rival Thibau Nys (Baloise Verzekeringen-Het Poetsbureau Lions), but came out second best in the first duel of the season between the pair.

Del Grosso said that he felt ‘sour’ losing to his Belgian rival after conceding the lead and failing to regain the front position in the snow during the final corners, while Nys stayed on the firmer ground.

“I don't think it was a bad performance, if you're close to winning. Of course, it's always sour to lose,” said Del Grosso afterwards to organisers.

“It was just a matter of having the lead and keeping the lead going into the last corner, at some point Thibau [Nys] came with quite some speed. I felt like there were some opportunities after, to still overtake him, but then I waited maybe a bit too long.

“The bit towards the final corner, there was only really one path where you could ride in. I tried to overtake, didn't really go anywhere.”

The Alpecin-Premier Tech rider burst onto the elite cyclo-cross scene last season by beating Wout van Aert in a dramatic sprint finish in the Superprestige at Heusden-Zolder. He then won the Dutch national championship and was runner-up at UCI Cyclo-cross World Championships to Mathieu van der Poel. While he didn't overtake Van der Poel in his first try as an elite, he did finish one spot ahead of Nys, who was third.

Del Grosso announced that he will ride 13 races this cyclo-cross season – all of the 12 World Cup rounds and the World Championships in Oostend.

Last season the Dutchman came into his first elite season from the under-23 ranks and finished 14th in his opening race at the World Cup round at Namur in mid-December. Before racing in Ostrava, the 23-year-old joked that a 13th place finish Friday would be an improvement of last year's first race.

“I think a lot of people think about my [cyclo-cross] races from last season,” said Del Grosso. “Last year I also needed some time to get into it. I didn’t prepare to be here in my best shape.”

Del Grosso looked comfortable on the slippery terrain in Ostrava and was able to follow Nys before putting his rival under pressure in the final laps.

“I have mixed feelings, I can be quite happy with my race today. The feeling was not yet where it was supposed to be. It was a really tactical race with how the course was. I think I played it relatively well, but then the final two minutes was not perfect," he reflected.

“I don't think it was a bad performance. Technically, I think it's a good 'cross. Some points for improvement, but also not crazy. A lot better than last year.”

Del Grosso competed on the road this season with Alpecin-Premier Tech and won the NXT Classic in April then adding 14th in Amstel Gold Race. The Dutchman took a two-month break following his last road race in the Flandrien Classic and National Coach Gerben de Knegt believed that it has allowed the youngster to ‘rest and train well’.

He told Wielerflits: "His road season has been somewhat disappointing for various reasons. He rested well and trained well. In other years, he also started the [cyclo-cross] season quite quickly after his road campaign.

“Now he is better prepared because he has been able to train for more weeks between the end of the road season and the start of his cyclo-cross winter.”

issues.title: Bad luck for Lucinda Brand with mechanical issues in snowy opening round of cyclo-cross World Cup in Ostrava
issues.summary: World Champion was one of several riders struggling to clip into pedals during the wintry conditions
issues.author: Ben Goddard
issues.content_html:
Cyclo-cross world champion Lucinda Brand and her podium rivals suffered mechanical problems in freezing conditions at the opening UCI Cyclo-cross World Cup round in Ostrava on Friday evening.

The picturesque venue was a step into the unknown, with the Czech Republic hosting its first-ever World Cup event.

While the snow and Christmas lights made for a unique setting at the former coal mine venue, the frozen surface and deep ruts made for dangerous conditions. The evening race saw temperatures drop below freezing, and Brand was one of several casualties of the frozen ground.

At the halfway point, Brand was fighting in the top 10 before she couldn't clip into her pedals, a problem that many riders suffered during the elite women's and elite men's race.

For the Baloise Verzekeringen-Het Poetsbureau Lions rider, though, she was left frustrated and shouting at her pit crew as they desperately tried to solve the issue from the pits.

Brand then lost over a minute and couldn't regain the time in the difficult conditions, finishing 15th and 2:25 behind race winner Marie Schreiber (SD Worx–Protime).

Brand was not the only rider to struggle with her equipment, as race winner Schreiber and third-placed finisher Manon Bakker were both forced to change bikes due to frozen pedals.

Despite having technical issues of her own, Bakker was hoping for more snow as the cyclo-cross World Cup continues in Tabor on Sunday.

“I made too many mistakes to really get into the win. I think everybody struggled with their pedals, I couldn’t clip in at all. I had a mechanical with my first bike and had to change, which is where I lost quite a lot of time," Bakker said.

“I came back, but that was it. I'd rather hope for more snow (at Tabor on Sunday). I think I'm the only one who was really smiling at the weather.”

It was Brand’s first outing in these snow conditions after missing previous World Cup rounds in Val di Sole.

“We haven’t had too often the chance for it,” said Brand on the snow conditions before the opening World Cup round. “I missed the World Cups in Val di Sole. This is something different again as there is not as much snow everywhere [on the course itself].”

Brand won the overall cyclo-cross World Cup series last year after sweeping the opening seven rounds in a commanding season.

However, this season the Dutch woman has found racing much closer and was beaten on two occasions last weekend by Sara Casasola. In the second of those races, Brand fell heavily at the X2O 'cross in Beringen and commented about suffering rib pain afterwards.

"My rib hurts a little. I now have to breathe well and calmly," Brand said. “It needs to heal again. It remains to be seen how this will develop in the coming days. You can do nothing but wait and let it recover.”

Brand won the World Cup overall by 97 points ahead of Aniek Van Alphen (777TV CX Team). However, with Van Alphen finishing runner-up in Ostrava, the pressure is on the two-time World Champion as they head to the second round in Tabor on Sunday.

issues.title: World Cup Ostrava: Thibau Nys surges ahead of Tibor Del Grosso to triumph in elite men's snowy first round
issues.summary: Michael Vanthourenhout takes third as Cameron Mason settles for fourth
issues.author: Jackie Tyson
issues.content_html:
Reigning European champion Thibau Nys (Baloise Verzekeringen-Het Poetsbureau Lions) held off Dutch champion Tibor Del Grosso (Alpecin-Premier Tech) on the final corner and won the opening round of the UCI Cyclo-cross World Cup in Ostrava, Czech Republic.

Michael Vanthourenhout (Pauwels Sauzen-Altez Industriebouw Cycling Team) then nabbed the final spot on the podium with a final push through blowing snow ahead of of Cameron Mason (777tv CX Team) in fourth and Jente Michels (Alpecin-Premier Tech) in fifth.

Nys continued his string of victories, dominating the X2O Trofee series with a trio of wins this month and taking the ’cross continental title.

"It was a really difficult one, but I think it's in my top three of most beautiful cyclo-cross victories. I think the fans, the atmosphere, the chorus, the snow makes it one to remember," Nys told broadcasters at the finish.

Nys let out a loud scream as he crossed the line, only able to drop Del Grosso in the final 200 metres with a more powerful sprint. Nys admitted he overcame two slow leaks and pitted for a fresh bike twice, then used "good technique" to seal the victory.

"I had two flat tyres, so it kept pushing me a little bit back. I didn't lose a lot because it [tyre pressure] was slowly going out, but it kept pushing me a bit out of the race. And then when I found my way to the front, I tried to make a move and push hard. Then on the last lap, I managed it perfectly and did a good sprint," he noted.

"I was feeling way, way better than the last two weekends, just physically. But then of course you come here on a circuit where it's difficult to release the full power, so the fact that I can finish it off like this is a proof that my cyclo-cross skills are still there."

Hot laps in cold temperatures

The World Cup season opened with two rounds in Czechia, the elite fields competing Friday in Ostrava in the only night races of the 12-round series. Floodlights illuminated a blanket of snow covering the venue, with the temperature holding steady for most of the afternoon at -1°C, but the wind chill making it feel five degrees colder.

Niels Vandeputte (Alpecin-Premier Tech Development) put on the power beside Nys from the start and took the front spot on the twisty course. Vanthourenhout and Del Grosso then led the long line of riders through the first pass of the finish line, riding in 6:36, which was the slowest lap of the nine.

There were narrow ruts instead of mud from the elite women’s race as the temperatures remained below freezing, and holiday lights sprinkled around the circuit. Amid the sounds of cowbells and cheers, the ringing of disc brakes was heard with constant speed changes as the track was slippery.

On the start of lap three, Gerben Kuypers (Pauwels Sauzen-Altez Industriebouw) took the lead ahead of Del Grosso and Pauwels teammate Vanthourenhout as small gaps began to form in the field of 75 riders.

At the mid-point of the contest, 10 riders settled in at the front - Del Grosso between the Pauwels Sauzen duo of Kuypers and Nieuwenhuis, then Vanthourenhout, Nys, Kuypers, Jent Michels, Yordi Corsus, Witse Meeussen, Felipe Orts and Cameron Mason.

It was Nys who drove the pace at the front to start the sixth and seventh laps, the second time carving a gap of five seconds to chasers across the stairs. However, he had to slow to bang one foot on the pedal to clear debris from his cleat and it was game-on again. Dutch ’cross champion Del Grosso, Vanthourenhout, Kuypers, Michels and Mason made it to his back wheel, but others were distanced for good.

On the final lap, Del Grosso took command at the front with Nys glued to his wheel, Vanthourenhout third and Mason in fourth. In a corner, Vanthourenhout dove to the front of the lead trio and held the position into the tricky descent from the stairs, while Nys made a pass of Del Grosso to nab second position.

With the wind blowing light snow, Del Grosso and Nys went back into the front positions, Vanthourenhout losing momentum in a corner before the barriers. Nys made the pass before the short steps feature and drove the sprint to the line and keep his winning streak alive.

issues.title: 'Bring great bike racing to the people' - Two events debut at USA CRITS for seven races compressed across 22 days in 2027
issues.summary: Tour of Newport News Criterium replaces Sunny King Criterium as opening race in early April
issues.author: Jackie Tyson
issues.content_html:
The Tour of Newport News Criterium and Charlotte Criterium make debuts in the USA CRITS series in 2027, with the compact collection of seven one-day races now spanning 22 days for overall elite rider and team titles, condensing the calendar by a full month.

In its 18th season, with races clustered in four states of the Mid-Atlantic and Southeast regions, the series opener will take place in Newport News, Virginia, on April 10. The finale is set for the High Line Criterium in Suwanee, Georgia, on May 1.

In between, regular stops at Athens Orthopedic Clinic Twilight Criterium, Winston Salem Cycling Classic, Greenville Cycling Classic and Spartanburg Criterium, all return from previous years. The biggest changes see Sunny King Criterium in Alabama off the schedule and the Winston-Salem, North Carolina race moving from a late-May slot to April 24.

Noticeably absent from the calendar is the Sunny King Criterium, which had been the lead-off event the past three seasons. Anniston has hosted races for state age-group championships as well as collegiate conference championships and organisers will continue to hold two days of racing for a 25th edition April 10-11.

“Nearly 20 years after launching the series, we're still bringing the best riders in the country to communities that embrace the excitement of professional cycling," Gene Dixon, founder of Athens Twilight Criterium and owner of Swagger LLC that produces USA CRITS, said in a press release.

"When we started Athens Twilight in 1980, the idea was simple: bring great bike racing to the people. USA CRITS was built on that same philosophy."

Dixon told Cyclingnews that the compact calendar helped simplify travel for riders and teams, especially those traveling from outside the US. While the final set of three races continue to conflict for some teams with Tour of the Gila, April 28-May 2, the earlier finish for the criterium series opens travel for all teams to compete at Tour de Bloom, May 12-16. Also a postivite is that the USA CRITS calendar does not bump into rushed travel to Washington, D.C. for the Amazon Armed Forces Cycling Classic, now early June.

All USA CRITS races will provide live streaming, produced by Swagger. Last year's prize purse totalled $200,000, with equal payouts for elite men and women across individual races and overall series classifications. The USA CRITS D1 Team programme also returns in 2027, with eligible teams provided travel stipends.

The Tour of Newport News is a three-day, five-race event that takes place on the Virginia Peninsula, on the banks of the Hampton Roads harbor near the Atlantic Ocean. USA Cycling-sanctioned events that comprise the omnium include a points race at Todd Stadium, a hill climb up an eight-story parking garage, a time trial and two criteriums. Only the Newport News Twilight Criterium, under the street lights on Saturday night, will set the standings for USA CRITS on Saturday, April 10.

The Charlotte Criterium is a new race that takes place on Friday, April 23, the night before the Winston Salem Cycling Classic. Specifics about the location of the course and start times will be confirmed in the coming months.

Ireland’s quality told in the end. Back-to-back victories to finish the year would have been a tonic for a much-criticised Wallabies team and while they started strongly, they were ultimately outclassed. They have lost seven matches in a row against Ireland: there was a time when such a statistic would have been unimaginable.

Sam Prendergast kicked brilliantly, off the tee and from hand, to orchestrate a success that was a classic Irish blend of power and finesse. The fly-half scored 13 points off the tee and his tactical kicking was world-class too. Two Ireland victories against the Wallabies have come in the Nations Championship and this was more one-sided than the 33-31 thriller in July.

Wesley Fofana, as a former Leicester player, might have expected the celebrating Nottingham Forest fans to give him a hard time. But, at the end of a week in which he invited opprobrium by making light of missing a penalty at Liverpool in an unsanctioned French interview, he endured the ultimate ignominy when Chelsea supporters followed a four-letter suggestion to tell the defender: “You’re not welcome here.”

Fofana was humiliated by Liam Delap before fouling the former Chelsea striker for a penalty that Morgan Gibbs-White converted for the first of his two goals. The result, coming after Forest’s win against Manchester City in their last match at the City Ground, means they climb three points clear of the Premier League’s relegation zone.

A sensational start for the Italian was swiftly followed by a dismal run and long faces in the team

This is the great known unknown in Manchester City’s run of one win – in addition to victory on penalties against Brighton in the Carabao Cup – in seven matches. After guilty verdicts were returned regarding the breaking of Premier League financial rules, Enzo Maresca’s team went to Anfield and handed Liverpool a 3-0 schooling. Yet this proved the falsest of dawns, with Andoni Iraola’s nascent side perhaps caught in a bad moment. City have since managed one league victory (3-2 over Ipswich, six days later) and two more wins in regulation time (in the Champions League) in 10 matches. The sequence includes one point from the past four league fixtures. Maresca argues that his, too, is an embryonic project so there will be uneven form. “I am not a magician,” he said on Friday. But it is also fair to ponder whether, after the adrenaline surge of an us-against-the-world mentality carried City to the Liverpool and Ipswich wins, the grim reality of what the guilty verdict may mean for careers is affecting players. City have appealed against the ruling, saying they are “innocent of the accusations”.

Offer England’s players a choice between a cut-price “Black Friday” deal and another super soaraway All Black Saturday and this week’s answer is unanimous. This may be an opportune moment to snap up pre-Christmas bargains on the high street but Maro Itoje and his side are rather more intent on securing a priceless little chunk of history.

Never before in 121 years have England’s men beaten New Zealand in three consecutive Tests and the last time their opponents lost six times in a calendar year was back in 1949. During that distant annus horribilis the All Blacks ended up contesting simultaneous Test series against South Africa and Australia and lost them both; this time around there would be no such asterisk.
