issues.author: Dan Maccarone
issues.content_html:
We have always tried to build things that outlast whatever comes next. AI makes that impossible. The solution is the opposite of what you think.

When creating products, the goal is often to try and future-proof it.

Create a tool that won’t be obsolete in a few years. Learn the skill the machines can’t take.

Build the architecture flexible enough to survive whatever comes next.

Draw the roadmap that still makes sense down the line.

It’s been the sensible approach for decades, the thing you do so you’re not betting the company on something that could kill. That’s an understandable fear. S. Patrick Viguerie and his colleagues at Innosight actually found the average lifespan of a company on the S&P 500 has collapsed from sixty-one years in the late 1950s to under twenty, with roughly half the index expected to turn over within a decade.

The thing you bet on really does die faster than it used to.

But to be frank, that mentality just doesn’t work anymore. Future-proofing was always a bet that you could see far enough ahead to build toward it, and the speed at which AI is evolving how we create things, how we interact with things, how we collaborate with AI itself, has made that bet impossible to win.

France found this out the hard way almost a hundred years ago. After the First World War they built the Maginot Line, a wall of concrete and guns along the German border so strong no army could punch through it. It was the most future-proofed thing on the planet. Then the Germans drove around it, through the forest everyone swore tanks couldn’t cross, and took France in six weeks.

The wall worked exactly as designed, but the strategy of the warfare outsmarted it.

Future-proofing has the same flaw. You take your known experience and armor up against a war you can picture, but in reality, the war goes in a completely different direction.

In a slower era you at least got years between building the wall and watching someone flank it. In our age of AI those years are gone.

When ChatGPT reached a hundred million users in two months, UBS analysts said they could not recall a faster ramp in twenty years of watching the internet, outpacing the nine months it took TikTok and the two and a half years for Instagram.

The situation gets worse, because we are no longer trying to predict just one thing that could change in the industry or technology or user habits. We are trying to predict three, all at once, all moving, all being shoved faster by the same technology.

The tech you build on.

The people you build for.

The company itself that you’re building.

Every one of them is a moving target, and future-proofing asks that we hit all three while they are in motion while we are standing on a platform that is moving too.

Let’s take them one at a time.

The tool you bet on is already dead

If we start with examining how companies rely on technology, it’s easy to see that people still pick the proven, well-funded, widely-used option because it seems like a safe bet.

Scott Brinker calls this Martec’s Law. Technology changes exponentially, and organizations change logarithmically. One curve shoots up, the other crawls, and the gap between what the tech can do and what your company can absorb gets wider every year.

Brinker was writing about marketing software, but the idea holds with where we are in the world of AI, and underneath that is Ray Kurzweil’s old observation that technology compounds on itself, each generation building on the last, so the pace does not just increase, the increase increases.

Patrick Neeman wrote a piece arguing the Double Diamond, the design process half the industry has leaned on for twenty years, is dead for software. His reasoning around this is what’s useful here, that the process was not wrong. The process was built for a world where making something was expensive and slow, so you spent a lot of time up front making sure you built the right thing before you committed. Then the cost of building a working prototype dropped from a two-week sprint to an afternoon.

One input fell by two orders of magnitude in under two years, and a process built on the way of working and pricing it survived into a world where that cost was no longer reasonable.

Future-proofing works exactly the same way. You pick the durable thing, the proven process, the safe stack, the tool with the big company behind it, because it feels like it will last, but that idea that it will continue to last is an illusion. Today, the thing that made it the right call at the time, the economics underneath it, is exactly what AI keeps disrupting.

Underneath all of this is a more straightforward problem. Future-proofing is a prediction, and people are famously terrible at prediction. Philip Tetlock spent decades studying expert forecasters, the people whose entire job is to see what is coming, and found they were barely better than chance, and sometimes worse than a crude rule of thumb.

These are the best-informed people in any room, and the future still makes fools of them regularly. Now hand that same impossible task to a product team and ask them to pick the tool that will still be right in three years, in the fastest technology shift any of us have worked through.

That’s just setting people up for failure where there are legit stakes.

The customer you designed for just changed on you

Let’s say you somehow beat the odds on the technology. You picked a stack or product that kept its place in the ranks of software. You still have the second problem.

AI is rewiring your user faster than you can build for them.

Think about what AI has done to the simplest thing a customer does, which is look for something. For twenty years, searching meant typing words into a box and scanning a page of blue links. People built entire companies, careers, and content strategies on that one stable behavior.

Natasha Sommerfeld and her team at Bain found that a large share of searches now end without anyone clicking through to a website at all, and that number climbs higher once AI starts answering the question directly instead of pointing at ten places that might.

The behavior that a generation of products was designed around is evaporating because of a technology most of those products never even considered.

It is not just search. Elizabeth Silliman and her colleagues at McKinsey surveyed around twenty-one thousand people about how they shop and found more than half already using AI somewhere in the process, with the behavior, in their words, shifting as fast as adoption itself, faster than the companies serving those customers can keep up.

The Capgemini Research Institute ran the same kind of study two years running, which is the useful part, because the year-over-year jump shows you the speed. This is not a new normal you can design for and settle into. It is a moving line.

Invoca, which sells software to marketers, found the share of people using a generative AI tool to research a serious purchase went from forty-one percent to fifty-eight percent in a single year. Among older buyers it tripled.

Imagine building a product around how your customer behaves, shipping it, and discovering that in the time it took to build, a third of them started researching an entirely different way. You tried to do everything right, but behavior just shifted to fast.

It doesn’t get better.

Lingxiu Dong, Kaiwen Luo, and Fasheng Xu studied what happens as people hand shopping over to AI agents, and found the scarce thing stops being the search and becomes the ability to say what you actually want, clearly enough for an agent to go get it. The whole shape of the interaction changes.

The thing you optimized, helping someone browse and compare, is not even the job anymore and, frighteningly, what you should have been designing for did not even exist when you started designing it in the first place.

This is the trap of the user you think you know. You do the research, you identify the behaviors, you ship the thing that fits who you think your audience is. By the time it hits the market, though, AI has given people a whole new set of habits and a new set of expectations that no longer fits.

Henry Ford supposedly said that if he had asked people what they wanted, they would have said a faster horse. The modern version is worse. Ask people what they want, and by the time you build it, the question itself has changed, because the thing answering their questions changed them while you tried to answer the original one.

The org chart you built is the thing slowing you down

Keeping it going, let’s assume you somehow future-proofed the tech and kept up with the customer (well done!). There is still a third thing you cannot pin down, and it is your own company.

Every org is built around a set of assumptions about how work gets done.

Who owns what.

Who hands off to whom.

Which role exists to coordinate, which to decide, which to make the thing.

You draw that structure to be stable, because stability is the point of a structure. The moment AI changes how the work actually happens, that carefully drawn stability becomes the thing you have to fight.

Remember Scott Brinker’s philosophy that technology moves exponentially and organizations move logarithmically. The org is the slow curve by design, and the slowness you built on purpose, the clear roles, the defined ownership, the approval chain, is exactly what cannot bend when the fast curve jumps.

A design leader I know has been watching the traditional product owner role dissolve in his very large organization, because the work that justified it, coordinating the handoffs, chasing the status, translating requirements between teams, is precisely the work AI and a good design process now absorb.

The experience is the product, he told me, and the people who understand the experience can own it end to end. So where does that leave the role built to coordinate it? The hardest thing to change, he said, is not the work. It is that the taxonomy of roles is what funds the roles.

The org chart is not just how work flows. It is how budgets, titles, and headcount are justified. You cannot just delete a box on it, because someone’s job, someone’s comp, someone’s sense of what they are, is inside that box.

It’s not just him, research backs it up. Sam Ransbotham and his colleagues at MIT Sloan found that AI only delivers real gains when companies redesign the work around it, the roles, the workflows, the decision rights, and that where the structure stays frozen, AI just gets absorbed into the old process and changes nothing.

This is an old idea in organizational theory. Michael Hannan and John Freeman called it structural inertia, the tendency of roles, processes, and reporting lines to persist long after the conditions that created them are gone. The structure outlives its own reason for existing, and everyone keeps staffing it anyway.

Wolfgang Rohde, in a paper on AI and organizational capability, points out that companies discover the value of human judgment right after they have cut the roles that produced it. You optimize the org chart for the work AI can do, you thin out the people who caught the problems and trained the next ones, and then the first time something genuinely novel breaks, you find you removed the exact capacity you needed to handle it.

The future-proofed org is not just slow. It is brittle in a way you cannot see until it is tested.

Most companies are using AI to get better at things they already do, inside the structure they already have. David M. Rothschild and his colleagues at Microsoft Research call this choosing optimization over reinvention, because it is safer and easier to make the current machine a little faster than to admit the machine is the wrong shape.

The structure you built to protect the future becomes the single biggest reason you cannot meet it.

Stop armoring. Start moving.

All three of these problems end up having same answer. Stop trying to predict the future and lean into moving with it.

Trying to future-proof is no longer possible, so strategize and build to respond instead.

The most direct approach to this of this came from Jeff Bezos, years before the AI wave, in a letter to Amazon shareholders. He split decisions into two kinds. Some are one-way doors, irreversible, and those you make slowly and carefully, because you cannot walk back through them. Most decisions are two-way doors. You can walk through, see what is on the other side, and come back if you were wrong.

His warning was that as companies get bigger, they start treating every decision like a one-way door, applying the slow, heavy, careful process to choices that are easily undone, and they grind to a halt. Future-proofing is the one-way-door mindset applied to a world made almost entirely of two-way doors. You are deliberating like the choice is permanent when the whole advantage available to you is that it is not.

Nassim Taleb conceived a whole book around this posture. He called it being antifragile, designing things that gain from disorder instead of trying to predict and prevent it. A fragile thing needs the future to arrive exactly as forecast. An antifragile thing gets stronger when the future shows up weird, because it was built to absorb surprise rather than to bet against it.

Future-proofing is a bet that the future behaves. The reality is that now we have to build things, teams, and careers that do better precisely because it will not.

It is worth noticing that Brinker himself, the one who named the gap, never prescribed better prediction as the fix. His advice for living with Martec’s Law was to choose selectively which changes you take on, stay agile enough to move, and every so often reset your whole approach at an inflection point instead of defending the old one.

He never says get better at predicting. He spent his career proving companies can’t keep pace with the tech, and his answer is to stop trying to.

In practice this is less exotic than it sounds. David Hoang frames it as stop thinking of the work as a factory, a machine that turns a fixed input into a fixed output, and start thinking of it as a garden, something you cultivate and adjust as it grows and as conditions change.

A factory built for one product is worthless when the product changes. A garden just gets replanted.

When you do have to commit, Sundeep Misra points at the one thing worth being sure of, which is not the tool or the plan but the decision underneath it. The scarce skill in all of this is knowing what is actually worth building, so that when everything around it moves, you still know why you are moving.

Responding does not mean acting on every piece of feedback you receive. That sort of reaction can thrash the product to death and burn out your team. The important thing is to filter feedback based on the source and the perspective and real knowledge behind it.

Everyone has an opinion. The ones worth listening to are the informed ones, with genuine expertise and the right context. I tell founders this constantly. I will not weigh in on your code, because I am not the expert there, and my opinion should carry no weight with you on that topic, but when it comes to user experience or patterns around process, things I’ve seen a thousand times, then my opinion is valid.

This is just as true for you as it is for your company. You cannot future-proof yourself as an employee either, for the same reason. The specific skill you are banking on, the tool you mastered, the process you are known for, is exactly the thing AI commoditizes first.

The World Economic Forum estimates that 39 percent of workers’ core skills will be transformed or outdated between 2025 and 2030. Hoarding one skill and hoping it lasts is the personal version of the Maginot Line.

Stop armoring a fixed skill set and build the thing that does not expire, your judgment, your taste, your ability to learn the next thing fast and decide what is worth doing. That is the one capability AI is not coming for.

The answer to the anxiety that started all this is that you were right to be scared of betting the company on the thing that dies, but you were wrong about how to fix it.

We’ve seen that just building a better wall wasn’t the answer. France built the best one ever and still found themselves in a losing position.

Stop building to last.

Make reversible bets.

Stay close enough to your customers to feel the shift before it’s obvious.

Put your effort into deciding what’s worth building, not into guessing what survives. That’s what you can actually control.

References and further reading

The window has collapsed

  • S. Patrick Viguerie, Ned Calder and Brian Hindo, “2021 Corporate Longevity Forecast” (Innosight). The average lifespan of an S&P 500 company has fallen toward under twenty years, with roughly half the index expected to turn over within a decade.
  • Reuters, reporting the UBS analyst note, “ChatGPT sets record for fastest-growing user base” (2023). ChatGPT reached a hundred million users in two months, a pace UBS called unmatched in twenty years of wa
  • World History Encyclopedia, “Maginot Line.” The French fortifications that Germany bypassed through the Ardennes in 1940, now a byword for an expensive defense that offers a false sense of security.tching the internet.

The tool you bet on is already dead

  • Scott Brinker, “Martec’s Law: The Greatest Management Challenge of the 21st Century” (chiefmartec). Technology changes exponentially, organizations change logarithmically.
  • Ray Kurzweil, “The Law of Accelerating Returns” (2001). The exponential, compounding nature of technological change.
  • Patrick Neeman, “The UX Double Diamond Is Dead, and in AI Only One Survives for Software” (UX Collective). A durable process made obsolete when the cost of building collapsed.
  • Philip Tetlock, “Superforecasting” (2015) and “Expert Political Judgment” (2005). Expert prediction barely beats chance.

The customer you designed for just changed on you

  • Natasha Sommerfeld and colleagues, “Goodbye Clicks, Hello AI: Zero-Click Search Redefines Marketing” (Bain & Company, 2025). The zero-click shift and the reset of search expectations.
  • Elizabeth Silliman, Jack Trotter, and Kelsey Robinson, with Desirae Oppong and Shreya Jaggi, “Who Wins When AI Does the Shopping?” (McKinsey, 2026, around 21,000 consumers). AI shopping behavior shifting as fast as adoption.
  • Capgemini Research Institute, “What Matters to Today’s Consumer 2026” (12,000 consumers, year over year). The rate of change in AI-driven expectations.
  • Invoca, 2026 B2C Buyer Experience Report. GenAI purchase research rose from 41 to 58 percent in a single year.
  • Lingxiu Dong, Kaiwen Luo and Fasheng Xu, “From Product Search to Preference Articulation: The Economics of Agentic Commerce” (2026). As AI agents take over discovery, scarcity shifts from search to preference articulation.

The org chart you built is the thing slowing you do

  • Scott Brinker, “Martec’s Law” (as above). Organizations change logarithmically.
  • Sam Ransbotham, David Kiron, Shervin Khodabandeh, Sesh Iyer and Amartya Das, “The Emerging Agentic Enterprise: How Leaders Must Navigate a New Age of AI” (MIT Sloan Management Review with BCG, 2025). AI delivers gains only when roles, workflows, and decision rights are redesigned around it.
  • David M. Rothschild, Jake M. Hofman, Markus Mobius, Brendan Lucier, Eleanor Dillon, Daniel G. Goldstein, Nicole Immorlica, Aleksandrs Slivkins at Microsoft Research, “From Augmentation to Reconstruction: Guiding the AI Disruption to the Good Place” (2026). Most organizations use AI to accelerate pre-AI workflows; real change favors reconstruction over local optimization.
  • Wolfgang Rohde, “Short-Term Gain, Long-Term Fragility: AI Labor Substitution and the Erosion of Sustainable Capability” (2026). Organizations discover the value of human judgment after they have made it scarce.
  • Michael T. Hannan and John Freeman, “Structural Inertia and Organizational Change” (American Sociological Review, 1984). The foundational theory of why organizations resist changing their structure even after the conditions that shaped it are gone.

Stop armoring. Start moving.

  • Jeff Bezos, Amazon 2015 Letter to Shareholders. One-way-door versus two-way-door decisions, and the cost of treating reversible choices as permanent.
  • Nassim Nicholas Taleb, “Antifragile: Things That Gain from Disorder” (2012). Build to gain from disorder rather than predict it.
  • Scott Brinker, “Martec’s Law” (as above). His own prescription: choose selectively, stay agile, reset at inflection points.
  • David Hoang, “Software Gardens” (Proof of Concept, 2026). Cultivate the work like a garden, not a factory.
  • Sundeep Misra, “AI Won’t Save an Organization That Can’t Decide What to Build” (2026). The scarce skill is deciding what is worth building.
  • World Economic Forum, “The Future of Jobs Report 2025.” On average, workers can expect 39 percent of their existing skills to be transformed or become outdated between 2025 and 2030; judgment, adaptability, and continuous learning are the durable capabilities.

issues.title: Vladimir Nabokov on What Makes a Good Reader
issues.summary: "A good reader, a major reader, an active and creative reader is a rereader."
issues.author: Maria Popova
issues.content_html:
“A good reader, a major reader, an active and creative reader is a rereader.”

“All attempts at gaining literary polish must begin with judicious reading,” H.P. Lovecraft advised aspiring writers. We’ve already seen that reading is a learned skill and an optimizable technique, and that non-reading is as important an intellectual choice as reading itself, so it follows that reading, more than the mere monolithic act of ingesting text, comes with degrees of mastery. But what, exactly, does it mean to be a good reader?

Vladimir Nabokov (April 22, 1899–July 2, 1977) was a man of wonderfully opinionated insights on literature and life. He was also, it turns out, equally opinionated in his criteria for what constitutes a good reader. In his collected Lectures on Literature (public library), Nabokov offers the following exercise, which he posed to students at a “remote provincial college” while on an extended lecture tour:

Select four answers to the question what should a reader be to be a good reader:

  1. The reader should belong to a book club.
  2. The reader should identify himself or herself with the hero or heroine.
  3. The reader should concentrate on the social-economic angle.
  4. The reader should prefer a story with action and dialogue to one with none.
  5. The reader should have seen the book in a movie.
  6. The reader should be a budding author.
  7. The reader should have imagination.
  8. The reader should have memory.
  9. The reader should have a dictionary.
  10. The reader should have some artistic sense.

The students leaned heavily on emotional identification, action, and the social-economic or historical angle. Of course, as you have guessed, the good reader is one who has imagination, memory, a dictionary, and some artistic sense–which sense I propose to develop in myself and in others whenever I have the chance.

He goes on to consider the element of time in reading, making a case for the value of rereading:

Incidentally, I use the word reader very loosely. Curiously enough, one cannot read a book: one can only reread it. A good reader, a major reader, an active and creative reader is a rereader. And I shall tell you why. When we read a book for the first time the very process of laboriously moving our eyes from left to right, line after line, page after page, this complicated physical work upon the book, the very process of learning in terms of space and time what the book is about, this stands between us and artistic appreciation. When we look at a painting we do not have to move our eyes in a special way even if, as in a book, the picture contains elements of depth and development. The element of time does not really enter in a first contact with a painting. In reading a book, we must have time to acquaint ourselves with it. We have no physical organ (as we have the eye in regard to a painting) that takes in the whole picture and then can enjoy its details. But at a second, or third, or fourth reading we do, in a sense, behave towards a book as we do towards a painting. However, let us not confuse the physical eye, that monstrous masterpiece of evolution, with the mind, an even more monstrous achievement. A book, no matter what it is—a work of fiction or a work of science (the boundary line between the two is not as clear as is generally believed)—a book of fiction appeals first of all to the mind. The mind, the brain, the top of the tingling spine, is, or should be, the only instrument used upon a book.

Complement with Mark Twain’s humorous list of the fourteen types of readers and Nabokov on the three qualities a great storyteller must have.

issues.title: The Third Thing: Poet Donald Hall on the Secret to Lasting Love
issues.summary: "Third things are essential to marriages, objects or practices or habits or arts or institutions or games or human beings that provide a site of joint rapture or contentment."
issues.author: Maria Popova
issues.content_html:
“Third things are essential to marriages, objects or practices or habits or arts or institutions or games or human beings that provide a site of joint rapture or contentment.”

“The encounter between two differences is an event,” French philosopher Alain Badiou wrote in his tremendous treatise on why we fall and how we stay in love. “On the basis of this event, love can start and flourish. It is the first, absolutely essential point.”

And yet at the heart of this essential event is often something beyond the two — something often improbable, almost always inessential in itself, which somehow magnetizes the two differences into a unit of belonging.

The power of that mysterious and magical something is what the poet and essayist Donald Hall (September 20, 1928–June 23, 2018) explores in a gorgeous essay titled “The Third Thing,” which appeared on the pages of Poetry — the world’s most enduring and visionary poetry magazine — in the autumn of 2004.

Reflecting on his life with the love of his life — the poet Jane Kenyon, herself the keeper and giver of uncommonly clarifying wisdom on writing and life — Hall considers the secret to the kind of lasting love that blooms between the mundane and the magical. An epoch after Virginia Woolf exulted in “the bead of sensation” that punctuates the dailiness of any durational love to make it last, Hall writes:

Jane Kenyon and I were married for twenty-three years. For two decades we inhabited the double solitude of my family farmhouse in New Hampshire, writing poems, loving the countryside. She was forty-seven when she died. If anyone had asked us, “Which year was the best, of your lives together?” we could have agreed on an answer: “the one we remember least.” There were sorrowful years — the death of her father, my cancers, her depressions — and there were also years of adventure: a trip to China and Japan, two trips to India; years when my children married; years when the grandchildren were born; years of triumph as Jane began her public life in poetry: her first book, her first poem in the New Yorker. The best moment of our lives was one quiet repeated day of work in our house. Not everyone understood. Visitors, especially from New York, would spend a weekend with us and say as they left: “It’s really pretty here” (“in Vermont,” many added) “with your house, the pond, the hills, but … but … but … what do you do?”

What we did: we got up early in the morning. I brought Jane coffee in bed. She walked the dog as I started writing, then climbed the stairs to work at her own desk on her own poems. We had lunch. We lay down together. We rose and worked at secondary things. I read aloud to Jane; we played scoreless ping-pong; we read the mail; we worked again. We ate supper, talked, read books sitting across from each other in the living room, and went to sleep. If we were lucky the phone didn’t ring all day… Three hundred and thirty days a year we inhabited this old house and the same day’s adventurous routine.

What we did: love.

But the substance of this daily love, Hall argues, is not the stuff of romantic tropes. Echoing Little Prince author Antoine de Saint-Exupéry’s beautiful insistence that “love does not consist of gazing at each other, but in looking outward together in the same direction,” Hall writes:

We did not spend our days gazing into each other’s eyes. We did that gazing when we made love or when one of us was in trouble, but most of the time our gazes met and entwined as they looked at a third thing. Third things are essential to marriages, objects or practices or habits or arts or institutions or games or human beings that provide a site of joint rapture or contentment. Each member of a couple is separate; the two come together in double attention. Lovemaking is not a third thing but two-in-one. John Keats can be a third thing, or the Boston Symphony Orchestra, or Dutch interiors, or Monopoly.

For Hall and Kenyon, the third thing was the pond near their home. He writes:

We had our summer afternoons at the pond, which for ten years made a third thing. After naps we loaded up books and blankets and walked across Route 4 and the old railroad to the steep slippery bank that led down to our private beach on Eagle Pond. Soft moss underfoot sent little red flowers up. Ghost birches leaned over water with wild strawberry plants growing under them. Over our heads white pines reared high, and oaks that warned us of summer’s end late in August by dropping green metallic acorns. Sometimes a mink scooted among ferns… Jane dozed in the sun as I sat in the shade reading and occasionally taking a note in a blank book. From time to time we swam and dried in the heat.

Hall’s most piercing point is that the third thing, rather than being an extraneous adornment of the relationship, is a central form of companionship. But while it is indispensable, it is not irreplaceable — it doesn’t so much matter what the thing is, only that it is.

When a landfill leakage destroyed their beloved pond, Hall and Kenyon still had their other third thing — poetry. Reflecting on its unparalleled power of perspective, its power to connect and console in the face of life’s darkest moments, he writes:

We lived in the house of poetry, which was also the house of love and grief; the house of solitude and art; the house of Jane’s depression and my cancers and Jane’s leukemia. When someone died whom we loved, we went back to the poets of grief and outrage, as far back as Gilgamesh; often I read aloud Henry King’s “The Exequy,” written in the seventeenth century after the death of his young wife. Poetry gives the griever not release from grief but companionship in grief. Poetry embodies the complexities of feeling at their most intense and entangled, and therefore offers (over centuries, or over no time at all) the company of tears. As I sat beside Jane in her pain and weakness I wrote about pain and weakness. Once in a hospital I noticed that the leaves were turning. I realized that I had not noticed that they had come to the trees. It was a year without seasons, a year without punctuation. I began to write “Without” to embody the sensations of lives under dreary, monotonous assault. After I had drafted it many times I read it aloud to Jane. “That’s it, Perkins,” she said. “You’ve got it. That’s it.” Even in this poem written at her mortal bedside there was companionship.

Hall’s 1999 poetry collection Without (public library) is the breathtakingly beautiful record of that abiding companionship. Complement it with Anna Dostoyevskaya on the secret to a happy marriage and Wendell Berry on what poetry teaches us about the secret of marriage and Adrienne Rich on honorable human relationships.

issues.title: How to Love the World More: Artist and Poet Rachel Hébert’s Breathtaking Catalogue of Gratitudes
issues.summary: Here we are, living these lives bright and perishable as a poppy, hard and shimmering as obsidian. We know that they are entirely improbable, that we bless that bright improbability with each flash of gratitude for it all, that if we pay attention closely and generously enough we are always repaid in gladness, that it is the handle of the door to the world. And yet over and over we choose to live
issues.author: Maria Popova
issues.content_html:
Here we are, living these lives bright and perishable as a poppy, hard and shimmering as obsidian. We know that they are entirely improbable, that we bless that bright improbability with each flash of gratitude for it all, that if we pay attention closely and generously enough we are always repaid in gladness, that it is the handle of the door to the world. And yet over and over we choose to live in the cage of complaint, too preoccupied with how the will of life betrayed our wishes, the wanting monster always growling in the other corner of the cage.

Imagine parting the bars and stepping out. Imagine waking up with a rush of gladness at everything we were never promised but got anyway — trees and music, clouds and consciousness, the cobalt eye of the scallop, the golden fan of the gingko, the alabaster chandelier of the ghost pipe.

In our age of competitive prostration, this is a headstand hard to hold for long. But it is trainable. It is possible to become strong enough to be tender, it is.

Artist and poet Rachel Hébert offers a bright patch of training ground in The Book of Thanks: A Catalogue of Gratitudes — one of the most miraculous books I have ever encountered, trembling with tenacious tenderness for the bewilderment of being alive.

Radiating from the pages is an invitation, extended in paintings and poems, to open “the sunlit fort of your attention” and let the world rush in, in all its minute and majestic loveliness: stalactites and Spanish moss, spiderwebs and skylights, snow and the call of the snowy owl, the heart’s capacity for “an urgent, flashing, interrupting kind of love.”

What emerges is prayerful (“more cellos, touch, and rain, please”) and singing with praise (“roots gripping, canyon carved, spine woven of baleen a thousand years old”) — a manual for how to live in gratitude (“what is working wants your praise”) and a theological statement (“there is nothing you must do to belong”).

A taste:

What do we say to longing?

If you have sat in the chill
of early morning bleakness

and watched as the deep blue
sighed and blushed, touched

by the warm curve of dawn
and pinker than pink then

apricot soft and spreading its
glow, you know. You know.

How
— in this dim parade of brutality —
might all be well?

But if we trouble it with light,
train our sights on
the rebellious good,

and work
to make it
truer.

Beneath the face
of the water,
wonder.

In dark woods,
a gate.

In the chapter
called lostness,
a friend.

All the help
we could not
yet see.

It cannot be always comfortable.
So love the thousand knives as they enter
and see your shape still sitting.

See that you too belong to paws
of soft silent hungers, to thirst-tangled
roots, to silver-spun constellations.

Know you’re no sicker than the rest of us.
The big secret is this: No one else can brave you.
Messy, yes. And marvelous.

What is more than we see
in this world we’re pressed into,
its blistered barking noise?

For what we build, speak, and ruin —
our efforts, our angers.

For music.

For wings.

issues.title: The Paradox of “Finding Yourself”
issues.summary: "The self is a style of being, continually expanding in a vital process of definition, affirmation, revision, and growth..."
issues.author: Maria Popova
issues.content_html:
“The self is a style of being, continually expanding in a vital process of definition, affirmation, revision, and growth…”

“No one can build you the bridge on which you, and only you, must cross the river of life,” thirty-year-old Nietzsche wrote in his treatise on how to find yourself. And yet in the century and a half since, a curious dissonance has begun to reverberate across culture: On the one hand, we have grown increasingly fixated on the self as the focal lens for interpreting the world — a fixation which Ian McEwan so brilliantly satirized and which has precipitated today’s tragic epidemic of militant identity politics; on the other hand, the rise of neuroscience has demonstrated again and again that the self we experience as so overwhelmingly real — the psychophysiological raft of experience through which we float along the river of life — is a sensory-perceptual byproduct of consciousness, completely illusory in its solidity.

Nearly half a century ago, the Pulitzer-winning poet Robert Penn Warren (April 24, 1905–September 15, 1989) cast a cautionary eye to the notion of “finding oneself” in Democracy and Poetry (public library) — his magnificent Jefferson Lecture about power, tenderness, and art’s role in a healthy society.

Decades before Harvard psychologist Daniel Gilbert’s witty and wise observation that “human beings are works in progress that mistakenly think they’re finished,” Warren challenges the cultural trend of young people taking “time off” from school or work in order to “get away from it all” and find themselves. He writes:

In the phrase [“to find myself”] lurks the idea that the self is a pre-existing entity, a self like a Platonic idea existing in a mystic realm beyond time and change. No, rather an object like a nugget of gold in the placer pan, the Easter egg under the bush at an Easter-egg hunt, a four-leaf clover to promise miraculous luck. Here is the essence of passivity, one’s quintessential luck. And the essence of absurdity, too, for the self is never to be found, but must be created, not the happy accident of passivity, but the product of a thousand actions, large and small, conscious or unconscious, performed not “away from it all,” but in the face of “it all,” for better or for worse, in work and leisure rather than in free time.

In consonance with my own deep belief in the ongoingness and fluidity of our becoming, Warren adds:

The self is a style of being, continually expanding in a vital process of definition, affirmation, revision, and growth, a process that is the image, we may say, of the life process of a healthy society itself.

In a sentiment that calls to mind Academy of American Poets executive director Jennifer Benka’s beautiful observation that “poems are physical sites of discovery [and] sense-records of our humanity,” Warren considers the role of poetry as a locus of our evolving being:

How does poetry come into all this? By being an antidote, a sovereign antidote, for passivity. For the basic fact about poetry is that it demands participation, from the secret physical echo in muscle and nerve that identifies us with the medium, to the imaginative enactment that stirs the deepest recesses where life-will and values reside. Beyond that, it nourishes our life-will in the process of testing our values. And this is not to be taken as implying a utilitarian aesthetic. It is, rather, one way of describing our pleasure in poetry as an adventure in the celebration of life.

Complement this particular portion of Warren’s thoroughly transcendent Democracy and Poetry with Walt Whitman on identity and the paradox of the self and philosopher Rebecca Goldstein on what makes you and your childhood self the “same” person despite a lifetime of change, then revisit Elizabeth Alexander on what poetry does for the human spirit.

issues.title: Some cities show traffic isn’t an inescapable fate
issues.summary: Tolls are just one solution.
issues.author: Sam Klebanov
issues.content_html:
Cities worldwide are demonstrating that the bane of your dad’s existence and your favorite excuse for being 20 minutes late can be solved. They’re doing this by embracing proven measures to fight traffic effectively.

(Lane) Change is possible

Aside from banning cars, the highest-impact anti-traffic measure is charging drivers to enter designated zones in the city, aka enacting congestion pricing. The toll is meant to spur some people to consider alternative routes or take public transit instead, reducing traffic and pollution in central areas:

  • After New York City imposed congestion pricing in 2025 in the zone below Central Park in Manhattan, traffic fell 12% in the first year, according to state data.
  • London implemented congestion pricing in 2003 and Stockholm, in 2007. Public opposition to both programs waned after people saw how it made driving less nightmarish.

This may seem expensive, but research firm INRIX estimates that traffic itself costs an average US driver 97 hours annually, or $1,348 in lost productivity.

But tolls are just one solution. For instance, NYC is testing so-called “low traffic zones,” using design elements like plastic bollards, speed bumps, and expanded sidewalks to steer drivers away from using certain residential neighborhoods as shortcuts. While meant to reduce congestion and pedestrian deaths, the measures have led some New Yorkers to complain that traffic now flows into their previously quiet streets instead.

Meanwhile…many cities are taking a simpler road to zero traffic: banning cars from select streets. This lets walkers saunter while letting their guard down, and local businesses benefit from the window-shopping.—SK

issues.title: Zeppelins might be making a comeback
issues.summary: A constellation of startups is betting that next-gen blimps are the future of cargo delivery.
issues.author: Sam Klebanov
issues.content_html:
Almost 90 years after the Hindenburg disaster gave blimps the worst reputation imaginable, gas-filled levitating ships might be returning to ferry your Temu orders. A constellation of startups is betting that next-gen blimps are the future of cargo delivery, pitching them as a cleaner and cheaper (albeit slower) alternative to freight planes:

  • Sergey Brin-backed LTA Research has been testing the 406.5-foot-long rigid airship Pathfinder 1—the world’s biggest aircraft—in the Bay Area skies. The company says that the prototype hybrid-electric blimp is a step toward building a fuel-efficient cargo vessel that can land in otherwise inaccessible areas.
  • French startup Flying Whales aspires to produce blimps for remote shipments of up to 66 tons at its Quebec factory.
  • Airship company Hybrid Air Vehicles, backed by the UK government, has $2.2 billion worth of orders for its anticipated gas-buoyed aircraft intended for civilian and defense purposes.

For those worried about Hindenburg 2.0: Modern safety advancements make a big difference. For one, these next-gen blimps use inflammable helium for buoyancy (instead of flammable hydrogen), and they’re built with more durable modern materials, like carbon fiber. Plus, digital controls allow for precise navigation, while improved wind prediction can help avoid storms.

But it’s a turbulent liftoff: Airship engineers have spent years tinkering with the unwieldy floating beasts, contending with the fact that they’re still more prone to weather disruptions than planes.—SK

issues.title: Shipping containers revolutionized global trade
issues.summary: The system cut unloading time by up to three weeks and allowed the containers to be moved seamlessly between ships, trucks, and trains.
issues.author: Dave Lozo
issues.content_html:
Before trucking company owner Malcolm McLean came along, shipping by water meant throwing everything into a cargo hold, much like cleaning your place when you have company coming over at the last second.

But McLean ushered in the era of maritime history known as containerization, which transformed global trade:

  • McLean helped create the shipping container that became the world’s standard by the 1970s (at 8’x8’x20’).
  • This made existing cargo ships obsolete and required new ones designed to increase cargo capacity by eliminating wasted space.
  • Docks were relocated and redesigned. Previously, they held sheds for storing cargo once it was unloaded.

Many shipping companies folded or changed course.Dockworkers who unloaded ships lost their jobs when cranes replaced them. The new system cut unloading time by up to three weeks and allowed the containers to be moved seamlessly between ships, trucks, and trains.—DL

issues.title: Keep on truckin’? In this economy?
issues.summary: Like a struggling stand-up comedian, the US economy is working through some delivery problems.
issues.author: Brendan Cosgrove
issues.content_html:
Like a struggling stand-up comedian, the US economy is working through some delivery problems. Due to high gas prices, fewer truck drivers, and tariffs, shipping and handling costs are through the roof. And, since a lot of things need shipping and/or handling, it’s impacting the price of…everything.

Fuel economy

Diesel costs have skyrocketed since the US and Israel attacked Iran in late February, and though prices have since eased off of their record highs above $6.50/gallon, not many people are celebrating rates well above last year’s sub-$4 price, per AAA data.

The freight of the world depends on it: Like Robert Pattinson, diesel plays a part in just about everything. Freight trucks, which typically run on the fuel, moved nearly 73% of US freight by weight in 2024, according to the American Trucking Associations. So, when truck transportation costs jump nearly 25% (like they did over the past year), it’s a wide-ranging problem. For example, the Independent Grocers Alliance estimates that fuel accounts for about 15% to 30% of the total cost of food.

Ship wrecked: Higher prices have forced a slew of freight companies to file for bankruptcy, and prompted FedEx, UPS, the US Postal Service, and even railroads to raise prices.

Higher shipping costs aren’t just about fuel, though: A shortage of truckers (thanks, in part, to a government crackdown on immigrant drivers) has made trucking more difficult, while port congestion and the conflict in the Middle East have driven container-shipping rates higher.

Trick of the trade: Shifting US tariff policies also led retailers to speed up their timeline for importing goods ahead of the holiday season, and that sudden increase in demand drove up transportation costs around the world.—BC

Ricky Hanlon is Leaving Meta (But Not React) — After years helping get React "from 4 million to 250 million weekly downloads", Ricky has left React's birthplace, noting "most of the React Core team have left Meta". This is more an 'end of an era' than big news, as he'll continue to work on React, and React getting its own foundation this year showed us the direction of travel.

Ricky Hanlon

💡 Paul O'Shannessy, who pushed React's first public code in 2013 and helped form the foundation, also left Meta this year and wrote a look back at his 14 years there.

Build Durable AI Agents & Workflows in TypeScript — Trigger.dev runs AI agents as tasks inside your codebase, in plain TypeScript with full control of runtime. No serverless timeouts, so even long agents run to completion, surviving refreshes, redeploys, and crashes. Write your logic, test it, and deploy agents that scale on demand.

Trigger.dev sponsor

The Roadmap to TanStack Query v6 — Dominik has shared the plan for TanStack Query's next major version, and it's focused on cleaning up, going ESM-only, React 19 as a baseline, etc. In his words, "we'll break things, but not too many." If you've got things to say, feedback is welcomed.

Dominik Dorfmeister

Your Tools are Hiding npm Audits From You — npm audit on a new create-next-app app shows '0 vulnerabilities' but Next vendors over 100 packages and the audit doesn't notice those. To help counter this, Zach has built the 📊 Prototype Pollution Report which compares numerous frameworks' behaviors and vendored dependency vulnerabilities.

Zach Leatherman

React Forms Beyond onSubmit — See the differences between a form built three ways (with onSubmit, React 19's action prop, and onSubmit plus useTransition). Each has pros and cons, shown in a comparison table.

Giorgi Moniava

📄 Can You Confidently Ship to Production From Your Phone? – How an Expo engineer fixed a bug and shipped an over-the-air update while on a walk. Rami Maalouf (Expo)

📄 Why Base44 Now Generates New Apps with TanStack Start – Bye to SPAs plus separate backend functions; hello full-stack apps. Netanel Gilad (Base44)

📄 Building Bulletproof React Components – A re-run of a classic from the co-creator of SWR. Shu Ding

📄 React Testing Library is Faster When It's Part of the DOM – An interesting approach. Scott Cooper

🛠 Code, Tools & Libraries

Generative Loaders: Loading States for Generative UI — Almost fifty elegant and accessible ways to show the 'thinking' moments in UIs, like when an LLM is generating text, an image is being generated, or even just while a background process is working on something.

Kasturi Khanke

🔊 Button Sounds: Tactile Click Sounds for Your UI — Popular dev blogger Josh (who I've just learnt has a background in audio) recorded numerous clicks and toggle sounds for us to use. There's a useButtonSounds hook, and the site lets you quickly check them all out.

Josh W. Comeau

Sashay: Sliding, Resizable Panes for React — A way to let users arrange your app the way they want by dragging and snapping edges between panes (and on phones, the edges become tabs). The homepage is a good demo itself.

Carl Vitullo

Exact: Expo's Experimental All-Platform App Framework — It's not React, but it's interesting to see the company behind so much React Native tooling building a Rust-powered multi-platform app framework. A big focus is on being 'agent native'.

Expo

File Viewer: A Browser-Native File Viewer for Internal Apps — Provides read-only views for Office, PDF/OFD, CAD files, archives, email and similar tricky formats, with integrations for React, Vue, and Svelte. The docs site has demos you can try out along with info on all the supported formats.

Flyfish Dev

  • react-pdf 11.1 – Display PDFs in your React app. Now on a newer version of PDF.js with better performance and text selecting. (Homepage with live demo.)

  • jest-dom 8.0 – Custom DOM matchers for Jest and Vitest. Note that Vitest users now need Vitest 5 or later.

  • Voltra 2.7 – A way to build iOS Live Activities and widgets as React Native components.

  • 📊 echarts-for-react 3.1 – React wrapper for Apache ECharts.

  • Material UI 9.6 – Comprehensive React component suite.

💡 If you're an existing user, there's a migration guide. Vue Flow has also now joined the xyflow family, alongside Svelte Flow.

How to Build Your Own Automated Debugging Workflow — Factory, Exa, and Bolt connected their coding agents to Sentry so production errors become fix PRs, not tickets. Get the recipes for Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, or bring your own coding agent.

Sentry sponsor

Why Next.js Has Had 51 Security Advisories This Year — You've surely noticed Next.js is getting a lot of security releases recently, but why? Unsurprisingly, it's AI, which is making old bugs easier to find, with 70% of this year's vulnerabilities found in code at least a year old. The team explains how it's responding and helping us stay up to date.

The Next.js Team

⚠️ In related news, a campaign dubbed React2STEAL is exploiting servers that are still unpatched against React2Shell and the old middleware bypass, in order to publish their secrets. Here's what to check on your apps.

🎬 Remotion Studio is Now a Visual Editor That Writes Back to Code — Remotion lets you make videos programmatically with React code, and this short video shows off how its Studio now works like a timeline editor, where you can drag/trim/keyframe something with the edit written back to your source. Your own components can also join in.

Jonny Burger

📄 When an Import Becomes a Zip Bomb: Catching Bundle Regressions in Next.js – By setting up per-route JavaScript budgets in CI. Sergey Patrakeev

📄 React 19.3's View Transitions, Tested: What Actually Animates? – Hint: not a plain setState. Esteban Trillo

📄 Shared Element Transitions Grow Up in Reanimated 4.8 – Now on by default, and they move the real view. Bartłomiej Błoniarz (Software Mansion)

🛠 Code, Tools & Libraries

React Anatomy: Explode a React Page into 3D Layers — A DevTools extension that splits a running React page into 3D layers mapped to the components that rendered it, with live props for whatever you click. You can try the demo without installing anything.

Nicolas Charpentier

Stepperize 9.0: Type-Safe Multi-Step Flows for React — A popular library for wizards, checkouts and onboarding where you define steps once and get typed navigation, plus guards that block a user from advancing until a step is valid.

Damian Ricobelli

Fate 2.0: The Async React Data Client Now Handles Client State Too — The Relay-inspired data client now manages client-only and offline state through the same views and mutations as server data, and works as a GraphQL client too. It's already replaced Relay and TinyBase in Christoph's game, Athena Crisis.

Christoph Nakazawa

Detent: A Wheel Picker for React with Real Inertia — An iOS-style wheel picker that uses its own physics rather than scroll-snap, meaning that a 'throw' has momentum and lands cleanly on options. The demo on the homepage is very cute and worth… a spin. 😎

Hayder

  • 📊 Recharts 3.11(above) – Popular charting library. Now with context-based themes and accessible fill patterns.

  • ⚠️ React Router 8.5.2 and 7.18.6 – Upgrade to either version for fixes covering seven security advisories, four rated high.

  • You Might Not Need an Effect 1.2 – ESLint plugin that flags unnecessary useEffect calls. Now 'sees through' popular third-party effect wrappers.

  • ka-table 13.0 – Lightweight React table component. Now a keyboard-accessible ARIA grid and has added fixed columns and virtual scrolling of columns.

  • Redux Toolkit 2.15 – Each store now gets its own RTK Query runtime, fixing long-standing SSR and test isolation problems.

  • 📱 React Native Bottom Sheet 1.0 – Software Mansion's bottom sheet goes stable.

📰 Classifieds

🔥 Let the cloud take the heat. Expo Simulators runs iOS simulators and Android emulators for your agents, and your laptop’s RAM stays free.

⚡ Next.js, Astro or React Router site? Fimo hosts it and runs AI agents that keep it found on Google and in AI answers.

🎬 Your app needs video, not a video team. Upload any format to Hyperserve's API, get back MP4 on a global CDN. Ship video in an afternoon.

📢 Elsewhere in the ecosystem

  • The Next.js team is experimenting with Switchyard, a Go-powered server that sits in front of next start. Currently, it forwards requests to Node, but the plan is to move routing work out of Node and into Switchyard. If you're self-hosting Next.js, this is one for your long-term radar.

  • Solid 2.0 is now stable. Async is now part of the signals graph and server functions have moved into core. There are also new diagnostics aimed at coding agents.

  • If you want to try speeding up your npm package installs, vlt's registry mirror serves much less metadata, making clean installs 20-70% faster and, now, it's open for all to use with no account/token needed.

  • 🐘 PostgreSQL 19 is finally here! If Postgres is part of your stack, our sister newsletter Postgres Weekly covered it in depth this week (please subscribe! 😅)

  • npkill 1.0 (npx npkill) no longer just clears out old node_modules folders, but build output and caches like .next and .turbo too.

e18e Project

  • ⚠️ Using Vite? A critical flaw allows remote code execution on dev servers exposed to the network with --host or server.host. Update to 8.3.7, 8.2.5, 8.1.7, 7.3.8 or 6.4.6.

  • Storybook 11 beta now has an official post. React projects get faster, more accurate component metadata, and there are type-safe stories and official skills for agents. The final release is due in December.

  • React's <form> docs now explain how to keep field values after an Action, and requestFormReset gets a reference page of its own.

UI SDK: Vercel and shadcn's Headless UI Behaviors Library — A low-level library of behaviors, like keyboard navigation, popups, drag and drop, that you compose into your own components. A core idea is to give a solid base for agents to build full components from. In beta, but you can get started now.

shadcn (Vercel)

How X is Rebuilding Its Web App with React, Relay and Vite — X/Twitter is replacing its decade-old client-rendered React app with a stack built around streaming SSR and Suspense. Lab tests show profiles displaying posts much sooner, and the hydration and chunking fixes make this an interesting case study.

Yagiz Nizipli (X)

#​496 — November 6, 2026

Read on the Web

React Status

Discord Dropping Electron and React Native for a Rust Rewrite — Discord, one of React Native's best-known users, is moving away, with its CTO 𝕏 showing off a Rust desktop client built on GPUI using 290MB of RAM, with mobile keeping native UI over Rust code shared with the desktop client.

Tom Warren (The Verge)

▶️ Just prior to this reveal, Software Mansion interviewed Discord's Chas Jhin about how React Native development works at Discord's scale, in the ominously titled 'Maybe React Native Is Impossible'.

Run AI Coding Models on Your Own Machine — Local models are now good enough for everyday coding. Learn to run them on your own Mac or GPU, wire them into your editor and terminal agents, and keep your code private with no per-token bill.

Master.dev sponsor

A Roadmap for Redux Toolkit v2.x and 3.0 — Mark Erikson has laid out the roadmap for Redux (complete with a neat history lesson) with RTK 3.0 expected in six to eight months, going ESM-only with 'React 19-scale' breaking changes. But a run of 2.x releases will ship the groundwork first, starting with 2.14 this week.

Mark Erikson

IN BRIEF:

  • ⚠️ Update to Next.js 16.4.5 or 15.5.29, as appropriate: the November security release fixes seven advisories. Most are Cache Components bugs, so the post is worth reading.

  • 🤖 TanStack Query maintainer Dominik Dorfmeister says work on Query v6 can start once 'slop PRs' stop coming in and taking up his time, leading to a thread on the effects of AI-made contributions on maintainers.

  • Vercel is folding Next.js's Data Cache into Runtime Cache with bigger allocations but… new per-read and per-write pricing. Hobby teams migrate on November 29, but check the dates and prices for your use case.

  • Vercel builds also now block known-malicious npm package versions before and during install, on all plans and with no configuration needed.

Next.js is Prototyping Go(lang) Route Handlers — A merged experimental PR lets an App Router route be a route.go file exporting GET and friends, compiled by Turbopack and run in supervised Go-powered workers. Tim says Rust could follow along the same path.

Tim Neutkens (Vercel)

Understanding React Internals: A Deep Dive — A seven-part, source-grounded tour of React's internals that, unusually, starts from the server end before getting to fibers, lanes and the commit phase.

Alexandre Trotel

Amazon's React Native-Based Vega OS Hits 2.0 — Vega, the React Native-based OS behind newer Fire TV devices, is out of beta. SDK 2.0 takes apps from RN 0.72 to 0.83, bringing the React Compiler and Hermes v1 into play. The release notes go into more detail than the post.

Barak Schlosser (Amazon)

📄 Why We Finally Left Next.js for TanStack Start – Production memory leaks in two Next.js 16.3 releases were the last straw. Harrison Milbradt

📄 Writable Derived State: Stop Synchronizing State – Using clientData ?? serverData instead of a useEffect that wipes user edits on refetch. Corbin Crutchley

🛠 Code, Tools & Libraries

Skullet: Skeleton Loading States Measured from Your Components — Hand it sample data and it renders your real component invisibly, measures everything, and draws a matching skeleton to reduce layout shifts when data arrives. The docs have a neat How it Works section explaining the technique.

Lochie Axon

Parcel 3 Alpha: A Rust Rewrite with React Compiler, Tailwind and RSC — Parcel's core is now a Rust binary with no Node dependency, and the team reports cold builds up to 100x faster than v2. React Compiler (opt-in), Tailwind and MDX are built in, with RSC support in beta.

Devon Govett (Parcel)

🤖 Reticle: Let Coding Agents Verify Their Changes Against Your Running App — A dev-only SDK and MCP server so coding agents can drive your running app, inspect network requests, application state, and console activity, and return a pass, fail or 'can't tell' verdict with what needs fixing.

Reticle Labs

react-resizable-panels Gets a VS Code-Style Workspace Component — Brian Vaughn's popular panel library now does dockable tabs you can drag to split or merge panes, and moved tabs keep their state rather than remounting. There's a live demo here.

Brian Vaughn

  • Preact 11.2 – Now has a runtime for React Compiler output via preact/compat, plus scoped custom element registries in shadow roots.

  • XState 6.0 Beta – "No further breaking changes are planned" for public APIs, and @xstate/react 7 is in beta alongside.

  • TanStack Redact 0.3 – The lightweight, synchronous-only React / React DOM replacement adds browser SPA plugins for Webpack and Rspack.

  • React Native 0.89 RC – Faster text layout and native module calls, legacy bridge APIs gone. Stable expected in December.

  • Storybook 11.0 Beta

📰 Classifieds

🤖 Fimo gives your marketers a visual editor and AI agents for SEO and GEO. No more tickets for your React devs. By the Strapi team.

QVAC allows you to run any AI capabilities for free, on your phone or laptop, privately. Try the QVAC SDK now on GitHub.

📢 Elsewhere in the ecosystem

  • James Long has been reviving Prepack, Facebook's abandoned JavaScript partial evaluator. There's a React demo where a pretend site is server rendered three ways, by React, by Prepack's output (which essentially 'compiles' React away), and a hybrid, with the render times to compare.

  • Node.js 27 Alpha has landed, the first version using Node's new release process (where a release will spend six months in 'alpha' before going Current), while Node 26 is now the new LTS line.

  • Chrome 157 rolled out this week with HTML-in-Canvas now stable. It provides a way to draw real DOM elements into 2D, WebGL and WebGPU canvases. The demos are striking.

  • Vercel has released Geist Serif, a new serif font that shares metrics with Geist Sans so the two can mix cleanly. It's not on Google Fonts yet, but the geist npm package includes it.

issues.title: 🎙️ How I AI: OpenClaw for executives: Automate every 1% annoyance
issues.summary: Your weekly listens from How I AI, part of the Lenny’s Podcast Network
issues.author: Lenny Rachitsky
issues.content_html:
OpenClaw for executives: Automate every 1% annoyance | Ankit Maheshwari (Innovaccer)

Listen now on YouTube • Spotify • Apple Podcasts

Brought to you by:

  • Parallel—Web search built for AI scale

  • GiveDirectly—Send cash to the world’s poorest

Ankit Maheshwari is the CTO of Innovaccer and the creator of a personal AI chief of staff he runs through OpenClaw on a Mac Mini. In this episode, he shows how his Jarvis handles work approvals, orders lunch, calls coworkers who miss Slack messages, books restaurants, and controls his smart home. He also explains how he uses soul files, specialist subagents, and strict guardrails to make the system trustworthy, and why he is testing local models against a $500 to $600 monthly Anthropic bill.

Biggest takeaways:

  1. The best reason to stick with an agent platform is control, not habit. Ankit remains on OpenClaw because it can use his credentials, act on his behalf, and complete tasks without requesting permission at every step. That autonomy is an architectural advantage, not brand loyalty.

  2. Start with the bottleneck, not the grand vision. Ankit’s first automation was a cron job that runs every four hours and briefs him on every resume awaiting approval, including candidate pedigree and GitHub history. Once it worked, he began spotting similar bottlenecks throughout his day.

  3. Specialized agents outperform generalist ones once the workload becomes complex. Ankit’s master agent struggled to maintain the right persona across restaurant bookings and coworker check-ins. Moving voice calls to a dedicated agent improved consistency and clarified the split between orchestration and execution.

  4. Configuring soul files requires more work than integrations. The hardest part was defining each agent’s personality, boundaries, permissions, and routing logic through files such as soul.md. Getting those instructions right required more iteration than connecting the underlying tools.

  5. Guardrails should cover the worst case before it happens. OpenClaw once approved expiring travel requests while Ankit was in transit, using the same budget and customer-impact criteria he would have applied. The decisions were sound, but the experience exposed other actions, such as job-role approvals, that needed explicit limits.

  6. The model bill is worth optimizing before the system becomes indispensable. Jarvis costs Ankit roughly $500 to $600 per month on Opus 5.5. Early tests suggest a nearly free local model can handle summaries, email, cron checks, and call orchestration, while complex browser work still requires a frontier model.

  7. The “1% annoyance” rule is an effective way to discover automations. If a task is even slightly frustrating and repeats a few times, Ankit automates it. That approach led to agents for lunch ordering, unanswered Slack messages, home automation, and potentially even calling the elevator.

  8. A terminal-first approach can keep agent building surprisingly simple. Ankit set up OpenClaw by opening its terminal interface and speaking to it like a new employee. When coding was required, OpenClaw launched Claude Code and managed the implementation itself.

  9. Teach agents the messy details, then let them keep learning. Ankit’s lunch agent confirms his order at 9:30 a.m. and acts independently if he does not respond. After one correction about ordering curry without bread, it learned both when to add bread and when a meal already includes it.

issues.summary: Sherif Mansour on why PMs are thriving in the AI era, the artist PM advantage, and why juniors are your secret weapon now
issues.author: Lenny Rachitsky
issues.content_html:
Sherif Mansour is Head of AI and Product Craft at Atlassian (the company behind Jira and Confluence), where he has spent 17 years building and scaling some of the most successful enterprise products in history. He joined Atlassian as its first PM on Confluence, eventually becoming its first Distinguished PM, and now leads both the craft of product management across the company and Atlassian’s AI product strategy.

Listen on YouTube, Spotify, or Apple Podcasts

We discuss:

Welcome back to This Week in Stratechery!

On that note, here were a few of our favorites this week.

  1. Obituaries and Exceptionalism. After several days to mull the shocking departure of Jensen Huang, Ben’s article on Monday delivered an omnibus obituary for a variety of American eras that may now be ending. Tracing the decisions that made Huang great, the strategies that made him a target, the implications of his demise for the rest of the tech ecosystem, and a shift in the U.S. government’s perspective on tech companies — and specifically AI companies — to which Huang never quite adapted, Monday’s piece was both comprehensive and poignant. —Andrew Sharp
  1. Arguments About Agents.Recurring Stratechery guest and advertising expert Eric Seufert is often aligned with Ben in his view of the digital advertising landscape, which is why this week’s Stratechery Interview was fun: Ben is a big believer in the potential upside in agentic commerce, while Eric has been (correctly) calling BS on a variety of hyped agentic commerce stories and trends over the past year. Both of them made their case Thursday, and it was sandwiched between thoughts on how Muse plans to monetize, why the market have misread Google’s recent earnings report, and ChatGPT’s progress building an ads business. — AS

  2. Ben Gets a Duo. In the middle of a heavy week of Nvidia takes and ominous infrastructure failures, I was delighted to find out that Ben not only purchased an iPhone Duo, but loved it. Come for his review at the end of Tuesday’s Update, and then stay for his discussion with John Gruber on Tuesday’s Dithering. We doubled back (Duo’d back?) to discuss all of it at the end of this week’s Sharp Tech , including some hands-on testing, comparisons to the iPhone Air, and a variety of shots fired at the iPhone Pro. —AS

Presented by

As AI models improve, you might expect the market will consolidate around a handful of providers. But user data tells a different story.

Among OpenRouter customers spending at least $100 a month, the median number of AI model families in use has doubled over the past year, from three to six.

Even as AI models become more capable, businesses are using more models, not fewer. This makes sense when you consider that intelligence isn’t one-dimensional. A model that’s exceptional at writing code may not be the fastest at answering customer questions, or the most economical at processing millions of documents.

The question is shifting from “which AI model should we build on?” to “which model should handle each task?” The answer, increasingly, is ‘it depends.’ Which is great for flexibility, less great for simplicity.

OpenRouter, which recently joined Stripe, allows businesses to access and govern hundreds of models with the flexibility to optimize for cost, performance, and reliability as the market evolves.

issues.title: 🔮 Certified human, twin primes, Anthropic++ #611
issues.summary: Your Sunday briefing on AI and exponential technologies
issues.author: Azeem Azhar
issues.content_html:
A must-read for asset allocators who are not tech specialists. – SHK, a paying member

Subscribe now

A big issue this weekend. Settle in with a cup of coffee.

The handmade’s tale

The year’s biggest launch is a testament to manual labor. Rockstar’s 5,000 staff built Grand Theft Auto VI without generative AI. Reports say that 30,000 unique characters in the game were made by hand. Proof of humanity paid handsomely – the game made $3.79 billion in sales by the end of the first day, including preorders.

Back in 2017, I argued that, in a world of AI, we should look for lessons from artisanal cheesemakers. AI would make perfection cheap, and what would be scarce is human imperfection. We do seem to love the human touch. In one study, people rated AI-generated paintings more favorably when they were labeled human-made.

William Morris and the British Arts and Crafts movement of the 19th century resisted industrial mechanization, only to find that manual labor couldn’t compete on price. In the end, only the well-heeled could afford the premium. He raged that he spent his “life ministering to the swinish luxury of the rich.”

Digital culture might escape the trap that held Morris. Created carefully by hand once, the costs can be spread across millions of buyers, as a mass-market phenomenon, not the plaything of the rich. But the specter of Morris (and the artisanal cheesemakers) still looms over a world flooded by generative content. An ocean of synthetic digital drivel (what my Instagram feed has become) might drown out a scarcer “certified human” tier.

👉 I’d love to hear how you are thinking about this. Leave your thoughts in the comments below.

Leave a comment

He starts nearly every piece by hand anyway Welcome to Model Behavior, our interview series featuring writers and creators on AI’s frontier. In previous editions, we spoke to author George Saunders and music producer Rick Rubin about AI and the creative process. Today we’re chatting with British entrepreneur and technology writer… Read more 7 days ago · 506 likes · Azeem Azhar and Arielle Swedback

Anthropic’s big week

Wall Street got a piece of Anthropic this week. What exactly did it buy?

  • The Exponential View view. Could Anthropic take a cut of the value its AI creates across the intangible economy? I shared my early analysis of what Anthropic is really listing.

  • From our AI Investment Brief desk.We model three futures for Anthropic, from licensing models that run on your devices to becoming an AI utility.

  • published a reflection on a year of conversations with people inside Anthropic. The firm has hallmarks of a religion: the only way to save humanity from an existentially dangerous technology is to race as fast as possible to build it first, and they are the only ones virtuous enough to wield that power.

Twin primes

You wait 167 years for a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, and then two come in the same day. Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, says he and Claude may have proved the Riemann hypothesis. That same day, Stanford mathematician Ravi Vakil rushed out a proof of the same conjecture by Alessandro Masullo: “all human, with no AI.”

I’ve not read either proof. Alpöge says his runs to 17.4m lines of Lean, a formal language used to prove logical arguments. Masullo’s proof was still being checked by a third party, but a team is now translating his argument into Lean, where it can be verified more quickly.

Scott Aaronson makes the case that no AI result that has been verified in Lean has ever been retracted. But it’s also a sign of the times that the human team wants to lean on Lean to prove Masullo’s work.

See also: Why the Riemann hypothesis is so important. (Lovely video.)

Wright of way

More than 2,000 gigawatts of new power plants and batteries are waiting to connect to the US grid. For perspective, that’s more than every power plant running in the country right now. About 85% of the queue is for solar, wind, and storage.

Meanwhile, solar modules keep getting 24% cheaper with every doubling of capacity — we have long believed this will open new markets that were previously unavailable (see our solar supercycle model). Well, since Wright’s law continues to deliver, the queue is pushing AI off the grid.

While an AI chip rents for about $3 an hour, a month spent waiting for power costs more than the power itself. In Friday’s edition, our Investment Brief showed how on-site solar and batteries are the cheapest option to power data centers in half of the United States.

issues.title: 🔮 What Anthropic is really listing
issues.summary: Tithes, not tokens
issues.author: Azeem Azhar
issues.content_html:
Azeem’s sketchbook is an experimental format we’re trialing for paying members, where we share raw research notes, early frameworks, and unfinished ideas. They are the earliest indication of what I’m thinking through.

It’s Anthropic’s big week. It will become the first real AI company in the West to list on a public market.

Anthropic has an extraordinary market opportunity. The battle hangs on the sustainability of its business model – whether falling token costs or competition from open-weight models won’t simply erode its margins. These forces, no doubt, exist. The bear case claims the company is merely a peddler of progressively devalued tokens. This misses the point.

Anthropic is building an ever-improving system that produces machine intelligence. That machine intelligence is valuable because of the nature of modern economies. Most value in our economies now comes from intangibles, scientific knowledge, patents, software, brand, and data. If Anthropic’s machine intelligence can create intangibles like these – breakthrough science, information, or software – then it should be able to create extraordinary value.

Over the past fifty years, value in the S&P 500 has shifted from tangibles, things you can count in warehouses or can stub your toe on. Most value now resides in that ethereal flim-flam of the intangible: brand, customer lists, patents, and software.

Put another way, Anthropic’s machine intelligence lets it compete for 92% of the value of the S&P 500 before it needs to deploy a single robot.

That is the big macro-level survey that paints the opportunity. But I’ve been digging deeper. My conclusion is that AI companies in general, and Anthropic, are in a unique position. Look at the chart below. Each time Anthropic announced a new product feature that encroached on a given sector, the stock prices of firms in that sector responded as you’d expect.

AI companies might be able to extract a permanent tithe on the economy. Anthropic, as the leading player, is best positioned to do that.

The following are my sketches. They’ll give you a sense of the direction that I think merits further exploration.

Capturing the intangible

Anthropic has three approaches to capturing value in an intangible economy:

  1. It can ask companies to pay to defend their assets. As I wrote in The Internet’s Wuhan moment, AI has laid bare the software’s non-existent security model. Anthropic’s Mythos is the world’s most powerful security-oriented AI.
