issues.title: Why Van Gogh Painted a Café Where a Man Could Lose His Mind
issues.summary: In September 1888, Vincent van Gogh made a painting that captured the “terrible passions of humanity.” This work, titled The Night Café, is one of the most significant paintings the artist made in his career. Instead of focusing on the beauty of nature or the honesty of peasant labor, this painting brings attention to […]
issues.author: Stuti Verma
issues.content_html:
In September 1888, Vincent van Gogh made a painting that captured the “terrible passions of humanity.” This work, titled The Night Café, is one of the most significant paintings the artist made in his career. Instead of focusing on the beauty of nature or the honesty of peasant labor, this painting brings attention to the ruin and self-destruction that human beings indulge in. Through its sharply contrasting colors and converging perspective, The Night Café evokes a feeling of uneasiness that characterized Van Gogh’s experience of this cafe.

Painting in Arles

Van Gogh moved to Arles, a city in southern France, in February 1888 after spending nearly two years living with his younger brother Theo in Paris. He spent this time modernizing his style and technique alongside his peers, discovering new ways to implement form, line, and color to create harmonious compositions. Van Gogh arrived in Arles with a fresh perspective on painting and color, ready to take on the job to capture the south of France on his canvases. The city provided him with a number of vistas and natural subjects to paint, such as wheatfields, orchards, hills and gardens, and the fifteen months he spent in Arles are recognized as Van Gogh’s most productive period. The artist wished to settle down in Arles and rented a small house with two floors and four rooms on 2 Place Lamartine.

He called this The Yellow House and hoped to establish it as an artists’ community where painters could share expenses and studio space. Before moving into this house in mid-September 1888, Van Gogh rented a small room in Café de la Gare located on 30 Place Lamartine and lived there between May and September. The café was run by the couple Joseph-Michel and Marie Ginoux, both of whom later posed for Van Gogh. The artist spent a good amount of time in the café and was intrigued by its atmosphere and character, which eventually led him to paint a night scene of its interior titled The Night Café.

The Night Café

Painted in September 1888, The Night Café depicts the interior of a café de nuit, which referred to a café that was open throughout the night. There is a billiard table in the middle of the room and several tables lined up against the wall, and the door lies on the opposite end of the room next to a small bar lined with bottles and a vase with a pink and green bouquet. The entire room is lit up with four gas lamps hanging from the ceiling, casting a large shadow directly underneath the billiard table. The cafe is populated by six people, including the landlord who stands next to the billiard table and five customers who appear to be drinking or sleeping.

The walls are painted a solid red, contrasting with the green ceiling. A clock hangs above the door and shows the time to be roughly quarter past midnight. Van Gogh used a converging perspective and the vivid contrast between the yellow, red, and green in The Night Café to create an atmosphere of uneasiness and restlessness that was characteristic of this space during the late hours. He described his deliberate choice of color in this painting in detail in a letter to his brother, writing,

“I’ve tried to express the terrible human passions with the red and the green. The room is blood-red and dull yellow, a green billiard table in the center, 4 lemon yellow lamps with an orange and green glow. Everywhere it’s a battle and an antithesis of the most different greens and reds; in the characters of the sleeping ruffians, small in the empty, high room, some purple and blue.”

The Night Café portrays the dark underbelly of society during the evening hours in Arles. His letter from September 9th shows his intentions with this painting. In it, he wrote, “In my picture of the Night Café I have tried to express the idea that the café is a place where one can ruin oneself, go mad or commit a crime. . . To express something of the power of the dark corners of a grog-shop.” This café was a hotspot for drinking and prostitution, and the customers who would spend their nights here usually had nowhere else to go, usually due to a lack of money or excessive drinking.

As Van Gogh spent many evenings in the establishment, he possibly witnessed many such scenes at night and considered it meaningful to portray this side of Arles on canvas. The Night Café was certainly an important work for Van Gogh as the artist worked on this painting over the course of three nights. He described the painting as “one of the ugliest I’ve done” and suggested that it was a counterpart to The Potato Eaters that he made in Nuenen in 1885. The Night Café was called “the equivalent, though different” of the painting of Brabant peasants, and both canvases illustrate completely different sides of society and human life. While The Night Café centers on addiction and ruin that people indulge in to escape their circumstances, The Potato Eaters portrays honest work and the simplicity of peasant life that perseveres despite material struggles.

The Night Café is also one of two prominent paintings by Van Gogh that feature a cafe setting. The other work, Café Terrace at Night, was also painted in Arles in September but depicts a different establishment on Place du Forum under a different light. This painting was inspired by Van Gogh’s fascination with night scenes and was intended to capture the effect of light and colors at night, while The Night Café presents a darker side of such establishments.

A Premonition to Personal Struggles?

A few months after The Night Café was painted, Van Gogh suffered from his first major psychological breakdown in Arles. After having an argument with his friend and peer, Paul Gauguin, Van Gogh cut off part of his left ear with a razor in his Yellow House. He was hospitalized the next day and treated by Dr. Félix Rey. This incident marked an important moment in the artist’s life as it was the beginning of his declining mental health. After returning from the hospital, he attempted to return to his normal routine and continued painting, but his breakdowns persisted and he had to be hospitalized on multiple occasions within the following months. By May 1889, Van Gogh’s condition had worsened, leading him to take the decision of admitting himself to a psychiatric asylum in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, where he had access to constant observation and professional support. He spent one year in this asylum before moving to Auvers-sur-Oise near Paris, where he ultimately died by suicide in July 1890.

While The Night Café was painted months before Van Gogh’s first breakdown, it can be interpreted as a premonition of his declining mental state. The people depicted in the work are lost in life and drowning in alcohol and prostitution. Van Gogh’s constant exposure to this life may have shaped his view of life and the world, and as an avid drinker and frequent visitor to brothels, he also partook in this lifestyle. In fact, scholars have considered the artist’s excessive drinking habits and lack of care for his health to be the main reasons for his worsening psychological state. To add to that, Van Gogh often struggled to cope with his failure to sell his work and found it difficult to remain hopeful.

He once wrote to his brother Theo from the asylum, “To succeed, to have lasting prosperity, one must have a temperament different from mine, I’ll never do what I could have and ought to have wanted and pursued.” However, while he struggled immensely for a significant period of his life, Van Gogh was never left without support. Theo remained a source of motivation and hope in the artist’s life until the very end. It was because of Theo’s encouragement and financial help that Van Gogh was able to pursue a career as an artist, and later, the efforts of Theo’s widow, Johanna, ultimately established Van Gogh’s name as one of the greatest artists in history.

issues.title: How the Sicilian Mafia Helped the Allies Invade Sicily in WWII
issues.summary: Before Allied boots ever touched the beaches of Sicily during World War II, unlikely allies began planning together in New York. The United States needed help gaining every advantage possible to break through Axis positions in the Mediterranean, and its primary target was Sicily, a heavily fortified gateway to mainland Italy. To secure a […]
issues.author: Mike Cohen
issues.content_html:
Before Allied boots ever touched the beaches of Sicily during World War II, unlikely allies began planning together in New York. The United States needed help gaining every advantage possible to break through Axis positions in the Mediterranean, and its primary target was Sicily, a heavily fortified gateway to mainland Italy. To secure a successful landing, American naval intelligence turned to an unexpected resource: the American Mafia. What ensued was a partnership forged in the deep, tumultuous world of espionage that also influenced post-war Sicilian politics.

How Mussolini’s Brutal Crackdown Forced the Mafia to Flee to America

After rising to power in Italy, dictator Benito Mussolini recognized the conventional Sicilian Mafia as a direct challenge to totalitarian rule. To tackle the syndicate, Mussolini chose a zealous official, Cesare Mori, widely referred to as the Iron Prefect. Mori went about his work with an iron fist and imprisoned thousands of suspected mafiosi. Some of their families were also subjected to harsh measures, and their properties were seized in a ruthless effort to stamp out organized crime. Many of these mafiosi, desperate to save their lives, fled to America and rose to prominence there. They harbored deep resentment for Mussolini.

How Sabotage Fears Led the US Navy to Partner With Lucky Luciano

By December 1941, when America entered World War II following the attack on Pearl Harbor, concerns regarding Axis sabotage and espionage had begun to rise. This was especially true after February 9, 1942, when the USS Lafayette, a luxury ocean liner formerly known as the SS Normandie, caught fire and capsized in New York Harbor while being converted into a troop transport vessel. Although later investigations found the fire accidental, fears of Axis sabotage prompted US naval intelligence to secure the docks by ensuring labor peace. To accomplish this, they turned to imprisoned Italian crime lord Charles “Lucky” Luciano.

Sentenced to 30 to 50 years in prison for compulsory prostitution, Luciano was contacted by intelligence agents, principally through Luciano’s associates like Meyer Lansky, to collaborate with the US Navy in exchange for a potential reduction of his sentence. Luciano promised to guarantee safe ports, ensure there would be no strikes, and watch for enemy spies.

How Mob Intelligence Prepared the Allies for Operation Husky

By early 1943, following a series of victories in North Africa, the Allies began planning an invasion of Sicily. Code-named Operation Husky, it would require a large amphibious landing in the Mediterranean Sea. For such an operation to succeed, Allied forces needed detailed knowledge of the geography, maps of ports, protected landing beaches, and contacts with locals who could sabotage enemy lines of communication. To aid this effort, the US military expanded its domestic wartime cooperation with the American Mafia.

Italian mafia boss Charles “Lucky” Luciano’s network of contacts on the New York waterfront was used to identify Italian-Americans who had family ties to Sicily. Through Luciano and others, the US enlisted the aid of Sicilian-born Americans who fervently wished to see Benito Mussolini and his fascist regime overthrown. These volunteers provided the information needed, as well as names of contacts they knew they could trust on the island. During the invasion on July 10, 1943, Allied forces used this intelligence to aid planning. The mafia would exploit the Allied occupation to help reestablish its political influence.

How the Allied Occupation Allowed the Sicilian Mafia to Rebuild

While the landings were successful, some serious fighting took place throughout the mountainous terrain of Sicily as Allied forces fought their way north against the Axis defenders. As towns fell to the Allies, military administrators turned to prominent citizens to help restore civil order and oversee food rationing. These men, who were in many cases members of the Mafia, used their newfound influence to piece back together mafia operations that had been ruthlessly crushed by Mussolini’s crackdown years earlier. The Allied forces basically gave the Sicilian Mafia room to grow.

Luciano’s actions did not go unrewarded. In 1946, his sentence was commuted on the stipulation that he agreed to be deported back to Italy. While he went to Italy initially, Luciano moved to Cuba briefly before pressure from America obliged him to return to Italy, where he resumed his criminal activities. He died in 1962 from a heart attack. The secret alliance between military intelligence and organized crime remains one of the most intriguing and controversial military operations.

issues.title: Actress Chloe Bridges and Dr. Charis Chambers on what moms need to know to help protect their baby against RSV infection
issues.summary: In a candid conversation on The Motherly Podcast, Chloe and Dr. Chambers get real about the challenging transition into motherhood, learning to ask for (and accept) help, and what every expecting mom should know about helping protect their newborn from RSV infection.
issues.author: Sara Goldstein
issues.content_html:
This episode is sponsored by Pfizer. This article is directed to a U.S. audience and may not be suitable for those outside of the U.S.We partnered with them to bring you this conversation, but everything you hear from me, Chloe, and Dr. Chambers is our own experience and opinion. Not medical advice, just a conversation between moms.

Pregnancy has a way of making you feel responsible for someone before you have ever met them. For actress Chloe Bridges and OBGYN Dr. Charis Chambers, that meant navigating the identity shift of new motherhood while also learning about respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), a highly contagious respiratory virus that is the number one cause of hospitalization for babies in the United States with nearly 50% of RSV hospitalizations occurring during the first 3 months of life. Both moms built a trusted village of support to help navigate – and have a lot to say about what they wish they had known sooner.

In a candid conversation on The Motherly Podcast, Chloe and Dr. Chambers get real about the challenging transition into motherhood, learning to ask for (and accept) help, and what every expecting mom should know about helping protect their newborn from RSV infection.

Chloe Bridges is an actress with a career spanning film and television. A Columbia University graduate, she welcomed her first child, her son Beau, with her husband, actor and comedian Adam Devine, in February 2024.

Dr. Charis Chambers is a board-certified OBGYN and fellowship-trained pediatric and adolescent gynecologist known to millions online as The Period Doctor. She is the Chief Medical Officer at the cycle-tracking app Clue and the author of The Period and Puberty Parenting Revolution. She lives with her husband, Zachary, and their son, Joshua.

What was the first lesson that motherhood taught you?

Chloe: I think for me it was that everything is a phase. In the early days, I would get so nervous if something went wrong that day, you know, if he didn’t nap or wasn’t a good sleeper. I’d be like, ‘Oh my gosh, he’s never going to sleep. He’s always going to be a bad sleeper.’ And I just had to learn that a good day today doesn’t necessarily mean a good day tomorrow. A bad day today doesn’t mean a bad day tomorrow. Everything is just constantly changing and in flux.

Dr. Chambers: The first lesson was really that I just can’t do it all by myself. I take pride in being able to accomplish things, and I am so proud of the things I have accomplished, professionally, personally. But motherhood is not one of those things where there’s a badge of honor when you suffer. So I had to learn, from the newborn phase to the late infancy phase to now, that I need help. Sometimes I need help because I can’t be in two places at once. Sometimes I need help because I don’t feel well. Sometimes I need help because I need to be restored, and I need a break. And all of those are really good reasons to ask for help.

How would you describe your mindset heading into motherhood for the first time?

Chloe: I didn’t know what I didn’t know. It was almost like I didn’t want to think about postpartum too much, because I truly didn’t know what to expect. Everyone talks about how it’s just such a big transition, and I did really feel that. What’s that thing that people say? Two people are born that day. The baby is born, but then you are also born as a mother. And I absolutely experienced that. You can try to prepare mentally for what it’s going to feel like, but it’s still so surreal when it actually happens.

Dr. Chambers: I immediately threw up my hands in thanks, and then I looked around like, ‘Wait a second.’ Everything is different. I felt like I didn’t even know which way to move or walk. I didn’t know what to do next. I just sat with that moment. My beliefs, my vision for tomorrow, my to-do list, it all just exploded, all in that moment. And it was immense joy, but a nervousness that I think is in proportion to just the depth and caliber of what this is.

You’ve both described an identity shift. Can you talk a little bit about that?

Dr. Chambers: As someone who spent so long not being a mother, I never thought that motherhood would ever fully define me, and I still don’t feel that way today. I also think when you desire something so much, it’s hard sometimes to verbalize that desire. So knowing that you’re stepping into this role, this space, that has never really been in your control to step into, but that door is opening. It was an identity shift, but like an identity shift I’d always hoped for but never had the power to change. Becoming a doctor, I knew that. I knew I was going to go to med school. Once I got that MD, I was going to be a doctor. But this is almost like it’s not an earned thing. It is given. I knew it was a forever shift, but spending so much time desiring to be in that role, and seeing that for myself and not knowing if it was going to happen, that was a real identity shift for me.

Pregnancy can feel like a crash course in invisible responsibility. What decisions felt hardest during your pregnancy journeys?

Chloe: I think a lot of the decisions I was making were just about being so much more cognizant of my own health. Before pregnancy, I don’t know if I was necessarily the healthiest person, but you get pregnant and suddenly it’s not about you, it’s about you and your baby. And your health is intertwined obviously. So it was just a lot of decisions about, you know, obviously I’m going to follow all the advice. I’m going to limit my caffeine intake and I’m going to avoid foods that could give me listeria. And I’m going to, you know, take my prenatal. All of a sudden I was thinking about my health so much more, in a way I hadn’t been before.

Dr. Chambers: So many of the decisions that I knew I had to make, it was almost like I had the answers to the test, just because I’m an OBGYN. But then I started to realize that what I really knew about pregnancy was related to a role that I wasn’t playing this time. I was the actual patient. I had a point in my pregnancy where my cervix was shorter, and they were measuring it, and wondering, are we going to need to do something more invasive, like a cerclage, or can we just do vaginal progesterone. And my very best friend, it was her bachelorette party, but it was in a remote area of Mexico, and I said, ‘How can I reconcile potentially delivering early in this extreme prematurity state that we would be looking at because I just want to be on this girls’ trip?’ I had to just sit with myself, ‘All right, what makes the most sense?’ Of course my friend was amazing and was like, ‘Girl, say less. No one’s going to feel bad. Take care of you and your baby.’ But it just was hard. You want to do so many things, but at the end of the day, you have to stand in your values and stand in your truths and trust that the people around you will be supportive of that.

There’s so much noise around pregnancy, social media, group chats, your mom, your OBGYN. How do you determine whose advice you can really trust?

Dr. Chambers: This day and age, it is just hard, but it depends on the topic. When I was making my registry, for whatever reason, I just couldn’t start it. There’s a billion strollers. What do you mean there’s this many cribs? I was so overwhelmed. So I gave my sister my login and said, ‘Go to town.’ But as it related to my health, being someone who had a high-risk pregnancy, it was a meeting of the minds. I made sure all of my doctors were on the same page, and I wanted a yes. Like when you’re in the emergency row of the flight and they’re like, ‘Yes, yes, yes.’ ‘Nephrologist?’ ‘Yes.’ ‘High-risk doctor?’ ‘Yes.’ OBGYN who’s doing the delivery, yes. I trusted my team.

Chloe: I was also overwhelmed by the whole registry process. But I don’t have a lot of friends who have been pregnant before me, so I was leaning on the internet a lot. Dr. Google, and honestly lots of YouTube videos, all those videos of people being like, ‘This is what’s on my registry,’ or ‘Day in the life.’ And then my OBGYN was so helpful. I would be lost without her. She was truly such a resource, and I really felt like I had built a trust with her, and it really paid off later during birth and everything. I felt like I could ask her anything and trusted her advice.

What is RSV, and why is it such a concern for infants, especially in those first six months of life?

Dr. Chambers: RSV, or respiratory syncytial virus, is a highly contagious respiratory infection that can get really serious for our youngest babies. When we think about the seasonality of it, it tends to run during the fall and winter months, and the seriousness is that it can lead to hospitalization. It can lead to infant mortality. This is a very serious thing.

What are some of the specific signs of RSV in infants, and how do they differ from a cold or flu?

Dr. Chambers: Cold and flu can look like fevers and things of that nature. Sometimes it isn’t terribly respiratory leaning. But RSV has a lot to do with how your baby breathes, the retraction signs, and the work of breathing is the term that we use. Babies can get really, really exhausted and tired, and that noisy type of rapid breathing, those are all red flags that something is wrong. These are not all the possible symptoms of RSV in infants, so it’s important to talk to your doctor. If you notice any symptoms in your baby, talk to your baby’s doctor right away.

If RSV is only vaguely on an expecting mom’s radar, what does she need to know about its potential impact during those early months?

Dr. Chambers: During those early months of life, that’s when your baby is at highest risk. Their immune systems are slowly building up, and when we’re thinking about the way RSV might affect an adult, it is not the same for your infant. So if it’s just vaguely on your radar, it’s important to know that this deserves more prioritization. It deserves more energy, more research. If eligible, pregnant women may have the power to help protect their babies by choosing to get vaccinated with ABRYSVO ® (Respiratory Syncytial Virus Vaccine), Pfizer’s respiratory syncytial virus vaccine that’s given during 32 through 36 weeks of pregnancy to help protect babies against RSV infection from birth through 6 months during September through January in most of the United States.

To avoid the potential risk of preterm birth, ABRYSVO should be given during 32 through 36 weeks gestational age. The most common side effects in pregnant women are injection site pain, headaches, muscle pain, and nausea. Low birth weight and jaundice can also occur in infants. Please keep reading for full Important Safety Information at the end.

How does maternal immunization for RSV actually work?

Dr. Chambers: Many moms don’t realize that they are constantly making antibodies to things they’re exposed to and passing those antibodies onto their babies naturally. The RSV vaccination uses that natural process by allowing the mom to create antibodies to RSV and pass them down to her baby. When you get the maternal RSV vaccine, you are helping to protect your baby from the moment they take their first breath. Maternal immunization is an important part of my prenatal care discussions because babies are at highest risk of infection from RSV during their first three months of life.

Chloe: RSV wasn’t on my radar. It was something that I learned about from my OBGYN. She recommended I get ABRYSVO for it, and I remain very happy that I listened to my OBGYN’s recommendation to get ABRYSVO when I was pregnant, and that helped protect him during his first six months of life when he is so vulnerable.

ABRYSVO should not be given to anyone with a history of severe allergic reaction (e.g., anaphylaxis) to any of its components. An increased risk of Guillain-Barré syndrome (severe muscle weakness) was observed after vaccination with ABRYSVO. Please keep reading for full Important Safety Information at the end.

How can moms care for their own anxiety and fear in new motherhood, especially around their baby’s health?

Chloe: I’m glad we’re talking about this, because sometimes it can feel like so many things are being thrown at you when you’re pregnant, especially if you don’t have a lot of knowledge going into it and then you’re hearing about things from your OBGYN. It can feel sort of rushed, where if I’m hearing about a vaccine in my 32-week appointment, but then they’re like, ‘Oh, by the way, you only have until your 36 weeks to get it.’ So the more you know going in, it can only help to be more informed, to have time to do research.

What about mental preparation for new motherhood, beyond the expected guidance?

Dr. Chambers: The mental shift that was required the most, that I still carry with myself today, is letting go of the whole independent aspect. I would pride myself in being someone who was very self-sufficient. ‘I got it. If you can’t do this, I’ll figure it out.’ And it’s not that I don’t believe in myself, it is that I fully acknowledge the weight of motherhood and all that is required, and I now welcome the help. I had to tell my older sister, ‘I need you to put together my pump,’ and she did. I had to tell my mother-in-law, ‘The only thing I need today is a nap.’ And she’s like, ‘Go nap.’ Until you learn to verbalize those things and truly believe that you’re worthy of it, not as a point of insufficiency, motherhood requires a village. It requires a team. It requires support. Your mental health will be that much better for it.

Chloe: You go from being an individual with all of your independence, and then suddenly you are putting this baby’s needs before your own. My advice would be to try to establish communication with your village early, whoever that is, and have some sort of plan. Learn how to delegate. I don’t think I had done a lot of delegating before becoming a mom, and then suddenly you’re delegating all the time.

When you think about your babies who have grown up already, what do you hope they say about you one day as a mom?

Chloe: I want him to see me as competent and capable, but I also want him to see me as playful and fun. I think that’s been a big part of it. Maybe especially having a little boy, I want to be playful with him, and I want him to be able to have that kind of relationship with me. The nurturing comes so easy, but the playfulness has come a little harder. I hope he looks back and he’s like, ‘You know what? We had fun.’

Dr. Chambers: I hope my son sees me as someone he can trust, as someone who can give him advice, as someone who always makes decisions that are grounded in love and goodness, and someone who’s been making decisions since before he was born to set him up to have the best possible life. I hope that he trusts me with every aspect of who he is, knowing that the love I have is profoundly unconditional, and it has been before I could even picture his face. Before I even knew who he was, he was always worthy of that love and support, and it’s not going anywhere.

This article has been edited and condensed for clarity. Watch the full episode of The Motherly Podcast on YouTube.

Important Safety Information & Use

  • ABRYSVO should not be given to anyone with a history of severe allergic reaction (e.g., anaphylaxis) to any of its components
  • An increased risk of Guillain-Barré syndrome (severe muscle weakness) was observed after vaccination with ABRYSVO
  • To avoid the potential risk of preterm birth, ABRYSVO should be given during 32 through 36 weeks gestational age
  • Fainting can happen after getting injectable vaccines, including ABRYSVO. Precautions should be taken to avoid falling and injury due to fainting
  • Adults with weakened immune systems, including those receiving medicines that suppress the immune system, may have a reduced immune response to ABRYSVO
  • Vaccination with ABRYSVO may not protect all people
  • In pregnant individuals, the most common side effects ( > 10%) were pain at the injection site, headache, muscle pain, and nausea
  • In clinical trials where ABRYSVO was compared to placebo, infants born to pregnant individuals experienced low birth weight (5.1% ABRYSVO versus 4.3% placebo) and jaundice (7.3% ABRYSVO versus 6.9% placebo)

Ask your healthcare provider about the risks and benefits of ABRYSVO. Only a healthcare provider can decide if ABRYSVO is right for you. Always talk to your healthcare provider about any side effects you may experience.

You are encouraged to report side effects of vaccines to the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Visithttp://www.vaers.hhs.govor call 1-800-822-7967.

Individuals who received ABRYSVO during pregnancy are encouraged to enroll in a pregnancy exposure registry at 1-800-616-3791. The registry will monitor pregnancy outcomes.

WHAT IS ABRYSVO?

ABRYSVO is a vaccine indicated for pregnant individuals at 32 through 36 weeks gestational age for the prevention of lower respiratory tract disease (LRTD) and severe LRTD caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) in infants from birth through six months of age.

Please see full Prescribing Information for ABRYSVO atpfi.sr/ABRYSVO_PI.

issues.title: Her friend died after giving birth. Now she’s writing legislation to save other moms
issues.summary: Mothering America is a regular column from Motherly and Chamber of Mothers sharing moms’ stories from across the country, showing the power of coming together to make change. Each piece is part of a larger effort to ensure every mother and family in the U.S. has the support and care to be well. In 2008, […]
issues.author: Cassie Shortsleeve
issues.content_html:
Mothering America is a regular column from Motherly and Chamber of Mothers sharing moms’ stories from across the country, showing the power of coming together to make change. Each piece is part of a larger effort to ensure every mother and family in the U.S. has the support and care to be well.

In 2008, Lauren Underwood was in graduate school at Johns Hopkins, earning a master’s in public health, when she met a woman with a big, bright smile named Shalon Irving.

She never would have imagined the impact that friendship would have on her life’s work. Underwood would eventually become a U.S. representative for the state of Illinois, fighting to protect moms like Irving, who died before she could see her friend take office.

At the time, Irving, who already had her PhD, was coming back to school for additional training in public health. “We were just like regular girlfriends, passing notes in class and everything,” Rep. Underwood says.

The two—Rep. Underwood, a registered nurse, and Irving, an epidemiologist—stayed in touch through the years. In January 2017, Rep. Underwood served as a senior advisor at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, and Irving worked for the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). She had also given birth to a beautiful baby girl named Soleil.

Three weeks later, though, Irving wasn’t feeling well. “She went to the doctor several times, explaining that something wasn’t right,” Rep. Underwood remembers. On January 28, Irving died of complications related to high blood pressure. She was 36.

“Shalon had a career focused on ending health disparities, and she was so excited to become a mom,” Rep. Underwood says.

Today, Rep. Underwood is the architect of a series of 14 bills called the Momnibus, which was reintroduced to Congress this spring. The Momnibus addresses “every clinical and non-clinical factor” leading to preventable maternal deaths and disparities in this country; it’s evidence-based, data-driven, and offers states, communities, providers, and nonprofits the resources to help save moms like Irving’s lives. For Rep. Underwood, the Momnibus is personal.

While a member of Congress, Rep. Underwood is also a woman and a friend who, like too many in this country, lost a dear friend and felt a fire to make change.

The maternal mortality crisis and moms who should be here today

Rep. Underwood recalls Irving’s funeral as devastating—particularly because many of those in attendance held positions of the highest authority in public health in this country. She remembers the head of the CDC speaking at Irving’s funeral and expressing bewilderment at her death.

For Rep. Underwood, it was no mystery why mothers like Irving die in childbirth and shortly thereafter. As a clinician, she had seen firsthand health disparities in action; as a Black woman, maternal mortality was an unfortunate “phenomenon where it’s just so common when you talk about the maternal crisis.”

Today, we know about 84 percent of pregnancy-related deaths like Irving’s are preventable—meaning that most of the moms who aren’t here today should be here, and could be here, with the proper supports in place. Black moms are more than three times as likely to die in pregnancy or the postpartum months than white women—a disparity that persists across income and education levels.

“People think higher education or higher income is protective. They think that if you are a healthcare worker, you’re going to get the best healthcare. If you know the risks, are self-aware, confident, and have agency, and you can speak up for yourself, then these kinds of things won’t happen to you. Shalon and her death fly in the face of all of those assumptions, and it breaks your heart.”

When she made the decision to run for Congress, Rep. Underwood knew that if she won, maternal mortality would be an issue she’d work on.

Why the political will to make change for moms is gaining momentum

In 2018, Rep. Underwood became the youngest Black woman ever elected to Congress. She teamed up with Rep. Alma Adams (D-NC), who also had personal experience with maternal health: Adams’ daughter had experienced a very challenging labor and delivery, known in medical terms as severe maternal morbidity, or an experience that has lasting impacts on a mother’s health.

Together, in April 2019, the two formed the Black Maternal Health Caucus. At a crowded press conference, Rep. Underwood fought back tears. “To be in this moment with the dome of the Capitol behind us and these cameras and people asking questions and it’s this diverse, multi-generational, multi-ethnic, male and female moment of speaking about an issue that was so personal to me—I was just overcome,” she says. “It was a moment of power and resolve. It was an invitation. We were planting a flag, saying, ‘We’re here. We’re going to do this work. We know that there’s an opportunity to bring change.’”

Rep. Underwood didn’t expect the Black Maternal Health Caucus to grow into one of the largest bipartisan caucuses on the Hill. “We left that press conference and our phones started ringing, and it never stopped.”

What moms everywhere can do to improve maternal health

Rep. Underwood has dedicated her career to ensuring everyone—moms included—has equitable healthcare so we can all feel our best. She’s also dedicated her career to ending the maternal mortality crisis. “We know exactly what to do. We just need to invest, have the resolve, and to say, ‘This is unacceptable. Let’s fix this issue.’”

She also reminds us that Congress works on the issues that members raise. “If a Member comes in and says, ‘This is important to my community, and this is an essential issue that we tackle,’ that’s how solutions advance.” Many of her ideas for bills, she says, come from your stories.

“Often, people think that their story doesn’t matter, and when they come in to advocate, they think they need to have statistics or be a walking encyclopedia,” Rep. Underwood says. “But we are in a relationship business, and connection is currency. The fastest way to build a connection is to share your humanity, tell your story, and invite space for that vulnerability.”

What that means for you: If you have a story to share, Members of Congress are home in their districts through the end of the month, with offices open Monday through Friday and available for meetings. (Not sure how to set up a meeting? Check out Chamber of Mothers’ ‘Moms at Recess’ guide, which includes step-by-step plans and tips for hosting a meeting with Members of Congress.)

Rep. Underwood also underscores the importance of being loud about solutions and progress in maternal health. She highlights the power of doulas, lactation consultants, and community support in maternal health—and the fact that, to date, one of the Momnibus’ 14 bills has been signed into law. Others have passed the House. The Momnibus has also unlocked more than $250 million for states, community organizations, researchers, and providers to save lives. (You can find out which projects are being funded with Momnibus dollars in your community through the Caucus’s Momnibus Money Tracker.)

“We want the news of a pregnancy to be a time of joy and hope and eager anticipation and wonder,” Rep. Underwood says. “This can’t just be a conversation around problems. We want people to know that we’re working on this, that we have their backs, and about the opportunities, help, and the resources that are available.”

issues.title: School meals decoded: What’s really on the lunch tray
issues.summary: The menu in your child’s cafeteria isn’t set by chance. It’s the result of a multi-year federal process, and you can weigh in on how it changes.
issues.author: Lauren Ramakrishna
issues.content_html:
In my son’s school district, entering middle school is a rite of passage. Sixth graders go to a new building, get their own locker, and experience freedoms they weren’t allowed in elementary school.

When my son came home from his first day of middle school, I couldn’t wait to talk about it. “What was the best part of your day?” I eagerly asked. “The food,” he replied.

I wasn’t surprised. Meals are a big deal for a growing boy. But it did make me wonder, what exactly will he eat for lunch every day?

Long gone are the days when I would pack my son a homemade lunch with a loving note tucked inside. In middle school, he wanted to walk into the cafeteria, review the day’s menu options, stand in line, and buy his lunch. I agreed to the plan because I wanted to support his thirst for independence. But I also hoped I hadn’t unwittingly given him permission to start a junk-food-only diet.

Luckily, there are guidelines schools are required to follow when it comes to serving our kids meals. Those rules aim to make lunchtime enjoyable and healthy for the 30 million students who eat school lunch every day in the United States through the National School Lunch Program (NSLP). Unsurprisingly, they’re a constant work in progress.

What are the School Nutrition Standards?

The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) sets federal requirements for school meals served through the NSLP and the School Breakfast Program. The rules attempt to align school food offerings with nutrition standards outlined in the Dietary Guidelines for Americans (DGA), the official dietary guidance published by the USDA and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) every five years. When the DGA gets an update, school nutrition standard changes will follow, as required by law.

Schools are currently implementing changes developed following the release of the 2020-2025 DGA. In April 2024, the Food and Nutrition Administration (FNA, formerly Food and Nutrition Service) , a government agency responsible for administering domestic nutrition programs, like the NSLP, issued a rule requiring schools to make changes to foods served at school, including:

  • Reducing added sugars. For the first time, starting last school year (2025-26), schools have a limit on the amount of added sugars allowed for specific sugary foods, like breakfast cereals, yogurt, and flavored milk. Next school year (2027-28), schools must also abide by serving no more than 10 percent of weekly calories from added sugars.
  • Reducing sodium. By school year 2027-28, schools must achieve a 10 percent reduction in sodium limits at breakfast and 15 percent at lunch.
  • Greater flexibility at breakfast. Previously schools were required to serve a separate grain item, such as a muffin, with breakfast. Now, meat or meat alternatives (eggs, cheese, tofu) can substitute the grain requirement or schools can serve a combination of the two.

These updates join a comprehensive list of nutrition standards for school breakfasts and lunches that outline weekly serving requirements for fruits, vegetables, grains, meats and meat alternatives, and milk, as well as calorie minimums and maximums, and limits on saturated fat.

When will school nutrition requirements change again?

Potentially soon.

The USDA and HHS released the 2025-2030 DGA on January 7, 2026, triggering the next wave of school nutrition reviews in preparation for new recommendations and requirements. The USDA will compare the new DGA guidelines against existing school nutrition requirements, then draft a proposed rule on which schools, state agencies, advocates, industry experts, and consumer advocacy groups, like Center for the Science in the Public Interest, can provide feedback. The USDA will read and respond to comments, sometimes changing planned provisions in response to the feedback received, then publish its final rule.

At face value, this may seem like a good thing.

The USDA and HHS appoints a Dietary Guidelines Advisory Committee (DGAC) every five years to serve as an independent, expert panel of scientists and researchers in nutrition, health and medicine. The committee spends years reviewing current nutrition science to write a scientific report that’s typically used as a foundational resource for new dietary guidelines. DGAs have historically followed the vast majority of the DGAC’s recommendations. But, as CSPI notes, USDA and HHS rejected more than half of the DGAC’s expert recommendations. Instead, the agencies, according to CSPI, “hand-picked authors whose work aligned with beef, dairy, and protein supplement industry interests and the administration’s preconceived policy goals.”

This group of hand-picked authors created a new “Scientific Foundation for Dietary Guidelines for Americans,” which includes contradictory advice, recommending folks stick to prior, science-based saturated fat limits, while suggesting high-fat foods like whole milk and beef tallow are part of a healthy diet.

CSPI has raised other concerns about the 2025-2030 DGA, arguing that it gives harmful guidance to emphasize animal protein; advises people to consume double or more of the scientifically-backed recommendation for daily protein; reduces clarity around how people can eat a balanced diet within vegetable and protein categories; and adopts an inverted food pyramid that doesn’t accurately visually represent the dietary recommendations found within the text of the guidelines.

As in cycles past, schools expect the USDA to use the most recent DGA as a guide to propose changes to school nutrition standards. It’s unclear exactly what changes will be put forth, but there will likely be a mix of nutrition wins and losses. It’s possible the new standards will reflect evidence-based nutrition guidance like increasing whole grains, protein, and whole fruit, and cutting back on added sugars, sodium, and refined grains in school meals.

However, it’s also likely the new proposed standards may stray from evidence-based guidance by calling for decreased vegetable variety and overall fiber intake due to a deprioritization of plant-based proteins and an overemphasis on high-fat foods like whole milk and beef (rather than a variety of protein sources). For example, students could see more protein, like eggs and yogurt, at breakfast but miss out on a rainbow of vegetables and inclusive protein options like beans and tofu at lunch. Zooming out, meals lower in added sugars could be prioritized, while progress made on reducing saturated fat and sodium in school meals will be lost.

How can I impact what my kids eat at school?

The best way to inform what your kids get on their breakfast and lunch trays at school is to make your voice heard. After proposing changes to nutrition standards, the government will open a public comment period where you can share your opinions about what should be included or excluded from school meals. When the proposed rule finally comes out, CSPI will make it easy to share your opinion through model comments and templates that will allow parents to comment directly on the proposed rule. Stay tuned for next steps by signing up for CSPI advocacy emails.

The regulatory red tape may seem overwhelming. That’s why non-profits like CSPI give parents tools to learn about school nutrition standards and enact change. To learn more about school nutrition standards, visit CSPI’s Healthier School Food advocacy page. If you’re ready to advocate for healthier school meals, check out CPSI’s Take Action page to get involved.

issues.title: Jennifer Garner reveals how Once Upon a Farm became a $724 million company without sacrificing its values at Motherly’s State of Motherhood event
issues.summary: Motherly hosted some of the country’s most influential women leaders for a State of Motherhood event that took a deep look at what the last decade reveals about moms, and what we need going forward.
issues.author: Audrey Goodson Kingo
issues.content_html:
Moms may be burned out and lonely right now – but we don’t have to accept it.

That was the theme of Motherly’s State of Motherhood event on Monday, which brought together some of the most powerful women in business, media and advocacy to diagnose how moms have fared during the last tumultuous decade, and detail what we need going forward.

The conversation was driven by an in-depth analysis of Motherly’s own research. Every year since 2018, we’ve polled thousands of moms (more than 60,000 in fact!) for our annual State of Motherhood survey. And every year, moms have told us they’re scaling back at work and having fewer children than they’d prefer, but they’re still feeling isolated and overwhelmed. In 2025, 70% of moms said motherhood is lonelier than expected and in 2026, 42% felt more burned out than in the previous year.

“The truth is that our expectations of what it means to be a good mom changed faster than the systems built around to support her, and Gen Z moms are running into that gap even earlier,” said Motherly’s CEO Sharon Yi in her opening remarks. “But none of us should have to sacrifice our sanity, our careers, our identities to have children, and no mother should have to carry it alone.”

Leaders from organizations at the Clinton Foundation, the Andrew Carnegie Foundation, the ACLU, and the Vote Mama Foundation, joined together with executives at JP Morgan, Pfizer, Coterie,IKEA, and Paramount, to hear from women who are working tirelessly to create a world where moms feel supported, connected, and respected.

That included actress Jennifer Garner, who talked about her work as an ambassador for Save the Children and as co-founder of organic children’s nutrition company Once Upon a Farm.

Jennifer Garner gets real about balancing mission-driven work with motherhood

Garner kicked off the event in a fireside chat that touched on everything from finding community as a mom to the importance of advocating for children and families.

“Every kid deserves healthy, real food, an education, and parents who have a roof over their heads, food in their bellies, and time and space and energy and support to love their kids,” she said. Traveling around the country for her work with Save the Children, she described seeing families stretch food-bank, WIC, and SNAP resources to feed their children.

That’s why Once Upon a Farm worked hard to become the first WIC-certified company offering organic refrigerated baby food, she said. The company is now WIC-certified in 22 states. For Garner, it’s about dignity and choice: families using public benefits should be able to access high-quality food.

It’s all baked in, pun intended, to the company’s social mission to “drive systemic change in childhood nutrition for a happier, healthier, more equitable world,” Garner says. In 2021, the company transitioned its corporate structure from an LLC to a Public Benefit Corporation (PBC), which legally requires it to balance profitability with its social and environmental impact. It’s a challenging path for a business to pursue, which is why there are fewer than 20 publicly-traded PBCs, and Once Upon a Farm is the only one focused on kids. Towards those goals, Garner said, the company has donated a million meals to kids in rural America, and it pays a premium for produce “so that the people who are growing and picking our food are recruited ethically, and have a say in their safety and what their workday looks like.”

When it comes to balancing the demands of her multi-hyphenite life with motherhood, Garner didn’t hold back. On her non-negotiables, she joked, “I work out every day… unless I don’t. I read every night until I fall asleep… one page or none. I go to church… when I can. My kids come first… except for weeks where it’s crazy and I tell them they come first from afar.”

Finding the right balance changes day by day, Garner said. She assesses who needs her most in a given moment, including herself. “You get to choose moment to moment what you do and what your family needs,” she said to the moms in the room.

She also encouraged moms to come together to help defeat the loneliness that Motherly’s data revealed. “We’re literally meant to be in community,” she described. “When my second was born, I joined a baby group for second-time moms, and that is the most active group chat on my phone to this day.”

Plus, she added, small groups of committed moms have the power to make real change.

“We all love our babies the same. And when you realize that, that every mother in the world loves their baby the way you love yours, which seems impossible, but it is true, that also connects you to every other mother,” she said. “And then you feel like, how can I help every other mother who doesn’t have the advantages I have?”

Reshma Saujani, Lauren Smith Brody and others detail the structural fixes moms need

Next up was a panel about the state of motherhood in 2026, breaking down Motherly’s data showing that moms are increasingly burned out, and figuring out fixes to help. Featuring some of the most influential women working to make the United States a better place for families, the panelists pointed out that burnout is a structural problem — not an individual failure — and that collective action can turn broad public support for family policies into change.

“I think motherhood in America is impossible by design,” said Reshma Saujani, the founder and CEO of Moms First, a national non-profit organization working to advance paid leave and affordable childcare for working families. “Why does the school day end at 2:30 and the workday end at six? Why do we pay more for our childcare than our mortgage? Why do one out of four women go back to work two weeks after having a baby?”

Lauren Smith Brody, the founder of The Fifth Trimester and co-founder of Chamber of Mothers, said she’s optimistic that federal lawmakers will soon advance legislation to help moms across the country, including paid family leave, affordable childcare for all, and measures to improve maternal health outcomes. “I feel a lot of hope as we walk into these offices on Capitol Hill and we make a lot of behind the scenes connections between Democratic offices and Republican offices, because guess what? They actually do want many of the same things,” she said. “Moms are top of the list. They know that our voting power is unmatched. They know that they need us. They know that we voted them in and can vote them out.”

“I am telling you standing right here, [affordable] childcare and paid leave will get passed in 2029 within the first hundred days,” Saujani said. “I don’t care who is elected president because we are getting this done.”

It’s all about moms coming together to hold leaders accountable, said Ailen Arreaza, the executive director of the national nonprofit parents organization ParentsTogether. “Moms often feel it’s our sole responsibility to protect our kids, and feel shame when we think we’ve failed — especially when it comes to technology,” she said. “One of the best ways that we can hold companies accountable is by sharing our stories. We do a lot of work with parents who have lost children to big tech, and their stories are so powerful,” she said. “That also helps with the shame. When we talk to each other about what we are struggling with, what we are facing, that shame evaporates.”

Michelle Jawando, the CEO of Omidyar Network, a philanthropy organization working to foster responsible technology and AI development, said she’s encouraged by the fact that the mistakes of the “move-fast-and-break-things” era in Silicon Valley are providing a roadmap for more responsible tech development going forward. “I believe that everything that happened in that proceeding era gives us an opportunity to get AI right,” she said, pointing to California, which recently passed the strongest AI companion chatbot legislation in the country.

Dr. Bayo Curry-Winchell and others spell out how moms can get better care, sleep, nutrition and support

The morning’s final panel, moderated by the host of Motherly’s new podcast, Daniela Gysler-Wood, provided practical ways mothers can protect their physical and mental well-being.

Dr. Bayo Curry-Winchell, a board certified family medicine physician and the author of the upcoming book How to Talk to Your Doctor, encouraged moms to keep seeking answers if they’re feeling unwell. Her advice? If a clinician says you are fine but you do not feel fine, say, “I understand that you think I’m fine, but I’m not. What are the next steps?”

She also suggested asking, “What three to five possibilities are on your working list?” This helps you understand the range of possibilities if your doctor is focused on just one diagnosis.

When it comes to getting enough rest, celebrate the small wins, said Megan Holm, the women’s sleep research lead at sleep technology company Eight Sleep. “Sleep when you can, and you don’t need to check off everything on your to-do list in order to put your head on the pillow. You can take a 30-minute nap,” she said.

“I think we’ve all just accepted that exhaustion is part of motherhood, and I don’t think that’s where we should be,” said Victoria Thain Gioia, the co-founder and CEO of Perelel, an OB/GYN-founded and doctor-formulated vitamin and supplement brand. “To get through the day and stay sane, and to take care of small children, and do your job, you need to be nutritionally sufficient, not depleted. So while it can sometimes be overhyped, the conversation about protein, collagen, lactoferrin and nutrients that can actually support your energy [is important]. We really need to focus on care for mom beyond just pregnancy and postpartum.”

When it comes to protecting our mental well-being, the panelists encouraged moms to let go of guilt and connect with other parents. “Check in on your friends, nurture your friendships, don’t ask everything of your partner or your spouse, and ask for help,” said Elise Hu, the host of TED Talks Daily, a flagship podcast from TED Conferences. “Asking for help doesn’t just benefit you, the person who needs the help, it also benefits the helper because think about all the times that you have been asked for advice or counsel. That’s such a tribute to you, right? Because somebody is saying to you, ‘I trust you and I trust your advice and I trust your counsel.’ It nurtures the connection on both ends, not only for the helpee, but also the helper.”

Perelel, Eight Sleep offer hands-on demonstrations and swag

The moms in the room didn’t just leave with actionable advice and encouragement – although there was plenty on tap – they also took home a Happ Paige Mini full of goodies, including Once Upon a Farm snacks, Perelel Collagen+ Defense Supplements, Shiseido Sun Protector Clear Stick Sunscreen, Then I Met You Cleansing Balm, Ursa Major Golden Hour Recovery Cream, Merit Shade Slick, and the new Bentgo Lift Chug Lid water bottle.

Guests also got a chance to try out a mini version of Eight Sleep’s pod, an intelligent mattress cover that uses built-in biometric sensors to track your sleep and automatically adjust its temperature. “In May, we released pregnancy mode, which is automatic temperature support to support women as they go through pregnancy and up to 24 weeks postpartum,” said Holm, Eight Sleep’s women’s research lead, during the second panel. “As you grow a child, the environment around you feels really hot and uncomfortable. So we automatically make sure that when you can rest, and even if it’s not for eight hours every night, you’re comfortable.”

And bestselling author Loryn Brantz greeted guests as they walked into the room, signing free copies of her new release, I Am a Spicy Nugget, as well as copies of her New York Times bestseller, Poems of Parenting. Some lucky guests also received a signed print.

Sharon Yi issues a call to find community and make change

Motherly’s CEO Sharon Yi closed out the day with a call to action for all of the “incredible, powerful, influential” women in the room: “From all these conversations, I heard over and over that we need community, and that community is power, big or small,” she began. “We need advocates, people who fight relentlessly for the care, the policies and the respect that moms deserve. And we need storytellers, people who show the real picture of this journey at every stage without judgment.”

That’s where Motherly can play a powerful role going forward, she noted.

“Motherly is growing from a trusted resource into an active community online and off,” she explained. “What does that mean in practice? It means we’re showing up in her group chat. We’re in her feed with a slate of new vertical video shows that I’m really excited about. We’re in her earbuds with a new podcast. And we’re popping up in her neighborhood with our new hyper local event series, coming to a neighborhood near you so that moms can find the people where they are.”

issues.title: Early Drafts and Process Notes Prove Little to Nothing About Authors’ AI Use
issues.summary: An author was dropped by her agent over suspected AI use despite showing 11 drafts and notes. But since writers can use AI throughout revision, process documents may prove less than they hope.
issues.author: Jane Friedman
issues.content_html:
Recently, an author was dropped by her agent because of suspicions about AI use raised by a UK publisher—reportedly Cornerstone, part of Penguin Random House UK—after it ran the manuscript through Pangram, the leading AI detection software. (Penguin Random House has said openly that it uses AI detection.) Publishers Marketplace reports that the author presented 11 drafts for review, plus character notes and plotting plans, to prove that she wrote the book herself. But it wasn’t enough to remove suspicion.

The reaction from writers has been outrage that an AI detection score is seen as credible, more so than the author’s own work process and notes. And some agents have expressed anger at the author’s agent for not defending the author from these accusations.

As with all such cases involving suspicions of AI use, there’s so much we don’t know and details that may never be made public. The author has taken down her social media accounts; her website remains up.

I’ve commented at length about the use of AI detection in previous articles, so here I want to address why process work may not prove anything about whether an author used AI.

Some people, especially those who don’t pay to use AI, may have a simplistic idea of what happens when writers use AI to write and edit. They might envision a writer opening up ChatGPT, typing in a prompt, generating a full novel, then submitting it—or some variation thereof, maybe one prompt per scene or chapter. I understand why people think this. After all, the New York Times article about romance novelist Coral Hart, a pen name used by an author who openly admits to publishing AI-generated romance novels, characterizes the process this way, and some authors are in fact doing that.

As time goes on, though, as AI becomes more and more advanced in its capabilities, it is being used as part of the creative process in myriad ways, especially as writers experiment beyond feeding a prompt into an LLM. Imagine a writer taking all of their process materials (especially for a project they’re stuck on), adding it to a project in Claude, then collaborating over a series of conversations: “We need to fix the plot hole in Chapter 4.” “Let’s develop a better ending.” “Fix the pacing throughout.” AI can help revise a problematic manuscript so that it becomes publishable; it can take a partial manuscript across the finish line. Moreover, there are any number of custom AI tools for writers, like Sudowrite, that specialize in fiction writing tasks like this.

The point is: Having process documents helps writers use AI more effectively to produce a commercially acceptable manuscript. And as AI is used more frequently in this way, I believe more agents and publishers will use AI detection to help assess AI’s role in a manuscript and if that role has gone too far, for as long as they care about the presence of AI assistance in a work.

Pangram’s AI detection is more refined than “This work is AI / This work is not AI.” It highlights specific areas of concern. It may assess Chapter 1 as human written for the first 7 paragraphs, but AI written for the next 18 paragraphs before returning to human-written for the last paragraph. It may show Chapter 17 as entirely human written while Chapter 30 is entirely AI written. It may show a mix of AI and human from paragraph to paragraph. In cases where the manuscript flip flops all over the place, the agent or editor may start wondering: Is this worth the risk? And how will the writer use AI going forward? Will they disclose? (As a side note, I do wonder how well AI detection can keep up with sophisticated use of AI to write and edit. Will it always be able to flag writing as AI assisted or AI generated when it is? Pangram does say it errs of the side of false negatives.)

Even if not perfect, Pangram can tell an editor or publisher, at minimum, if an author has relied maybe too much on AI to write and edit a book-length manuscript. A publishing professional at that point might ask the writer, “I can tell AI has been involved in some way, and I’d like to understand how you used it.” 1 While writers might be tempted to flatly deny AI use given that it’s so hard to prove, some agents and publishers don’t trust the word of writers any longer. And reviewing writers’ process documents isn’t likely to be convincing or definitive either. This is why I don’t think it helps writers to take special efforts to create a process trail that they wouldn’t ordinarily be able to provide—I don’t think it matters in the end. (In the case of Haitian-Canadian poet and author, Thélyson Orélien, having early drafts may have in fact hurt his case. He was accused of using AI assistance for his novel, It Was That or Die, after it appeared on the longlist for the Prix Goncourt in France. His Canadian publisher, Les Éditions du Boréal—the one that discovered the book—dropped him some weeks later after finding evidence of AI use in early versions of the manuscript.)

Many wonder why lawsuits aren’t happening around these cases, either lawsuits against the publishers or agents using AI detection or against the AI detection companies. Cases are expensive to litigate and take a long time. Most writers don’t have money to bring such cases, but might lawyers work on contingency—or how about organizations with lawyers, like the Authors Guild? If they thought they could win, maybe they’d take up such cases. But no one seems to be stepping forward and it’s been many months since the first of these cases made headlines. And the authors who would bring such cases have to be prepared for a very bruising process of discovery.

If you comment: Some people will immediately comment to say AI detection tools are inaccurate and not to be trusted. These claims are usually based on misinformation, outdated information from 1–2 years ago, and/or random statements seen on social media. When I see claims that AI detection isn’t accurate, typically the person (1) isn’t using Pangram, which agents/publishers largely use, (2) isn’t using the paid version of Pangram, and (3) isn’t testing passages beyond a couple thousand words, if that. AI detection becomes incredibly useful and reliable for book-length work.

  1. With credit to Emily Broadmore ︎

issues.title: Writing for Small Screens: How to Structure Text for E-Readers
issues.summary: You finish a chapter on your laptop and it looks perfect. Then you open the same file on a six-inch e-reader, bump the font up two sizes, and your tidy paragraph becomes a gray wall that fills three screens. To structure text for e-readers, you have to plan for that moment. Keep paragraphs short, use The post Writing for Small Screens: How to Structure Text for E-Readers first appeared on DAILY WR
issues.author: Daily Writing Tips
issues.content_html:
You finish a chapter on your laptop and it looks perfect. Then you open the same file on a six-inch e-reader, bump the font up two sizes, and your tidy paragraph becomes a gray wall that fills three screens.

To structure text for e-readers, you have to plan for that moment. Keep paragraphs short, use real headings, keep lists simple, and remove anything that depends on a fixed page. This guide shows you how to do each one, with examples you can apply to your next manuscript.

Why Does Text Behave Differently on an E-Reader?

E-reader text behaves differently because it reflows. The words rearrange themselves to fit the screen, the font, and the size the reader chooses.

Understanding Reflowable Text

Most ebooks use reflowable text. The W3C’s EPUB 3 overview describes EPUB as a format built for content that adapts to different screens and reading settings, rather than one that locks every line in place.

That flexibility shifts control from you to the reader. You can’t decide where a line breaks or where a “page” ends. You can only decide how the text is organized.

What This Means for Your Writing

On paper, a long paragraph looks like one solid block. On a phone-sized screen at a large font, the same paragraph may stretch across several screens with no visual break. The same happens when a print PDF is converted carelessly, so if you’re starting from one, use a pdf to epub tool and then check the result.

Structure is the only layout that survives reflow. If your ideas are broken into clear units, the reader can follow them on any device.

How Long Should Paragraphs Be for E-Readers?

Paragraphs for e-readers should be shorter than they would be in print. Aim for one idea per paragraph and two to four sentences in most cases.

Following the One-Idea Rule

The Purdue OWL’s guide to paragraphs gives the classic rule: each paragraph develops one idea, and a new idea gets a new paragraph. On a small screen, that rule matters even more, because each break gives the reader a place to rest.

Plain-language guidance points the same way. The Digital.gov guide to short sentences and paragraphs recommends paragraphs of no more than 150 words and notes that long blocks can discourage readers from continuing.

Examples: Splitting a Dense Paragraph

  • Weak: The new policy takes effect in March, and every team will need to update its forms, which means managers should schedule training in February, although teams that already use the digital forms can skip the first session and go straight to the review meeting.
  • Why it fails: Four ideas share one sentence. On a narrow screen, the reader loses the thread before the end.
  • Strong: The new policy takes effect in March. Every team will need to update its forms. (New paragraph) Managers should schedule training in February. Teams that already use the digital forms can skip the first session.
  • Why it works: Each paragraph carries one point, and the break signals a shift from what is changing to what managers should do.

Shortening Sentences Too

Long sentences cause the same problem as long paragraphs. Front-load the subject and verb so the reader knows who does what before the line wraps.

The active voice helps here, since active sentences are usually shorter and more direct than passive ones.

How Should You Use Headings in an Ebook?

Use headings often, keep them short, and apply them as true heading styles, not as bold body text. Headings are how readers find their place on a device with no visible page numbers.

Applying Real Heading Styles

When you format a heading with your word processor’s Heading 1 or Heading 2 style, conversion tools recognize it as a heading. That allows the ebook to build a working table of contents and helps screen readers announce the structure.

Bold text at a larger size looks like a heading to you but often converts as an ordinary paragraph. The reader then loses navigation for that section.

Keeping Headings Short and Specific

A heading that runs three lines in print may run five on a phone. Keep headings to a few words and make them describe what follows.

  • Weak: Some Additional Thoughts on the Various Considerations Involved
  • Why it fails: It’s long, vague, and tells the reader nothing about the section.
  • Strong: Choosing a File Format
  • Why it works: The reader knows the topic at a glance, even on a small screen.

Checking Heading Alignment

Amazon’s Kindle text guidelines for reflowable books note that reflowable body text is fully justified by default, so they recommend setting an explicit alignment for headings. Without it, a short heading can stretch with uneven gaps between words.

How Do You Format Lists, Tables, and Notes for Small Screens?

Format them as simply as possible. Short vertical lists work well, wide tables rarely do, and footnotes need a different approach entirely.

Keeping Lists Short and Parallel

Bulleted lists are easy to scan on a small screen, but only if each item is brief and built the same way. Start every item with the same part of speech, and keep nesting to one level.

The Chicago Manual of Style’s Q&A on vertical lists covers how to punctuate and capitalize list items. Whatever style you choose, apply it the same way throughout the book.

  • Weak list items: Saving drafts often / You should back up files / Version names
  • Strong list items: Save drafts often / Back up your files / Name each version clearly

Replacing Wide Tables

A table with five columns may fit a printed page but force sideways scrolling on an e-reader, or shrink to an unreadable size. Ask whether the content truly needs a grid.

  • Two-column tables: Usually display well. Keep them.
  • Wide comparison tables: Convert each row into a short subsection or a bold-label list.
  • Data tables that must stay intact: Consider an image with a full text description nearby.

Handling Footnotes and Page References

E-readers don’t have fixed pages, so phrases such as “see page 42” or “as shown on the facing page” stop making sense. Replace them with section names or internal links: “see Choosing a File Format.”

Footnotes usually convert into linked notes that open in a pop-up or jump to the end of a chapter. Keep notes short, and move anything essential into the main text so readers don’t have to tap away to understand it.

How Do You Prepare and Test Your File?

Prepare your file from a clean, well-styled manuscript, then test it on more than one screen size before you publish.

Starting From the Right Source

A word processor file with consistent styles converts more cleanly than a print-ready PDF, because a PDF locks every line in place. If your manuscript only exists as a print layout, convert it to a reflowable format first, then check every heading, list, and paragraph break by hand.

Separating Paragraphs Correctly

Amazon’s guidelines require body paragraphs to be distinguished with either a first-line indent or extra space between paragraphs. Pick one method and use your paragraph style settings to apply it, never the Tab key or the space bar.

Testing Like a Reader

Before you publish, open the file and read it the way your audience will:

  1. Change the font size: Try the smallest and largest settings.
  2. Switch orientation: Read a chapter in portrait and landscape.
  3. Use the table of contents: Tap every entry to confirm it lands in the right place.
  4. Follow every link: Check internal cross-references and notes.
  5. Read one chapter start to finish: Watch for paragraphs that feel too long on screen.

What Are the Most Common Structure Mistakes in Ebooks?

The most common mistakes come from writing for a printed page that the reader will never see. Watch for these five:

  1. Page-number references: “See page 12” points to nothing on a device.
  2. Fake headings: Bold body text that never shows up in the table of contents.
  3. Overlong paragraphs: Print-length blocks that fill several screens.
  4. Spacing with the keyboard: Tabs, extra spaces, or blank lines used for layout often disappear or behave unpredictably after conversion.
  5. Passive, wordy sentences: Long constructions are harder to follow when lines wrap often. These examples of passive voice and how to fix them show how to tighten them.

How Can You Summarize Writing for Small Screens?

Writing for e-readers means building structure into the words themselves. Keep paragraphs to one idea, keep sentences direct, and use real heading styles so readers can navigate.

Simplify lists and tables, replace page references with section names, and test your file at several sizes before release. For more practical guides on clear, correct writing, subscribe to the Daily Writing Tips newsletter.
