issues.title: A Former Appliance Store Becomes a Hong Kong Cocktail Bar
issues.summary: Kevin Yiu of Minus Workshop pairs mid-century modern influences with warm wood, metallic finishes, and clever spatial solutions at Mius
issues.author: Anna Zappia
issues.content_html:
Good design is all about transformation and turning the everyday into memorable spaces. Kevin Yiu, principal at Minus Workshop, did just that with his recent conversion of a former appliance store into Mius, a cocktail bar in Hong Kong.

Nestled at 29 Gough Street in the SoHo district, the space reflects owner Shelley Tai’s belief in simple things done right, from libations that honor the classics to comfort food without complication. “Her desire for a genuine neighborhood bar challenged me to translate that specific vibe into spatial design,” Yiu explains.

Photography by Steven Ko

Yiu embraced mid-century modern design, and with only eight months to complete the project, he turned constraints into assets. High ceilings and a curated system of leather blinds capture sunlight by day, then offer layered illumination in the evening. A low structural beam clad in oak now doubles as an element that guides circulation and visually organizes the spaces. Electrical and mechanical systems remain hidden by joinery, which still allows access for maintenance.

Photography by Steven Ko

The material palette blends a range of contrasting textures. Wood veneer adds an organic appeal, while bronze and silver metals cast a subtle sheen, paired with shades of copper and brown. Minimal paint, rather than the artificial brightness of lacquer, keeps the aesthetic grounded.

Photography by Steven Ko

The 14-foot stainless steel bar top is both a statement piece and a functional surface that integrates essential equipment for the staff. Slabs of travertine form high tables where guests enjoy small plates or signature drinks. Reflective accents and strategic voids make the compact interior look more expansive.

Yiu decided to split bar operations across four counters to ease peak-hour congestion, keeping service clean and efficient. The queue flows from the front to the bar, with stools framing the activity in the main area.

Photography by Steven Ko

A floating chandelier by Lee Broom features celestial orbs that cast even light over the crowd. Plush velvet curtains drape over storage room doorways, and accent lamps round out a style that is bespoke but never stuffy.

For Yiu, it is a place that unfolds quietly, meant to be savored like the fare on the menu. “Mius is a sanctuary of simplicity, designed with a contemplative approach, which allows the interior architecture to elevate the hospitality experience,” he says.

issues.title: Friday Five with Nick Doyle: Seeing America Through Shades of Blue
issues.summary: Ahead of Art Basel Miami Beach, the Brooklyn-based artist shares the inspirations behind his latest exhibition
issues.author: Danine Alati
issues.content_html:
Creative minds can seemingly turn anything into art—from household items and food to packing supplies and bottle caps. For Los Angeles-born interdisciplinary artist Nick Doyle, the material of choice is denim. Even when working in other mediums, he often gravitates toward a denim-blue palette, as in his latest exhibition, “Lonely but Free I’ll Be Found.”

Presented at Pace Prints’ New York gallery this fall, the exhibition marks Doyle’s first venture into printmaking, using graphic interpretations of everyday objects to examine American preoccupations with risk and reward, escapism, and the myth of the self-made man. The gallery will present a selection of these works at Art Basel Miami Beach 2026.

‘Quick Fix’ (2026) by Nick Doyle. Photography courtesy of Pace Prints.

Now based in Brooklyn, Doyle earned a BFA in interdisciplinary arts from the San Francisco Art Institute and an MFA in sculpture from Hunter College, in addition to studying at Skowhegan School of Painting and Sculpture. He cites his discovery of denim as an artistic medium as a turning point in his career.

“I had been doing a ton of research on American history and making work exploring our relationship to nostalgia,” he recalls. “One day a fashion designer moved out of the neighboring studio and threw away a ton of stuff. I found a bolt of denim, and my brain flashed across a network of ideas I had already been considering. I intuitively knew I had stumbled across something significant.”

Photography courtesy of Pace Prints

Represented by Perrotin and Brussels-based Stems Gallery, Doyle typically uses denim collage to explore what he calls the “underlying structures in American culture.” His practice encompasses “painting-like wall works as well as interactive installations,” he says.

Doyle’s recent exhibition, Collective Hallucinations, presented at Perrotin New York this past spring, featured wall-mounted collages and an interactive installation called “Mirror Mirror.” The denim-clad structure featured a sign reading “Psychic Readings $10 Special,” while inside, a sassy AI avatar named Ava greeted visitors. The installation marked Doyle’s first foray into AI.

In another unexpected move, he presented his corporate-themed kink bar, Human Resources, at Basel Social Club in Switzerland this June. Built from repurposed cubicles and office furniture, the installation plays with the power dynamics inherent in both corporate and kink culture.

‘The Price of Ascension’ (2026) by Nick Doyle. Photography courtesy of Pace Prints.

Doyle calls his work “more of a reflection of American culture than an individualist perspective.” Reflecting on being raised Quaker, he says, “It’s a very consensus-driven community that is slow-paced and meditative. It’s culturally very counter to a fast-paced, consumer-driven way of life typical of growing up in a large American city.” The tension between these two ways of life surfaces throughout his work.

In this week’s Friday Five, we spent five minutes with Nick Doyle ahead of Art Basel Miami Beach, where Pace Prints will present selections from Lonely but Free I’ll Be Found, to discuss the inspirations behind his exploration of the contradictions of American life.

‘Empty’ (2026) by Nick Doyle. Photography courtesy of Pace Prints.

The Project: Lonely but Free I’ll Be Found

As with much of Doyle’s work, his latest exhibition examines the greed, excess, and toxic masculinity of American culture, this time through bold representations of the minutiae of everyday life: a folded shirt, a necktie, a lottery ticket, a gas gauge on empty, a Coca-Cola machine. Rendered in blue tones reminiscent of denim, the imagery evokes American labor and the archetype of the self-made man.

Together, the works question the country’s deep-rooted belief in self-reliance, drawing parallels between the ideal of the independent American and today’s “America First” mentality, in which individual freedom can come at the expense of collective responsibility. A selection of these works will be on view at Art Basel Miami Beach, Dec. 2–6, 2026.

Here, Doyle discusses his inspirations for the exhibition in his own words.

Photography courtesy of Pace Prints

What Inspired Lonely but Free I’ll Be Found?

The Ken Burns Documentary: Country Music

“This documentary has everything: It traces the origins of country music alongside American history and is a deeply emotional story about the search for salvation and community.

“One of the musical groups featured is The Sons of the Pioneers. The title of this exhibition Lonely but Free I’ll be Found is a lyric in their song ‘Tumbling Tumbleweeds.’ Originally a poem written by Bob Nolan in the 1930s, it describes lonely cowboys adrift on the range.”

The Neon Museum in Las Vegas, Nevada. Photography courtesy of Nick Doyle.

The Neon Museum in Las Vegas

“I take a lot of road trips in the Southwest. Vegas is a great access point, and one of my favorite places is the Neon Museum with a collection of old signage from the last century. There’s something about these retrofuturistic signs rotting away in the desert that I relate to. They exude a sad psychological aura of something that once served a purpose, sitting in functionless rows like a graveyard.

“I think of this body of work functioning similarly to these signs, although different in the sense that what I’m drawing attention to is an idea rather than something that can be purchased.”

‘The Itch’ (2026) by Nick Doyle. Photography courtesy of Pace Prints.

The Suicide Belt

“For this show, I was considering the perspective of a man who lived in the ‘suicide belt,’ a term coined by Matt Wray in the early 2000s to describe the high-suicide-rate region of the U.S. Mountain/Intermountain West. The belt includes Arizona, Colorado, Idaho, Montana, Nevada, New Mexico, Oregon, Utah, and Wyoming.

“Wray describes ‘the Intermountain West as a place that is disproportionately populated by middle-aged and aging white men, single, unattached, often unemployed, with access to guns.’ I often think about suicide as a larger social symptom and connect it to broader social issues in the U.S.”

issues.title: The Best Gifts Under $50 for Design Enthusiasts
issues.summary: Clever, colorful, and thoughtfully designed finds that make a big impression on a limited budget
issues.author: Design Milk Staff
issues.content_html:
There’s something particularly satisfying about finding a great gift at a reasonable price point. And when it comes to design, a smaller price tag doesn’t have to mean settling for something ordinary. Some of the most memorable objects are also the simplest: a cleverly designed kitchen tool, a colorful accessory, or an everyday essential with an unexpected twist.

For this year’s selection, we’re looking for gifts that bring a little more personality to the everyday. Think playful forms, interesting materials, useful details, and objects that reflect the creativity of the people who designed them. Whether you’re shopping for a friend, a coworker, or someone who’s notoriously difficult to buy for, these gifts under $50 offer plenty of reasons to think beyond the usual suspects.

Photography courtesy of Shelton Metal

Shell Espresso Spoon Set by Shelton Metal

Inspired by treasures found along the seafloor, these miniature spoons bring an unexpected sculptural element to everyday rituals. Jewelry and homeware designer Colby Shelton Byrd hand-carves the shell-inspired forms, which are cast in solid brass and designed to develop a natural patina over time. The two-piece set is equally suited to stirring espresso or serving sugar, salt, and other small accompaniments.

The Shell Espresso Spoon Set is available at bloomingdales.com for $42.

Photography courtesy of Original Duckhead

Matisse Duck Umbrella by Original Duckhead

Rainy days get a little more colorful with Original Duckhead’s Matisse-inspired umbrella. Its graphic canopy is made from recycled plastic bottles, while a carved wooden duck-head handle adds an unexpected touch of whimsy. Designed with a wind-resistant frame and automatic opening mechanism, the compact umbrella combines everyday practicality with enough personality to make even a gloomy forecast feel more interesting.

The Matisse Duck Umbrella is available at originalduckhead.com for $45.

Photography courtesy of Goodee

Niwaki Y-Type Tool Box

Who says a toolbox has to live in the garage? Made in Japan from durable steel, Niwaki’s Y-Type Tool Box brings a little personality to everyday organization with its distinctive pitched lid, rounded edges, and compact industrial design. Available in yellow or gray, it’s just as useful for storing art supplies, sewing essentials, or desk accessories as it is for actual tools. At approximately 14 inches long, it’s a practical little storage solution that looks good enough to leave out.

The Niwaki Y-Type Tool Box is available at goodeeworld.com for $40.

Photography courtesy of Present & Correct

1Y 52W 365D Planner by Present & Correct

A planner that’s as thoughtfully designed on the outside as it is on the inside. The 1Y 52W 365D Planner pairs a bold, striped cover with textured paper and foil lettering for a graphic take on everyday organization. Inside, 208 pages provide space to map out the year, while the undated format means there’s no pressure to start on January 1. A ribbon bookmark adds a practical finishing touch.

The 1Y 52W 365D Planner is available at presentandcorrect.com for $47.

Photography courtesy of Mark & Graham

Graham Leather Travel Tech Organizer

Tangled charging cables and misplaced earbuds are an inevitable part of traveling, but this sleek leather organizer from Mark & Graham helps keep the chaos under control. Its compact, zippered design keeps everyday tech essentials together, whether tucked into a carry-on, work bag, or backpack. The understated silhouette and leather exterior make it feel more like a thoughtfully designed accessory than a utilitarian storage pouch. Add a monogram for a personal touch that makes it an especially nice gift for frequent travelers.

The Graham Leather Travel Tech Organizer is available at markandgraham.com for $49.

MORE GIFT INSPIRATION

Still shopping? Explore Design Milk’s Complete 2026 Holiday Gift Guide for more thoughtful finds for everyone on your list.

Photography courtesy of McGee & Co.

Stoneware Fish Plate by McGee & Co.

A little coastal charm goes a long way with this sculptural stoneware fish plate from McGee & Co. Its softly raised details capture the fish’s distinctive shape, while a white reactive glaze adds subtle variations in color and texture, making each piece slightly different. Measuring just over seven inches long, it’s perfectly sized for serving small bites, holding a few favorite trinkets, or adding a playful touch to an open shelf. Proof that a thoughtful gift doesn’t need a big price tag.

The Stoneware Fish Plate is available at mcgeeandco.com for $26.

Photography courtesy of Galison

Frank Stella Harran II 750-Piece Shaped Puzzle by Galison

Frank Stella’s bold geometric artwork becomes a hands-on experience with this 750-piece puzzle. Featuring Harran II (1967), from the artist’s celebrated Protractor series, the design transforms colorful, overlapping arcs into an unconventional jigsaw with an irregular silhouette. Packaged in a handsome drawer-style box, it’s a thoughtful gift for art enthusiasts who enjoy a creative challenge.

The Frank Stella Harran II 750-Piece Shaped Puzzle is available at galison.com for $35.

Photography courtesy of Goodee

Pepin Olla Self-Watering Pot

For the plant lover who occasionally forgets to water, Pepin’s Olla offers a clever solution rooted in centuries-old irrigation techniques. Handcrafted in Portugal’s historic Leiria region, the small clay vessel is designed to be partially buried in a planter, where its porous walls slowly release water directly into the soil. Simply refill it every week or two, and let the plant take what it needs. Finished with a rich burgundy glaze and a natural cork stopper, it’s a charming little object that makes plant care a bit easier.

The Pepin Olla Self-Watering Pot is available at goodeeworld.com for $35.

Photography courtesy of Valsa Home

Stainless Steel Egg Cup Set by Valsa Home

A little retro and entirely practical, these stainless steel egg cups bring a sculptural touch to the breakfast table. Made in Portugal, their polished finish and gently flared silhouettes recall midcentury tableware, while the simple design feels right at home in a contemporary kitchen. Sold as a set of four, they’re a charming gift for anyone who appreciates the ritual of a leisurely breakfast.

The Stainless Steel Egg Cup Set is available at valsahome.com for $30.

Photography courtesy of Design Within Reach

Spirale Bowl by Emma Kohlmann for Hay

Artist Emma Kohlmann brings her expressive, painterly style to the table with this charming stoneware bowl. Part of Hay’s La Pittura collection, it draws inspiration from Renaissance apothecary jars and traditional Tuscan pottery. Each piece is hand-painted by artisans in Sri Lanka, making every bowl slightly different. At just under five inches across, it’s perfectly sized for snacks, sauces, or small treats.

The Spirale Bowl is available at dwr.com for $45.

Photography courtesy of Printworks

Yatzy Bazaar by Printworks

Swedish brand Printworks has a knack for turning classic games into objects worth displaying, and its Bazaar edition of Yatzy is no exception. Colorful, graphic packaging gives the traditional dice game a contemporary makeover, making it as at home on a coffee table as it is on game night. It’s a fun gift for anyone who appreciates good design and a little friendly competition.

Yatzy Bazaar is available at printworksmarket.com for $35.

Photography courtesy of Toast

Longpi Oil Burner by Toast

Hand-molded from a mixture of ground black stone and locally sourced clay, this oil burner showcases a centuries-old pottery technique unique to two villages in northeastern India. A tea light tucked into the opening below gently heats a mixture of water and essential oils in the bowl above, releasing fragrance throughout the room. Pair it with a favorite essential oil for a gift that engages multiple senses.

The Longpi Oil Burner is available at ⁠us.toa.st for $50.

Photography courtesy of Urban Outfitters

Kodhi Mini Table Lamp by Urban Outfitters

An exercise in playful proportions, the Kodhi Mini Table Lamp pairs a colorful, spherical base with an elongated, tapered woven shade in coordinating hues. The contrast between the rounded base and the angular shade gives the petite lamp an almost cartoonish quality. Sized for a bedside table or bookshelf, it’s an affordable way to introduce both color and ambient lighting into a small space. Just be sure to include the required bulb with your gift, as it’s sold separately.

The Kodhi Mini Table Lamp is available at urbanoutfitters.com for $40.

Photography courtesy of Coming Soon

White Elephant Gift from Coming Soon

Take the white elephant gift exchange quite literally this year with a cup that conceals a miniature white elephant inside. The unexpected detail reveals itself as you sip, bringing a little humor to an everyday ritual. It’s a clever choice for a holiday gift swap, but one that’s equally fun to give outside of the party game.

The White Elephant Gift is available at comingsoonnewyork.com.

Photography courtesy of Joon Loloi

Valene Vase by Joon Loloi

With its rounded silhouette and glossy moss-green finish, the Valene Vase makes a small but memorable statement. Handmade in India from EcoMix, a material incorporating upcycled paper, the sculptural vessel offers an unexpected alternative to traditional ceramic. At just 6.5 inches wide, it’s sized for a bookshelf, desk, or bedside table, where it can stand alone or hold a few dried stems. Just note that it’s not watertight, so fresh flowers are off the table.

The Valene Vase is available at joonloloi.com for $39.

Photography courtesy of Native Union

Pop Phone by Native Union

Native Union brings the familiar silhouette of a traditional telephone handset into the smartphone era with its Pop Phone. Complete with a coiled cord and oversized receiver, the retro-inspired design offers a more tactile alternative to taking calls on a touchscreen. It’s a fun nod to analog technology for anyone nostalgic for the days of landlines.

The Pop Phone is available at nordstrom.com for $40.

Photography courtesy of Wms&Co.

Task Roller by Wms&Co.

An upgrade from the ubiquitous sticky note, the Task Roller pairs a continuous roll of paper with a streamlined stainless steel dispenser. The compact design keeps a fresh writing surface within reach without cluttering a desk or countertop, making it particularly appealing to those who prefer handwritten reminders, grocery lists, and daily to-dos.

The Task Roller is available at wmscoshop.com for $46.

Photography courtesy of Areaware

Everybody Grinder by Dusen Dusen for Areaware

Leave it to Dusen Dusen to give the humble salt and pepper grinder a personality of its own. Designed for Areaware, the Everybody Grinder features a graphic face rendered in the Brooklyn-based studio’s signature playful style. The unexpected design makes a case for leaving your seasonings out on the counter, adding a little character to an otherwise utilitarian corner of the kitchen.

The Everybody Grinder is available at areaware.com for $48.

Photography courtesy of West Elm

Pigeon Glasses Holder by Emma Chamberlain for West Elm

For the friend who’s constantly misplacing their glasses, this unlikely little companion offers a solution. Part of Emma Chamberlain’s collaboration with West Elm, the pigeon-shaped holder brings a dose of absurdist humor to a nightstand or desk. Even when it’s not sporting a pair of spectacles, it makes for an amusing decorative object.

The Pigeon Glasses Holder is available at westelm.com for $35.

Photography courtesy of Studio Arhoj

Riso Works 2027 Calendar by Studio Arhoj

Give someone a colorful start to the new year with Studio Arhoj’s Riso Works calendar. Available in orange, pink, and red, the poster celebrates the distinctive aesthetic of risograph printing, turning a practical everyday reference into a piece of graphic art. It’s a particularly fitting gift for design enthusiasts who appreciate the tactile qualities of printed matter in an increasingly digital world.

The Riso Works 2027 Calendar is available at arhoj.com for $45.

Photography courtesy of MoMA Design Store

Multicolor Glass Jars by Ingo Fremer

For the person who finds as much joy in organizing as they do in decorating, this set of four colorful glass jars makes everyday storage a little more interesting. The transparent glass keeps contents visible while introducing playful pops of color to kitchen counters, bathroom shelves, and desktops.

The Multicolor Glass Jars are available at ⁠store.moma.org for $35.

Photography courtesy of Maharam

Memory Three by Maharam

A childhood favorite gets a design-minded makeover with Maharam’s third edition of its memory game. Featuring 36 distinct patterns drawn from the brand’s archive of classic and contemporary textiles, the game doubles as a miniature lesson in textile design. Even the packaging offers an element of surprise, with one of four cover designs selected at random.

Memory Three is available at ⁠maharam.com for $40.

issues.title: Burlwood Is Making a Comeback With a Modern Twist
issues.summary: 4 interior designers share their thoughts on burlwood’s enduring appeal, their favorite material pairings, and how to incorporate it into contemporary spaces
issues.author: Colleen Sullivan
issues.content_html:
Few materials make a visual statement quite like burlwood. Its swirls and naturally irregular patterns give it a depth and individuality that are difficult to replicate. That distinctive grain comes from burls, rounded growths that develop on tree trunks or branches and are often associated with injury, stress, or infection.

Burlwood gained popularity during the Art Deco era of the 1920s and ’30s before becoming a defining feature of furniture design in the 1970s. Today, it’s experiencing another moment. Yet its current appeal is less about recreating the past and more about rethinking how the material fits modern spaces.

Design Milk spoke with four designers to learn why burlwood continues to resonate and the fresh ways they’re using it.

Bookmatched burlwood creates a striking symmetrical pattern across this three-drawer chest, set against a sculptural curved wood bed frame. Photography by Emily Hart.

Why Burlwood Continues to Captivate Designers

“Burlwood does what a great print does,” says Tiffany Brooks, principal designer of Tiffany Brooks Interiors. “It gives your eye somewhere to go. Up close, you see all these little swirls and knots, and from across the room, it reads as one rich surface. Even two pieces made from the same wood can have completely different personalities.”

Abbe Fenimore, owner of Studio Ten 25, shares that appreciation for burlwood’s organic qualities, seeing the material as a way to introduce visual interest without relying on patterned textiles.

The tightly patterned grain of this burlwood chest extends across its drawer fronts, while colorful glass candlesticks and art books add color to the display. Photography by Ellen Renee.

For Eddie Maestri, founder, principal, and creative director of Maestri Studio, burlwood’s appeal lies in its departure from the predictable. “To me, the imperfections are the beauty,” he says. “Every piece of burl is different, and you can’t fake it.”

The designers we spoke to see burlwood as having staying power, particularly as homeowners move toward spaces that feel more personal and collected.

“The material is timeless,” Brooks says. “What changes is how we use it. Right now, I think people are a little tired of rooms that look like they all came from the same inspiration board. Burl brings some individuality back.”

A honey-toned burlwood table features a richly figured top and tapered legs, standing out against the darker wood cabinetry behind it. Photography by Ellen Renee.

Fenimore sees a similar appeal in burlwood’s ability to bridge different eras and styles. Its balance of modern and vintage sensibilities, she explains, can give even a brand-new piece the character of something collected over time.

Maestri points to its long history, from French cabinetmakers to the Art Deco era and the 1970s, as evidence of its enduring draw. “It keeps coming back because people want warmth and things made by hand,” he says, noting that burlwood can bring a sense of soul to interiors that otherwise feel overly polished.

Choosing the Right Burlwood

Walnut, maple, and mappa burl each bring a different quality to a piece, with variations in color, grain, and visual weight influencing how designers use them.

Brooks reaches for walnut burl when she wants to introduce depth and create a moodier atmosphere, while maple burl offers similar movement in a lighter, softer palette. For a bolder grain pattern, she favors mappa burl.

A burlwood nightstand introduces warmth and a touch of traditional detail to this otherwise contemporary bedroom, adding a rich wood accent against the sculptural charcoal headboard and modern lines. Photography by Nick Sargent.

Maestri, meanwhile, has a clear go-to: mappa burl, also known as poplar burl. “It’s my favorite because it’s lighter and more golden than walnut, so you get all that movement without the room feeling heavy,” he says.

While Mimi Meacham, founder and principal designer of Marian Louise Designs, gravitates toward rich walnut burl and lighter mappa burl, the individual piece matters more to her than the wood species. “The color, scale of the figuring, and finish all affect how it will feel in a room,” she says. “I want the grain and the shape of the furniture to complement each other.”

A close-up reveals the distinctive natural markings of a burlwood table, with brass-and-acrylic drawer pulls adding a mix of warm and modern finishes. Photography by Emily Hart.

Pairing Burlwood with Other Materials and Finishes

Because burlwood already has so much movement, surrounding colors and finishes can either complement its natural pattern or create an intriguing contrast. Brooks likes combining burl with warm brass, matte paint, and textiles such as nubby linen and velvet. “I’d put a honey-toned burl next to a deep aubergine or an inky blue in a heartbeat,” she says. Fenimore also likes pairing burl with color and pattern, especially soft blues, olive greens, warm neutrals, and even unexpected pops of pink or red.

A burlwood tray with a gold-toned rim highlights the wood’s warm coloring and varied markings, with stacked books providing a colorful backdrop. Photography by Ellen Renee.

Meacham gravitates toward warm wood tones paired with blues and greens, from soft periwinkle to deep green, along with antique brass, linen, velvet, and plaster. She also considers the finish of the burl itself when choosing surrounding materials. A glossy burlwood surface, for example, can be balanced by a matte wall or softly textured fabric.

For a warmer, earthier direction, Maestri recommends tobacco, ochre, olive, and soft plaster white, complemented by brass, stone, linen, and mohair. He also prefers finishes with a subtle luster to emphasize the grain’s richness. Fenimore likes the contrast burlwood creates with lacquered surfaces, brass, upholstery, and contemporary furniture silhouettes.

A curved burlwood console showcases the wood’s richly varied grain across its drawer fronts and rounded frame, with pale green stools and white fringe adding a touch of color and texture. Photography by Emily Hart.

How Designers Are Reimagining Burlwood

Burlwood is finding its way into a wider range of applications throughout the home. Brooks likes seeing it incorporated into architectural details, such as the back of a kitchen island or as an inset on a painted door. “A little restraint makes the detail feel more special,” she says. For larger pieces, she points to Worlds Away for its clean-lined interpretations of burlwood, as well as Ambella Home, Chairish, and 1stDibs for finding distinctive designs.

Maestri also appreciates seeing burl used beyond traditional furniture, including on lamp bases, picture frames, and cabinet doors. At home, he has a burlwood bar cabinet from Soho Home, and he’s drawn to the brand’s Wallace collection, which uses mappa burl in sculptural, curved forms.

A burlwood coffee table showcases the wood’s warm tones and naturally irregular markings, while art books and a decorative bowl give the tabletop a relaxed, collected feel. Photography by Ellen Renee.

Contemporary furniture designs also explore the interplay between burlwood, contrasting materials, and simpler silhouettes. Jonathan Adler’s Bond collection, for example, combines burl with acrylic on a dresser and metal on a dining table. Meacham points to Made Goods’ Bradley mirror, which lets the mappa burl frame take center stage. Fenimore recommends looking at brands like Modway and TOV Furniture, particularly for smaller items such as chairs, ottomans, and drink tables with burl accents.

The rich, swirling grain of the half-moon burlwood console complements the delicate branches and floral motifs in the botanical artwork above. Photography by Emily Hart.

Making Room for Burlwood

For anyone hesitant to introduce such a distinctive material, the designers recommend beginning with one piece, such as a side table, mirror, or tray. Brooks suggests starting with something that serves an existing need, even if it’s as small as a drink table next to a chair. Maestri puts it simply: “Pick one piece and let it be the star. Keep what’s around it simpler so the grain can stand out.”

Fenimore encourages mixing burlwood with other wood tones rather than trying to match everything. She also sees the material as a way to ground a room that already has plenty of color and pattern. Meacham recommends giving the grain some breathing room through intentional styling and a variety of finishes. “That doesn’t mean everything else needs to be neutral—I love burl with color—but you want your eye to have somewhere to rest.”

Burlwood’s latest resurgence doesn’t require a revival of any particular decorating style. The same material that characterized Art Deco cabinetry and 1970s furniture feels equally at home alongside contemporary silhouettes, unexpected colors, and contrasting finishes. Its history is part of its appeal, but it needn’t dictate how we use it.

issues.title: DD416 / Adrift in a world of options
issues.summary: Issue 416: Adrift in a world of options – Read the full issue in the archive.
issues.author: Kai Brach
issues.content_html:
I left Germany at 20 and, looking back, never quite stopped leaving. A year of travelling around Australia and parts of Asia kicked off two decades of freelancing from wherever I happened to be. I never held a ‘real’ job for more than three months. I wasn’t in a serious relationship until my thirties. Above all, I wanted to keep my options open. Australia became home, but something kept pulling me elsewhere, sometimes for months at a time.

I’m grateful for those years. Few people enjoy that kind of privilege. But I can also see what all that freedom did to me: it turned me into a commitment-phobe. Without really noticing, I’d become uncomfortable with anything that might anchor me to a place. Leases, girlfriends, gym contracts – if it had a whiff of long term obligation, I’d look for a reason to stay clear.

In the last few years, that’s changed. Relationship, mortgage, dog, lovely neighbours. Age surely plays a part, but this work here has also taught me that one of the best responses to the many crises of our time is to stop running from obligations and become a person of place.

Rosie Spinks and Spencer R. Scott, two of my favourite Substackers, verbalised this perfectly in a recent video chat to discuss Scott’s new book As If We Were Staying (see below).

Spinks quotes a line from the book that feels very apt: “One cannot learn to engage in reciprocal partnership with the local environment while planning to flee it at the first inconvenience.” You may swap ‘local environment’ for a person, a city, a child, a pet…

Spinks admits that, like me, not long ago she’d hear the word ‘obligation’ and instinctively file it under ‘bad things’. The goal was always to have as few as possible. Then she became a mother, and suddenly her life was full of them.

I agree with her that our cultural fear of obligation explains a lot of the emptiness people feel. It’s never been easier to live without obligations, and whenever we do need help, there’s a paid service to spare us the inconvenience of relying on other people. But does that add up to a good life?

Scott, who gave up a biotech career to buy a farm in a small US town, went through a similar reckoning. His book argues that capitalism has sealed us into tidy units of individualism. An obligation is the opposite: a draw on your time and energy that you can’t simply outsource. He resisted at first, until it dawned on him that all of his obligations were really relationships. The effort was what made them matter.

And it’s not just about the people closest to us. It’s the local birdlife, that old tree on the corner, the barista who knows our order, the councillor who lives down the road. All those little connections add up to a network of reciprocity.

I guess my generation was the first, though not the last, to be sold this mirage of independence, sometimes for reasons we didn’t choose – insecure work, unaffordable housing, a phone that turns every evening into a sea of options. Other towns, other partners, other careers always look better in the feed, so we never stay long enough to collect what staying gives us. Spinks calls it “floating in the void”.

I’m wary of making obligation a virtue in itself. Plenty of people are stuck in commitments they never chose, and for some of them leaving is the healthiest thing they can do. I also know it was my drifting years that let me put down roots knowing what I was giving up. What matters, I think, is that we pick our obligations with our eyes open, then commit to them. In other words: fuck stick around and find out.

And now to this week’s discoveries. – Kai

issues.title: DD415 / MBA: school of profit
issues.summary: Issue 415: MBA: school of profit – Read the full issue in the archive.
issues.author: Kai Brach
issues.content_html:
When I finished high school and started exploring my study options back in Germany, I came across the then-new MBA (Master of Business Administration) and found it a bit baffling. I thought you first had to master a craft, then turn it into a business. The MBA seemed to suggest that the craft was not important and you could just learn how to run any business. The course description was thick with English jargon, which didn’t help. I vaguely remember someone describing it as learning how to make more money without producing anything.

That description came back to me while reading a recent opinion piece by Christopher Marquis, who has spent more than 20 years teaching at famous business schools. His verdict on his own industry: business schools can’t be repaired; it’s time to shut them down.

“I’ve come to realize that business schools don’t just reflect our economic system – they actively manufacture its priorities and normalize its harms, training the future leaders who will design and defend the structures driving our overlapping global crises. Tinkering at the margins with a class on corporate responsibility or ethics is not going to help. We don’t need to ‘fix’ business schools. We need to abolish them.”

Marquis points to research showing that managers with business degrees cut wages, yet didn’t become any more productive. He concludes:

“What registers as managerial acumen turns out to be wealth transfer – value moved away from workers and toward profits, shareholders and executives.”

He also puts into words what I couldn’t as an adolescent:

“A medical school’s core justification is health, and a law school’s is justice – undisputed public goods. Business schools are organized explicitly around a private good: the pursuit of profit. The American sociologist Thorstein Veblen identified this tension a century ago, criticizing university schools focused on commerce because they ‘need imply nothing in the way of serviceability to the common good.’”

The tension is usually glossed over with the comforting ‘win-win’ story:

“These aspirations are built on the delusional but widely accepted idea of ‘stakeholder capitalism’: that companies can produce climate stability, fair wages, healthy communities and functioning democracies while also delivering profits. Executives promise that technology will solve our environmental problems; voluntary measurement systems are offered as appropriate alternatives to public accountability; ethics is rebranded as competitive advantage rather than moral obligation.”

So what should we teach instead? Marquis points to the idea of “schools for organizing” rather than schools for business:

“Students would study co-ops, unions and social movements alongside the shareholder corporation. The central question would shift from ‘How do we maximize shareholder value?’ to ‘How do different forms of organization distribute power, risk and reward – and which should we strengthen?’”

“The goal is not to write off the students as aspiring selfish capitalists; it is to stop funneling them through a machine that narrows their sense of possibility. Many of my students arrive on campus wanting to work on the crises that our economic system has created. What they lack is an institution that is worthy of their better impulses.”

To me, this is what rethinking our economic system could look like at its most basic level. An ethics elective won’t do it. The work starts with how we teach people to think about power and capital: how currently both tend to accumulate at the top, while the ecological and social mess gets filed under ‘externalities’ and left for future generations to sort out.

We need people who can read a balance sheet and run a payroll, of course. But we could also teach them to build co-operatives, strengthen communities and organise around shared interests. Extracting value for personal gain is one model of doing business, with a long track record of consequences, but certainly not the only one.

And now to this week’s discoveries. – Kai

issues.title: DD414 / Organising the discontent
issues.summary: Issue 414: Organising the discontent – Read the full issue in the archive.
issues.author: Kai Brach
issues.content_html:
I can still feel it – the collective exhale. Ann Friedman calls it ‘the great unclenching’, and Rebecca Solnit writes that a win for democracy of this size deserves a proper celebration. Fair enough.

But while the rest of us were glued to swing-state maps, something remarkable was unfolding in a corner of Europe that rarely makes our news feeds.

In Serbia, a movement led by students forced snap elections and then won them outright, ending more than a decade of autocratic rule. It started in 2024, when a train station canopy collapsed and killed 16 people. To many Serbians, it was corruption made visible. Students blockaded their universities and demanded accountability. Within months, farmers, actors, judges and pensioners had joined them, filling city squares in some of the largest protests the country has ever seen.

What’s amazing is that this ideologically mixed movement hasn’t splintered into rival factions. Instead, it has built a shared identity without a single face on the poster. Its electoral list had no leader. The 250 candidates on the ballot papers were nominated, grilled and voted on by student plenums – open assemblies at each university. This produced something that represents a decent slice of the country: a cardiologist, a grammar school teacher, a coal miner, a social worker, a former central bank governor and, for good measure, a retired basketball star.

I’ve been a fan of citizens’ assemblies for years (see DD220). There is lots of evidence that ordinary people, given time, reliable information and a genuine stake in the outcome, can make remarkably good and fair decisions. Serbia’s plenums aren’t a textbook citizens’ assembly – nobody was picked by lottery – but they share the spirit. The power to choose sat with big, messy rooms full of people. And few people have a bigger stake in the outcome than students, who’ll be living with the results long after today’s power brokers have retired to their holiday homes.

It’s hard not to see echoes of Serbia in the Gen Z protests spreading across the world. Of course, some protests turn ugly, and the looting and vandalism deserve condemnation. But the media is often far more interested in pictures of ghouls smashing shop windows than in understanding why so many people took to the streets in the first place, why so many young people can’t see a future worth studying for. Serbia shows what that frustration can build once it gets organised.

The proof is in the pudding, of course. Leaderless movements can be great at opposing and clumsy at governing. Decision-making by committee isn’t pretty. Consensus takes time, patience and a healthy tolerance for disagreement. But there’s something very inspiring about a political movement that started by asking who should represent it, not who should lead it.

And now to this week’s discoveries. – Kai

issues.title: DD413 / The lost art of having people over
issues.summary: Issue 413: The lost art of having people over – Read the full issue in the archive.
issues.author: Kai Brach
issues.content_html:
As a kid, I loved our big lunch and dinner parties. There are photos of 30-odd people – friends, family, neighbours – squeezed into our apartment on borrowed chairs around tables that didn’t match. It was chaotic, loud and a lot of fun. They didn’t happen nearly often enough, and I sometimes wonder why something we all enjoyed so much was saved for birthdays and other rare occasions.

Over the years, we’ve actually made them rarer still. Derek Thompson has the numbers to prove it:

“In the last 30 years, Americans have seen double-digit declines in practically every measure of socializing. ... The share of Americans who say they host friends or family at their home at least monthly has fallen from 42 percent in 1975 to 12 percent in 2026 – a 70 percent collapse in a half-century.”

These days, the convenience economy has made staying in so easy that inviting people over feels like a self-inflicted chore.

Elizabeth Oldfield went the other way. For more than a decade, she and her husband have hosted shared dinners every other week, first squeezing eight people around a table in a tiny London flat, now feeding up to 16 at a time in their community house. By her count, around 1,500 people have come through the door. The trick, she says, is putting it in the calendar and refusing to renegotiate:

“This bizarre culture of possessive individualism will always give us reasons not to be together, so sometimes it takes a strong container to push back. ... Always keeping our options open and autonomy over our time sounds good but leaves us lonely and disoriented. Make a commitment and your future self will thank you.”

I love how unbothered she is about the state of the house. As her husband puts it, hospitality is ”not the same as entertaining”:

“To be invited into someone else’s imperfect house is, it turns out, a blessing. I do not tend to find very primped, spotless, Instagram-ready homes especially relaxing to be in. If we are going to move towards each other and build real community we have to let go of the desire to impress people.”

I wrote about the radical act of regular open-door dinners a while back (DD331), and Oldfield’s dinners are about the most practical version of that idea I’ve come across. (Do check out her list of tips in the essay.)

So why don’t more of us do it? Thompson has a pretty good theory:

“Everybody might prefer, in the abstract, a world of dinner parties, neighborhood friendships, and spontaneous gatherings. But on any given Wednesday at 7:45pm., it is easier to look at a screen than to host a party; easier to listen to a podcast while doing yoga than to plan a gathering. This is not so much an individual failure as a coordination failure. ... Compared to TikTok, a dinner party is a terrible leisure technology. It requires matching schedules, cleaning the house, buying food, accommodating children and allergies, tolerating awkwardness, and taking the risk that the evening is mediocre. By contrast, what does television ask of us? Nothing. TikTok? Even less.”

When I look at those old photos and my mum’s kitchen, I notice who’s doing the cooking. Those parties ran on a lot of unpaid labour, mostly by women, and Thompson points out that the social calendar frayed when they took on paid work and the men didn’t pick up the slack. Today’s cost-of-living pressures and two exhausted working parents make the couch and screens combo look very appealing.

Oldfield offers us a way back that doesn’t require a kitchen full of women doing all the work and stressing about being a perfect host. Her dinners run on cheap dahl and wine from Lidl. Guests chop, set the table and stay for the clean-up. Nobody performs, nobody keeps score, and somehow everyone leaves a little less alone.

And now to this week’s discoveries. – Kai

What do you think?

What are your perspectives on the debate? Has the i-frame vs. s-frame debate influenced your work? Where do you agree, and where do you disagree? What related questions are you grappling with? Where do you think the applied behavioral science goes next?

Share your perspective via our “letter to the editor” form.

Share your perspective

Five questions to consider

In advance of the event, I asked each of our five guests to prepare a question for the group. We didn't get to all of them during the discussion, so I thought it might be valuable to share them with everyone. The questions can serve as leaping off points to advance your own thinking and for your discussions with colleagues.

Here they are:

1. Systems-level change (from Nick): How can behavioral science most effectively help with system-level (s-frame) change?

2. Inadvertent harm of the i-frame vs. s-frame argument (from Michael): From where you sit, do you think the i-frame vs. s-frame argument could inadvertently diminish interest in applying behavioral science to public policy?

3. Equity (from Crystal): How does an equity focus complicate (or settle?) the i-frame/s-frame question?

4. The case of gambling (from George): Considerable research suggests that online gambling is causing extensive harm, particularly to poor and young people. How can behavioral insights inform interventions at both the individual level and the system level? And which level do you expect to be more effective?

5. The next generation of behavioral scientists (from Chiara): How does this debate translate into action, such as the training and mentoring of the next generation of behavioral scientists?

issues.title: Frontiers: A Roundtable Discussion on the I-Frame vs. S-Frame Debate
issues.summary: Applied behavioral scientists believe their work can influence people’s lives for the better. But what is the most effective way to make that happen? Is it through interventions focused on influencing individual behavior while maintaining freedom of choice? Is it by changing policies and laws, and thereby the systems, that individuals operate within? Is it a combination of the two? Is the distinct
issues.author: Evan Nesterak
issues.content_html:
Applied behavioral scientists believe their work can influence people’s lives for the better. But what is the most effective way to make that happen?

Is it through interventions focused on influencing individual behavior while maintaining freedom of choice? Is it by changing policies and laws, and thereby the systems, that individuals operate within? Is it a combination of the two? Is the distinction between an individual- or systems-focus a helpful one? Or, is the world too messy and complex? How should applied behavioral scientists navigate the financial and political influences on the work they’re asked to do, as well as the work they’d like to do?

These are all questions that applied behavioral scientists are grappling with as they try to realize the promise of the field—to leverage the scientific understanding of psychology, behavior, society, and culture to help one another live happier, healthier, and more peaceful lives.

On October 14, join Editor-in-Chief Evan Nesterak and five leading behavioral scientists—Nick Chater, George Loewestein, Crystal Hall, Michael Hallsworth, and Chiara Varazzani—for a roundtable discussion about these questions and more. The leaping off point will be the i-frame vs. s-frame debate initiated by Chater and Loewenstein, first in an academic article and now in their new book, It’s on You. (Further background on the debate below.)

The guests of the roundtable don’t all agree on how to answer the questions above. In fact, in many cases they sharply disagree. But they all have extensive experience working in both academic and applied settings, especially in public policy, so we have the opportunity for an interesting and constructive conversation. The goal isn’t to settle the debate but to explore areas of agreement and disagreement, open a dialogue about how applied behavioral scientists approach their work, and surface the questions that can move the debate forward.

The event will take place online and is free to attend. You can reserve your spot here.

  • Date: Wednesday, October 14
  • Start time: 9:00am San Francisco | 12:00pm New York | 5:00pm London | 6:00pm Berlin | 7:00pm Nairobi | 9:30pm Delhi
  • Duration: 90 minutes
  • Location: Online
  • Cost: Free to attend
  • Register:Reserve your spot
Reserve your spot

A recording will be made available to all registrants after the event, in case you're not able to attend live.

We hope to see you there,

Evan Nesterak, Editor-in-Chief

Background on the debate

In their 2022 article in Behavioral and Brain Sciences, psychologist Nick Chater and behavioral economist George Loewestein ignited the i-frame vs. s-frame debate within applied behavioral science. The two argued that, in the decade since the field burst on the scene, applied behavioral scientists, themselves included, had focused too much on trying to influence individual behavior (i-frame) and not enough on trying to influence the systems in which individuals behave (s-frame).

The result, they said, especially as it related to public policy, was that interventions were coming up short, attention was being directed away from system-level solutions that could have a tangible impact, and, perhaps most seriously, that applied behavioral scientists “may have unwittingly promoted the interests of the opponents of systemic change.”

Perhaps unsurprisingly, not everyone agreed. One focus of Chater and Loewenstein’s criticism was nudging, which for them epitomized the i-frame approach. The format of the journal Behavioral and Brain Sciences is to feature a target article (in this case Chater and Loewestein’s) and then invite other scholars to respond to that article. Both Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein, authors of Nudge, issued a response. “Nudging is being framed,” Thaler wrote. Sunstein argued, “Their complaint is baseless. In the real world of policymaking, behavioral science is mostly being used to reform systems, not to alter individual behavior.”

And Michael Hallsworth, a leader of the Behavioural Insights Team, wrote:

“I greatly respect the authors of the target article. However, in contrast to the target article's assertion, practitioners of behavioral public policy are indeed involved in developing and promoting systemic solutions. Its ‘i-frame’/‘s-frame’ distinction is incoherent, unhelpful, and obscures promising future directions for behavioral public policy. Its content and presentation undermine its stated goals and encourage sweeping dismissals of the field.”

Chater, Loewenstein, Thaler, Sunstein, and Hallsworth all believe that applied behavioral science can be a positive force in improving people’s lives. The question is: How does the field get there?

Earlier this year, Chater and Loewenstein expanded their argument about the i-frame and s-frame in their book, It’s on You. And the question of how applied behavioral scientists should approach their work continues to bubble up in commentaries and conversations.

We wanted to use this moment to bring together diverging viewpoints about the i-frame vs. s-frame debate and how the field fulfills its promise. At the roundtable discussion, in addition to Nick Chater and George Loewestein, we’ll be joined by Crystal Hall (Professor, University of Washington and President, Behavioral Science & Policy Association), Michael Hallsworth (Chief Behavioral Scientist, BIT), and Chiara Varazzani (Lead Behavioral Scientist, OECD).

Reserve your spot

About the roundtable guests

Nick Chater is a professor of behavioral science at the Warwick Business School. In 2023, he was awarded the Rumelhart Prize for lifetime achievement in cognitive science. He has advised the UK Government and co-founded Decision Technology, a research consultancy. He is the coauthor of It’s on You (with George Loewenstein).

George Loewenstein is the Herbert A. Simon University Professor of Economics and Psychology at Carnegie Mellon University. He is one of the founders of behavioral economics, neuroeconomics, and behavioral public policy and has advised many leading companies and government bodies. He is the coauthor of It’s on You (with Nick Chater).

Crystal Hall is the John and Marguerite Walker Corbally Endowed Professor in Public Service at the University of Washington, as well as the president of the Behavioral Science & Policy Association. She has served as a fellow with the White House Social and Behavioral Sciences Team and the Federal Office of Evaluation Sciences at the General Services Administration, and has advised government agencies, nonprofits, and community organizations. She is the coauthor of Antiracist by Design (with Mindy Hernandez).

Michael Hallsworth is the chief behavioral scientist at BIT. He has two decades of experience in developing policy and designing services for national governments and international organizations. He is also a distinguished lecturer at the University of Pennsylvania, and was previously visiting lecturer at Princeton University and assistant professor (adjunct) at Columbia University. He is the author of TheHypocrisy Trap and coauthor of Behavioral Insights (with Elspeth Kirkman).

Chiara Varazzani is lead behavioral scientist at the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD). She is also a senior visiting fellow at the London School of Economics and Political Science. Previously, she served as a member of the Technical Advisory Group on Behavioural Insights for the World Health Organization (WHO), advised the Australian government, and was an adjunct research fellow at Monash University.

issues.content_html:
AppLovin at 55% Growth and 66% Net Margins, Zeta Accelerating to 46%, and The Trade Desk Shrinking in the Same Quarter

For most of the last decade, adtech was the part of B2B that investors avoided. It had low multiples, was exposed to whatever Apple and Google did to privacy, and seemed to be one platform change away from getting wiped out. Most B2B founders wouldn’t pitch it, and most VCs wouldn’t take the meeting.

Now look at Q3 2026. In a quarter when HubSpot guided down to 12% growth and most seat-based B2B was fighting to hold its growth rate, two adtech companies posted some of the best numbers in public software. AppLovin did $2.2 billion in a quarter, growing 55%, with a 66% net income margin. Zeta Global grew 46%, organic growth sped up to 30%, and it turned GAAP profitable. Investors responded the same week.

Adtech didn’t get hot as a category, though. The Trade Desk, the adtech darling of the 2020s, shrank. The companies that are winning share three traits: an AI model sits in the middle of the product, customers can see exactly what each dollar returns, and the money comes from marketing budgets, not software budgets.

The short version:

  • AppLovin: net income grew 72% year-over-year to $1.44 billion on record revenue of $2.18 billion, up 55% year-over-year, with 66% net income margin and 84% Adjusted EBITDA margin.
  • Nearly all of AppLovin’s growth came from price. Net revenue per installation rose 55% and installation volume increased 2%.
  • Zeta: revenue of $493 million for the third quarter, an increase of 46% Y/Y or 30% Y/Y excluding Marigold and political candidate revenue, an acceleration from 28% growth excluding Marigold last quarter.
  • The stocks: AppLovin closed at 228.50 on Friday 30 October and at 391.22 on Friday 6 November, up 71.2% in five trading days. Zeta is trading at the top of its 52-week range.
  • The Trade Desk: third-quarter 2026 revenue of $736 million, down 0.5% from $739 million a year earlier, the first year-over-year revenue decline since the demand-side platform listed in 2016.

1. AppLovin Did $2.2 Billion in a Quarter With Fewer Than 900 Employees

The absolute numbers matter here as much as the growth rate. Revenue exceeded the top of the $2,055M–$2,085M range by about $99.8M, and the sequential increase was the largest quarterly dollar step in 12 quarters. Operating income: $1.71bn, up 58%, a 78% operating margin.

A 78% operating margin at an $8 billion+ run rate. Full-year 2026: Midpoint implies roughly $8.33bn revenue, about 52% growth. As of Nov 12, 2026, the company has 898 employees. That works out to more than $9 million of revenue per employee. A very efficient B2B company runs at $500K to $1M.

Cash conversion follows. Q3 free cash flow was $1.4B, equal to 77% of adjusted EBITDA and ~65% of revenue, versus 53% conversion in Q2.

AppLovin also hasn’t finished rolling out its main growth driver. CEO Adam Foroughi said AppLovin’s gaming business “grew nearly 50% year-over-year, re-accelerating right alongside the rollout” of a new generation of its ad models, which have so far only been partially deployed. Most companies at $8B are guiding toward slower growth. AppLovin is telling investors the next model upgrade is mostly still ahead of them.

2. Installs Grew 2%. Revenue Per Install Grew 55%.

This is the most useful number in the quarter for B2B founders.

AppLovin didn’t grow by finding more volume. Over nine months it actually shrank on volume: revenue per install rose 68% while installs fell 7%. The growth came from a better model predicting which user will install, pay, and stay. That makes each outcome worth more to the advertiser, so AppLovin gets paid more for each one.

Meta shows the same pattern at much larger scale. Ad impressions rose 10% and average prices climbed 14% in Q3 2026, on the way to a 26% year-on-year increase in advertising revenue, reaching $63.1 billion.

In both cases the AI improvement shows up directly as price, in the same quarter, on the same invoice. Nobody has to build an ROI calculator. The advertiser sees a better return and spends more.

Compare that to most of B2B + AI, where better models currently show up as a COGS line. At HubSpot, cost of subscription revenue +28% against subscription revenue +18%; subscription and hosting costs rose $23.2m, which the 10-Q attributes primarily to customer growth and also to growth in usage of AI features. HubSpot files no AI revenue. It’s the same AI wave with the opposite effect on the P&L. In seat-based software, a better model costs more to serve the same customer. In outcome-priced adtech, a better model earns more from the same customer.

3. AppLovin Spends About 3% of Revenue on Sales and Marketing

Sales and marketing: $68.8M (up 42%). Against $2.185 billion of revenue, that’s about 3.1%. HubSpot, Salesforce, and Atlassian spend roughly 25% to 45% of revenue on sales and marketing.

The product sells itself because the results are measurable. Advertisers don’t need a rep to explain why it works. They need to see the return and raise the budget.

There’s one caveat, and it comes from Foroughi himself. AppLovin’s newer business is still very hands-on. Foroughi said results still depend heavily on support. He said customers who work with AppLovin’s team succeed much more often than customers who come in through self-serve, and small merchants are not yet the target market. The 3% figure belongs to a mature gaming business. The e-commerce expansion is being sold the old way.

4. Zeta Grew 46%, 30% Organic, and It Accelerated

Zeta is the smaller, messier story, and in some ways the more relevant one for B2B founders, because it sells to enterprise marketers through a platform, not an ad network.

The headline 46% includes an acquisition and an election year, so the number to watch is organic growth. Organic went from 28% to 30%. Revenue exceeded the midpoint of guidance by $22 million, or 5%. Zeta generated $121 million of adjusted EBITDA and expanded adjusted EBITDA margin by 140 bps Y/Y to 24.6%, reflecting the rule of 71. Free cash flow: $81.5M, up 73% Y/Y (16.5% margin).

The full year got raised again. Management raised full-year revenue guidance by $37 million at the midpoint to $1.855 billion, representing 42% year-over-year growth. This was its 21st straight beat-and-raise quarter.

Go-to-market got more efficient as growth accelerated. Sales & marketing: $109.4M, about 22% of revenue, down from about 25% a year earlier ($85.3M).

5. Zeta’s Biggest Customers Spend $2.0 Million Each, Up 22%

Super-Scaled Customers: 212, up 18% Y/Y. Super-Scaled Customer ARPU: $2.0M, up 22% Y/Y. One analyst noted that spending per large customer broke out to $2.0 million after seven quarters in a narrow range.

The CFO credits Zeta’s AI agent for the expansion. On the call, Greiner highlighted that customers with multiple use cases have doubled year-over-year.

David Steinberg explained where that money comes from: “Marketers are recognizing the strong return on investment delivered by Zeta and increasingly view us as a revenue center for their business, not a cost center”.

That’s the budget point. A revenue center gets more money when it works. A cost center gets consolidated. Most B2B software is still bought out of a software budget that CIOs are cutting to pay for tokens. Zeta and AppLovin are paid out of the marketing budget, which is much larger and gets bigger when ROI improves. This is why I won’t invest in an agentic B2B company unless it unlocks budget beyond the software budget. Zeta’s $2.0M ARPU, growing 22%, is what that looks like when it works.

6. The Stocks: Zeta Is at Its High. AppLovin Is Rebounding From a Crash.

These two stock charts look very different.

Zeta is on a real run. The stock had previously closed at $32.42 before earnings, and then on November 11, 2026, Zeta Global Holdings Corp ZETA shares rose by 7.6%, bringing the current price to $37.74. The stock has experienced significant price movements recently, with a 52-week range of $14.37 to $38.46. That’s up about 2.6x from its low, and it rose on two straight days after the report. The company has a market capitalization of $9.44 billion, so it trades at roughly 5x this year’s revenue guide.

AppLovin’s week was bigger, but it came from a lower starting point. Going into the print, it had declined approximately 60% in 2026 through Wednesday’s close, making the company the S&P 500’s worst performer, according to MarketWatch. Then the report hit. AppLovin (NASDAQ:APP) ended up 31.04% on November 5, 2026, a rare advance as the Nasdaq Composite dropped 5.52% and the S&P 500 lost 4.36%. It’s trading around $404 today, with a Market Cap 134.109B.

Even so, it sits well below its peak. The 52 Week High 738.01, 52 Week High Date 12/22/25, which puts today’s price about 45% under the high. Before the report, the stock went into the report at about 13x forward earnings, around half its five-year average of 25x.

Put together, the market is paying up for Zeta’s acceleration and is just starting to forgive AppLovin. A company growing 55% with 66% net margins was priced like a no-growth company a week ago. The decline came from fear about sustainability, competitors, and a pending securities class action, not from the numbers. The numbers kept getting better the whole time.

7. The Trade Desk Shrank in the Same Quarter

To see that this isn’t “adtech is back,” look at The Trade Desk.

A year earlier, the same quarter had grown 18%. The trend is what matters: Q1 2026: +12%. Q2 2026: +3%. Q3 2026: -0.5%. Profitability is down too: operating margin: 12.6% (down from 21.8%). The stock still jumped after the report because it beat a lowered bar.

The Trade Desk is in the same category, selling to the same advertisers, in the same midterm-election quarter, and it went backwards. The difference is structural. TTD is a buying platform for the open internet. It doesn’t own the user, the outcome data, or a closed loop where its model learns which ad produced which purchase. AppLovin owns that loop inside mobile apps, and Meta owns it inside its own apps. In 2026, owning the loop is where all the value goes.

8. HubSpot Sells to the Same Marketer and Is Guiding to 12%

HubSpot is the other control case. It sells to marketers too, but it’s priced per seat and bought out of the software budget.

Total revenue was $947.6 million, up 17% on an as-reported basis and in constant currency. The guide is where it slows: Total revenue is expected to be in the range of $945.0 million to $947.0 million, up 12% year over year, which would be flat to down sequentially. Net revenue retention as filed 103.5% in FY2025 against 115.2% in FY2021 (prior method); 101% in Q3 2026, stated on the call.

So the same buyer is giving 101% net retention to the seat-priced tool and 22% ARPU expansion to the outcome-priced platform. The marketer isn’t spending less. They’re moving money to vendors that can show a return.

Where the Budget Beyond Software Comes From

Founders can take three things from this quarter.

Get paid out of the budget that grows when your product works. AppLovin and Zeta both get paid from marketing budgets. When their models improve, their customers make more money and spend more with them. HubSpot gets paid from the software budget, and its AI improvements so far have mostly added cost. If your AI product saves a customer money, expect to fight for a share of a shrinking budget. If it makes them money, the customer finds more budget.

Price the unit your model improves. AppLovin’s 55% growth came almost entirely from revenue per install rising, not install volume. Meta’s came more from price than from impressions. If your pricing unit is a seat, a better model doesn’t show up in revenue. If it’s an outcome, a better model raises revenue the same quarter.

Own the loop, or plan around whoever does. The Trade Desk is a well-run company with 95%+ retention, and it shrank in a quarter when Meta grew ads 26%. What separates the winners is whether the company sees the result of the ad it served. In B2B + AI, that’s whether you see the outcome of the work your agent did. If you don’t, someone who does will train a better model on it.

Every other B2B category is still trying to work out how to charge for AI. Performance adtech already gets paid for it, and Q3 2026 showed the numbers.
