issues.content_html:
Plus Cognition at $75B, a Sierra vs. Databricks vs. Ramp investment committee, CrowdStrike’s $43.9B Zscaler deal, and why marketing automation may be a dead category

Rory O’Driscoll was on holiday this week, and Matt Murphy of Menlo Ventures took his seat. Matt was one of Anthropic’s earliest investors and joined the same week Anthropic went public, so he had the inside view from the opening bell. The rest of the episode covered Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia, a week of serious breaches, Cognition’s step-up to $75B, and a run of M&A that showed what 2021-vintage B2B companies are worth now. Here are the takeaways that matter.

1. Nvidia Reinstated Jensen Huang Less Than Two Weeks After He Resigned

The news: Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s CEO after reports of extramarital affairs, including one involving a suspected Chinese spy that raised questions over exports of the company’s advanced AI chips to China. On November 23, Nvidia’s board reinstated Huang as President, CEO and board director, and said it will continue to cooperate with ongoing government investigations and inquiries. Harry said the stock added about a trillion dollars on the news, and he read out the FT’s headline calling it “the triumph of money over morals.”

Matt’s read: The board moved too fast. Directors feared government action and made a rash call. People close to the administration later signaled the push went further than intended. Many of those directors had worked with Jensen for 20+ years, and Matt thought they should have held the line longer.

Jason’s read: Every American with an index fund owns this outcome. Nvidia is roughly 6% of QQQ and 7% of VTI, and last week there didn’t seem to be a floor. He compared it to Steve Jobs and the backdated options: there’s a limit to the pass you give a generational founder, but this was too much, too fast. His counterintuitive point was that the return is better than Jensen staying on under a cloud of hearings and gossip. It has a cleansing effect, the same way nobody really talks about Sam Altman’s missing week anymore. The cost is less social capital. Jason expects Jensen to lock in on product and pull back on roundtrip deals, the China narrative and startup investing, which would be a marginal negative for venture.

Why is it better for Jensen that he was let go and came back than investigated without leaving?

“In a way, it is better this happened than that he did not step down, because there is a cleansing effect.

If he had stayed at Nvidia while all these congressional hearings happened… https://t.co/BiMag7bVoSpic.twitter.com/5U0xR5qTKI

— Harry Stebbings (@HarryStebbings) November 26, 2026

2. Anthropic Priced at $83 and Opened at $111.50

The news: Anthropic priced its IPO of 980 million shares at $83 per share and opened at $111.50, against an initial range of $70 to $78. That values it at about $1.08T on shares outstanding, and about $1.5T counting every share including options and employee plan reserves.

Matt’s read: First came a program for investors and partners, with Dario, Daniela and the founders all accessible. Then the opening bell and speeches on trust, safety and humanity. Then three hours of waiting, a countdown on the floor, a five-minute delay for incoming volume, and “wild energy, high fives and hugs” when the first trade went live.

His benchmark used to be Google, which he followed as a board observer alongside John Doerr. Google went from $10B to $100B over 15 years, and Anthropic is doing it in one. He also argued this wave is unusually broad. Past waves had one to three big winners, and this one has tens. Some companies valued as winners won’t end up as winners, but the breadth is real.

3. Harry’s Worry: What If ANT Just Trades Flat?

The news: Harry pointed to the stock dipping in its first days. He paired that with OpenRouter data showing more usage on Google models than OpenAI’s. His question was whether a soft Anthropic stock could cool the whole ecosystem, OpenAI included.

Jason’s read: Facebook was flat for a while after its IPO. Even if Anthropic just holds its IPO price for a year, that’s still epic. The real question is how permanent model leadership is. Harry and Rory used to mock Jason for using Claude, until the 4-series models changed the growth ratio between the two companies, and that kind of shift can happen again. Jason also repeated a take that gets him hammered in the comments: China-based open-weight models are in permanent decline because CIOs don’t want them. And ARR multiples are breaking. They worked for every B2B company through about 2020, and now they only fit a middle slice of decent growers. “Maybe they’re all cheap.”

Matt’s read: The market won’t fail to reward the absolute leader in AI at this scale, growth, gross margin and net retention. Matt doesn’t see this as a closed vs. open-weight bet. The whole ecosystem is growing faster than anyone imagined, and Anthropic is now the public way to own it: “Where else are you going to put your capital?”

4. A Brutal Cyber Week, and Zero Data Retention Has to Actually Work

The news: Harry ran the list. OpenRouter models were compromised, JPMorgan Chase’s high-net-worth division was hacked, the US head of cyber was fired, and the FBI issued a flash alert. OpenRouter also admitted some models on its platform sent data back to China, and Cursor is weighing a phase-out of Chinese open-weight models.

Jason’s read: 2027 will be the death of a lot of B2B apps and of vibe-coded production apps, because you can’t trust them. He listed examples: Optimizely leaks, 2021-era vendors that laid off their SecOps teams, Gainsight offline for a month over Salesforce security audits, and a Shopify ecosystem breach caused by tokens that never expired. SOC 2s got so cheap they were “thrown out of the airplane for free.” Jason expects most classic B2B companies to fail next year’s security reviews, because they can’t stand up to “a thousand-agent cyber swarm.” Apps can increasingly maintain themselves, but they can’t secure themselves. On OpenRouter, the lesson is that everyone relied on the model provider’s piece of paper. Zero data retention has to actually work, and every breach costs the China-based models more share.

Matt’s read: Brian Armstrong says Coinbase will build more internally, but most companies don’t have the time or team to rebuild and maintain their CRM, even with great models. Hard, brittle, custom workflows still need forward-deployed engineers, so we’ll see both build and buy for a long time. On model disclosure, the Fortune 5000 doesn’t care whether you run on AWS or Azure, but it will demand to know which models are underneath. The result will be more open-source models from other players and more competition.

5. Vibe Coding vs. Horizontal Agents, and HubSpot’s Problem

The news: Harry played arbiter after Jason declared vibe coding dead, pointing to Lovable’s latest round as evidence against him. Then he asked whether HubSpot, with Brian Halligan back, is the natural owner of SMB agents.

Jason’s read: “Vibe coding as we knew it died about 90 days ago, and we just haven’t attended the funeral yet.” He means vibe coding your own production apps, which was a marketing dream. Replit and Lovable will still hit $2B next year and do great. What wins in 2027 is horizontal agents that you just tell what to do, like Meta’s Muse. Horizontal apps won through 2021, and horizontal agents win next. On HubSpot, a new SMB has no system of record, and Jason pointed to HubSpot’s net new customer adds falling from roughly 10K a quarter toward under 5K. Harry described his own Muse workflow, which scrapes LinkedIn daily for founders leaving 25 high-talent companies. Jason said HubSpot would need a year and a $15,000 mandatory implementation to do that, and Muse did it in an hour.

Matt’s read: Vibe coding isn’t dead. It’s evolving from “build a prototype” to “run your business.” The bigger shift is that a platform like Lovable can now cover everything from CRM to the app to inbound and outbound calls, and that’s more exciting than picking the next narrow application.

“What is going to happen in 2027 is SMB agents are going to do everything. Another reason vibe coding is dying is because vibe agents have just begun.

Instead of trying to vibe code your app, build the spec and figure out security, you just tell Muse or whatever you want what to… https://t.co/BiMag7bVoSpic.twitter.com/EWaHtd4bjd

— Harry Stebbings (@HarryStebbings) November 26, 2026

6. Cognition’s $75B Round, and Valuing the Number Four Player

The news: Cognition announced on September 8 that it had raised more than $2 billion at a $48 billion valuation, and it’s now raising about $2B at $75B. Matt said he’s heard from people close to the deal that it’s real.

Matt’s read: Menlo backed Factory’s last round instead. Matt sees the products as comparable, with Cognition differentiated on on-prem and air-gapped work, and the market as a jump ball. At $75B, the question is whether you’re underwriting a $400B company, and how often that happens. Factory and Cognition are expanding from coding agents into the full SDLC and other personas, which is how they grow TAM. A slightly better coding agent alone isn’t a good bet at this price. Matt’s pattern is to back the number two challenger that can out-execute on product: Factory over the leader, and Anthropic over OpenAI.

Jason’s read: Anthropic is now a troubling comp. A 10x at $75B, after dilution, means a roughly $1 trillion exit, and Jason can’t see Cognition getting bigger than Anthropic. “At $700 million I’m in.” He brought up what Sequoia internally called the Postmates effect: when spaces get big enough, the failing number three can still be worth billions. That only holds when times are hot. His warning: “The biggest sign of a bubble of all is when we’re comfortable investing in the number six player.”

Harry’s read: He was taught you have to be number one or two or you’re irrelevant, and here the number four player is doing close to $2B in revenue.

7. Investment Committee: Sierra at $30B vs. Databricks vs. Ramp at $70B

The news: Harry framed three late-stage deals. Sierra is in talks to raise about $1.5B at a roughly $30B valuation, up from $15.8B in May, and said in October it had hit $400M+ in annualized revenue. Ramp is in preliminary talks to raise at least $1 billion above $70 billion, roughly a month after an October $1.85 billion raise at $60 billion. Databricks was on the table at $225B. It last closed a $5bn round at $190bn, with run-rate revenue past $7bn and growth above 80%.

Jason’s read: He went with Sierra for $250M, possibly stretching to $300M. Databricks is the safest bet, but he can’t see a clean 10x to $3 trillion. Sierra has the clearest path to $300 to $400B, because everyone in enterprise software thinks it’s the next Salesforce or bigger. Salesforce is approaching $60B in revenue, and Bret Taylor shows up as the number one competitor in every incumbent’s diligence. Jason still thinks Databricks accelerates next year. It stumbled into becoming the trusted, cost-effective place to run agents, at a fraction of legacy enterprise pricing. What he’s learned from SaaStr’s own agents is that they’re stubborn. Raise prices, go down, or get breached and they want to leave right away. If the platform works and the cost is right, they never leave.

Matt’s read: If he had to pick the likeliest 10x, he’d agree on Sierra, but he’s skeptical any of the three get there. Ramp has made a boring category monstrous, but the new products are less tangible bets. Matt doesn’t know Bret’s strategy well enough to underwrite the Salesforce analogy. For late-stage capital he’d pick Databricks for a 3 to 5x: a stacked team, data gravity, and smart moves like the Neon acquisition. “I don’t see a 10x from anything in this basket.” He’d add Modal as an infrastructure-level agent beneficiary.

Harry’s read: He backed ClickHouse for the same reason Matt likes challengers: it’s the slightly-behind provider that can out-innovate on product, and he expects it to accelerate too.

8. Palo Alto Buys Applied Compute for $4.5B, and Why Acquired Teams Go Stale

The news: Palo Alto Networks agreed to buy Applied Compute in an all-stock deal valued at $4.5 billion, to train, deploy and secure open-weight AI models for enterprises. Two weeks earlier, Applied Compute had raised $350 million at a $3.25 billion valuation. Harry noted the ex-OpenAI founders are in their early twenties and credited Neo’s Ali Partovi with another big win.

Jason’s read: Nikesh Arora is one of the best M&A operators of all time, so this is at least a thoughtful bet. The pattern Jason has seen over the past year is that a great team acquired outside the ultra-core goes stale. Integration takes too long, motivation slips, and within a year the product isn’t competitive. He also took a victory lap for giving both Matt and Ali VC of the Year awards back in 2024.

Matt’s read: Acquisitions only work if they’re front and center, with their own mandate. His example is Ramp, which bought a small company whose founder Rahul is now Ramp’s CTO and runs all AI innovation outside core payments.

Harry’s read: His acquisition of the year is Meta’s deal for Alex Wang’s team, which everyone scratched their heads at until Muse shipped. Jason added that it might have looked like a failure if OpenClaw hadn’t shown the world that people want agents doing the work, not chatbots.

9. Mailchimp Sells for $3.68B, Bill Goes Private, and What 2021 B2B Is Worth

The news: Intuit agreed to sell Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for $3.68B, less than a third of the $12B it paid in 2021. Mailchimp revenue fell 1% to $313M last quarter, while Intuit’s total revenue grew 12%. The same week, BILL agreed to be acquired by TPG in partnership with Corpay in an all-cash deal valuing it at $6 billion. Harry opened with: “The Italian mafia have been raiding corporate America again.”

Matt’s read: What is a shrinking business worth? Mailchimp stopped being core and wasn’t a growth driver, so Intuit deserves credit for finding it a home rather than winding it down in three years. What scares him is that PE apparently didn’t bid for two years on a likely profitable asset. “That’s pretty scary in terms of where the off-ramp is for a lot of these 2021 companies.” Bill.com at high-teens growth is a head scratcher, because plenty of similar companies aren’t getting bought.

Jason’s read: Mailchimp had been on the block for about two years, after every possible price increase. With Airtable, Miro and Mailchimp, Bending Spoons was the only buyer, or the sellers would have taken a higher price. Bending Spoons will raise prices again, 20% of customers will churn, and the rest will pay two to three times more. His uncomfortable question for year-end marks: can any 2021 investment that isn’t growing at top-quartile rates be worth more than 2x revenue? Where’s the comp?

Jason’s bull case for Bill is that it’s an agentic beneficiary. SaaStr’s 10K agent runs finance and billing on top of Bill. Bill costs $20 a month, has a great API, and the agents won’t move. Marketing automation is the opposite. “It is anachronistic to have humans send emails.” SaaStr moved from Marketo to Salesforce Marketing Cloud and now doesn’t need either, because agents plus Resend plus Lovable do the work. He called the category walking dead.

Matt’s read: So much is being abstracted away that you won’t know or care which tools your agents use. They’ll find the cheapest path, and point products get squeezed along the way.

10. CrowdStrike Buys Zscaler for $43.9B, and Founders Thinking About Their Own Exit

The news: CrowdStrike agreed to acquire Zscaler in a transaction valuing it at approximately $43.9 billion, with Zscaler shareholders receiving 1.135 CrowdStrike shares per share. Harry noted CrowdStrike fell 9.6% and Zscaler rose 13% on the day.

Jason’s read: In the week of Jensen’s return, Jason looked at the human side. Jay Chaudhry largely self-funded Zscaler and owned a huge stake at IPO, and he’s a billionaire on his fourth startup. Why sell? Probably because he’s around 70. Jason thinks Zscaler as a standalone brand may not exist in two years, but the deal makes sense: complementary, efficient, and accretive.

Matt’s read: Security is consolidating. The Fortune 5000 wants one vendor that covers it on all fronts, from endpoint runtime to network runtime to AppSec. Niche products won’t disappear, but a leader at this market cap has to broaden. Zscaler may have seen the squeeze coming, and George Kurtz has the energy to build one of the two main platforms.

11. Claude Helps Crack the Riemann Hypothesis, and the Anthropic Wealth Wave

The news: An Anthropic mathematician used Claude to solve the Riemann Hypothesis, a result many thought was five to 10 years away for LLMs. Harry then noted that around 600 people made over $100M in the IPO.

Jason’s read: This wasn’t Claude alone. It was one of the best mathematicians in the country paired with Claude, which makes it a bionic result. That contrasts with sales, where AI didn’t create super reps, only reps who do less prep. Breakthroughs from the best humans plus frontier models make the next 12 to 18 months less predictable, from drug discovery onward. On wealth, it isn’t brand new. Some 2,000 Nvidia employees already hold $20M+ liquid, and Palo Alto has almost no houses for sale at any price. The bigger 2027 issue is comp. Anthropic has about 6,000 people at $100B in revenue, so it can pay whatever it wants in cash. A startup that raised $5M after YC can’t pay $600K engineers.

Matt’s read: Model progress combined with agents collaborating like clones means 10 to 100x faster breakthroughs, and life sciences shouldn’t be laughed at. It also explains why labs are holding back models: if Riemann can fall, what does that mean for hackers? On wealth, expect a flood of new angel capital and more early-stage competition. On comp, the ship sailed when researchers became worth 5 to 10x and everyone else’s pay trickled up. The old “low salary, big options” model is very hard to sell now. Inside Menlo, Matt said there was no single champagne moment, because the run-up was so long and predictable. Menlo bought more in the IPO and plans to hold.

issues.author: Jason Lemkin
issues.content_html:
Dear SaaStr: How Long Should a Free Trial Be for B2B Products?

It doesn’t really matter as long as it’s long enough to really try the product. Although the latest ReveneuCat data does suggest, longer is better.

What I mean is, this is one of those things in B2B that is over-analyzed, as if it will make a magical difference.

The sales team will like a shorter period, often, to help them close a deal that month, to shorten sales cycles. This is the real reason you often see 14 day (vs 30 day) trials: it helps the sales team. And that’s OK. It’s fine. Just bear in mind that’s the real history behind the extremely common 14 day duration you’ll see at many sales-led B2B leaders. To help sales get the deal in this month.

Sometimes 14 days really isn’t enough to get enough usage out of the product, for sure. Then you make need to make it longer. On a one-off basis, or for all customers, or per edition. Say, 30 days. Which is also fine.

But …

What really matters is engagement. How do you get the prospect to even use the trial period at all? Many customers, for many products, won’t just automatically start on their own. Most prospects aren’t like you and me. They don’t just grab-and-go. Almost all of us underinvest in getting those Free and Free Trial users really going as quickly as they could.

So what’s generally most important is investing in on-boarding, both programmatic and human assisted and driven.

Not arguing over how many days goes into the trial. Just do what creates the best user experience there.

Why are free trials 14 days? Not for your customers.

"The Salesforce sales team wanted to close deals that month, so they forced the move from 30 days to 14. There was no evidence it was better for the customer."

From my conversation with Lenny Rachitsky on Lenny's Podcast. pic.twitter.com/ljPt2LXdKl

— Jason ✨👾SaaStr.Ai✨ Lemkin (@jasonlk) November 16, 2026

___

RevenueCat now has data from 17,000+ subscription apps, and at least for mobile, length does matter. ~30 Days vs. 2 Weeks is Much Better.

On annual plans, trials of 17 to 32 days converted 44.6% of users vs. just 24% for trials of 4 days or less, and first renewals more than doubled. Monthly plans were different: conversion peaked at 10 to 16 days, so the standard 14-day trial is about right there. And AI apps hit a wall at 16 days. The B2B read: if you want a 12-month commitment, give buyers closer to 30 days to decide. Full data here: https://www.saastr.com/what-17000-subscription-apps-tell-us-about-free-trial-length-annual-plans-convert-86-better-with-30-day-trials-monthly-tops-out-at-two-weeks-and-ai-apps-hit-a-wall-at-16-days/

And Tom Tunguz did a deep analysis here of over 600 startups. He found it didn’t really matter how long the trial was, 14 vs 21 vs 30-day free trials didn’t matter. More here from SaaStr AI Annual:

issues.content_html:
You barely notice high churn on the way to $2m-$3m ARR. You are just growing so fast, and are so new.

It starts to impact growth somewhere in the $5m+ range. Numbers are often still OK though.

At $10m ARR, high churn starts to stop growth

At $20m ARR, it can end your startup

— Jason ✨👾SaaStr.Ai✨ Lemkin (@jasonlk) April 25, 2021

Q: What can you do to lower your customers’ churn rate?

One update for the agent era: don’t just assume an agent can do it all. No matter what any vendor tells you. Agents are great. But they need to be able to escalate to humans. Especially when a customer is on their way out.

A few basic thoughts:

  1. Have every customer have a named customer success rep . Every customer. Yes, this is hard if your price point is low. But it can be done. If every customer knows “Casey” is her rep, and who she can turn to … churn will go down.
  2. Measure NPS constantly, and set quarterly goals to drive it up . If you don’t measure it, you can’t improve it. If you haven’t measured your NPS yet, you may be surprised that it is lower than you think.
  3. Segment your Customer Success, and Sales, teams . Different size customers need different approaches. If you segment your CS team, you can get folks that specialize in different deal sizes and customer needs. And if you segment your sales team by deal size, the smaller customers will get better attention upfront. Leading to less churn. Don’t lump your smaller customers together with the big ones, or they will churn at a much higher rate.
  4. Stop with churn-and-burn deals . Selling deals you can’t service is worse than not closing them at all. More here: 5 Tips To Minimize “Churn and Burn” Behavior in Your Sales Team | SaaStr
  5. Do phone support . No one wants to pick up the phone. But customers that need help want their call answered. More here.
  6. Answer all tickets in < 5 minutes . Yes, it can be done.
  7. Visit as many customers via Zoom and in-person as you can . You can’t visit the tiny ones, but at least visit all the bigger ones. The more you visit, the fewer that churn. Zoom isn’t the same as in-person, but it’s much better than not connecting directly. Try to do 6 customer Zooms a week. More here.
  8. Do a weekly webinar for all prospects and customers, every week . This is another chance for folks to get their questions answered.
  9. A wiki or answer database is NOT enough. Technology alone is NOT enough. Don’t use cheats. There are no shortcuts . People need help from people. Self-service is great for solving some problems, but not for a lot of them. Don’t be lured into thinking technology alone is the answer.
  10. Add a great free trial . If your free trial experience is truly awesome, customers that might churn will select out during the free trial. That’s not all bad.
  11. Finally: let them go. In fact, make it easier to go . Yes, churn is painful. But if you treat them well on the way out, they may come back at some point in the next decade. If you don’t, they’ll never come back unless they have to. More here: You’ll Lose Customers. It Hurts. But Don’t Let Them Become Angry Ex-Customers. | SaaStr

And a related, bonus point:

12. Do more customer marketing . How much of your marketing time and budget is focused on getting folks to know more, love you more, and buy more from you? Not enough. More on that here.
